# THE MATHNAWÍ
## OF
# JALÁLU'DDÍN RÚMÍ <note>Jalálu'ddín Rúmí (1207–1273) was a 13th-century Persian poet, Islamic scholar, and Sufi mystic whose influence transcends national borders and ethnic divisions.</note>

->EDITED FROM THE OLDEST MANUSCRIPTS<-
->AVAILABLE: WITH CRITICAL NOTES,<-
->TRANSLATION & COMMENTARY<-
->BY<-
->REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON<-
->DOCTOR OF LETTERS, DOCTOR OF LAWS, FELLOW OF THE BRITISH ACADEMY<-
->*Sir Thomas Adams's Professor of Arabic and sometime*<-
->*Lecturer in Persian in the University of Cambridge*<-

->VOLUME III & VI<-
->CONTAINING THE TRANSLATION<-
->OF THE THIRD & FOURTH BOOKS<-

->1925–1940<-

### INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the Mathnawí <note>The term "Mathnawí" refers to a poem written in rhyming couplets; here it refers specifically to Rúmí's masterpiece of Sufi wisdom.</note> were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have hitherto been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2000 were translated by Whinfield in his abridged version (Trübner's Oriental Series, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and so far as I am aware, this is the only contribution that has yet been made by a Western scholar towards the study of Books III–VI. Good as his renderings are from a general point of view, I cannot say that I owe much to them, since they are seldom precise enough to afford help in dealing with obscure and doubtful passages. Regarding the character and purpose of my translation I have nothing to add to what was said in the Introduction to the previous volume. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. Growing familiarity with the author's thought and style has removed some difficulties and lightened others; but there are still many to be cleared up.

For reasons which are set forth in the Introduction to volume III, I consider the Qóniya Manuscript (G), dated 677 After the Hijra <note>677 A.H. corresponds to approximately 1278 A.D., only five years after Rúmí's death.</note>, to be the most authoritative text of the Mathnawí. The text of the present edition from Book III, verse 2836, to the end of Book IV is founded on that ancient and admirable manuscript, and in the Appendices to volume III I have recorded those readings of G which differ from the text of my edition in the First and Second Books and in the first half of the Third Book. The present volume, therefore, contains an Appendix showing what changes the adoption of these readings would involve in the English version of the corresponding portions of the poem. As it will be some time before the Commentary on the First and Second Books can appear, a few suggestions for improving the translation of these Books are now brought together in a separate list.

**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**

CAMBRIDGE,
*April 1930*

# BOOK III

->In the Name of God the Compassionate, the Merciful.<-

The sciences of Divine Wisdom <note>original: "al-hikmah al-ilahiyyah"</note> are God's armies, wherewith He strengthens the spirits of the initiates <note>those who have begun the spiritual path</note>, and purifies their knowledge from the defilement of ignorance, their justice from the defilement of iniquity, their generosity from the defilement of ostentation, and their forbearance from the defilement of foolishness; and brings near to them whatever was far from them in respect of the understanding of the state hereafter; and makes easy to them whatever was hard to them in respect of obedience to Him and zealous endeavour to serve Him. And they—these sciences—are amongst the evidences and proofs of the prophets, giving information concerning the mysteries and sovereignty of God, the knowledge whereof is bestowed on the gnostics <term>gnostics: from 'arifun, those who possess direct, experiential knowledge of God</term> exclusively, and how He causes the revolution of the Luminous Sphere appertaining to the *Rahmán* <note>The All-Merciful</note> and the Pearl, the Sphere which rules over the vaporous globular sphere, even as the intellect rules over the bodies created of dust and over their external and internal senses; for the revolution of that spiritual Sphere rules over the vaporous sphere and the gleaming meteors and the radiant lamps of heaven and the fostering winds and the outspread earths and the flowing waters. May God benefit His servants thereby by these sciences and increase their understanding! 

Now every reader understands according to the measure of his intelligence, and the devotee practises devotion according to the measure of his power to exert himself therein, and the mufti <term>mufti: a legal expert empowered to give rulings on Islamic law</term> decides questions of law according to the amount of judgement he possesses, and the alms-giver gives alms in proportion to his ability, and the donor is generous in proportion to his means, and the recipient of generosity obtains only so much of his bounty as he, the donor, approves. But nevertheless he who searches for water in the desert will not be prevented from seeking it by his knowledge of what is contained in the seas, and he will be earnest in seeking the Water of this spiritual life ere he is cut off from it by preoccupation with the means of subsistence and hindered by illness and want, and ere other objects come between him and that goal to which he is hastening, since none who prefers vain desire or is inclined to ease or turns back from his search or has fears for himself or feels anxiety about his means of livelihood will ever attain unto Knowledge, unless he take refuge with God and prefer his spiritual affairs to his temporal and take from the treasure of Wisdom the great riches, which neither lose their value nor are inherited like riches of this world, and the majestic lights and noble jewels and precious estates of Wisdom, giving thanks for His bounty, glorifying His dispensation, magnifying His allotment; and unless he seek refuge with God from the vileness of worldly interests and from an ignorance so blind that he makes much of the little which he sees in himself and makes little of the much and great which he finds in others, and admires himself on account of that self-conceit for which God hath not given him permission. 

But it behoves one who hath knowledge and is seeking God that he should learn whatever he does not know, and teach others what he knows already, and deal gently with those of weak intelligence, and neither be made conceited by the stupidity of the stupid nor harshly rebuke him that is dull of understanding. *Such were ye aforetime, but God hath been gracious unto you.* <note>A reference to the Qur'an 4:94, reminding the learned that they too were once ignorant.</note> Transcendent is God and exalted above the sayings of the blasphemers, and the belief of those who attribute partners to Him, and the imputation of defect to Him by those deficient in knowledge, and the comparison of Him by the comparers, and the evil conceptions of the thinkers, and the descriptions of Him by those who vainly imagine. And to Him be the praise and the glory for the composition of the Divine, Lordly Book of the *Mathnawí*, since He is the Helper to success and the Giver of bounty, and to Him belongs the power of conferring abundant benefits and favours, especially upon His servants, the gnostics, in despite of a party who desire to extinguish the Lights of God with their mouths—but God will bring His Light to completion, even if the unbelievers are loth. Verily, *We have sent down the Warning (the Qur'án) and verily We will* <note>The text breaks off here, quoting Qur'an 15:9: "and verily We will be its guardian."</note>

<summary>This preface to Book III of the Mathnawí describes spiritual knowledge as a divine army that purifies the soul and governs the physical universe. It emphasizes the necessity of prioritizing spiritual pursuit over worldly anxieties and calls for humility and patience when teaching those with less understanding.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Wisdom, gnosticism, spiritual discipline, Mathnawí, humility, providence, intellect vs. spirit</keywords>

> *guard it. And whoever shall alter it after he hath heard it, surely the guilt thereof is upon those who alter it: verily, God is Hearing and Knowing. And praise be to God, the Lord of all created beings!* <note>This is a traditional closing formula, often citing the Quran, to protect the integrity of the sacred or inspired text from unauthorized changes.</note>

->IN THE NAME OF GOD THE MERCIFUL, THE COMPASSIONATE<-

**1. O Light of the Truth, Husámu’ddín <note>The spiritual successor and beloved disciple of the author, Rumi</note>, bring (into verse and writing) this Third Book, for “three times” has become a <term>sunna</term> <note>A traditional practice or custom, often referring to the deeds and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad</note>.**
Open the treasury of mysteries; in respect of the Third Book leave excuses alone.
Thy power flows from the power of God, not from the veins which throb because of (bodily) heat.
This lamp, the sun, which is bright—it is not (made bright) by means of wick and cotton and oil.

**5. The vault of heaven, which is so enduring, is not supported by any tent-rope or pillar.**
The power of Gabriel <note>The Archangel of Revelation</note> was not from the kitchen; it was from beholding the Creator of existence.
Likewise, know this power of the <term>Abdál</term> <note>A class of high-ranking saints or "Substitutes" in Sufi cosmology who help maintain the spiritual balance of the world</note> of God to be (derived) from God, not from viands and from trays (of food).
Their bodies too have been moulded of the Light, so that they have transcended the Spirit and the Angel.
Inasmuch as thou art endowed with the qualities of the Almighty, pass beyond the fire of the maladies (of the sensual self), like <term>Khalíl</term> <note>A title for the Prophet Abraham, meaning "The Friend of God," referring to the miracle where the fire he was thrown into became a garden</note>.

**10. To thee also the fire will become *coolness and safety*, O thou to whose complexion (constitution) the elements are slaves.**
The elements are the substance of every complexion, but this complexion of thine is superior to every grade.
This complexion of thine is of the simple (uncompounded) world; it has now gathered up (amassed and absorbed) the attributes of Unity.
Oh, alas, the area of the people's understandings is exceeding narrow: the people have no throat <note>A metaphor for the capacity to receive and digest spiritual truths</note>.
O Light of the Truth, through the keenness of thy perception thy sweetmeat bestows a throat (even) on (one dull as) stone.

**15. Mount Sinai in the (Divine) epiphany gained a throat, so that it quaffed the wine; but it could not bear the wine.**
Thereby the mountain was shattered and cloven asunder: have ye seen a mountain amble like a camel? <note>A reference to the Quranic account of Moses on Sinai, where the mountain crumbled when God revealed His glory</note>
Bestowal of mouthfuls comes (to pass) from every clustered fruit-tree (well-to-do person), (but) bestowal of a throat is the work of God alone.
He bestows a throat on the body and on the spirit; He bestows a separate throat for every part of you.
This He bestows at the time when you become Majestical and become void of vanity and deceit,

**20. So that you will not tell the King's secret to any one nor pour out sugar before flies.**
The secrets of the (Divine) Majesty are drunk in by the ear of that one who, like the lily, hath a hundred tongues and is dumb <note>A poetic image of the lily, which has petal "tongues" but remains silent, symbolizing the mystic who knows secrets but does not speak them</note>.
The grace of God bestows a throat on the earth, to the end that it may drink water and make a hundred herbs to grow.
Again, He bestows on the creature of earth (the animal) a throat and lip, in order that it may eat its (the earth's) herbage in desire.

<summary>This page opens the Third Book of the Masnavi with an invocation to Husámu’ddín, emphasizing that spiritual power and understanding are gifts from God rather than physical sustenance. It uses metaphors of "throats" and "complexions" to describe the capacity of the soul to receive divine mysteries.</summary>
<keywords>Husámu’ddín, Sunna, Abdál, Khalíl, Mount Sinai, spiritual capacity, divine revelation, Sufi mysticism</keywords>

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse on the nature of consumption, spiritual nourishment, and the transformation of the soul from a physical to a divine state.</meta>

When the animal has eaten its herbage, it becomes fat: the animal becomes a mouthful for Man and goes (disappears). <note>The author describes the food chain as a cycle of transformation where lower forms of life are absorbed into higher ones.</note>

❦25. In turn it becomes earth and becomes a devourer of Man, when the spirit and the sight are separated from Man.
I beheld the atoms <note>original: "the particles of created existence"</note> with their mouths all open: if I should tell of their food, it (the tale) would become long.
Provisions have (their) provision from His bounty; His universal grace is the nourisher of them that nourish.
He bestoweth gifts (of sustenance) on the gifts (which sustain life), for how should wheat spring forth without (receiving) any sustenance? <note>Even the soil and the grain require divine "sustenance" to exist and grow.</note>
There is no end to the explanation of this matter. I have told a portion: you may know the (remaining) portions (by analogy).

❦30. Know that all the world is eating and eaten; know that those who have everlasting life (in God) are fortunate and accepted.
This world and its inhabitants are (in the end) dispersed; that (other) world and its travellers are continuing (for ever).
This world and its lovers are cut off; the people of that (other) world are eternalised and united.
The (truly) noble, then, is he that gives to himself the **Water of Life** <note>A common metaphor for divine knowledge or the Holy Spirit that grants immortality to the soul.</note> that remains unto everlasting.
The noble one is (the very essence of) *the good works which endure*: he has been freed from a hundred banes and perils and fears.

❦35. If they (the noble) are thousands (externally), there is no more than one (in reality): 'tis not like the fancies of him that thinks of number. <note>This refers to the concept of "Unity of Being," where all enlightened souls are one in the Divine.</note>
(Both) the eater and the eaten have a throat and windpipe: (both) the victor and the vanquished have understanding and mental perception.
He (God) bestowed a throat on the **rod of justice** <note>A reference to the staff of Moses, which transformed into a serpent and swallowed the illusions of the magicians.</note>, (so that) it devoured all those many rods and ropes;
And in it was no increase from all that eating, because its eating and its form were not animal.
To Faith also He gave a throat like (that of) the rod, so that it devoured every vain fancy that was born.

❦40. Hence the spiritual and intelligible things, like the concrete (sensible) things, have throats, and the giver of food to the throat of the spiritual and intelligible things is also (none but) God.
Therefore from the **Moon to the Fish** <note>An idiomatic expression meaning "from the highest heavens to the depths of the ocean," encompassing the entire universe.</note> there is nothing in creation that hath not a throat in respect of its drawing sustenance (from God).
(When) the spirit's throat is emptied of thought for the body, then its apportioned sustenance becomes **Majestical** <note>original: "Jalāl"—referring to the awe-inspiring glory of God.</note>.
Know that the necessary condition (for gaining this sustenance) is the transformation of the (sensual) nature, for the death of evil men is (arises) from (their) evil nature.
When it has become natural to a human being to eat clay, he grows pale and ill-complexioned and sickly and miserable;

❦45. (But) when his ugly nature has been transformed, the ugliness departs from his face, and he shines like a candle.
Where is a nurse for the suckling babe?—that with kindness she may sweeten the inner part of its mouth,
And, though she bar its way to her teat, may open up for it the way to a hundred gardens (of delight)?—
Because the teat has become to that feeble (infant) a barrier (separating it) from thousands of pleasures and dishes (of food) and loaves (of bread). <note>The weaning of a child is used as a metaphor for the soul being "weaned" from worldly pleasures to discover spiritual delights.</note>

<summary>This text explores the metaphysical concept of "eating" as a universal law of transformation, arguing that just as the body requires physical food, the soul must be "weaned" from the world to consume divine sustenance. It emphasizes that spiritual reality is a unified state where the many become one through faith and divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, spiritual nourishment, Moses' staff, Water of Life, divine sustenance, transformation of the soul, unity of being</keywords>

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual maturation, using the metaphor of the embryo's development to explain the soul's transition from the material world to the divine.</meta>

Our life, then, depends on weaning. Endeavour to wean yourself little by little. The discourse is now complete.

❦**50.** When man was an embryo his nourishment was blood: in like fashion the true believer draws purity from filth. <note>The poet suggests that just as an embryo transforms blood into life, the believer transforms the "filth" of the material world into spiritual purity.</note>
Through his being weaned from blood, his nourishment became milk; and through his being weaned from milk, he became a taker of solid food.
And through his being weaned from food he becomes a sage like <term>Luqmán</term> <note>A legendary wise man mentioned in the Qur'an, often associated with Aesop; he represents profound spiritual insight.</note>; he becomes a seeker and hunter of the hidden game.
If any one were to say to the embryo in the womb, “Outside is a world exceedingly well-ordered,
A pleasant earth, broad and long, wherein are a hundred delights and so many things to eat,

❦**55.** Mountains and seas and plains, fragrant orchards, gardens and sown fields,
A sky very lofty and full of light, sun and moonbeams and a hundred stars.
From the south-wind and from the north-wind and from the west-wind the gardens have the appearance of wedding-feasts and banquets.
Its marvels are beyond description: why art thou in tribulation in this darkness?
Why dost thou drink blood on the gibbet of this narrow place—the womb—in the midst of confinement and filth and pain?”—

❦**60.** It, the embryo, in virtue of its present state, would be incredulous, and would turn away from this message and would disbelieve it,
Saying, “This is absurd and is a deceit and delusion,” because the judgement of the blind has no imagination.
Inasmuch as the embryo's perception has not seen anything of the kind, its incredulous perception would not listen to the truth;
Just as in this world the <term>Abdál</term> <note>Literally "The Substitutes"; a high rank of saints in Sufi cosmology who help maintain the spiritual order of the world.</note> speak of that other world to the common folk,
Saying, “This world is an exceeding dark and narrow pit; outside is a world without scent or colour”: <note>Meaning a world beyond physical sensory qualities.</note>

❦**65.** Naught of their words entered into the ear of a single one of them, for this sensual desire is a barrier huge and stout.
Desire closes the ear and hinders it from hearing; self-interest closes the eye and hinders it from beholding,
Even as, in the case of the embryo, desire for the blood which is its nourishment in the low abodes
Debarred it from hearkening to the news of this world: it knows no breakfast but blood.

### ***Story of those who ate the young elephant from greed and because they neglected the advice of the sincere counsellor.***

Hast thou heard that in India a sage espied a party of friends?

❦**70.** Left hungry, lacking provisions, and naked, they were coming from travel on a far road.
His wisdom's love was stirred within him, and he gave them a fair greeting and blossomed like a rose-bush.
“I know,” he said, “that anguish has gathered upon you from this <term>Karbalá</term> <note>A reference to the site of the martyrdom of Husayn; used here as a metaphor for a place of extreme suffering and trial.</note> of suffering in consequence of hunger and emptiness;
But, for God's sake, for God's sake, O illustrious company, let not your food be the young of the elephant!
The elephant is in this direction that ye are now going; do not tear in pieces the elephant's offspring, but hearken to me.

<summary>This passage uses the metaphor of an embryo's refusal to believe in a world outside the womb to illustrate humanity's spiritual blindness to the afterlife. It concludes by introducing a cautionary tale about travelers tempted by greed to eat a forbidden young elephant.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual weaning, embryo metaphor, Luqmán, Abdál, Karbalá, spiritual blindness, Sufi wisdom, greed</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on the spiritual dangers of harming the friends of God, using the metaphor of the elephant mother protecting her young to illustrate Divine protection over the saints.</meta>

**75.** The young elephants are on your road: to hunt them down is what your hearts desire exceedingly.
They are very weak and tender and very fat, but their mother is searching after them and lying in wait.
She will roam a hundred leagues' distance in quest of her children, moaning and making lament.
Fire and smoke issue from her trunk: beware of hurting those cherished children of hers!
O son, the saints are God's children: both in their absence and presence He is well aware of what befalls them.

**80.** Do not deem absence from Him to be the result of imperfection on their part, for He takes vengeance for the sake of their spirits <note>The poet suggests the souls of the saints are unified with the Divine essence</note>.
He said, 
> "These saints are My children in exile, sundered from My dominion and glory;
> They are despised and orphaned for the sake of probation <note>Testing or spiritual trial</note>, but secretly I am their friend and intimate.
> All of them are supported by My protections: you may say they are in truth parts of Me.
> Take heed! Take heed! These are My dervishes <note>term: Dervish (a member of a Muslim religious order, often associated with poverty and austerity)</note>; they are a hundred thousand thousand and yet they are one body."

**85.** Else, how should a Moses have overthrown Pharaoh by means of one goodly rod?
Else, how should Noah have submerged East and West in his Flood by means of one evil curse?
One prayer of the generous Lot would not have razed to the ground all their city and left them in despair.
Their city, resembling Paradise, became a lake of black water: go, behold the sign!
This sign and this admonition lies in the direction of Syria: you will see it as you pass on the way to Jerusalem.

**90.** Hundreds of thousands of prophets who worshipped God—truly there have been chastisements inflicted by them in every generation.
If I should tell on and if this narration should increase in length, not only men's hearts but the very mountains would bleed.
The mountains bleed and again become solid, but you do not see them bleed: you are blind and reprobate.
A marvelous blind man, who is far-sighted and keen-eyed, but sees naught of the camel except the hair! <note>A metaphor for focusing on trivial physical details while missing the grand spiritual reality</note>
Man, from the stinginess of greed, inspects hair by hair: like a bear, he keeps dancing to no purpose.

**95.** Dance only where you break yourself <note>Mortify the ego</note> and when you tear away the cotton from the sore of lust.
Holy men dance and wheel on the spiritual battle-field: they dance in their own blood.
When they are freed from the dominion of self, they clap a hand; when they escape from their own imperfection, they make a dance.
From within them musicians strike the tambourine; at their ecstasy the seas burst into foam.
You see it not, but for their ears the leaves too on the boughs are clapping hands.

**100.** You do not see the clapping of the leaves: one must have the spiritual ear, not this ear of the body.
Close the ear of the head to jesting and lying, that you may see the resplendent city of the soul.
The ear of Mohammed draws out the hidden meaning in the words of the religious hypocrites, for God says of him in the Qur'án, "*He is an ear.*" <note>original: "Qul udhunu khayrin lakum" (Say, he is an ear of goodness for you) - Surah At-Tawbah 9:61</note>
This Prophet is entirely ear and eye; we are refreshed by him: he is as the suckler and we as the infant boy.

<summary>This passage warns against mistreating the saints (dervishes), explaining that God protects them as a mother elephant protects her calves. It describes the spiritual "dance" of the saints who have overcome their egos and emphasizes the need for a "spiritual ear" to perceive divine truths.</summary>
<keywords>saints, dervishes, divine protection, Moses, Noah, Lot, spiritual dance, ego, Mohammed, spiritual perception</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the moral discourse following the parable of the elephant calves, transitioning from a literal story into a spiritual warning about divine judgment and the fleeting nature of life.</meta>

This discourse hath no end. Go back to those who had to do with the elephant, and start at the beginning.

## ***The remainder of the Story of those who molested the young elephants.***

105. “The elephant takes a sniff at every mouth and keeps poking round the belly of every man,
To see where she will find the roasted flesh of her young, so that she may manifest her vengeance and strength.”
You eat the flesh of God's servants: you backbite them, you will suffer retribution. <note>The poet compares backbiting—speaking ill of others—to the literal consumption of flesh, a common Quranic metaphor.</note>
Beware, for he that smells your mouths is the Creator: how shall any one save his life except him that is true (to God)?
Woe to the scoffer whose smell shall be tested in the grave by Munkar or Nakír! <note>Munkar and Nakír are the two angels who, in Islamic tradition, question the deceased in the grave regarding their faith.</note>

110. There is no possibility of withdrawing the mouth from those mighty ones, nor of sweetening the mouth with medicinal ointments.
(In the grave) there is no water and oil to cover the face, there is no way of evasion (open) to intelligence and sagacity.
How many a time will the blows of their maces beat upon the head and rump of every vain gabbler!
Look at the effect of the mace of ‘Azrá'íl, <note>‘Azrá'íl is the Angel of Death.</note> (even) if you do not see the wood and iron in (their material) forms.
Sometimes too they appear in (material) form: the patient (himself) is aware thereof.

115. The patient says, “O my friends, what is this sword over my head?”
(They reply), “We do not see it; this must be fancy.” What fancy is this? (Nay), for it is (the hour of) departure (to the other world).
What fancy is this, from terror of which this inverted sphere (the sky) has now become (as insubstantial as) a phantom?
To the sick man the maces and swords became perceptible (visible), and his head dropped down.
He sees that that (vision) is for his sake: the eye of foe and friend (alike) is barred from it.

120. Worldly greed vanished, his eye became keen: his eye became illumined at the moment of bloodshed (death).
That eye of his, from the result of his pride and his anger, became (like) the cock that crows unseasonably. <note>A metaphor for realizing the truth too late, when the knowledge can no longer save the person.</note>
It is necessary to cut off the head of the bird that rings the bell (crows) at the wrong time.
At every moment thy particular spirit is struggling with death: in thy spirit's death-struggle look to thy faith!
Thy life is like a purse of gold: day and night are like him who counts the gold coins (the money-changer).

125. He (Time) counts and gives the gold without stopping, until it (the purse) is emptied and there comes the eclipse (death).
If you take away from a mountain and do not put (anything) in the place (of what you have taken), the mountain will be demolished by that giving.
Therefore, for every breath (that you give out), put an equivalent in its place, so that by (acting in accordance with the text) *and fall to worship and draw nigh* <note>original: "wa-sjud wa-qtarib" (Quran 96:19). This encourages replacing spent life with spiritual proximity to God.</note> you may gain your object.
Do not strive so much to complete (your worldly) affairs: do not strive in any affair that is not religious.
(Otherwise) at the end you will depart incomplete, your (spiritual) affairs marred and your bread unbaked.

<summary>The author uses the imagery of an elephant searching for its lost young to illustrate how God detects and punishes those who harm others through backbiting. The text warns that death and the subsequent interrogation in the grave are inevitable, urging the reader to prioritize spiritual growth over worldly greed.</summary>

<keywords>divine retribution, backbiting, Munkar and Nakir, Azrail, deathbed visions, spiritual preparation, transience of life</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the moral teachings of Rumi's Masnavi, transitioning from a discourse on spiritual burial to the illustrative parable of the young elephant.</meta>

**130.** And the beautifying of your grave and sepulchre is not done by means of stone and wood and plaster;
Nay, but by digging for yourself a grave in spiritual purity and burying your egoism in His egoism <note>The "His" refers to the Divine; the poet argues that true rest is found by losing one's self-centeredness in God's will</note>,
And by becoming His dust and buried in love of Him, so that your breath may gain replenishments from His breath.
A tomb with domes and turrets—that is not approved on the part of the followers of Reality <term>Reality: (Haqiqat) the ultimate spiritual truth sought by Sufis</term>.
Look now at a living person attired in satin: does the satin help his understanding at all?

**135.** His soul is in hateful torment, the scorpion of grief is in his grief-laden heart.
Outside, on his exterior, broideries and decorations; but within he is sorely lamenting from bitter thoughts,
While you may see another in an old patched frock, his thoughts sweet as the sugar-cane and his words like sugar.

### **_Returning to the Story of the elephant._**

Said the sincere adviser, “Hearken to this counsel of mine, so that your hearts and souls may not be afflicted.
Be content with herbage and leaves, do not go in chase of the young elephants.

**140.** I have discharged the debt of admonition: how should the final result of admonition be anything but felicity <note>happiness or spiritual success</note>?
I came to deliver the message, that I may save you from fruitless repentance.
Beware! Let not greed waylay you, let not greed for victual <note>food or provisions</note> tear you up by the roots!”
This he said, and gave a farewell and departed; their famine and hunger waxed great on the way.
Suddenly, in the direction of a highroad, they espied a fat young elephant, newly born.

**145.** They fell upon it like furious wolves, ate it clean up, and washed their hands.
One of the fellow-travellers did not eat of it and exhorted the others to abstain, for the sayings of that dervish <term>Dervish: a member of a Muslim religious order, often known for poverty and austerity</term> were remembered by him.
Those words hindered him from eating its roasted flesh: old intelligence bestows on thee a new fortune.
Then they all fell down and slept, but the hungry one was awake like the shepherd in the flock.
He saw a frightful elephant approaching: first she came and ran towards him who was keeping guard.

**150.** She smelt his mouth thrice: no disagreeable smell came from it.
She paced round him several times and went off: the huge queen-elephant did him no hurt.
She smelt the lips of every sleeper, and the smell of her young one's flesh was coming to her from each of those slumbering men.
Each man had eaten of the roasted flesh of the young elephant: the mother elephant quickly tore him to pieces and killed him.
At once she set about rending the people of that company one by one, and she had no awe of doing it.

**155.** She tossed each one in the air recklessly, so that he dashed on the earth and was cloven asunder.
O drinker of the people's blood, begone from the way, lest their blood wage war against thee.
Know for sure that their property is as their blood, because property is acquired by strength of body.

The mother of those young elephants will exact vengeance: her retribution will slay him that eats the young elephant.
O eater of bribes, thou eatest the young elephant: from thee too the Master of the elephant <note>A reference to the "People of the Elephant" mentioned in the Quran, symbolizing divine protection against the powerful.</note> will wring the breath.

160. The smell put to shame the deviser of fraud: the elephant knows the smell of her child.
He that perceives the smell of God from distant Yemen <note>A reference to Uways al-Qarani, a contemporary of the Prophet who lived in Yemen and was known for his spiritual connection despite never meeting him in person.</note>, how should not he perceive the smell of falsehood from me?
Inasmuch as Mustafá <term>Mustafá: "The Chosen One," a title for the Prophet Mohammed</term> smelt this from far away, how should not he smell the odour from our mouths?
He does smell it, but he conceals the fact from us: the good and bad smells go up to Heaven.
Thou art sleeping, and meanwhile the smell of that unlawful deed of thine is beating on the azure sky.

165. It accompanies thy foul breaths, it ascends to the smellers—the examiners—in the celestial sphere.
The smell of pride and the smell of greed and the smell of concupiscence will become, in speaking, like the smell of onions.
If thou take oath, saying, "When have I eaten them? I have abstained from onions and garlic,"
The breath of thy oath will inform against thee and will strike upon the noses of those who sit beside thee.
Many prayers are rejected because of the smell thereof: the corrupt heart shows in the tongue.

170. The answer to such a prayer is "Get ye gone": the requital for every knave is the cudgel of repulse.
But if thy words be wrong and thy meaning right, that wrongness of expression is acceptable to God.

->***Explaining that in the sight of the Beloved a fault committed by lovers is better than the correctness of strangers.***<-

The veracious Bilál <note>Bilál ibn Rabáh, the first muezzin in Islam, known for his devotion and his slight speech impediment.</note> in uttering the call to prayer used, from ardent feeling, to pronounce *hayya* as *hayya* <note>original: "hayya as hayya" — Bilál reportedly pronounced the Arabic letter 'sh' as 's' due to his dialect or an impediment.</note>,
So that some people said, "O Messenger of God, this fault is not right now when 'tis the beginning of the edifice of Islam.
O Prophet and Messenger of the Creator, get a muezzin <term>muezzin: the official who proclaims the call to prayer</term> who speaks more correctly.

175. At the commencement of religion and piety, it is a disgrace to mispronounce *hayy 'ala 'l-faláh* <note>original: "hasten to success" — a central phrase in the Islamic call to prayer.</note>."
The Prophet's wrath boiled up, and he gave one or two indications of the hidden favours which God had bestowed upon Bilál,
Saying, "O base men, in God's sight the mispronounced *hayy* of Bilál is better than a hundred *há's* and *khá's* <note>Refers to the precise phonetic pronunciation of Arabic letters, emphasizing technical skill over spiritual sincerity.</note> and words and phrases.
Do not stir me to anger, lest I divulge your secret—both your end and your beginning."
If thou hast not a sweet breath in prayer, go and beg a prayer from the pure in heart.

->***How God most High commanded Moses, on whom be peace, saying, "Call unto Me with a mouth with which thou hast not sinned."***<-

180. God said, "O Moses, beseech Me for protection with a mouth thou hast not sinned withal."
Moses said, "I have not such a mouth." God said, "Call unto Me by the mouth of others."

<summary>This passage explores the spiritual reality behind outward appearances, arguing that God values the sincere intention of a "lover" over the technical perfection of a "stranger." It uses the examples of Bilál's mispronunciation and Moses's humility to show that true prayer arises from a pure heart or the intercession of others.</summary>

When did you sin by the mouth of others? Invoke God by the mouth of others, crying, “O God!”
Act in such a way that their mouths may pray for you in the nights and days.
Ask pardon by a mouth with which you have committed no sin—and that will be the mouth of others— <note>The poet suggests that since we cannot sin with another person's tongue, their prayers on our behalf are inherently "pure" for us.</note>

❦ **185.** Or else make your own mouth pure; make your spirit alert and nimble.
Praise of God is pure: when purity has come, defilement packs up and leaves.
Opposites flee from opposites: night flees when the light of dawn shines forth.
When the pure, holy Name <note>original: "Name" refers to the Dhikr or remembrance of God's specific attributes.</note> comes into the mouth, neither impurity remains nor any sorrows.

## ***Showing that the supplicant's invocation of God is essentially the same thing as God's response to him.***

One night a certain man was crying “Allah!” <note>original: "Allah" is the Arabic proper name for God.</note> until his lips were growing sweet with praise of Him.

❦ **190.** The Devil said, “Please, O talkative one, where is the response ‘Here am I’ <note>original: "Labbayk," the traditional response of a master to a servant or God to a pilgrim.</note> to all this ‘Allah’?
Not a single response is coming from the Throne: how long will you cry ‘Allah’ with a grim face?”
He became broken-hearted and laid down his head to sleep: in a dream he saw Khadir <note>A legendary immortal figure in Islamic tradition who acts as a spiritual guide; often associated with greenness and hidden knowledge.</note> amidst the greenery.
Khadir said, “Listen, you have held back from praising God: why is it that you regret having called unto Him?”
He said, “No ‘Here am I’ is coming to me in response, hence I fear that I may be a rejected soul who is driven away from the Door.”

❦ **195.** Khadir said, “God says: That ‘Allah’ of yours is My ‘Here am I,’ and that supplication and grief and passion of yours is My messenger to you.
Your efforts to find a way to Me were in reality My drawing you towards Me, which released your feet from the bonds of the world.
Your fear and love are the noose to catch My favor: beneath every ‘O Lord’ of yours are many responses of ‘Here am I’ from Me.”
The soul of the fool is far from this prayer, because he is not permitted to cry “O Lord.”
On his mouth and heart are a lock and bolt, so that he may not moan unto God in the hour of misery.

❦ **200.** God gave to Pharaoh <note>The archetypal tyrant and egoist who claimed divinity for himself.</note> a hundredfold possessions and riches, so that he claimed divine might and majesty.
In his whole life, that man of evil nature felt no spiritual headache, lest he should moan unto God.
God gave him all the empire of this world, but He did not give him grief and pain and sorrows.
Grief is better than the empire of the world, so that you may call unto God in secret.
The call of the griefless comes from a frozen heart; the call of the grieving one comes from rapture:

❦ **205.** It is to pull the voice back under the lips, to bear in mind one's origin and beginning;
It is the voice become pure and sad, crying “O God!” and “O Thou whose help is sought!” and “O Helper!”
Even the moan of a dog for His sake is not empty of Divine attraction, because everyone who desires Him is a captive of His love—
As, for example, the dog of the Cave <note>A reference to the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus (mentioned in the Quran), whose dog was granted a spiritual status for guarding the holy youths.</note>, which was freed from eating carrion and sat at the table of the spiritual emperors:
Until the Resurrection, before the Cave, it drinks the water of Divine mercy in a gnostic <note>term: gnostic (Arif) - one who possesses direct, experiential knowledge of spiritual truths rather than just book learning.</note> way without needing a cup.

<summary>This passage explains that the very act of longing for God and calling His name is itself the divine response, suggesting that spiritual suffering is a gift that draws the soul closer to the Creator. It contrasts the "painless" life of the tyrant Pharaoh with the "blessed" grief of the sincere seeker.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the internal state of prayer to the external practice of spiritual vigilance. ❦ **210.** Oh, there is many a person dressed in a dog’s skin <note>This refers to the "hidden saints" or the *Malamatiyya*, who purposely lived in a way that drew public reproach or appeared lowly to hide their high spiritual rank.</note> who has no name or fame, yet is not without the cup of Divine knowledge in secret.
Give your life for this cup, my son; for how can victory be won without spiritual warfare and patience?
To show patience for the sake of this is no hardship: show patience, for patience is the key to joy. <note>original: "al-sabru miftahu'l-faraj," a famous Arabic proverb meaning "Patience is the key to relief."</note>
From this ambush of the world, none escaped without some patience and prudence: indeed, to prudence, patience is like the hand and the foot.
Exercise prudence in what you eat and drink, for the food and drink of this world are like poisonous weeds; to exercise such caution is the strength and light of the prophets.

❦ **215.** He that jumps at every breath of wind is like straw, but how should a mountain attach any weight to the wind?
On every side a ghoul <note>A shape-shifting desert demon in folklore that mimics voices to lure travelers off the path to their death.</note> is calling to you—"Hark, O brother, if you wish to find the way, come hither!
I will show you the way, I will be your kind fellow-traveler; I am the guide for you on this intricate path."
She—the ghoul of the world—is no guide, and she does not know the way. O Joseph, do not go toward that wolfish one! <note>The soul is compared to the beautiful Prophet Joseph, while the deceptions of the world are compared to the wolf that his brothers claimed had devoured him.</note>
Prudence consists of this: that you be not beguiled by the rich foods, sweets, and snares of the World;

❦ **220.** For she has neither fat nor sweet: she simply chants magic spells and breathes them into your ear,
Saying, "Come in as my guest, O light of my eyes: the house is yours, and you are mine."
Prudence is this, that you say to her, "I have indigestion," or "I am ill, I am a sick man in this charnel-house";
Or "My head aches: take away my headache," or "The son of my maternal uncle has invited me"—
For she will give you a single draught of honey mixed with venomous stings, so that her honey will plant many sores within you.

❦ **225.** Whether she gives you fifty or sixty pieces of gold, she gives you—O fish—nothing but flesh on a hook.
If she gives, when does that deceitful one ever truly give anything? The words of the swindler are like rotten walnuts.
Their rattling robs you of your understanding and your brain, and does not value even ten thousand understandings as worth a single one.
In your travels, your spiritual bag and purse are your only true friends; do not care for anything else. If you are Rámín, seek none but your Wísa. <note>Ramin and Wisa (Vis) are the protagonists of a famous 11th-century Persian romance. Here, they symbolize the seeker and the true Beloved or the essential self.</note>
It is your essential self that is your Wísa and beloved, and all these external things are nothing but causes of ruin to you.

❦ **230.** Prudence is this: that when worldlings invite you, you should not say, "They are enamoured and fond of me."
Know that their invitation is like the bird-whistle which the fowler <term>bird-catcher</term> gives while concealed in his place of ambush.
He has put forward a dead bird, pretending that this bird is making this plaintive noise and cry.
The living birds think he is one of their kind: they gather round, and he rends their skins—
Except, of course, the bird on which God has bestowed prudence, so that it may not be fooled by that bait and enticement.

<summary>This passage teaches the necessity of spiritual caution (prudence) and patience in navigating the world's deceptions, using metaphors like the ghoul, the fowler, and the romance of Vis and Ramin to distinguish between the ego's traps and the soul's true essence.</summary>

❦ **235.** Imprudence is surely followed by regret. Listen to this story as an explanation of this truth.

### *How the countryman deceived the townsman and invited him with humble entreaties and great importunity.*

In the past, my brother, there was a <term>townsman</term> <note>Representing the person of intellect or the urban soul</note> who was close friends with a man from the country.
Whenever the countryman traveled to the city, he would set up his quarters in the street where the townsman lived.
He would remain as a guest for two or three months at a time, spending his days in the townsman’s shop and eating at his table.
And the townsman would provide, entirely free of charge, everything the man required during his stay.

❦ **240.** One day, the countryman turned to the townsman and said, “Sir, will you never come to the countryside for a holiday?
Bring all your children, I beg you in God’s name, for this is the season when the rose-gardens bloom and the spring is at its height.
Or come in the summer, during the harvest, so that I may gird my belt and devote myself to serving you.
Bring your servants, your children, and your kinsfolk, and stay in our village for three or four months.
In the spring, the countryside is truly delightful; there are flowering fields and beautiful <term>anemones</term> <note>Wild red poppies or windflowers common in the Persian landscape.</note>.”

❦ **245.** The townsman continually put him off with promises, until eight years had passed since the first invitation was given.
Every year the countryman would ask, “When will you begin your journey? For the month of December is already here.”
And the townsman would make an excuse, saying, “This year we have a guest who has arrived from a distant district;
But next year I will certainly travel to your region, if I can escape the pressing affairs that keep me at home.”
The countryman replied, “My family is anxiously expecting your children, O benefactor.”

❦ **250.** Every year he returned, like a migrating stork, to reside in the townsman’s quarters.
And every year the <term>Khwája</term> <note>A Persian title of respect for a master, teacher, or merchant; literally "Lord."</note> would spend his gold and wealth upon him, opening his wings wide in hospitality.
On this last occasion, that <term>paladin</term> <note>Used here ironically to mean a 'champion' of receiving favors.</note> sat before dishes of food provided for him every morning and evening for three months.
Feeling a sense of shame, he said again to the Khwája, “How much longer will you give me nothing but promises? How long will you deceive me?”
The Khwája replied, “My body and soul are eager for our meeting, but every change in life depends on the decree of God.

❦ **255.** Man is like a ship or a sail: he must wait to see when the <term>Driver of the wind</term> <note>A poetic metaphor for God as the ultimate controller of human destiny.</note> shall send a favorable breeze.”
Once more the countryman implored him, crying, “O generous man, take your children and come to witness the pleasures of the country!”
Three times he took the townsman’s hand in a solemn <term>covenant</term> <note>A formal, binding agreement or oath.</note>, saying, “In God’s name, come quickly, make your greatest effort!”
After ten years of these same sugared entreaties and promises, the Khwája’s children finally spoke.
They said, “O father, even the moon, the clouds, and the shadows have their journeys.

❦ **260.** You have placed this man under many obligations; you have taken great pains on his behalf.
He wishes to repay some part of that debt when you become his guest.
He gave us many instructions in private: ‘Bring him to the country,’ he said, ‘by coaxing him to come.’”

The townsman said, “This is true, but, O Síbawayh <note>Síbawayh was a famous 8th-century Persian grammarian. Here, the name is likely used as an archetype for a person of learning or intellect who may still be vulnerable to deception.</note>, be on your guard against the malice of the person to whom you have shown kindness.

Love is a seed sown to bear fruit at the moment of one’s final breath; I fear that it may be spoiled by neglect or estrangement.”

❧ **265.** There is a friendship that acts like a sharp sword, as destructive as the month of December in gardens and cornfields;
But there is also a friendship like the season of spring, from which comes healing and harvests beyond calculation.
Prudence is this: that you think of potential evil, so that you may flee and be free from it.
The Prophet <note>Referring to a traditional saying (Hadith) of Muhammad: 'Prudence consists in being suspicious' (al-hazmu su’u ’l-zanni), suggesting one should not be naively trusting in a world of hidden dangers.</note> has said, “Prudence consists in thinking evil”: know that for every footstep there is a snare, O fool!
The surface of the plateau looks level and broad, but at every step there is a trap; do not advance so boldly.

❧ **270.** The mountain-goat runs along, saying, “Where is the snare?” But as it speeds onward, the snare catches its throat.
O you who said “Where?” look and see! You saw the open plain, but you did not see the ambush.
Without an ambush, a snare, and a hunter, O cunning one, why would there be a sheep’s tail <note>A fatty sheep's tail was considered a delicacy and was commonly used as bait in traps.</note> lying in the middle of a cornfield?
Consider those who walked boldly upon the earth—look at their bones and skulls now!
When you go to the graveyard, O you with whom God is pleased, ask those bones about the things of the past,

❧ **275.** So that you may see clearly how those blind, intoxicated men fell down into the pit of delusion.
If you have eyes, do not walk blindly; and if you do not have eyes, take a staff in your hand.
When you lack the staff of prudence and judgment, make the eye of a seer <note>A spiritual guide or someone with higher perception.</note> your leader;
And if you have no staff of prudence or judgment, do not stand on every road without a guide.
Walk in the same way a blind man walks, so that your foot may escape the pit and the hound.

❧ **280.** The blind man plants his foot tremblingly, with fear and caution, so that he does not fall into distress.
O you who have jumped away from smoke only to fall into a fire—you who sought a mouthful of food and instead became a mouthful for a snake!

->***(Story of the people of Sabá and how prosperity made them forward.)***<-

You have not read the story of the people of Sabá <note>Sabá (Sheba) refers to an ancient kingdom in modern-day Yemen. In Islamic tradition, they were blessed with incredible abundance but were destroyed by a great flood after they turned away from God and became ungrateful.</note>, or perhaps you read it and heard nothing but the echo.
The mountain itself, which produces the echo, is not aware of the sound; the mind of the mountain has no way to access the true meaning.
Without an ear or a mind, it continues making a noise; when you are silent, it also becomes silent.

❧ **285.** God bestowed great ease upon the people of Sabá—thousands of castles, palaces, and orchards.

But those of a bad nature showed no gratitude for those bounties; in loyalty, they were lower than dogs.

When a dog receives a piece of bread from a door, he will stay and serve at that threshold.
He will become the watcher and guardian of that door, even if he suffers violence or harsh treatment.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual loyalty and the dangers of ingratitude. Still will he stay and abide at that door: he will deem it ingratitude to prefer another.

**290.** And again, if a strange dog comes by day or night to a particular quarter of the town, the dogs there will at once teach him a lesson,
Saying, “Begone to the place that was your first lodging! The obligation for that kindness is the heart’s pledge, which it must redeem.”
They will bite him, saying, “Begone to your place! Do not any longer leave unpaid the obligation for that kindness.”
From the door of the spirit and of spiritual men, how long did you drink the **water of life** <note>A common Sufi metaphor for divine knowledge or the presence of the Master that grants eternal life to the soul.</note>, so that your eyes were opened!
Much food from the door of the spiritual—in the form of mystical intoxication, ecstasy, and selflessness—did you cast upon your soul.

**295.** Afterwards, through greed, you abandoned that door, and now you are going round about every shop like a bear.
For the sake of worthless **bread-broth** <term>tharīd: a traditional dish made of pieces of bread soaked in meat broth; here it symbolizes meager, worldly rewards.</term> you are running to the doors of those worldly patrons whose pots are full of fat.
Know that here, where the saints abide, the meaning of “fat” is that the soul becomes flourishing, and know that here the plight of the desperate is made right.

### ***How the suffering would assemble every morning at the door of the cell of Jesus—peace be upon him—craving to be healed through his prayer.***

The table of the spiritual is like the cell of Jesus: O afflicted one, beware, beware! Do not forsake this door!
From all sides the people would gather—the blind, the lame, the paralyzed, and those clothed in rags—

**300.** At the door of the cell of Jesus in the morning, so that he, by his **breath** <note>In Islamic tradition, Jesus (Isa) is celebrated for his "life-giving breath" (*nafas*), by which he healed the sick and raised the dead by God’s leave.</note>, might deliver them from tribulation.
As soon as he finished his litanies, that man of goodly religion would go forth at morning tide,
And he would see troops of afflicted, feeble folk seated at the door in hope and expectancy.
Then he would say, “O you who are smitten, the wants of all you here present have been granted by God.
Listen! Set off and go without pain or trouble toward the forgiveness and kindness of God.”

**305.** All of them, like tethered camels whose knees you unbind with foresight,
At his prayer would begin to run on their feet, hastening gladly and joyously to their homes.
So too, you have experienced many maladies in yourself and have gained health from these **kings of religion** <note>A title for the great saints or Sufi masters who rule over the spiritual realm.</note>.
How often has your limping been turned into a smooth, easy gait! How often has your soul been made void of grief and pain!
O heedless one, tie a string to your foot <note>An idiom suggesting one should take measures to remain mindful or "tethered" to reality so as not to lose one’s way.</note>, so that you may not become lost to yourself even, O sluggard!

**310.** Your ingratitude and forgetfulness did not call to mind your former drinking of honey.
Necessarily, that way by which spiritual blessings were conveyed became barred to you, since the hearts of the **men of heart** <note>original: *ahl-e dil*; those who possess spiritual insight and are in union with the Divine.</note> were made sore by you.
Quickly overtake them and ask pardon of God; weep lamentably like a cloud,
In order that their rose-garden may open its blossoms to you, and that the ripe fruits may burst and reveal themselves.
Pace round that same door: do not be less than a dog, if you have become a fellow-servant with the **Dog of the Cave**. <note>A reference to the loyal dog, Qitmir, who guarded the Seven Sleepers (Ashab al-Kahf) in the Qur'anic and Christian tradition; though a dog, his devotion earned him a place in Paradise.</note>

<summary>This passage uses the analogy of a dog's loyalty to its master to rebuke those who abandon spiritual paths for worldly gain. It highlights Jesus as the supreme healer of both body and soul, urging the seeker to seek forgiveness from the "men of heart" to restore their spiritual health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual loyalty, extending the metaphor of the faithful dog to shame those who are ungrateful to their Divine Creator. It transitions from the animal analogy to a theological argument regarding the priority of God’s rights over even the most sacred human bonds, such as those with one's mother, citing God's protection of humanity since the time of Noah.</meta>

❦ **315.** Even dogs warn one another, saying, “Keep your heart fixed on your first home. <note>In Sufi thought, the "first home" refers to the soul's origin with God before entering the physical world.</note> Hold fast to that first door where you were fed, and fulfill your duty; do not leave that debt unpaid.”
They continue to bite the stray dog so that, out of a sense of duty, he might return there and find success in his original dwelling.
They bite him, saying, “O wicked dog, be gone! Do not become an enemy to your benefactor.
Be attached to that same door like a door-ring; stay on watch, nimble and ready to spring.”

❦ **320.** “Do not be the one who breaks our tradition of faith; do not recklessly make our disloyalty famous.
Since loyalty is the very badge by which dogs are known, go away and do not bring shame and a bad name upon all dogs.”
Inasmuch as unfaithfulness has always been a disgrace even for dogs, how could you think it right for a human to show such treachery?
God the Most High has boasted of His own faithfulness: He has asked, “*And who is more faithful to his covenant than God?*” <note>original: "wa-man awfā bi-ʿahdihi mina llāh," a reference to the Quran, Surah At-Tawbah 9:111.</note>
Know that any "faithfulness" to others that requires the rejection of God is actually unfaithfulness; no one has a claim that comes before the rights of God.

❦ **325.** Even your mother’s right to your devotion only arose after that **Bounteous One** <term>The Bounteous One: One of the names of God (Al-Karim), referring to His role as the ultimate Giver who requires nothing in return.</term> made her the debtor for your very embryo.
He fashioned your form within her body; He gave her ease during pregnancy and helped her grow accustomed to the weight.
She considered you a part of her own self; yet it was His providence that eventually separated that which was joined.
God prepared thousands of clever means and arrangements so that your mother would pour her love upon you.
Therefore, God’s right to you exists before the mother’s: anyone who does not recognize this is a fool. <note>The original uses the word "ass" to denote someone who lacks spiritual perception.</note>

❦ **330.** If you deny this, then you must also refuse to admit that He created the mother, the breast, and the milk, and that He united her with your father!
O Lord, O You whose kindness is eternal, everything I know and everything I do not know belongs to You.
You commanded us, saying, “Remember God, for My right shall never grow old.”
Remember the kindness I showed you on that morning when I protected you in the Ark of Noah.
At that time, I gave the lineage of your ancestors safety from the Flood and from its crashing waves.

❦ **335.** Water—which is like fire in its deadly nature—had covered the earth; its waves were washing over the highest mountain peaks.
Yet I protected you; I did not reject you, even while you were still in the bodies of your ancestors' ancestors.
Now that you have grown to adulthood, how could I strike the sole of your foot? How could I let My own handiwork go to waste?
How is it that you become devoted to those who are unfaithful, turning away from Me because of your dark thoughts?
I am free of all negligence and betrayal, yet you come to Me and think such evil of Me.

❦ **340.** Save those evil thoughts for the world—for the places where you crawl before people who are just like yourself.

<summary>Rumi uses the loyalty of dogs to highlight human ingratitude toward God, arguing that the Divine "right" to a person's devotion precedes even that of their parents, citing God's protection of the human race since the Great Flood.</summary>
<keywords>faithfulness, ingratitude, Divine Right, motherhood, Noah's Ark, Covenant, Rumi, Masnavi</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual loyalty and the consequences of neglecting one's Divine debt. It moves from the metaphor of the faithful dog to the transient nature of human friendships compared to the eternal presence of God. It also introduces the Sufi psychological concepts of "contraction" and "expansion" as indicators of one's spiritual health.</meta>

You have many powerful friends and companions; yet if I ask you, “Where is so-and-so?” you will only be able to say, “He is gone.”
Your good friend has ascended to the highest Heaven, while your wicked friend has descended to the depths of the earth.
You are left in the middle, helpless, like the embers of a fire left behind by a departing caravan.
O valiant friend, take hold of the cloak of Him who is beyond the limits of “above” and “below.”

**345.** He neither ascends to Heaven like **Jesus**, nor is He swallowed by the earth like **Qárún**. <note>Qárún is the Quranic name for Korah, a man of immense wealth who was swallowed by the earth as punishment for his pride and refusal to pay alms.</note>
He is with you in physical space and in the spaceless realm, even when you leave your house and shop behind.
He draws purity out of defilement; He accepts your flawed attempts at goodness as if they were faithful performances of duty.
When you commit a wrong, He sends a punishment so that you might turn away from imperfection and move toward perfection.
When you have neglected a portion of your **orisons** <term>orisons: traditional ritual prayers or spiritual devotions (salat)</term> on the Path, you feel a painful, burning sensation of **contraction**. <note>original: "qabd," a Sufi term for a state of spiritual distress, anxiety, or "tightness" of the heart.</note>

**350.** That feeling is God’s corrective act, meaning: “Do not break the ancient covenant.”
Act before this mental contraction becomes a physical chain, and before this grip on your heart becomes a shackle on your feet.
Your mental suffering will eventually become visible to the senses and manifest in the world. Do not ignore these spiritual warnings.
In this life, the contractions caused by sin affect only the heart; after death, these same contractions manifest as actual chains.
“*Whosoever turns away from My remembrance, We shall surely give him a narrow life and gather him blind on the Day of Resurrection.*” <note>original: "wa-man aʿraḍa ʿan dhikrī..." Reference to the Quran, Surah Taha 20:124.</note>

**355.** When a thief steals someone's property, a feeling of contraction and tightness pricks his conscience.
He wonders, “I what is this distress?” It is the distress of the victim who wept at his wickedness.
When the thief ignores this feeling, the wind of persistence in evil fans the fire of his wrongdoing.
The contraction that once gripped the heart eventually turns into the physical grip of the policeman; inevitably, internal thoughts materialize and show themselves.
The inner pangs transform into the prison and the cross: the pang is the root, and the root eventually produces branches.

**360.** The root was hidden, but now it is revealed. View your inner **contraction** and **expansion** <term>expansion: "bast," a state of spiritual joy, openness, and divine grace</term> as spiritual roots.
If the root is bad, strike it down quickly so an ugly thorn does not grow in your garden.
When you feel the contraction, seek a remedy, for all outward growths begin from the hidden root below.
When you feel the expansion, nurture it; and when the fruit of that joy appears, share it with your friends.

### *The remainder of the Story of the people of Saba.*

The people of **Saba** <note>Saba (Sheba) refers to an ancient South Arabian civilization. In the Quran, they are cited as a people who were blessed with great gardens but were destroyed by a flood after they became ungrateful and arrogant.</note> were a folk given over to idle pleasure and folly; it was their habit to show ingratitude toward the Generous One.

<summary>This passage explores the internal spiritual signals of "contraction" (distress) and "expansion" (joy), explaining how inner states eventually manifest as external rewards or punishments. It concludes by introducing the historical example of the people of Saba to illustrate the dangers of ingratitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of spiritual discipline, moving from the internal feeling of "contraction" (qabd) to the historical and metaphorical example of the people of Saba. It illustrates how the human ego, or carnal soul, perversely rejects Divine blessings and wisdom, leading to its own destruction through pride and ingratitude.</meta>

**365.** By way of illustration, it would be ingratitude to dispute with your benefactor,
> Saying, “O do not want this kindness, I am annoyed by it: why are you troubling about it?
> Do me a favor, take away this kindness; I do not desire an eye: blind me at once!”
Hence the people of **Saba** <note>Saba (Sheba) refers to a wealthy ancient civilization mentioned in the Quran that was destroyed after the people rejected God's blessings and perversely asked for hardship instead of ease.</note> said,
> “(O Lord), put a far distance between us: our blemish is better
> for us, take away our adornment.
> We do not desire these palaces and orchards, nor fair women nor that safety and ease which we
> now enjoy.

**370.** “Towns near to each other are bad; the desert, where the wild beasts are, is good.”
Man craves winter in summer, and when winter comes, he likes it not,
For he is never content with any state of things, neither with poverty nor with a life of plenty.
“May Man be killed! How ungrateful he is!” <note>original: "qutila 'l-insán," a quote from the Quran (80:17) expressing Divine sorrow over the stubbornness of humanity.</note> Whenever he obtains guidance, he spurns it.
The **carnal soul** <term>carnal soul: (nafs) the lower self or ego that drives worldly desires and resists spiritual growth.</term> is of this sort, hence it ought to be killed: that Exalted One has said, “Kill yourselves.” <note>A reference to the Quranic command for the Israelites to slay their egos as an act of repentance.</note>

**375.** It is a **triagonal thorn**: <note>A caltrop-like thorn that always has one point facing up; used here as a metaphor for the ego, which causes pain no matter how you try to manage it.</note> however you may place it, it will pierce, and how will you escape from its stab?
Set the thorn on fire with renunciation of sensual passion, and cling to the righteous friend.
When the people of Saba carried their ingratitude beyond bounds, saying, “In our opinion, pestilence is better than the zephyr,”
Their counselors began to admonish them and restrain them from impiety and ingratitude;
But they sought to take the lives of their counselors, and sowed the seed of impiety and unthankfulness.

**380.** When the **Divine Decree** <term>Divine Decree: (Qadar) the preordained will of God that overrules human planning and perception.</term> comes to pass, this whole world becomes cramped so that there is no escape; by the Decree, sweetmeat becomes anguish to the mouth.
He, the **Prophet**, <note>Referring to Muhammad, who spoke of the overwhelming nature of God's will.</note> said, “When the Decree comes, the widest expanse is narrow; when the Decree comes, the eyes are veiled.”
The eye is bandaged at the time of the Decree, so that the eye does not see the eye’s **collyrium**. <term>collyrium: a medicinal eye salve used both for healing and enhancing vision; here, it represents spiritual insight.</term>
When the cunning of that **Horseman** <note>A metaphor for God's hidden agency; the "dust" represents the physical world and secondary causes that distract us from the true Actor.</note> has raised the dust, the dust keeps you from calling for aid.
Go towards the Horseman, go not towards the dust; else the cunning of the Rider will beat upon you.

**385.** God said,
> “He whom this wolf devoured, he saw the wolf’s dust; how did he not make
> piteous moan?”
Did he not know the wolf’s dust? Then, with such knowledge, why did he graze?
Sheep know the smell of the harmful wolf and creep away in every direction.
The brain of animals knows the smell of the lion and bids farewell to grazing.
You have smelled the lion of God’s wrath. Turn back! Consort with prayer and dread!

**390.** That multitude of Saba did not turn back from the wolf’s dust, and after the dust, the wolf of tribulation came in his might.
In wrath he tore to pieces those sheep which shut their eyes to the shepherd, **Wisdom**.
How often did the shepherd call them! And they came not: they were throwing the dust of resentment in the eyes of the shepherd,
> Saying, “Begone: we ourselves are better shepherds than you.
> How should we become your followers? We are chieftains, every one of us.
> We are food for the wolf, and we are not for the Friend; we are fuel for the Fire, and we are not
> for dishonor.”

**395.** A heathen pride was in their brains: the raven croaked disaster over the traces of their habitation.

He explains that when the Divine Decree arrives, human perception is clouded, making the wide world feel narrow and blinding us to the true source of our trials.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual lesson following the story of the people of Saba. Having shown how the ego rejects divine ease, the text now illustrates the suffering of the spiritual heart—likened to prophets like Joseph and Mohammad—when it is trapped by the "old wolf" of the carnal soul and the distractions of the material world.</meta>

“They were digging a pit for the oppressed” but they themselves fell into that very pit, crying “Alas!”
They tore the coats of the **Josephs** <note>In Sufi tradition, Joseph (Yusuf) represents the ultimate beauty of the soul and the heart. Tearing his coat refers to the way worldly people persecute the saints and prophets.</note>, and that which they gave to others they received back themselves, piece by piece.
Who is that Joseph? It is your own God-seeking heart, held as a captive within your physical body.
You have bound a **Gabriel** <note>The Archangel Gabriel represents the highest spiritual intellect; here, the poet laments how we stifle our divine spirit within the "pillar" of our physical existence.</note> to a pillar, and you have wounded his wings and feathers in a hundred places.

❦400. You set a roasted calf before him, or you fetch ground straw and bring him to the straw-barn,
Saying, “Eat; this is a dainty meal for us,” even though for him there is no food but meeting God face to face.
Because of this torment and trial, that afflicted heart is complaining about you to God,
> Crying, “O God, deliver me from this **old wolf**!” <note>The "old wolf" is a metaphor for the carnal soul or ego (nafs), which falsely "devours" the spiritual heart, much like the wolf was falsely accused of eating Joseph.</note> God says to it, “Behold, the hour is almost here: have patience.
> I will demand justice for you from every heedless person: who provides justice but God, the Dealer of Justice?”

❦405. The heart says, “My patience is lost because I am separated from Your face, O Lord.
I am like **Ahmad** <note>original: "Ahmad," another name for the Prophet Mohammad.</note> left forsaken among the enemies, or like **Salih** <note>Salih was a prophet sent to the people of Thamud; they rejected his miracle of the she-camel and were eventually destroyed.</note> fallen into prison among the people of **Thamud**.
O You who bestowed happiness on the souls of the prophets, either slay me, call me back to You, or come Yourself!
Even the unbelievers cannot endure to be separated from You: every one of them is saying, ‘*O, would that I had been dust!*’” <note>A quote from the Quran (78:40), expressing the deep regret of those who realize they have missed their spiritual purpose.</note>
This is the state of the one who belongs to the other side; how then could one who belongs to You remain patient without You?”

❦410. God says, “Yes, O pure heart; but listen to Me and have patience, for patience is better.
The dawn is near. Hush, do not wail! I am working for you; do not you struggle.”

### *The rest of the Story of the Master’s going to the village on the invitation of the countryman.*

This digression has gone too far: return now, O brave friend. The countryman, you see, finally took the **Khwaja** <term>Khwaja: a title of respect for a master, teacher, or wealthy merchant.</term> to his house.
Put aside the story of the people of Saba: tell how the Khwaja arrived at the village.
The countryman used flattery to worm his way into favor, until he made the Khwaja’s common sense go crazy.

❦415. The Khwaja was distracted by message after message, until the clear water of his wisdom became muddy.
At the same time, his children—approving of the invitation—were joyfully shouting, “*Let us frolic and play!*” <note>This phrase mirrors the words of Joseph’s brothers in the Quran (12:12) when they plotted to lead him away from his father’s protection to throw him in the pit.</note>
Just like Joseph, whom the mysterious hand of Divine destiny allowed to be carried away from his father’s protection by those words, “*Let us frolic and play.*”
That is not true play; no, it is playing with one’s life. It is cunning, deceit, and a fraudulent trap.
Whatever would pull you away from the **Friend** <note>In this context, "the Friend" refers to God.</note>, do not listen to it, for it holds only loss upon loss.

❦420. Even if the profit seems to be a hundred times over, do not accept it: for the sake of a little gold, do not break your bond with the Treasurer, O **dervish**! <term>dervish: a spiritual seeker who has taken a vow of poverty and austerity, focusing on the "inner wealth" of God.</term>
