<meta>This page continues the spiritual warnings about the soul's distractions. Having previously discussed the inner struggle of the "Joseph" of the heart against the "wolf" of the ego, the text now turns to historical and parabolic examples of how worldly greed and the lures of the Devil can pull a believer away from divine presence.</meta>

Listen to the many rebukes—some stern and others gentle—that God directed toward the Companions of the Prophet <note>The *Sahaba*, or the early followers of Muhammad.</note>. 
This occurred during a year of famine, when the sound of a drum announcing a trade caravan caused them to abandon the Friday sermon without hesitation. They emptied the mosque, rushing out to the marketplace,
Thinking to themselves, “We must hurry, lest others buy the goods at a lower price and gain an advantage over us.”
The Prophet was left standing almost entirely alone in prayer, with only two or three impoverished men who remained firm in their faith and devotion.

❧**425.** God said: “How could a drum, a fleeting pastime, or a mere business deal pull you away from a man of God? 
You have scattered and run like madmen toward a shipment of wheat, leaving a Prophet standing alone in prayer.
For the sake of grain, you have sown the seeds of vanity and abandoned the Messenger of God. 
To be in his company is far better than any amusement or wealth. Open your eyes and see who it is you have forsaken! 
In your greed, did you forget the truth—that I am the Provider, and the best of all who provide?” <note>original: "Khayr al-Raziqin." This refers to the Quranic concept that God is the ultimate source of all sustenance, making worldly anxiety unnecessary.</note>

❧**430.** If God is the one who grants life and substance to the wheat itself, how could He ever let your acts of trust in Him go to waste? 
For the sake of a handful of grain, you have separated yourselves from the One who sent that grain down from the Heavens.

### ***How the falcon invited the ducks to come from the water to the plain.***

The falcon says to the duck, “Come up out of the water! Come and see the plains, which are blooming with sweetness.”
But the wise duck replies, “Stay back, O falcon! The water is our fortress, our safety, and our joy.”
The Devil is like that falcon. O ducks of the spirit, hurry to safety! Beware, and do not leave your stronghold in the "water" of spiritual life.

❧**435.** Say to the falcon: “Begone! Turn back and take your claws off us, you 'kind' friend! 
We have no need of your invitation. Keep it for yourself! We will not listen to your words, you deceiver! 
This water is enough for us; you can keep your sugar and your fields of sweets. I do not want your 'gifts'—take them away! 
As long as there is life in the body, God's nourishment will not fail us; where there is a king’s army, the banners of victory will always fly.”
The prudent **Khwája** <note>A title for a master, teacher, or gentleman of high status.</note> offered many excuses and pretexts to the countryman, who represents the stubborn Devil.

❧**440.** “At this moment,” the Khwája said, “I have serious business to attend to. If I come to visit your lands, my affairs will fall into disorder.
The King has entrusted me with a very delicate matter; he has even stayed awake all night anxiously waiting for my report. 
I dare not neglect the King’s command, for I cannot risk falling out of favor with him. 
Every morning and evening, a high-ranking officer arrives to ask for my help in finding a solution to these difficulties. 
Do you really think it is right for me to go off into the countryside, only to have the King knit his brows in anger?

❧**445.** How could I ever calm his wrath after that? To offend him so would be like burying myself alive.”

<summary>Rumi uses the historical abandonment of the Prophet's Friday sermon and the parable of the Falcon and the Duck to warn against choosing material gain over spiritual safety. He offered a hundred excuses of this kind, but his plans did not align with God’s command. If every atom in the world conspired to make a plan, they would be nothing—absolutely nothing—against the will of Heaven. How can this earth escape the sky? How can it hide? Whatever descends from Heaven to the earth, the earth has no shelter, no trick, and no hiding place.

❦**450.** If fire rains down from the sun, the earth bows its face before that flame; 
And if the rain creates a flood, destroying the cities upon it, 
The earth remains patient and resigned like Job, saying:
> “I am a prisoner; bring upon me whatever You will.” 
O you who are made of this earth, do not raise your head in pride; when you see God's command, do not turn away. Since you have heard the words, “*We created you from dust,*” <note>original: "Minha khalaqnakum," a reference to Quran 20:55, reminding humanity of their humble origins.</note> understand that He requires you to be as humble as dust; do not turn your face away from Him.

❦**455.** God says: 
> “Look at how I have sown a seed in the ground: you are the dust of the earth, yet I have raised you up high. 
> Adopt once more the way of the earth—humility and self-abasement—so that I may make you a prince over all princes.” 
Water falls from above to below, then from below it rises back up. Wheat was buried beneath the earth from above, and then it became ears of grain and sprouted quickly. The seed of every fruit entered the earth, then raised its head from the buried root.

❦**460.** The source of every blessing descended from Heaven to the earth and became nourishment for the pure vital soul. Because it came down from Heaven with humility, it became part of a living and brave human being. Thus, that lifeless matter—the rain and sun—was transformed into human virtues and soared joyously above the highest heavens, saying: 
> “We came first from the world of the living, and now we have returned from below to the heights.” 
Every particle of existence, whether moving or still, speaks and declares: “*Truly, to Him we are returning.*” <note>original: "Inna ilayhi raji'un," a Quranic phrase often recited during times of loss, signifying that all life originates from and returns to God.</note>

❦**465.** The praises and songs of the hidden particles have filled the Heavens with a great sound. When the Divine Decree began its work, a simple countryman defeated a clever city-dweller. <note>This refers to a parable in the Masnavi where a sophisticated city man is outmatched by the simple circumstances of the countryside, orchestrated by fate.</note> Despite thousands of good intentions, the Master <term>Khwája: a title for a person of high status, a teacher, or a merchant</term> was defeated and fell into calamities during his journey. He relied on his own stability, but though he was like a mountain, a mere trickle of a flood swept him away. When the Decree reveals itself from Heaven, all the intelligent become blind and deaf;

❦**470.** Fish are thrown out of the sea; the snare cruelly catches the bird in flight. Even powerful spirits and demons are trapped in a bottle; even a Hárút <note>Hárút and Márút were two angels mentioned in the Quran who were tested with human desires in Babylon; Hárút was eventually imprisoned in a pit.</note> falls into the pit of Babylon. All are lost except for the one who has found refuge in the Divine Decree: no unlucky alignment of the stars <term>quadrature: an astrological term referring to a 90-degree angle between planets, often considered an omen of conflict or misfortune</term> can ever harm them. Unless you take shelter in the Decree itself, no clever plan will ever set you free from it.

## ***The Story of the people of Zarwán and how they plotted to harvest the fruit in their orchards without being troubled by the poor.***

You have read the story of the people of Zarwán <note>Zarwán refers to the "People of the Garden" mentioned in the Quran (Surah Al-Qalam), who plotted to harvest their crops in secret to avoid sharing with the needy.</note>: then why have you persisted in seeking clever tricks to avoid your duties?

❧ **475.** Several harmful men who stung like scorpions were plotting to cut off the daily bread of some poor folk.
During the entire night, they were devising a scheme; many a person like ’Amr and Bakr <note>’Amr and Bakr are traditional Arabic placeholder names, similar to "every Tom, Dick, and Harry."</note> had put their heads together in conspiracy.
Those wicked men were whispering their inmost thoughts in secret, hoping God would not discover them.
Did the clay plot evil against the <term>Plasterer</term> <note>The "Plasterer" is a metaphor for God, the Creator who shapes human beings from clay.</note>? Is the hand doing any work that is hidden from the heart?
He (God) has said, "Does He who created you not know your desires, and whether there is sincerity or mere flattery in your secret conversations?"

❧ **480.** How could a traveler who set out at dawn be ignored by the One who sees clearly where he will stay tomorrow?
Wherever he has descended into a valley or climbed a mountain, God has taken charge of it and *perfectly accounted for it.* <note>original: "ahsahu 'adadan," a reference to God’s total knowledge of all things.</note>
Now clear your ears of forgetfulness and listen to the lonely plight of the sorrowful soul.
Know that when you listen to his story, that is the alms you give to the sad;
For you will hear the sorrows of the heart-sick—the starvation of the noble spirit trapped within the water and clay <note>In Sufi tradition, "water and clay" refers to the physical human body.</note> of the physical world.

❧ **485.** Though the spirit is filled with knowledge, it lives in a house filled with the smoke of worldly cares: open a window for it by listening.
When your ear becomes a vent for its relief, the bitter smoke will decrease and vanish from its house.
Show sympathy with us, O prosperous one, if you are traveling toward the most high Lord.
This indecision is a prison and a jail that will not let the soul move in any direction.
One motive pulls you one way, and another motive pulls you elsewhere, each one saying, "I am the right way."

❧ **490.** This indecision is a cliff on the Way to God: oh, blessed is the one whose feet are freed from its bonds.
He travels the right path without hesitation: if you do not know the way, look for where his footprints lead.
Follow the footprints of the deer and move forward safely, so that from those tracks you may eventually find the <term>musk-gland</term> <note>The musk-deer's scent is a common metaphor for the scent of divine truth or the presence of God.</note>.
By means of this spiritual travel you will ascend to the brightest heights, my brother, if you are willing to walk through the fire of hardship.
There is no fear of the sea, the waves, or the foam, since you have heard the Divine word: "*Do not be afraid.*"

❧ **495.** Know that the promise of *Do not be afraid* <note>original: "La takhaf," a Quranic phrase used to reassure prophets during times of trial.</note> is fulfilled when God has given you the holy fear that keeps you from sin. He will provide the bread, since He has already sent the tray to you.
True danger is for the one who has no fear of God; true suffering is for the one who does not visit the place where God is honored.

## ***The Merchant’s Departure for the Country and the Warning of Reason***

The <term>Khwaja</term> <note>A Persian title for a man of high status, such as a master, merchant, or lord.</note> set to work and made his preparations. His resolve to set out, like a bird in flight, sped rapidly toward the country.
His relatives and children prepared for the journey and loaded their baggage upon the ox of departure.
They were rejoicing and hastening toward the country, saying, "We have already tasted the fruit in our minds; give us the glad news of our arrival!"

❧ **500.** "The place we are heading for is a sweet pasture," they said, "and our friend there is kind and charming.
He has invited us with a thousand wishes; he has planted for us the sapling of kindness.
From him, we shall bring back to the city the harvest of the countryside to sustain us during the long winter.
Indeed, he will give up his whole orchard for our sake; he will make a place for us in the very center of his soul."
"Hasten, friends, so that you may find profit!" But Reason, speaking from within, was saying to them, "*Do not rejoice!*" <note>original: "la tafrahu," a reference to Quran 28:76, warning against exulting in worldly possessions.</note>

❧ **505.** Seek gain through the gain of God: *Truly, my Lord does not love those who rejoice overmuch.* <note>original: "inna 'llaha la yuhibbu 'l-farihin," quoting Quran 28:76.</note>
Rejoice only moderately *because of what He allows to come to you*: <note>A reference to Quran 57:23: "In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you."</note> for everything that comes and preoccupies you only serves to divert you from Him.
Rejoice in Him, and do not rejoice in anything except Him. He is like the spring, and all other things are like the cold month of December.
Everything other than He is a means of leading you gradually to your end, even if it appears to be your throne, your kingdom, or your crown.
Rejoice even in sorrow, for sorrow is the snare used to achieve union with God; on this spiritual Path, the way up is actually down. <note>This paradox suggests that spiritual "ascent" is achieved through "downward" humility and the breaking of the ego.</note>

❧ **510.** Sorrow is a hidden treasure, and your pain is like the mine where it is found, but how can such a saying take hold of children?
When children hear the word "play," they all run toward it with the speed of a wild donkey.
O blind donkeys! In that direction, there are snares; in that direction, there are bloodbaths hidden in ambush.
The arrows are flying, but the bow is hidden. From the <term>Unseen World</term> <note>original: "Ghayb," the hidden spiritual realm that lies beyond physical perception.</note> come a hundred arrows of old age to strike down youth.
You must set foot on the plain of the heart, because in the plain of the body's clay, there is no path for spiritual progress.

❧ **515.** The heart is the home of security, O friends; it has fountains and rose gardens within rose gardens.
Turn toward the heart and journey on, O night-travelers; within the heart are trees and many a flowing spring.
Do not go to the country: the country makes a fool of a man; it robs the intellect of its light and splendor.
O chosen one, hear the <term>Prophet’s saying</term>: "To dwell in the country is the grave of the intellect." <note>A traditional saying (Hadith) often cited in Sufi literature to contrast the "City" (the place of the Master and spiritual community) with the "Country" (the place of isolation and worldly ignorance).</note>
If anyone stays in the country for even a single day and evening, his intellect will not be fully restored for a month.

❧ **520.** For a whole month, foolishness will stay with him. What else should he reap from the parched grass of the country?
And he who stays a month in the country—ignorance and blindness will be his lot for a long time to come.

<summary>This passage warns against the distractions of the material world, symbolized by "the country," and urges the seeker to find joy only in God and the inner life of the heart.</summary>
<keywords>Khwaja, Reason, Worldly Joy, Sorrow as Union, Unseen World, Plain of the Heart, Grave of the Intellect, Sufi Parable</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Khwaja (the Merchant) and his family as they journey away from the city—which represents Universal Reason—toward the countryside, a symbol of spiritual distraction and the entrapment of the senses. The text transitions from a philosophical warning about the "outward form" of things to the physical journey of the characters.</meta>

What is "the country"? It represents the <term>Shaykh</term> <note>A spiritual teacher or elder.</note> who has not achieved union with the Divine, but has instead become addicted to mere convention and intellectual argument.
Compared with the town—which represents <term>Universal Reason</term> <note>In Sufi philosophy, the cosmic intellect that reflects Divine Wisdom.</note>—these senses of ours are like asses going round and round in a mill with their eyes bandaged.
Leave this inner meaning for a moment and look at the outward form of the tale: let the "pearl-seed" of essence alone and look at the "corn-seed" of the story.

**525.** If you cannot find the path to the pearl, come, take the wheat; if that direction is closed to you, push on in this one.
Observe the outward form! Although the outward form may fly crookedly, it will eventually lead you to the inward meaning.
Truly, the first stage of every human being is the "form"; only after that comes the "spirit," which is the beauty of one's inner disposition.
Is the first stage of every fruit anything but its outer form?
Only after that comes the delicious taste, which is its true reality.
First, people make or buy a tent; only afterwards do they invite the <term>Turcoman</term> <note>In this context, the Turcoman represents the beloved guest or the soul inhabiting the "tent" of the body.</note> as a guest.

**530.** Consider your physical form to be the tent and your real essence to be the Turcoman; regard your essence as the sailor and your form as the ship.
For God’s sake, let us leave this topic for a moment, so that the <term>Khwaja’s</term> <note>The merchant or master of the house.</note> donkey may ring its bell and proceed on its journey.

### How the Khwaja and his family went to the country.

The Khwaja and his children prepared their gear and galloped on their beasts toward the countryside.
Merrily they rode through the fields; they chanted, "Travel, so that you may gain advantage"; <note>A reference to a traditional saying (hadith) encouraging travel for both physical and spiritual profit.</note>
For it is through traveling that the moon becomes as splendid as <term>Kay Khusraw</term>; <note>A legendary and heroic King of ancient Persia.</note> how could it ever become an emperor (*khusraw*) without wandering through the sky?

**535.** Through travel, the humble pawn becomes a noble queen <note>original: *farzin*, the vizier or queen in chess.</note>, and through travel, Joseph reached the heights of his desire.
By day, the sun scorched their faces; by night, they learned the way by observing the stars.
The rough road seemed good to them: because of their delight in reaching the country, the path felt like Paradise.
From the lips of a sweetheart, even bitterness becomes sweet; because of the rose-garden, even the thorns become charming.
The bitter <term>colocynth</term> <note>A desert plant known for its extreme bitterness.</note> turns into sweet dates when it comes from the beloved; a cramped house is made to feel like spacious fields by the presence of a dear companion.

**540.** Oh, there is many a delicate youth who endures the thorns of anguish in the hope of winning a moon-faced sweetheart.
Oh, there is many a porter with a back torn by heavy loads for the sake of the beautiful one to whom he has lost his heart.
The blacksmith blackens his own beauty with soot so that when night comes, he may kiss the face of a beloved as radiant as the moon.
The merchant sits, exhausted, on his shop-bench until nightfall because the image of one as tall and slender as a cypress has taken root in his heart.
A trader travels over sea and land, making swift and dangerous journeys for the love of the one who sits waiting at home.

**545.** Whoever has a passion for that which is "dead" (the material world) only does so in the hope of gaining that which possesses the features of the "living" (the Divine Essence).

<summary>This passage uses the Khwaja's literal journey to the countryside to explain the relationship between outward form and inward spirit, arguing that even mundane or difficult journeys are motivated by a search for beauty and essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the deception of outward forms. Having previously warned that the "countryside" represents a state of spiritual distraction, the text now explains why human affections are often misplaced. It transitions from the philosophical concept of "borrowed beauty" to the narrative of the Merchant (Khwaja) and his family, eventually introducing the famous allegory of Majnun and the dog to illustrate how a lover sees the essence behind the form.</meta>

The carpenter turns his attention to wood, in the hope of rendering service to a fair one whose face is like the moon <note>A common Persian poetic metaphor for a beautiful beloved.</note>.
Do thou exert thyself in hope of the Living One who does not become lifeless after a day or two!
Do not out of meanness choose a mean person as thy friend: that friendship in him is merely borrowed and not part of his true essence.
If thy friends other than God possess any permanence, where is the friendship you once had with your mother and father?

**550.** If any one but God were worthy to be relied upon, what has become of the friendship you had with your nurse and your tutor?
Thy friendship with the milk and the breast did not endure, nor did thy shyness of going to school.
That beauty was merely a radiance cast upon their "wall": when the sign of the Sun departed, the light went back towards the Sun.
On whatsoever thing that radiance may fall, thou fallest in love with it, O brave man.
On whatsoever existent thing thy love is bestowed, that thing is merely gilded with <term>Divine qualities</term> <note>The attributes of God reflected in creation, such as beauty, mercy, or strength.</note>.

**555.** When the "gold" has returned to its original source and only the "copper" remains, thy nature is surfeited and proceeds to discard it.
Withdraw thy foot from that which is merely gilded by His qualities; do not out of ignorance call the base alloy beautiful;
For in a base coin, the beauty is borrowed: beneath the lovely surface, the substance is uncomely.
The gold is returning from the face of the false coin back into the mine; do thou also go towards that Mine to which it is returning.
The light is going from the wall back up to the sun: do thou go to that Sun which ever moves in accordance with eternal justice.

**560.** From now on, take the water that comes from Heaven, for thou hast found no faithfulness in the man-made aqueduct.
The lure to catch the wolf is the sheep’s tail; it is not the shop where the sheep’s tail grew: how should that fierce wolf know the place of its origin?
They <note>The <term>Khwaja</term> (Merchant) and his family.</note> imagined they would find "gold tied in knots" <note>An idiom for wealth or a secure reward.</note>, so the deluded party were making haste to reach the countryside.
Thus they went alone, laughing, dancing, and caracoling <note>Prancing or performing half-turns like a horse.</note> toward the water-wheel.
Whenever they saw a bird flying in the direction of the country, their patience rent its garments in excitement;

**565.** And they would joyfully kiss the face of anyone who came from the country, or even from that neighborhood,
Saying, “You have seen the face of our friend, therefore to the beloved Soul you are as the soul, and to us you are as the eye.”

->### ***How Majnún petted the dog that lived in Layla's abode.***<-

They behaved like <term>Majnún</term> <note>The "Madman" for love; the protagonist of the classic romance *Layla and Majnun*, symbolizing the soul's intense longing for the Divine.</note>, who was seen petting a dog, kissing it, and melting with fondness before it.
He was pacing round it, stooping humbly in <term>circumambulation</term> <note>The act of walking around a sacred object; Majnun treats the dog as a holy site because it lived near his beloved.</note>; he was also giving it pure sugar-julep <note>A sweet, medicinal drink made of rosewater and sugar.</note> to drink.
An idle talker said, “O half-baked Majnún, what hypocrisy is this that thou art always displaying?

**570.** A dog's muzzle is ever eating filth; a dog scrapes its <term>séant</term> <note>Archaic term for the backside or buttocks.</note> with its lips!”

<summary>This passage argues that all earthly beauty is a temporary reflection of Divine light, like gold leaf over copper. It uses the story of Majnun's devotion to a common dog to show how a true lover looks past outward "impurity" to see the connection to the Beloved.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how outward appearances deceive the eye. Having previously discussed "borrowed beauty," the text now uses the famous story of Majnun and the dog to show how love transforms one's perception. It then transitions into the story of the Merchant (Khwaja) who is led astray by false promises, serving as a warning about the necessity of a spiritual guide.</meta>

He spoke at length about the dog’s flaws, but one who only notices faults <gloss>original: 'aybdán</gloss> has never caught even a scent of the One who knows all that is hidden <gloss>original: ghaybdán</gloss>.
Majnun <note>A famous figure in Eastern literature known as "The Madman" because of his total, self-sacrificing love for Layla.</note> replied, "You are made entirely of outward form and physical body. Come inside! Look at this dog through my eyes.
For this creature is a wonder protected by the Lord’s own seal; he is the guardian of the home of Layla <note>Majnun's beloved, often representing the Divine in mystical poetry.</note>.
Look instead at his high purpose, his heart, his soul, and his wisdom. Consider where he chose to live and make his dwelling-place."

### 575. The Dog of the Cave

**575.** "He is a dog with a blessed face, like the dog of the Cave <note>A reference to the faithful dog that guarded the 'Seven Sleepers' in religious tradition; a symbol of loyalty that transcends its animal nature.</note>; no, he is the one who shares in my grief and woe.
How could I trade even a single hair of a dog that stays in her home for the greatest of lions?
When lions themselves are humble slaves to her dogs, there is no more to be said. Silence, and farewell!"
If you look beyond outward appearances, my friends, you will find a Paradise—gardens of roses within gardens of roses.
Once you have broken and destroyed the 'form' of your own ego, you will have learned how to break the form of everything else.

**580.** After that, you will shatter every false image. Like the hero Ali <note>Specifically called 'Haydar' (The Lion) here; the cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, renowned for his spiritual and physical strength.</note>, you will tear down the gates of Khaybar <note>A famous fortress; in this context, it symbolizes the massive obstacles of the material world that only a spiritual hero can overcome.</note>.
That simple Master <gloss>original: Khwája</gloss> was tricked by appearances, for he was heading to the countryside based only on weak and empty promises.
He ran joyfully toward the trap of that flattery, just as a bird flies toward the hunter's bait.
The bird thinks the bait is a sign of kindness, when in truth that 'gift' is the height of greed and not true generosity at all.
Driven by desire for the bait, the little birds fly happily toward their own deception.

**585.** If I told you the full story of the Master’s joy, I fear it would make you late on your own journey, traveler.
I will be brief: when the village finally came into view, it was not the village he was looking for, so he had to take another road.
For about a month, they hurried from village to village because they did not truly know the way to the countryman's house.
If anyone travels a path without a leader, a journey of two days becomes a journey of a hundred years.
Whoever rushes toward the Ka'ba <note>The holy house in Mecca, the ultimate goal of the pilgrimage.</note> without a guide becomes lost and pathetic, just like these bewildered men.

**590.** Anyone who takes up a trade or a profession without a teacher becomes a laughingstock in both the town and the country.
Except for a few rare miracles, has any descendant of Adam ever entered this world without parents?
Wealth comes to those who work for it; it is a truly extraordinary event when someone simply stumbles upon a buried treasure.
Where is there a Mustafa <note>A title for the Prophet Muhammad, meaning 'The Chosen One.'</note>—one whose very body is pure spirit—so that God the Merciful might teach him the Qur'an directly?
For all those who are still attached to the physical body, God, in His great bounty, provided the 'Pen' <note>A reference to the Qur'anic verse 'He taught by the Pen,' implying that most people require study, tools, and teachers to learn.</note> as the means of gaining knowledge.

**595.** My son, every greedy person is deprived of spiritual blessings. Do not run headlong like the greedy; move more slowly and with care.

<summary>Rumi uses the story of Majnun's love for a dog to illustrate that spiritual truth is found by looking past outward forms, and warns that traveling the spiritual path without a guide leads to exhaustion and failure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative illustrating how the "Master" (the Khwája) was misled by the false promises of a countryman. On that journey, the party of the Master <term>Khwája: A Persian title for a man of high status, such as a wealthy merchant or scholar.</term> suffered such pains and distress that they were like a land-bird struggling in fresh water <note>A metaphor for being completely out of one's element and in a state of suffocating misery.</note>.
They grew weary of the village and the countryside, and of the sweet-talking lies of that uneducated boor.

### How the Master and his kinsfolk arrived at the village, and how the countryman pretended not to see or recognise them:

When, after a month, they arrived in that region—themselves without food and their animals without fodder—
See how the countryman, out of evil intent, still heaps upon them calamities both small and great.

❦ **600.** He keeps his face hidden from them by day, afraid that they might look longingly toward his orchard.
It is better that a face like that, which is made entirely of hypocrisy and spite, should be hidden from the eyes of the faithful <note>original: "Moslems"</note>.
There are some faces where demons gather like gnats, acting as his guards.
When you look upon such a face, those demons fall upon you; either do not look at that face at all, or if you do, do not smile at it.
Concerning such a wicked, sinful face, God has said in the Holy Scripture:
> “Verily, We will drag him by the forelock.” <note>A reference to the Quran (96:15), describing the humiliating punishment of the arrogant.</note>

❦ **605.** When the Master's party had made inquiries and finally found the countryman's house, they hurried to the door like close relatives.
Thereupon, the people inside his house bolted the door. At this spiteful act, the Master nearly lost his mind with rage.
But indeed, it was no time for anger: when you have already fallen into the pit, what is the use of being enraged?
For five days they remained at his door, passing the nights in the freezing cold and the days in the scorching blaze of the sun.
Their staying there was not out of forgetfulness or stupidity; rather, it was out of desperate necessity and because they lacked even a single donkey to carry them away.

❦ **610.** Out of necessity, the good are often forced to associate with the vile; out of extreme hunger, even a lion will eat a rotting carcass.
The Master would see the countryman and greet him, saying, “I am so-and-so, this is my name.”
The countryman replied, “Perhaps; but how should I know who you are? Are you a person of ill-repute or an honest gentleman?”
“This moment,” the Master said, “is like the Resurrection <note>The Day of Judgment, a time of such terror that all social and family ties are broken.</note>, since a brother has come only *to flee from his brother*.” <note>A reference to Quran 80:34, describing how even the closest relatives will turn away from each other on the Day of Judgment.</note>
He tried to explain to the countryman, saying, “I am the one from whose table you ate many kinds of food <term>viands: an old-fashioned word for choice food or a feast.</term>.

❦ **615.** On such and such a day, I bought that merchandise for you. Every secret that goes beyond the two who share it becomes public knowledge.
The people all heard the secret of our friendship; usually, when the throat has tasted someone's generosity, the face shows some sign of shame.”
The countryman would say to him, “Why are you talking nonsense? I know neither you, nor your name, nor where you live.”
On the fifth night, there began such a storm of clouds and rain that the very sky seemed astonished by its own downpour.
When the suffering became unbearable <note>literally: "when the knife reached the bone"</note>, the Master knocked at the door, crying, “Call your master!”

<summary>This page describes the Master’s arrival at the countryman’s village, where he is met with cold indifference and a total denial of their former friendship. The scene serves as a cautionary tale about the fickleness of worldly relationships and the cruelty of those who forget past kindnesses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the ordeal of the Master (the Khwája) and his family. Having been rejected by the countryman they once helped, they are now forced to beg for the humblest shelter during a storm. ❦**620.** When at last, after a hundred urgent pleas, the countryman came to the door, he asked,
“Why, what is the matter, my dear sir?”
The Master replied, “I give up those claims to your gratitude; I renounce the reward I was imagining.
I have suffered five years of pain, and for five days my miserable soul has been trapped in this heat and blaze.”
A single injustice from one's own kin, friends, or family weighs as heavily as three hundred thousand wrongs from others.
This is because the sufferer did not anticipate such cruelty and injustice; his soul was accustomed only to kindness and faithfulness from that person.

❦**625.** Whatever tribulation or bitter grief men face, know for certain that it feels so heavy because it is contrary to what they are used to.
The Master said further, “O you, the sun of whose love is now setting, if you have shed my blood, I forgive you.
On this night of rain, just give us a small corner to shelter in, so that on the Day of Resurrection you may receive a <term>viaticum: Originally a Latin term for provisions given to a traveler; here it refers to the spiritual merit or 'provisions' earned for the afterlife through good deeds.</term>.”
“There is a small hut,” the countryman replied, “which belongs to the keeper of the vineyard. He stays there to watch for wolves.
He keeps a bow and arrow in his hand because of the wolf, so that he may shoot if a fierce one appears.”

❦**630.** “If you will perform that service, the place is yours; if not, have the kindness to look for another place.”
The Master said, “I will perform a hundred services, only give us the place and put that bow and arrow in my hand.
I will not sleep; I will guard the vines. If the wolf shows its head, I will fire the arrow at it.
For God’s sake, do not abandon me tonight, you double-hearted hypocrite, with the rainwater pouring from above and the mud clinging from below!”
A corner was cleared, and the Master went there with his family; it was a narrow place with no room even to turn around.

❦**635.** They were huddled on top of one another like locusts, crowded into the corner of that cavernous hut out of terror of the flood.
Throughout the night, the entire night, they all cried out, “O God, we deserve this! This is our own doing!”
This is the fate deserved by one who associates with the wicked, or who shows their own worth for the sake of those who have none.
This is the fate deserved by those who, out of empty desire, stop honoring the very dust beneath the feet of the noble.
Licking the dust and the walls of the <term>elect: The spiritually pure or chosen ones.</term> is better for you than the company of the vulgar and all their vineyards and rose gardens.

❦**640.** Becoming a slave to a person with an enlightened heart is better for you than walking upon the heads of kings.
From the kings of this earth, you will gain nothing but the empty noise of a drum, O you who travel so many roads.
In comparison to the Spirit, even the city-dwellers are like bandits. And who is the "countryman"? He is the fool who possesses no spiritual gifts <note>Rumi uses "townsman" and "countryman" as metaphors for the spiritually enlightened and the spiritually ignorant, rather than literal geography.</note>.
This is the fate deserved by the one who, hearing the cry of a <term>ghoul: A desert demon in folklore that mimics the voices of friends to lead travelers off the path to their deaths.</term>, chose to follow it without using their reason.
When regret has moved from the core of the heart to the <term>pericardium: The membrane surrounding the heart; here it signifies that the regret has become an all-encompassing, externalized pain.</term>, it is no longer of any use to confess one's sins.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Master (the Khwája) who, after being forced into the rain by his ungrateful former friend, is now tasked with guarding the vineyard against wolves. The scene shifts from physical hardship to a sharp moral critique of hypocrisy and selective perception.</meta>

**645** (Holding) the bow and arrow in his hand, he searched for the wolf all night, pacing to and fro.
The wolf, indeed, was given power over him like sparks of fire: he was hunting the wolf (outside), unaware of the wolf (within his own soul). <note>Rumi frequently uses the "wolf" as a metaphor for the *nafs*—the lower, carnal self or ego—suggesting that the Master's external struggle mirrors an internal one.</note>
Every gnat and every flea had become like a wolf, inflicting wounds upon them in that desolate place.
There was no chance even to drive away those gnats, for they lived in dread of an attack from the defiant wolf,
Lest the wolf should cause some harm, and then the countryman would vent his rage by tearing out the **Master’s** <note>original: "Khwája"</note> beard.

**650** In this way, they remained gnashing their teeth until midnight; their very souls were rising from their bellies to their lips.
Suddenly, the silhouette of a solitary wolf appeared, raising its head from the top of a small hill.
The **Master** released the arrow from the <term>thumbstall: A protective leather ring worn on the thumb by archers to help draw and release the bowstring.</term> and shot the animal, so that it tumbled to the ground.
As it fell, the animal broke wind: at this, the countryman let out a wail and beat his hands together,
Crying, “O cruel wretch, that is my young donkey!” “No,” the Master replied, “this is that devilish wolf.

**655** The signs of a wolf are plain to see; its very shape reveals its wolfish nature.”
“No!” the countryman cried, “I recognize the sound of the wind that escaped its backside as clearly as I know water from wine.
You have killed my young donkey in the meadows—may you never be free from your sorrow!”
“Look more closely,” the Master replied; “it is night, and at night physical objects are hidden from the observer.
The night causes many things to appear wrong or altered from their true state; not everyone has the power to see clearly in the dark.

**660.** Moreover, it is night, there are clouds, and it is raining heavily: these three layers of darkness lead to great mistakes.”
The countryman said, “To me, it is as clear as bright day: I know it is the wind of my young donkey.
Among twenty such sounds, I would recognize that one, just as a traveler knows his own provisions for the road.”
The **Master** leapt up, and losing all patience, he seized the countryman by his collar,
Crying, “O fool and thief, you have shown your hypocrisy! You must have eaten both <term>beng: An intoxicant made from henbane or hemp, often used by those seeking a false or drugged state of spiritual ecstasy.</term> and opium together!

**665.** In the midst of three layers of darkness, you claim to recognize the flatulence of a donkey, yet how do you not recognize *me*, you dizzy-headed fool?
He who can identify a colt at midnight—how could he fail to recognize his own companion of ten years?”
You are only pretending to be a <term>gnostic: From the Arabic 'ārif, referring to one who possesses direct, mystical knowledge of God.</term> lost in divine love; you are merely throwing dust in the eyes of my generosity,
Saying, “I have no awareness even of myself; in my heart, there is no room for anything but God.
I have no memory of what I ate yesterday; this heart finds joy in nothing but spiritual bewilderment.

**670.** I am both sane and driven mad by God; remember this, and since I am in such a state of selflessness, hold me blameless.”
The religious Law counts the one who eats carrion—that is to say, one who drinks <note>original: "date-wine"</note>—among those who are excused.
The drunkard and the one who consumes intoxicants are not held to their vows of divorce or trade; they are like children, absolved and set free.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical reflection following the story of the Master and the countryman. In the previous scene, a countryman recognized his own donkey—which the Master had accidentally shot—simply by the sound of it breaking wind. Rumi now uses this absurd incident as a metaphor to critique hypocrites who claim spiritual "intoxication" but are still tied to their worldly egos.</meta>

The intoxication that arises from the scent of the unique King—a hundred vats of wine never wrought *that* ecstasy in the head or the brain. <note>The "King" here refers to God; Rumi frequently contrasts the spiritual "wine" of divine love with literal, worldly alcohol.</note> 
To such a man, then, how could the obligations of the Law still apply? The horse of his reason has fallen and can no longer move.

❦ **675.** Who in the world would place a heavy load upon a young donkey? Who would try to teach Persian to <term>Bú Murra: Literally "Father of Bitterness," an Arabic nickname for Iblis (Satan), implying he is beyond instruction.</term>?
When lameness occurs, the burden is removed: as God has said, *There is no blame upon the blind.* <note>original: "Laysa ‘ala ’l-a‘má haraj"—a reference to the Quran (24:61), which exempts the disabled from certain physical duties, here applied to spiritual "blindness" to the self.</note>
I have become blind to myself but see through the grace of God; therefore, I am released from all obligations, both small and great."

In this way, God exposes hypocrisy; in this way, He catches the prey that has tried to flee.
There are hundreds of thousands of trials, my friend, for anyone who claims, “I am the master of the Gate.”

When a common man pretends to be a master tailor, the king will throw a piece of fine satin before him,

❦ **685.** Saying, “Cut this into a wide <term>baghaltáq: A specific type of military undervest or tunic worn under armor.</term>.” Under the pressure of that test, the pretender's true nature is revealed.

Even if a coward puts on a coat of mail, as soon as he feels a blow, he will surrender like a captive.
How could one truly intoxicated with God be brought back to his senses by a soft breeze? A man drunk on God would not even wake up at the blast of the Resurrection trumpet!
The wine of God is real, not a sham; you, however, have only been drinking buttermilk—nothing but buttermilk!

❦ **690.** You have tried to pass yourself off as a <note>Junayd (d. 910) and Báyazíd (d. 848) were two of the most famous early Sufi masters, representing the "sober" and "intoxicated" paths of mysticism.</note> Junayd or a Báyazíd, saying, “Leave me be, for I cannot tell a hatchet from a key.”
O weaver of lies, how can you use hypocrisy to hide your inner depravity, your spiritual laziness, your greed, and your lust?
You pretend to be a <term>Mansúr-i Halláj: A famous mystic executed in 922; his name literally means "the wool-carder."</term> and set fire to the "cotton" of your friends, <note>Rumi plays on Halláj’s name; by claiming high spiritual states, the hypocrite "burns" the faith or resources of those around him.</note>

Oh, what a fool of a donkey is he who would believe a donkey like you, making himself blind and deaf just for your sake!

❦ **695.** Do not count yourself among the true travelers on the spiritual Way; you are merely a companion to those who defile it—stop talking such rubbish!
Flee from hypocrisy and run toward true Reason; how can the wings of a shadow fly to Heaven?
You have feigned to be a lover of God, but in truth, you have only been playing at love with a dark devil.

### *How a braggart greased his lips and mustache every morning with the skin of a fat sheep's tail and came amongst his companions, saying, "I have eaten such and such fine foods."*

❧ 735. For this is the witness to the truth of my words, and this is the token of my eating greasy and delicious food."

### **How Bal'am the son of Bá'úr felt secure because the Lord had tested him many times and he had come through them honorably.**

Bal'am the son of Bá'úr <note>A biblical and Quranic figure known for his great knowledge and prayers, who eventually fell into sin because of pride and greed.</note> and the accursed Iblís <note>The name for the Devil or Satan in Islamic tradition.</note> were both brought to shame during their final test. 
The boastful hypocrite, through his pretenses, desires to be seen as wealthy, yet his hungry belly curses his own mustache. 
The belly cries out: "Reveal what he is hiding! He has consumed me with the pangs of hunger: O God, expose him!"

❦ **750.** Every part of his body is his opponent, for he prattles on about the flowers of spring while his limbs are shivering in the cold of December. 
Vain talk drives away acts of kindness and tears the branch of pity from the trunk of the tree. 
Practice honesty, or else remain silent; only then can you witness true pity and enjoy it. 
That belly became the enemy of his mustache and secretly turned to prayer, 
Crying, "O God, expose this empty bragging of the lowly, so that the hearts of the noble may be moved to pity me."

❦ **755.** The belly's prayer was answered: the heat of its desperate need raised a signal flag. 
God has said, "Even if you are a sinner or an idolater, I will answer when you call to Me."

When the belly surrendered its fate to God, a cat arrived and snatched away the skin of that sheep's tail <note>The man used this fatty skin to grease his mustache every morning to trick people into thinking he had eaten a rich, fatty meal.</note>. 
They chased after the cat, but she escaped. The man's child, fearing a scolding, turned pale with fright.

❦ **760.** The little child ran into the middle of the company and accidentally stripped the boastful man of his reputation. 
The child said, "That sheep's tail you used every morning to grease your lips and mustache— 
The cat came and suddenly snatched it away! I ran as hard as I could, but it was no use." 
Those who were present laughed in astonishment, and their feelings of pity began to stir again. 
They invited him to eat and kept him well-fed; they sowed the seeds of true mercy in the soil of his life.

❦ **765.** Once he had tasted the fruits of honesty from the noble-hearted, he let go of his arrogance and became devoted to the truth.

### **Comparison of Pharaoh and his pretence of divinity to the jackal which pretended to be a peacock.**

### **Explanation of the scripture: "And thou wilt surely know them in the perversion of their speech."**

When you are buying clay pots, you test them, O buyer.
You tap the pot with your hand—why? So that you can recognize a cracked one by the sound it makes.
The sound of a cracked pot is distinct; the voice is like a <term>cháwúsh</term> <note>original: "cháwúsh" (a herald or beadle). The voice acts as a messenger that announces the inner state of a person.</note>: it runs out ahead of the person.

**795.** The voice comes forward to make the truth known: it defines the character, just as the verb reveals the meaning of the <term>masdar</term>. <note>original: "masdar" (the verbal noun or root). # **The Story of Harut and Marut and Their Boldness in Facing the Trial of God Most High**

We have spoken a little of this story before; but what can we truly tell? We can only share one part out of thousands.
I wished to speak of the spiritual truths contained within it, but until now, various obstacles have kept them untold.
Now, once again, a small portion of its vast meaning shall be shared—the description, as it were, of a single limb of the elephant. <note>An allusion to the famous parable of the blind men and the elephant, where each person perceives only a fragment of the whole truth.</note>

❦**800.** Listen to the tale of Harut and Marut, <note>Two angels mentioned in the Quran (2:102) who were sent to Babylon and tested with human desires.</note> O you to whose presence we are devoted slaves and servants.
They were intoxicated with the vision of God and with the wonders of the King’s "gradual temptation."
Such intoxication arises even from God's subtle testing, so you can imagine what ecstasies are produced by actually ascending to Him!
If the bait in His snare produced such drunkenness, what wonders must the table of His true bounty reveal!
They were drunken and felt freed from every noose; they were shouting cries of rapture like passionate lovers.

❦**805.** But in their path, there was an ambush and a trial; its mighty wind was strong enough to sweep a mountain away like straw.
This Divine trial was turning them upside down, but how could someone who is so intoxicated be aware of such things?
To a drunkard, the pit and the open field look the same; to him, a dungeon is as pleasant as a well-trodden path.
Consider the mountain goat that runs up the high peaks in search of harmless food:
While he grazes, he suddenly sees another trick played by the decree of Heaven.

❦**810.** He casts his gaze upon another mountain, and on that distant peak, he spots a she-goat.
Straightway his vision is clouded by desire; he leaps madly from his mountain toward the other.
To him, the distance seems as short and easy as running across the courtyard of a house.
Those thousands of ells <note>An old unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm.</note> are made to appear as only two, so that his mad infatuation will give him the impulse to leap.
As soon as he leaps, he falls into the abyss between the two pitiless mountains.

❦**815.** He had fled to the mountain to escape the hunters, but his very place of refuge shed his blood.
The hunters sit between the two mountains, waiting for this awesome decree of God to take effect.
The capture of the mountain goat is usually accomplished in this way; otherwise, it would be difficult, for he is agile, nimble, and quick to spot an enemy.
Even if a man were <term>Rustam</term> <note>The legendary hero of the Persian epic *Shahnameh*, symbolizing ultimate strength and masculinity.</note> with a mighty head and mustache, lust will certainly be the snare that catches his feet.
Cut yourself off, as I have, from the intoxication of lust; look at the frenzy of lust even in the camel!

❦**820.** Know, then, that this intoxication of lust in the physical world is a small thing compared to the intoxication of the angels.
The spiritual ecstasy of an angel makes human lust seem insignificant; why then would an angel show any leaning toward worldly desire?
It is because until you have tasted sweet water, the salty water of the world seems delicious—as sweet as the light in one's own eye.

He uses the metaphor of a mountain goat blinded by lust to illustrate how even the most agile and powerful beings can fall into a trap when their perception is distorted.</summary>

Just a single drop of the wine of Heaven is enough to snatch the soul away from the wine and the cupbearers of this world—

**825.** Those who have set their hearts on that celestial wine after only a single scent, and have shattered the jar of this worldly existence;—
Except, perhaps, for those who live in despair and are far from God, like those who lack faith and are already hidden in their graves.
Such people have lost all hope in both this life and the next; they have sown nothing but endless thorns.
This is why the angels Harut and Marut, <note>original: "Hárút and Márút"</note> in their state of spiritual intoxication, said: "Alas! If only we could rain down upon the earth like clouds;
We would spread justice, equity, devotion, and faithfulness across this land of wrongdoing."

**830.** They said this, even as the Divine Decree was warning them: "Stop! Many an unseen pitfall lies before your feet."
Take care! Do not run so boldly into the desert of sorrow. Beware of pushing blindly into a Place of Suffering <note>original: "Karbalá"; here used to signify a place of immense trial and tribulation, referencing the historical site of martyrdom.</note>,
For the feet of travelers can find no path through the hair and bones of those who have already perished there.
The entire road is covered in bones, hair, and sinews; many are the things that the sword of Divine Vengeance has reduced to nothing.
God has said that His servants—those who are supported by His help—walk upon the earth with quietness and humility.

**835.** How could a barefoot man enter a thicket of thorns without hesitating, reflecting, and moving with caution?
The Divine Decree was speaking these truths to them, but their ears were muffled by the veil of their own hotheadedness.
The eyes and ears of everyone are closed, except for those few who have escaped from the trap of their own "self."
Who but Divine Grace can truly open the eyes? Who but Divine Love can soothe the Wrath of God?
Truly, may no one in this world have to labor without God’s blessing to make it prosper! And God knows the right course best of all.

### ***The Story of Pharaoh's dream about the coming of Moses (peace be upon him) and how he plotted to protect himself from the predicted danger.***

**840.** Because Pharaoh’s efforts were not blessed by God, every stitch he made was actually an act of tearing things apart.
He had a thousand astrologers at his command, along with a countless number of dream-interpreters and magicians.
He was shown a dream of the coming of Moses, the one who would eventually destroy Pharaoh and his entire kingdom.
He asked his interpreters and astrologers, "How can the fulfillment of this dark vision and dream be prevented?"
They all replied to him, "We will devise a plan; we will waylay the birth of this child like bandits."

**845.** They waited until the night arrived when the conception of Moses was meant to take place. Pharaoh's advisors thought it best,
Early that day, to set up the King’s banquet and throne in the public square, <note>original: "maydán"; an open arena or public space used for ceremonies.</note>
Proclaiming, "Welcome, O people of Israel! The King calls for you to join him there."

## **How they summoned the Israelites to the public square, as a device to prevent the begetting of Moses, on whom be peace.**

**855.** “O captives, go ye to the square <note>original: "maydán"</note>, for there is hope for you of seeing Pharaoh and experiencing the generosity of the King of kings.”
When the Israelites heard the glad news, they were thirsting and longing exceedingly for that spectacle.
They swallowed the trick and hastened in that direction and made themselves ready for the promised unveiling.

### **Story.**

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the narrative focuses on the terrifying transformation of Moses’ staff into a dragon. With its breath, it sucked stone and iron into its jaws and visibly chewed the iron into small fragments.

**1105.** The gnashing of its teeth would break one's heart; even the souls of "black lions" <note>a metaphor for the bravest warriors</note> were distraught with terror.

That pure wine is the portion allotted to the **selfless** <note>those who have annihilated the ego</note>; since they are still with "themselves" (not freed from the ego), how could it be shown to them?
“With us, one must be a 'waking sleeper,' so that in the state of wakefulness, he may dream spiritual dreams.”

**1115.** Thoughts of created, worldly things are an enemy to this sweet, spiritual sleep: until one's worldly thoughts are asleep, the throat of the soul is shut.

The more perfect a person is in **worldly science** <note>original: "‘ulūm" — intellectual or academic learning</note>, the more backward he is in **Reality** <note>original: "haqīqat" — the inner spiritual truth</note> and the more forward he is only in outward appearance.
God has said, “Verily, to Him we are returning”; and the return is in the same way a herd of animals turns back and goes home.

**1120.** And the lame goat that was last is now in front: the return caused the faces of those who were frowning before to laugh.
How did this party (the prophets and saints) become "lame" and give up worldly glory to purchase what seemed like ignominy?
This party goes on the **pilgrimage** <note>the journey to the Divine Reality</note> with "broken legs," because there is a secret way that leads from narrowness to ease.
This company washed their hearts clean of **exoteric** <note>outward, literal, or intellectual</note> kinds of knowledge, because that knowledge does not know this Way.
To tread this Way, one needs a knowledge whose root is "Yonder" <note>in the Divine realm</note>, just as every branch is a guide back to its root.

**1125.** How should every wing be able to fly across the breadth of the Sea? Only **esoteric** <note>inward, mystical</note> knowledge will bear you to the Presence of God.
Why, then, should you teach a man the kind of knowledge that he actually needs to purify from his breast?
Therefore, do not seek to be in front in this world: be "lame" on this side, and you will be the leader at the moment of the return to God.

If you are not yet one of these "awakened hearts," then stay vigilant; be a seeker of the heart and remain in constant struggle against your lower self.

**1225.** But if your heart has truly been awakened, then sleep soundly: your spiritual eye is never absent from the seven heavens or the six directions. 
The Prophet said, "My eyes may slumber, but when does my heart ever fall into drowsiness?" 
The King is awake; even if the guard falls asleep, what does it matter? May my soul be sacrificed to those sleepers whose hearts see clearly! 
The description of a heart's wakefulness, O spiritual man, could not be contained in thousands of rhymed couplets. 
When the magicians saw him lying there outstretched, they began their preparations to steal the rod.

**1230.** The magicians quickly approached the rod, saying, "We must go behind him and then snatch it away." 
But as they moved a little closer, the rod began to shake.

### ***How the magicians from the cities assembled before Pharaoh and received robes of honour and laid their hands upon their breasts, pledging themselves to subdue his enemy, Moses, and saying, “Write this down against us.”***

<margin>**1245.**</margin>

<margin>**1250.**</margin>

The lineage of Moses continues until the Resurrection: the Light remains the same, even though the lamp has changed.

<margin>**1255.**</margin>

### ***The disagreement regarding the description and shape of the elephant***

The elephant was in a dark house; some people from India had brought it for exhibition. 

<margin>1260</margin>
In order to see it, many people were going, one by one, into that darkness. 
As seeing it with the eyes was impossible, each one was feeling it in the dark with the palm of his hand. 
The hand of one fell on its trunk: he said, "This creature is like a water-pipe." 
The hand of another touched its ear: to him it appeared to be like a fan. 
Since another handled its leg, he said, "I found the elephant's shape to be like a pillar." 

<margin>1265</margin>
Another laid his hand on its back: he said, "Truly, this elephant is like a throne." 
Similarly, whenever anyone heard a description of the elephant, he understood it only in respect to the part that he had touched. 
Because of their different points of view, their statements differed: one man called it "bent" <note>original: "dál" — the Persian letter D, which is shaped like a curve.</note>, another called it "straight" <note>original: "alif" — the Persian letter A, which is a straight vertical line.</note>. 
If there had been a candle in each one's hand, the disagreement would have vanished from their words. 
The eye of sense-perception is only like the palm of the hand: the palm does not have the power to reach the whole of the elephant.

<margin>1270</margin>
The eye of the Sea is one thing, and the foam is another; leave the foam and look with the eye of the Sea. 
Day and night, there is the movement of foam-flecks from the Sea: you see the foam, but not the Sea. How marvelous! 
We are dashing against each other like boats; our eyes are darkened, even though we are in the clear water. 
O you who have gone to sleep in the boat of the body, you have seen the water, but look now upon the *Water of the water* <note>The spiritual essence or Divine power that gives life and motion to the physical world.</note>. 
The water has a Water that is driving it; the spirit has a Spirit that is calling it.

<margin>1275</margin>
Where were Moses and Jesus when the Divine Sun was giving water to the sown field of all existing things? 
Where were Adam and Eve at the time when God fitted this string to the bow <note>A metaphor for the moment of Creation or the setting in motion of destiny.</note>? 
This manner of speech is also imperfect and limited; the speech that is truly complete is found only in the Beyond. 
If the saint speaks from that source, your foot will stumble; and if he speaks nothing of it, then alas for you! 
And if he speaks using the likeness of a material form, you will become stuck to that form, O youth.

<margin>1280</margin>
You are rooted in the earth like grass; you nod your head at every breath of wind, though you lack certainty. 
But you have no spiritual "foot" to make a departure, or to drag yourself out of this mud. 
How could you pull your foot away? Your very life is drawn from this mud; it is incredibly difficult for this earthly life of yours to set out on the Way to God. 
But when you receive life from God, O dependent soul, then you will become independent of the mud and you will rise upward.

Just as a nursing babe is eventually separated from its nurse to become an eater of solid food, so too must the seeker outgrow the comforts of the physical world.

<margin>1285</margin>
You are like a seed, held in bondage by the "milk" of the earth. Strive to wean yourself so you may partake of spiritual food.

<margin>1290</margin>

This world is like a tree, O noble ones, and we are like the half-ripened fruit upon its branches.

<margin>1295</margin>

When the "mouth" of the soul has been sweetened by spiritual felicity, the kingdoms of this world lose their appeal to Man.
To hold tight to the world and attach oneself strongly to it is a sign of unripeness. As long as you are a spiritual embryo, your only nourishment is "blood" <note>A metaphor for base, worldly sustenance compared to the "milk" of wisdom.</note>.
There is more to be said, but the Holy Spirit will tell you the rest of the story without my help.
Indeed, you will tell it to your own ear—neither I nor anyone else, for you are essentially "Me"—

<margin>1300</margin>

In your dreams, you hear things from yourself, yet you imagine that someone else has secretly told you these things in the dream.
You are not a single "you," my good friend; you are the entire sky and the deep sea.
Your Great Self, which is a hundred times more vast than your ego, is an ocean that can swallow a hundred "yous."
Truly, why do we even speak of "wakefulness" and "sleep"? I shall say no more, for God knows best what is right.

<margin>1305</margin>
Remain silent, so that you may hear from the Great Speakers that which cannot be put into words or explanations.
Remain silent, so that you may hear from the Sun of Truth that which was never written in a book or spoken in an address.
Remain silent, so that the Spirit may speak for you. In the Ark of Noah, give up your own swimming!
Do not be like Canaan <note>In Islamic tradition, Canaan was a son of Noah who refused to enter the Ark, believing he could save himself from the Flood by his own strength.</note>, who tried to swim on his own, saying, "I do not need the Ark of Noah, for he is my enemy."
Noah cried out, "My son, come and sit in your father’s Ark, so that you are not drowned in the Flood, O wretched one!"

### **_Reconciliation of these two Traditions: "To be satisfied with infidelity is an act of infidelity," and "If any one is not satisfied with My ordainment, let him seek a lord other than Me."_** <note>These are two famous "Hadiths" (sayings) in Islamic thought that seem to contradict: one forbids being happy with sin/unbelief, while the other demands total acceptance of God’s decree, which includes the existence of sin.</note>

Yesterday an inquirer put a question to me, because he was fond of disputation.
He said, “This Prophet uttered the deep saying, ‘To be satisfied with infidelity is an act of infidelity’; his words are conclusive like a seal.
Again, he said that the Moslem must be satisfied and acquiesce in every ordainment, must be satisfied.

❦**1365.** Is not infidelity and hypocrisy the ordainment of God? If I become satisfied with this infidelity, ’twill be opposition and disobedience to God,
And if I am not satisfied, that too will be detrimental: between these two alternatives, then, what means of escape is there for me?”
I said to him, “This infidelity is the *thing ordained*, it is not the *ordainment*; this infidelity is truly the effects of the ordainment. <note>Rumi solves the paradox by distinguishing between the "Decree" (the eternal knowledge/will of God) and the "Decreed" (the specific earthly outcome).</note>
Therefore know and distinguish, sire, the ordainment from the thing ordained, so that thy difficulty may be removed at once.
I acquiesce in infidelity in that respect that it is the ordainment of God, not in this respect that it is our contentiousness and wickedness.

❦**1370.** In respect of the ordainment, infidelity indeed is not infidelity. Do not call God ‘infidel,’ do not stand here.
Infidelity is ignorance, and the ordainment of infidelity is knowledge: how, pray, should <term>hilm</term> (forbearance) and <term>khilm</term> (anger) both be one and the same? <note>original: "hilm" (divine patience/forbearance) and "khilm" (here used to imply the human object or the state of being a 'friend' or 'enemy'). The poet contrasts the Divine attribute with the human condition.</note>
The ugliness of the script is not the ugliness of the artist; nay, ’tis an exhibition of the ugly by him.
The power and skill of the artist is that he can make both the ugly and the beautiful.”
If I develop the investigation of this subject methodically, so that question and answer become lengthy,

❦**1375.** The savour of Love's mystery will go from me, the form of piety will be deformed.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical shift from the story of Noah to the nature of spiritual experience. Previously, Noah accepted God’s will regardless of personal grief. A certain man, whose hair was of two colors, came in haste to a highly esteemed barber. 
He said, “Remove the white hairs from my beard, for I have chosen a new bride, O young man.” 
The barber cut off the entire beard and laid it all before him, saying, “You pick them out yourself, for I have more important business to attend to.” 
That “picking out” represents logical hair-splitting <note>original: "dialectic." Rumi uses this to mock those who waste time on minor theological or legalistic details instead of focusing on the heart of the matter.</note>, for true religious passion has no care for such trivial disputes.

❧**1380** A certain man slapped Zayd <note>A common name used in Islamic legal and philosophical examples, similar to "John Doe."</note> on the neck; Zayd at once rushed at him with a warlike purpose. 
The attacker said, “I will ask you a question first; answer me, and then you may strike me. 
I struck the back of your neck and there was the sound of a slap. I have a question about this in good faith: 
Was this sound caused by my hand, or by the back of your neck, O pride of the noble?” 
Zayd said, “Because of the pain, I have no time to stop and engage in such reflection and consideration. 

❧**1385.** You, who are without pain, may ponder on this; he who feels the pain has no room for such thoughts. Take heed!”

### Story

Amongst the Companions <note>The *Sahaba*, or the immediate followers of the Prophet Muhammad.</note> there was scarcely anyone who knew the Qur’án by heart, even though their souls had a great desire to memorize it. 
This was because, as the "kernel" <term>kernel: the inner, spiritual meaning of a text</term> had filled them and reached maturity, the "rinds" <term>rinds: the outward form or the literal words of the scripture</term> became very thin and burst. 
Similarly, when the meat of a walnut, pistachio, or almond fills the shell, the rind decreases. 
As knowledge—the kernel—increases, its rind decreases and vanishes, because the lover is entirely consumed by his Beloved.

❧**1390.** Since the state of being "Sought" <note>Referring to God as the Object of desire.</note> is the opposite of "seeking," the Revelation and the flashing of the Divine Light consume the prophet with a burning heat. 
When the Attributes of the Eternal have shone forth, then the mantle of temporality <note>The "mantle of temporality" refers to our temporary, physical existence in this world.</note> is burned away. 
In those days, anyone who knew even a quarter of the Qur’án by heart was greeted by the Companions with the words, “Great is he among us.” 
To combine the outward form with such a deep inner meaning is not possible, except for a mighty spiritual king. 
In such mystical intoxication as theirs, the strict observance of the letter of the law will not be there; or if it is, it is a miracle.

❧**1395.** To maintain humility while in a state of spiritual independence is to combine two opposites, like "round" and "long." 
Truly, a staff is loved by the blind; the inwardly blind man himself is like a chest full of the Qur’án. 
A certain man said, “In truth, the blind are chests full of the words of the Qur’án, of remembrance, and of warning.” 
Then again, a chest full of the Qur’án is better than a man who is like an empty chest in one's hand. 
And yet again, a chest that is empty of any load is better than a chest that is full of mice and snakes <note>Here, "mice and snakes" represent dark thoughts, vices, or malicious intentions.</note>.

❧**1400.** The sum of the matter is this: when a man has attained Union <note>The mystical state of *Fana*, where the individual self is lost in God.</note>, the go-between becomes worthless to him.

<summary>Through several parables, Rumi argues that intellectual theorizing and literal memorization of scripture are merely "rinds" that must eventually give way to the "kernel" of direct spiritual experience and Union with God.</summary>
<keywords>parables, logic vs. passion, the Qur'an, Companions of the Prophet, spiritual maturity, Divine Union, Zayd, inner meaning</keywords>

Following the previous parables about the "pain" of love making legalistic hair-splitting irrelevant, Rumi now uses the metaphor of a ladder and a love letter to show that once the Beloved (the Divine) is reached, the tools used to get there—including books and even certain spiritual "states"—become secondary.</meta>

Since you have reached the object of your search, O elegant one, the search for knowledge has now become a hindrance <note>Literally "evil" or "bad" in this context because it distracts from the goal already achieved.</note>.
Since you have climbed to the roofs of Heaven, it would be futile to seek a ladder.
After attaining happiness, the way that leads to happiness is worthless, except for the sake of helping and teaching others.
The shining mirror, which has become clear and perfect—it would be folly to apply a polisher to it.

❧**1405.** When you are seated happily beside the Sultan <note>A metaphor for God or the Perfect Master.</note> and are in his favor, it would be disgraceful to look for a letter or a messenger.

### ***Story of a lover being engrossed in reading and perusing a love-letter in the presence of his beloved, and how the beloved was displeased by it. It is shameful to seek proof in the presence of the one who is proved, and blameworthy to occupy oneself with external knowledge after having reached the one who is known.***

A certain man, when his beloved allowed him to sit beside her, produced a letter and read it to her.
In the letter were verses of praise and glory, lamentations of his wretchedness, and many humble entreaties.
The beloved said, "If this letter is for me, reading it at the moment we are meeting is a waste of your life.
I am here beside you, and you are reading a letter! This, at any rate, is not the mark of true lovers."

❧**1410.** He replied, "You are present here, but I am not yet feeling my pleasure fully.
The feelings I had for you last year are not here at this moment, even though I am united with you.
I have drunk cool water from this fountain; I have refreshed my eyes and heart with its water.
I still see the fountain, but the water is not there; perhaps some bandit has blocked the flow of my water."
She said, "Then I am not your beloved: I am in Bulghár <note>A region on the Volga, representing the far West.</note>, and the object of your desire is in Qutú <note>A city in East Turkestan, representing the far East. She is telling him that his heart and her presence are poles apart.</note>."

❧**1415.** "You are in love with me and also with a <term>state of feeling</term> <note>original: *hal*. In Sufism, this is a temporary spiritual mood or ecstasy granted by God.</note>; but you do not possess that state of feeling, O youth.
Therefore, I am not the entirety of what you seek; I am only a part of your quest at this moment.
I am only the house of your beloved, not the beloved herself; true love is for the gold, not for the coffer that holds it."
The real beloved is the One who is unique, who is your beginning and your end.
When you find Him, you will not wait for anything else; He is both the manifest world and the hidden mystery.

❧**1420.** He is the lord of all <term>states of feeling</term>, not dependent on any one state; the months and years are slaves to that Moon.
When He commands a "state," it obeys His order; when He wills, He turns physical bodies into pure spirit.
One who is stuck on the road is not at the journey's end; he will remain seated, waiting and seeking a "state."
But the hand of the perfect saint is the <term>elixir</term> <note>In alchemy, the substance that turns base metals into gold.</note> that transforms any state; if he moves his hand, the "copper" of the soul becomes intoxicated with him.
If He wills, even death becomes sweet; thorns and stings become narcissus and wild roses.

❧**1425.** He who is dependent on a "state" is still just a human being; at one moment he is made great by the state, and at another moment he declines.

<summary>This passage uses a story of a lover reading a letter to his beloved to argue that intellectual study and even temporary spiritual ecstasies (states) are merely tools. Once a seeker achieves true union with the Divine, these tools and fluctuating moods should be transcended in favor of the "Lord of States."</summary>
