<meta>This page continues the discourse on the transition from spiritual seeking to spiritual realization. Having previously explained that ladders and letters are useless once the goal is reached, Rumi now distinguishes between the "Sufi," who is still bound by the fluctuations of time and spiritual states, and the "Safi" (the Pure One), who has transcended them. This leads into a new narrative regarding the importance of the "Search" itself, illustrated by a man in the time of the Prophet David.</meta>

In likeness, the **Súfí** <term>Sufi: A mystic seeker on the path to God.</term> is "the son of the moment," <note>original: "ibn al-waqt". This refers to one who acts according to the spiritual requirements of the present instant.</note> but the pure one (**ṣáfí**) is unconcerned with "time" and "spiritual states."
Spiritual states are dependent on his decision and judgment; they are brought to life by his Messiah-like breath <note>A reference to the breath of Jesus, which in Islamic tradition could raise the dead; here, it refers to the spiritual power of the purified saint to revive hearts.</note>.
God says: "You are in love with your 'spiritual state,' you are not in love with Me; you are attached to Me only in the hope of experiencing that 'state.'"
He who at one moment is lacking and at another moment perfect is not the One who was worshipped by **Khalíl** <note>Khalíl: "The Friend," a title for the Prophet Abraham.</note>; he is like the celestial bodies that set and disappear.

**1430.** And he that is liable to sink—now being this and now being that—is not the true Beloved: "I love not those that set" <note>original: "Lā uḥibbu 'l-āfilīn" (Quran 6:76). This refers to Abraham’s realization that the sun, moon, and stars could not be God because they disappear.</note>.
He who is now pleasing and now unpleasing, at one time water and at another fire,
May be the dwelling-place of the Moon, but he is not the Moon itself; he may be the image of the Adored One, but he is not the consciousness of it.
The Súfí who seeks purity is "the son of the moment"; he has clasped "the moment" tightly as though it were his father.
But the pure one (**ṣáfí**) is plunged in the Light of the Glorious God; he is not the son of anyone, for he is free from the fluctuations of "times" and "states"—

**1435.** He is plunged in the Light which is unbegotten: the description *He neither begets nor is He begotten* <note>original: "Lam yalid wa lam yūlad" (Quran 112:3). A core definition of the Divine's eternal nature.</note> belongs to God alone.
Go and seek a love like this, if you are spiritually alive; otherwise, you remain a slave to the changing "time."
Do not look at your own ugly or beautiful form; look instead at Love and the object of your search.
Do not regard the fact that you are weak or infirm; look upon your high aspiration, O noble one.
In whatever state you find yourself, keep searching; O you with the dry lip, always be seeking the water,

**1440.** For that dry lip of yours provides the evidence that at last it will reach the springhead.
The dryness of the lip is a message from the water, saying: "This anxious search will certainly bring you to the water."
For this seeking is a blessed movement; this search is a killer of obstacles on the Way to God.
This search is the key to the things you seek; it is your army and the victory of your banners.
This search is like the rooster crowing, proclaiming that the dawn is near.

**1445.** Although you have no equipment, keep on seeking: equipment is not necessary on the Way of the Lord.
Whomever you see engaged in the search, O son, become his friend and bow before him,
For by being the neighbor of seekers, you yourself will become a seeker; and under the protection of the conquerors, you yourself will become a conqueror.
If an ant has sought to attain the rank of **Solomon**, do not look with contempt upon its quest.
Everything you possess of wealth or professional skill—was it not, at first, merely a quest and a thought?

### *Story of the person who, in the time of David (peace be upon him), used to pray night and day, crying, "Give me a lawful livelihood without any effort on my part."*

**1450.** In the time of the Prophet **David**, a certain man—in the presence of every wise man and every simpleton—
Used to always utter this prayer: "O God, bestow on me riches without any trouble!
Since Thou hast created me a lazybones, a receiver of blows, a slow mover, and a sluggard..."

<summary>Rumi distinguishes between the seeker (Sufi) and the realized saint (Safi), emphasizing that while the saint transcends time, the seeker must persevere in a relentless "Search." This transitions into the story of a man in David's time who prays for effortless sustenance, testing the boundaries of divine providence and human effort.</summary>

☙**1460.** "Since the infant has no foot to seek nourishment, its mother comes and pours the ration of milk upon it.

☙**1465.** "The way to get daily bread is through work, trouble, and fatigue; God has given everyone a handicraft and the capacity for seeking a livelihood:

☙**1470.** "When has anyone, from the time of Adam until now, had a melodious voice like an organ,

### ***How a cow ran into the house of him that was praying importunatey <note>Importunate prayer refers to the act of asking God persistently, almost to the point of annoyance, which Rumi suggests is a sign of deep devotion.</note>. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, has said, "God loves them that are importunate in prayer," because the actual asking of anything from God most High and the importunity itself is better for the petitioner than the thing which he is asking of Him.***

❦1485. Until suddenly one day, when he was uttering this prayer with moaning and sighs at morningtide,
Suddenly a cow ran into his house; she butted with her horns and broke the bolt and key.
The cow boldly jumped into the house; the man sprang forward and bound her legs.
Then he at once cut the throat of the cow without pause, without consideration, and without mercy.
After he had cut off her head, he went to the butcher, in order that he might quickly rip off her hide forthwith.

### ***The Poet's excusing himself and asking help.***

❦1490. O Thou that makest demands within me, like the embryo—since Thou art making a demand, make easy

Since Thou art demanding gold from an insolvent <note>One who is bankrupt or has no money.</note>, give him gold in secret, O rich King!

Poesy and homonymy <note>The use of words that sound the same but have different meanings, a common stylistic device in Persian poetry known as "tajnis."</note> and rhymes, O Knowing One, are the slaves of Thy Command from fear and dread,

1500. Since I am heedless of the glorification uttered by one who speaks, how should my heart know the glorification performed by that which is mute? <note>Rumi refers to the Islamic concept that all creation, even inanimate objects, praises God in a "silent" language.</note>

Every person can distinguish mercy from vengeance, whether they be wise, ignorant, or even wicked.

The rest hold only an opinion of these two qualities: they fly toward their nest with only a single wing.

### **_Explaining that Knowledge has two wings, and Opinion has only one: "Opinion is defective and curtailed in flight"; and a comparison illustrating opinion and certainty in knowledge._**

1510. Knowledge has two wings, while Opinion has only one wing: Opinion is defective and cut short in flight.
The one-winged bird soon falls headlong; then it flies up again for a few paces or a little more.
The bird of Opinion, falling and rising, goes on with its single wing in hope of reaching the nest.
But when he has been delivered from Opinion, Knowledge shows its face to him: that one-winged bird becomes two-winged and spreads his wings.
After that, he walks erect and straight, no longer falling on his face or suffering.

1515. He flies aloft with two wings, like the Archangel Gabriel, without opinion, without doubt, and without argument.
If the whole world should say to him, “You are on the Way of God and are following the right religion,”
He will not be made more fervent by their words: his solitary soul will not need their company.
And if they all should say to him, “You are astray; you think you are a mountain, but in reality you are a blade of straw,”
He will not fall into doubt because of their taunts, nor will he be grieved by their rejection.

1520. Indeed, if the seas and mountains should find speech and say to him, “You are joined with destruction,”
Not for a single moment will he fall into delusion or sickness because of the taunts of those who scoff.

### **_Parable of a man's being made spiritually ill by the empty conceit of being worshipped by the people and the pleas of those seeking his favor; and the following story of the Teacher._**

The boys in a certain school suffered from weariness and toil at the hands of their master.
They consulted together about how to stop his teaching, so that the teacher would be forced to let them go.

### *How Pharaoh was made (spiritually) ill by vain imagination arising from the people's reverence (for him).*

**1555.** The people's prostrating themselves—women, children, and men—smote the heart of Pharaoh and made him ill.
Every one's calling him lord and king made him so tattered (infamous) from a vain imagination,
That he dared to pretend to divinity: he became a dragon and would never be sated.
Imagination and opinion are the bane of the particular (discursive) reason, because its dwelling-place is in the darkness.
If there be a path half an <term>ell<note>A historical unit of measurement, often the length of a man's arm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note></term> wide on the ground, a man will walk safely without imagining;

**1560.** (But) if you walk on the top of a high wall, you will stagger even if its width be two ells;
Nay, through (the force of) imagination and from trembling of heart, you will be (on the point of) falling. Consider well and understand the fear that is due to imagination.

### *How the teacher was made ill by imagination.*

The master became unnerved by imagination and dread; he sprang up and began to drag his cloak along,
Angry with his wife and saying, “Her love is weak: I am in this state (of health), and she did not ask and inquire.
She did not even inform me about my colour: she intends to be freed from my disgrace.

**1565.** She has become intoxicated with her beauty and the display (of her charms) and is unaware that I have fallen from the roof, like a bowl.”
He came (home) and fiercely opened the door—the boys (were following) at the master's heels.
His wife said, “Is it well (with thee)? How hast thou come (so) soon? May no evil happen to thy goodly person!”
He said, “Are you blind? Look at my colour and appearance: (even) strangers are lamenting my affliction,

**1570.** His wife said, “O sir, there is nothing wrong with thee: ’tis (only) thy vain unreal imagination and opinion.”

'My wife has an evil design, for she is making arrangements to be alone.
She is getting me out of the house, she is plotting and cajoling for the purpose of some wickedness.'"
She prepared his bed, and the master fell down upon it: sighs and moans were arising from him.
The boys sat there, reciting their lesson with a hundred sorrows in secret,

❧1585. Thinking, "We have done all this and still we are prisoners: it was a bad building <note>a metaphor for a poorly devised plan</note>, and we are bad builders."

### *How for the second time the boys made the master imagine (that he was ill), saying that their recitation of the Qur’ān would increase his headache.*

The clever boy said, "O good fellows, recite the lesson and make your voices loud."
When they were reciting loudly, he said, "Boys, the noise we are making will do the master harm.
The master's headache will be increased by the noise: is it worth while that he should suffer pain for the sake of a few pence?"
The master said, "He is speaking the truth: depart. My headache is worse: go out of the house!"

### *How the boys escaped from school by this trick.*

❧1590. They bowed and said, "O honoured sir, may illness and danger be far from you!"
Then they bounded off to their homes, like birds in desire of grain.
Their mothers became angry with them and said, "A school-day and you at play!"
They offered excuses, every one of them, saying, "Stop, mother! This sin does not proceed from us and is not caused by our fault.
By the destiny of Heaven our master has become ill and sick and afflicted."

❧1595. The mothers said, "It is a trick and a lie: ye bring forward a hundred lies because of your greed for <term>buttermilk<note>original: "dugh," a savory yogurt-based drink; here used to represent the boys' desire for snacks and leisure rather than study.</note></term>."

<summary>The schoolboys' psychological trick succeeds as the master, now convinced of his illness, takes to his bed and dismisses the class. The boys escape to their homes, though they face skepticism and accusations of laziness from their mothers.</summary>

### *How the mothers of the boys went to visit the sick master.*

The next morning, the mothers arrived. They found the master in bed like a man gravely ill, perspiring under a heavy stack of blankets, his head bandaged and his face buried in the quilt.

**1600.** He was moaning softly. Upon seeing him, the women all began to cry out, "There is no power or strength except in God!" <note>original: "Lá hawl," a common Arabic phrase used to seek God's protection or express dismay at a misfortune.</note>
They said, "Master, we hope all will be well. This headache—by your soul, we were completely unaware of it."
He replied, "I also was unaware of it; it was those scoundrels—those sons of harlots—who made me realize it, mark you.
I did not notice it because I was so busy with my lectures, but all the while, such a severe malady was hidden within me."
When a man is earnestly occupied, he is blind to his own physical pain.

**1605.** It has become a famous tale how the women of Egypt lost their senses when they saw the beauty of Joseph <note>This refers to the story where women were so entranced by the beauty of the Prophet Joseph that they accidentally cut their own hands with knives while peeling fruit, feeling no pain at the time.</note>.
They cut their forearms to pieces, for the spirit was so distracted that it looked neither behind nor before.
Consider the brave man in battle: his hand or foot may be sliced by a sword’s blow,
yet he carries that same hand into the heat of combat, believing it is still whole.
Only later does he see the injury and realize how much blood he has lost without knowing it.

### *Explaining that the body is as a garment to the spirit, and that this bodily hand is the sleeve of the spirit's hand, and that this bodily foot is the shoe of the spirit's foot.*

**1610.** I mention this insensibility to pain so that you may know the body is like a garment.
Go, seek the wearer of the garment; do not simply kiss the fabric.
To the spirit, the knowledge of the Divine Oneness <term>Tawhid: the core Islamic concept of the absolute unity of God</term> is sweeter than the body; the spirit possesses hands and feet different from those you see.
In your dreams, you may see your spiritual hands and feet and their connection to your spiritual form; believe that vision to be a reality, do not think it is in vain.
You are such a being that you possess a spiritual body independent of your material one; therefore, do not fear the soul's departure from the physical body.

### *Story of the dervish <term>Dervish: a member of a Sufi Muslim religious order, often known for vows of poverty and austerity</term> who had secluded himself in the mountains, with an account of the sweetness of detachment from the world and seclusion and of entering upon this path, for God has said: "I am the companion of those who remember Me and the friend of those who take Me as their friend. If you are with everyone, you are without everyone when you are without Me; and if you are without everyone, you are with everyone when you are with Me."*

There was once a dervish dwelling in a mountain wilderness; solitude was his closest companion and his dearest friend.

**1615.** Because a refreshing breeze of Divine favor was blowing toward him from the Creator, he grew weary of the empty chatter of men and women.

Discern the outcome of an affair from its very beginning, so that you do not find yourself repenting on the Day of Judgement.

### **_How a goldsmith discerned the end of the affair and spoke in accordance with the end to one who wished to borrow his scales._**

A certain man came to a goldsmith and said, "Lend me your scales so that I may weigh some gold."

**1625.** The master goldsmith replied, "Go away, I do not have a sieve."
"Give me the scales!" the man replied. "Stop making such jokes."
The goldsmith said, "I have no broom in my shop."
"Enough, enough!" cried the man. "Leave these jests aside. Give me the scales I asked for; do not pretend to be deaf, and do not beat around the bush."
The goldsmith replied, "I heard what you said; I am not deaf. Do not think I am speaking nonsense.
I heard your request, but you are a shaky old man: your hand trembles and your body is bowed.

**1630.** Furthermore, that gold of yours consists of tiny, fine filings. Because your hand shakes, the fragments of gold will surely fall;
Then you will say, 'Sir, bring me a broom so I can search for my gold in the dust.'
Once you have swept the floor, you will have gathered dust along with the gold, and then you will say to me, 'O brave man, now I need a sieve.'
From the very beginning, I saw the entire process to its end. Now, go from here to another place—and farewell!"

### **_The rest of the Story of the ascetic of the mountain who had made a vow that he would not pluck any mountain fruit from the trees or shake the trees or tell any one to shake them, either plainly or in veiled terms, and that he would only eat what the wind might cause to fall from the trees._**

With eyes and ears wide open and the snare right in front, it flies toward the trap on its own wings.

### **_A comparison showing that the bonds and snares of Destiny, though outwardly invisible, are manifest in their effects._**

**1650.** You may see a nobleman’s son in a tattered cloak, bareheaded and fallen into affliction.
He is consumed with passion for some ne’er-do-well; he has sold his furniture and his properties.
His household is gone; he has become ill-famed and despised. He walks along like a shadow of misfortune, to the joy of his foes.
If he sees an ascetic, he will say, "O venerable sir, bestow a blessing on me for God’s sake,
For I have fallen into this ugly misfortune and have let wealth, gold, and happiness slip from my hand."

**1655.** "Give me a blessing, so that perhaps I shall be delivered from this woe and escape from this dark clay." <note>A metaphor for the physical body or the material world that weighs down the soul.</note>
He begs this prayer of high and low, crying, "Release me! Release me! Release me!"
Yet his hand is free and his foot is free; there is no chain, no guard standing over him, and no iron shackles.
From what chain are you seeking release, and from what imprisonment are you seeking to escape?
It is the hidden chain of fore-ordainment and destiny, which none but the elect spirit may behold.

**1660.** Though it is not visible, it lies in ambush; it is worse than any prison or chains of iron.
Because an ironsmith may break those iron bonds, and an excavator may even dig up the foundations of a prison;
But, O wonder, the ironsmiths of the world are powerless to shatter this heavy, hidden chain.

### ***How the dervish who had made the vow was reduced by hunger to plucking pears from the tree, and how God’s punishment arrived without delay.***

He spotted several pears on a branch; once again he acted with patience and restrained himself. 
But the wind came and lowered the end of the branch, allowing his carnal nature <term>nafs</term> <note>The 'nafs' represents the lower self or ego, the seat of worldly desires and impulses that the mystic seeks to master.</note> to prevail and eat that fruit.

When he plucked fruit from the pear tree, he became false to his promise. 
At that very instant, God’s chastisement arrived; it opened his eyes and "pulled his ear" as a warning.

### **The reason why the magicians of Pharaoh had courage to suffer the amputation of their hands and feet.**

Is it not a fact that the accursed Pharaoh threatened the magicians with punishment on this earth,
Saying, “I will cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, and then I will hang you; I will not let you escape punishment”? <note>original: "min khilāfin" (on opposite sides). This refers to the Quranic account where Pharaoh threatens the magicians who turned to Moses.</note>
He believed they were still trapped in the same illusions, terrors, and doubts as others,
Thinking they would be trembling and terrified by the empty threats of the <term>carnal soul</term> <note>The "nafs" or lower ego that prioritizes physical survival and comfort over spiritual truth.</note>.

**❧1725.** He did not realize that they had been set free and were now resting at the window of the heart’s light;
They had recognized the difference between their bodily shadows and their true selves, and they were joyful, alert, and full of spirit.
Even if the mortar of Fate were to crush them into dust a hundred times in this muddy world,
They would not fear what happens to the physical body, for they have seen the eternal Origin from which all things are composed.
This world is a dream—do not rely on mere opinion; if a hand is lost in a dream, no real harm is done.

**❧1730.** If in a dream a blade has cut off your head, when you wake, your head is still in its place and your life continues.
If in a dream you see yourself split into two halves, you are perfectly healthy when you rise, not ill at all.
The point is this: in dreams, it does no harm if the body is maimed or torn into two hundred pieces.
The Prophet <note>Referring to Muhammad, who is often quoted in Sufi literature as saying, "Humans are asleep; when they die, they awaken."</note> said of this world—which looks so solid—that it is merely a sleeper’s dream.
You have accepted this statement as a matter of tradition, but the <term>travellers</term> <note>A term for those actively walking the mystic path toward God.</note> have seen this truth with their own eyes, needing no one to tell them.”

### ***How the mule complained to the camel, saying, "I am often falling on my face, while you fall but seldom."***

The mule said to the camel, “O good friend, whether on the hills, in the valleys, or on the most difficult paths,
You never stumble onto your head but travel along happily. Meanwhile, I am constantly falling on my face, like someone who has lost their way.
At every moment I am tripping, whether the ground is dry or wet.
Explain the cause of this to me, so that I may know how I ought to live.”

1750. The camel replied, “My eyes are clearer than yours; furthermore, I am looking from a higher vantage point.
When I reach the top of a high hill, I look carefully toward the end of the mountain pass.
Then, God reveals to my sight all the highs and lows of the path ahead.
Because of this, I take every step with clear vision and am saved from stumbling and falling.
You, however, cannot see more than two or three steps in front of you; you see the bait, but you do not see the hidden pain of the trap. <note>The "bait" represents worldly pleasures, while the "trap" represents their spiritual consequences.</note>

1755. In your opinion, are the blind and the seeing equal in how they settle, how they rest, and how they travel?”
When God grants a soul to the embryo in the womb, He places within its nature the power to draw life-particles together.
By using food as a tool, the soul gathers these particles and weaves the "warp and woof" <note>The vertical and horizontal threads of a loom.</note> of its own body.
Until the age of forty, God makes the soul eager to gather these particles for the purpose of growth.

1760. The one who assembled all these specks of dust was the Divine Sun; He knows how to seize your bodily particles and draw them together again, even without the need for food.

### ***The story of Daqúqí and his miraculous gifts.***

1925. He walked upon the earth like the moon moves through the heavens: through him, the spirits of those wandering in the dark became enlightened.

1935. Because you are all parts of me.” Why, then, would you tear the part away from the Whole?
When a part is severed from the Whole, it becomes useless; when a limb is cut from the body, it becomes a lifeless thing.

And even if it seems to move, it has no foundation—even a freshly severed limb twitches for a moment.
If a part is severed and falls away from this spiritual Whole, the Whole itself does not suffer; it is the part that is diminished.

While he walked the road, he would say, “O God, make me a companion of Your elect.
O Lord, to those saints whom my heart already knows, I am a slave—one who has girt his loins and stands ready to serve them;
And as for those whom I do not yet know, O God of the soul, make them look kindly upon me, for I am currently barred from their company.”

1950. The Lord would say to him, “O noble prince, what passion is this? What unquenchable thirst is this?
You already possess My love: why are you seeking others? When God is with you, why do you seek mere men?”
He would answer, “O Lord, O Knower of secrets, You are the one who opened this path of supplication in my heart.
Even if I am seated in the middle of the Sea, I still set my desire on the water kept in the jug. <note>The "Sea" represents God's infinite presence, while the "water in the jug" represents God's presence as manifested through a human saint.</note>
I am like David: I have ninety-nine ewes of my own, and yet a longing for my neighbor's single ewe has risen within me.” <note>This refers to the Quranic and Biblical parable where the Prophet David is tested by his desire for more, here re-interpreted as a holy "greed" for spiritual growth.</note>

1955. Greed for Your love is glorious and grand; but greed for anything besides You is shameful and corrupt.”
The desire and "greed" of the spiritually strong leads to advancement, while the greed of the weak leads only to disgrace and loss of faith.
The greed of true men moves forward on the path, but the greed of the effeminate moves backward toward the world.
One type of greed belongs to the perfection of manliness, while the other is a cause for reproach and disgust.
Ah, there is a very hidden mystery here—the reason why even a prophet like Moses sets out to run toward a guide like Khizr. <note>Khizr (or Khidr) is a mysterious, immortal figure in Islamic tradition who guided Moses, representing "hidden" knowledge vs. Moses's "revealed" law.</note>

1960. By God, do not linger in any spiritual station you have already reached; crave more, like a man with dropsy who can never be satisfied with water. <note>Dropsy (edema) causes an insatiable thirst; Rumi uses it as a metaphor for the mystic's endless longing for the Divine.</note>
This Divine court is an Infinite Plane. Leave the "seat of honor" behind; the journey itself is your true seat of honor.

### *The mystery of Moses seeking Khizr, notwithstanding his perfection as a prophet and as one nigh unto God.*

Learn from the one who spoke with God, O noble sir! See what the <term>Kalím<gloss>The Interlocutor (Moses)</gloss></term> says in his longing!

### ***Resuming the story of Daquqi***

That man Daquqi—may God have mercy on him—said: "I traveled for a long time across the horizons of the world. ❦**1975.** Someone asked him, "Why do you walk barefoot over thorns and stones?" He replied, "I am bewildered, out of my mind, and consumed by love."

And for a heart that is drunk with the presence of the Sweetheart, what does it matter if the road is long or short, or where the next stop might be?

❦**1980.** The journey of the spirit exists outside the limits of Time and Space; our physical bodies only learned how to move by imitating the spirit.

As I walked toward a certain shore, the day grew late, and evening began to fall.

### ***The appearance of what seemed like seven candles in the direction of the shore***

The birds and the fish know the real meaning of the veiled style in which I have briefly praised this man of good name,

Where would an envious man even find a true concept of him? When has a parrot ever made its home in the nest of a mouse?

---

**2120.** That false idea of him arises in the mind of the envious man through his own trickery; it is like seeing a stray hair from one's own eyebrow and mistaking it for the new moon.
I sing your praise beyond the five <note>The five physical senses.</note> and the seven <note>The seven layers of heaven in traditional cosmology.</note>. Now write: "Daquqi stepped forward."

### ***How Daquqi went forward to lead that company in prayer.***

In the greetings and blessings addressed to the righteous saints, the praise of all the prophets is blended together.
These praises are all mixed and united; it is like many jugs being poured into a single basin.
Because the One who is praised is Himself no more than One, from this perspective, all religions are actually one single religion.

---

**2125.** Know that every act of praise ultimately belongs to the Light of God, and is only borrowed by created forms and people.
How could people praise anyone except Him who alone has the right to be praised? But they wander astray, following a hollow fantasy.
The Light of God, in relation to physical things, is like a light shining upon a wall—the wall is merely a focal point for these splendors.
Inevitably, when the reflection moves back toward its source, the one who was lost in the reflection loses sight of the moon and stops his praise;
Or again, a reflection of the moon might appear in a well, and a misguided person might put his head into the well to praise that very reflection.

---

**2130.** In truth, he is a worshiper of the moon, even though his ignorance has turned his face toward a mere reflection.
His praise belongs to the moon, not to that reflection, but his praise becomes a form of unfaith when the situation is misunderstood;
For that bold man was led astray by his own ruin: the moon was high above, while he imagined it was down below.

### *How the company followed the leadership of Daquqi.*

**2140.** <term>Daquqi</term> <note>A saintly protagonist in this section of the Masnavi who represents the perfect spiritual guide.</note> stepped forward to lead the prayer; the company of saints was like a fine silk robe, and he was its embroidered border.

**2145.** The body is like <term>Ishmael</term> <note>In Islamic tradition, the son of Abraham who was offered for sacrifice as an act of total submission to God.</note>, and the spirit is like Abraham; the spirit has pronounced the sacred praise over the noble body.

While performing the prayer, they were drawn up in ranks before God, as if at the Resurrection, engaged in self-examination and intimate prayers,
Standing in God’s presence and shedding tears, like one who rises erect from the grave on the Day of Judgment.
On that day, God will say: “What have you produced for Me during this time of respite I gave you?

**2150.** In what work have you spent your life? In what have you consumed your food and your strength?
Where have you dimmed the light of your eyes? Where have you exhausted your five senses?
You have spent your eyes, ears, intellect, and the pure heavenly substances of your soul—what have you purchased from the earth in return?
I gave you hands and feet like a spade and a pickaxe to till the soil of good deeds; when did they ever exist only for themselves?”
Even so, hundreds of thousands of such sorrowful messages come from the Lord.

**2155.** At the time of standing in prayer, these words return from God to the worshiper, and out of shame, the worshiper is bent double in <term>bowing</term> <note>original: "ruku," the physical genuflexion in prayer.</note>.
From shame, the power to remain standing is lost, and out of embarrassment, the worshiper recites a litany of glorification while their knees are bowed.

<meta>This page transitions from the physical descriptions of the ritual prayer (Salah) to a vivid narrative illustration of the human soul’s desperation. It compares the terror of the Day of Judgment to a ship caught in a violent storm, where even the most hardened skeptics are forced into a state of sincere, albeit late, devotion.</meta>

❧**2180.** There were night, clouds, and massive waves: a triple darkness, coupled with the terrifying fear of being swallowed by the whirlpool.
A fierce wind, like **Azrael** <note>original: "‘Azrá’íl," the Angel of Death who separates the soul from the body.</note>, arose; the waves tossed the ship violently to the left and right.
The people on board were faint with terror; cries of "woe!" broke out.
In their lamentation, they beat their heads with their hands: both the **unbeliever** and the **materialist** <note>original: "káfir" and "dahrí," the latter referring to those who believe the universe is eternal and governed only by time rather than a Creator.</note> became sincere in their devotion to God.
In that hour, they made heartfelt promises and vows to God with a hundred humble entreaties.

❧**2185.** Men whose faces, due to their perversity, had never once turned toward the **Qibla** <note>original: "qibla," the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca which Muslims face during prayer.</note> were now bare-headed in the posture of prostration.
They used to say, “This worship of God is useless”; but in that moment of despair, they saw a hundred lives—precious advantages—within it.
They had entirely abandoned all hope in their friends, their uncles, and even their fathers and mothers.
At that moment, the ascetic and the sinner alike became God-fearing, just as a wicked man does when he faces the agony of death.
There was no help for them on the left or the right; when all worldly strategies are dead, that is the time one invokes God.

❧**2190.** They were engaged in invocation, lamentation, and moaning; a black smoke of grief rose from them toward heaven.
Then the Devil cried out in enmity, “Away with you! Away! O worshippers of dogs, you shall be afflicted with two maladies!
Death and woe to you! O unbelievers and hypocrites, this will be your end:
That after your rescue, you will joyfully return to being your own private devils for the sake of your lusts,
And you will not remember that on the day of peril, God took your hands to save you from His own decree.”

❧**2195.** This cry was coming from the Devil, but such words are unheard except by a "good ear" <note>A spiritual ear capable of perceiving the unseen world.</note>.
**Mustafa** <note>original: "Mustafá," meaning 'The Chosen One,' a title for the Prophet Mohammed.</note>—the Pole, the Emperor, and the Sea of Purity—has told us truly:
That what the ignorant see only at the very end, the wise see from the first step.
If matters are hidden and secret at the beginning, the wise man sees them immediately, while the obstinate man sees them only when it is too late.
The beginning of an event is concealed, and both the wise and the ignorant will eventually see the outcome when it is manifest;

❧**2200.** But if you, O stubborn one, do not see the hidden event before it happens, when was it that the torrent of life swept away your prudence?
What is prudence? It is to "think ill" <note>original: "sū-i zann," a technical term for suspicion or expecting the worst, used here as a spiritual safeguard to avoid complacency.</note>. In this world, the prudent man expects to see a sudden calamity at every moment.

### ***The ideas of the prudent man.***

It is as when a lion has suddenly appeared, seized a man, and dragged him into the jungle.
At the moment of being carried off, what will that man think of? Consider this, and think of that same thing, O you who are learned in the **Religion of Mohammed**.
The lion of **Destiny** is dragging our souls—which are preoccupied with worldly business and trades—into the jungles of death.

❧**2205.** This situation is like the fact that people in this world fear poverty, even while they are plunged up to their throats in the "briny water" <note>A metaphor for the bitter, unsatisfying nature of worldly pursuits.</note> of material life.
If they were to fear the Creator of poverty instead, treasures would be opened to them upon the earth.

### ***Daquqi’s Humble Prayer and Intercession for the Rescue of the Ship***

When Daquqi witnessed that chaotic scene, his heart was moved with deep compassion and his tears flowed freely.
He prayed,
> “O Lord, do not look at their shameful deeds! Take their hands and help them, O Blessed King! <note>original: "sháh-i-khujasta," referring to God as the auspicious Sovereign.</note>
> 
> 2210. Bring them back safely and soundly to the shore, O You whose power reaches across both the ocean and the dry land!
> O Gracious One, O Merciful and Eternal One, overlook this wickedness committed by those who plot evil!
> O You who have given us a hundred eyes and ears for free, and who has granted us intellect and understanding without asking for a bribe;
> Who bestowed Your gifts before we even existed to deserve them, even though You have endured nothing but ingratitude and sin from us:
> O Almighty One, You are able to pardon our greatest sins in the secret of Your mercy.
> 
> 2215. We have consumed ourselves with **lust** <term>original: "shahwat," meaning carnal or worldly desire</term> and greed, and even this prayer we are saying is something we learned from You.
> We beg You, out of respect for the fact that You taught us how to call upon You, and for lighting the lamp of prayer in the midst of such deep darkness.”

This was the prayer flowing from his tongue at that moment, spoken with the tenderness of a devoted mother.
Tears streamed from his eyes, and that prayer ascended to Heaven while he was in a state of **spiritual ecstasy** <term>original: "bíchishí," literally "beside oneself" or unconscious of the physical world</term>.
That prayer offered in a state of self-loss is, in truth, something unique: that prayer does not come from the man himself; it is spoken by the Divine Judge.

2220. God Himself is the one making that prayer, since the speaker has reached the state of **annihilation** <term>original: "faná," the Sufi concept of the ego dissolving into the Divine presence</term>: the prayer and the answer to it are both from God.
The "middleman"—the created human personality—is no longer present: the body and the soul are both unaware that they are even making a plea.
The chosen servants of God are merciful and patient: they share the very nature of God when it comes to setting things right.
They are kind and seek no reward; they are helpers in times of dire trouble and on the day of heavy grief.
Listen! Seek out this company of saints, O you who suffer! Listen! Cherish them as a great prize before the next affliction arrives.

2225. Through the breath and prayer of that spiritual hero, the ship was saved. Yet, the people on the ship believed they were saved by their own efforts—
Supposing that perhaps, in the moment of terror, their own strength had skillfully shot an arrow into the bullseye of safety.
Foxes, when being hunted, are saved by their legs; yet the foolish foxes believe their safety comes from the beauty of their tails.
Therefore, they play fondly with their tails, thinking, “These save our lives when we are caught in the trap of calamity.”
O fox, protect your legs from being broken by stones; once you have no legs, what use is your tail, you bold-eyed creature?

2230. We are like those foxes, and the noble saints are like our legs: they rescue us from a hundred different kinds of divine justice.
Our clever tricks and strategies are like our tails: we play fondly with them, waving them to the left and the right.

### **How David (peace be upon him) ordered that retaliation should be taken on the murderer after his conviction.**

He ordered that <term>retaliation</term> <note>original: *qisas*; the legal principle of "life for a life"</note> be carried out with that very same knife the man had used. How could any human trickery hide a person from the knowledge of God? Although God’s mercy grants many kindnesses and delays punishment, when a sinner goes beyond all bounds, God exposes him. 

Blood does not remain hidden; the desire to investigate and solve a mystery is planted by God in every heart. The urge to uncover the truth, prompted by the Lord of Judgment, springs up in the conscience of everyone.

❧ **2490.** People began to ask, “How did this happen to him? What was his fate? Where did he end up?”—just as a sown seed eventually shoots up from the soil. Those constant questions, the pricking of the public conscience, and the relentless investigations were all the "stirring" of the murdered man’s blood seeking justice.

When the mystery of the murderer’s case was finally revealed, David’s miracles became twice as clear to the people. All the people came with their heads bared in humility and prostrated themselves on the earth, saying: “We have all been like those born blind, even though we have seen a hundred kinds of marvels from you!”

❧ **2495.** “The very stones spoke to you openly,” they cried, “saying, ‘Take me for Saul’s campaign against <term>Goliath</term>!’ <note>In both the Bible and the Quran, David famously defeats the giant Goliath with a sling and stones.</note> You went out with only three pebbles and a sling and routed a hundred thousand men. Your pebbles shattered into a hundred thousand pieces, and each one found its mark. 

Iron became soft as wax in your hand when you were taught the craft of making coats of mail. Even the mountains became your grateful companions; they sing the <term>Psalms</term> <note>original: *Zabur*; the holy book revealed to David</note> along with you, like students following a master of recitation.”

❧ **2500.** “Hundreds of thousands of spiritual eyes were opened by your breath and made ready to see the <term>Unseen</term> <note>the spiritual realm hidden from the physical senses</note>. This miracle is greater than all others because it lasts: you bestow a life that endures forever!”

Indeed, this is the essence of all miracles: that they should give everlasting life to those who are spiritually dead. The wicked man was executed, but an entire world of people was brought to life; everyone became a devoted servant of God once more.

### **Explaining that Man’s fleshly soul is in the position of the murderer who had become a claimant on account of the cow; that the slayer of the cow is the intellect; and that David represents God or the Spiritual Master (Shaykh). By means of their strength, it is possible to kill the wicked ego and be enriched with spiritual sustenance that requires no hard labor.**

Kill your <term>fleshly soul</term> <note>original: *nafs*; the ego or lower self that drives selfish desires</note> and bring the world to spiritual life. This ego has "killed" its true master—your spirit; now, make it your slave.

<summary>David executes the murderer, sparking a public realization of David's many miracles and his role as a spiritual life-giver. Rumi then pivots to the allegorical meaning: the murderer is the ego (nafs) which must be "killed" by the intellect to achieve spiritual freedom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the external judgment of the murderer in the story of David to the internal, spiritual interpretation of the "cow." The text shifts from the historical narrative to a metaphorical teaching on the soul, the intellect, and the nature of divine miracles.</meta>

❦ **2505.** Listen! Your carnal soul <note>original: *nafs*; the lower, ego-driven self</note> is like the man who claimed the cow: it has set itself up as a master, though it is actually a thief. The true slayer of this "cow" is your <term>intellect</term> <note>original: *'aql*; specifically the rational or spiritual soul that seeks God</note>. Do not be offended by the slayer of this cow, which is merely your physical form. 

The intellect is currently a captive and begs God for "daily bread won without toil"—the spiritual bounty served on a heavenly tray. What does this effortless bread depend upon? It depends on killing the "cow," for the carnal soul is the source of all evil. 

The carnal soul cries out, “How could you kill my cow?”—it says this because the "cow" of the carnal soul is the outward, material form of the body.

❦ **2510.** Thus, the intellect (the rightful master’s son) is left destitute, while the carnal soul (the murderer) has become the leader and master. 

Do you know the nature of this "bread won without toil"? It is the nourishment of spirits and the sustenance of the prophets. But it requires the sacrifice of the cow. Know that the spiritual treasure is found within that sacrifice, O you who dig in dark corners!

“Last night I ate something,” I might say; otherwise, I would have handed the reins of this explanation over to your understanding. But saying “I ate something” is just an idle story; in truth, everything that happens comes from the secret chamber of Divine Destiny.

❦ **2515.** Why have we fixed our eyes on secondary causes <note>The physical laws and material reasons we see in the world</note>, when those with spiritual vision have shown us how to look toward the Beloved? Beyond these secondary causes, there are primary, Divine causes. Do not look only at the physical means; let your gaze fall upon the Creator of those means.

The prophets came specifically to cut the cords of secondary causes. They threw their miracles against the very stars of heaven. Without physical means, they parted the sea; without sowing seeds, they found heaps of grain. By their spiritual work, sand was turned into flour, and coarse goat’s hair became silk as it was pulled from the hide.

❦ **2520.** The entire Qur’an is concerned with this: the breaking of secondary causes. Its theme is the glory of the spiritually poor and the destruction of the arrogant, like <term>Abu Lahab</term> <note>A relative of the Prophet Muhammad who became a symbol of fierce opposition to spiritual truth</note>.

Think of how a small swift drops two or three pebbles and shatters the mighty army of Abyssinia <note>A reference to the "Year of the Elephant," when a bird (the Ababil) miraculously defeated an invading army</note>. The pebble of a bird flying high lays low a massive elephant, leaving it riddled with holes.

God said: “Strike the murdered man with the tail of the sacrificed cow, so that he may come back to life in his shroud.” At that touch, the man whose throat was cut sprang up from his place and demanded justice from the one who shed his blood.

❦ **2525.** In this same way, from the beginning of the Qur’an to the end, the message is about abandoning your reliance on material causes and means. And now, we leave that subject.

This mystery cannot be explained by a meddlesome, purely logical intellect. Perform your service to God so that the truth may become clear to you. The philosopher is a prisoner to things he can perceive with his mind; but the pure saint is the one who rides as a prince upon the "Intellect of intellects."

This "Intellect of intellects" is your kernel <note>the essence or soul</note>, while your everyday intellect is merely the husk. The bellies of animals are always seeking husks. He who seeks the essence has a hundred loathings for the outer shell. To the righteous saints, only the kernel is truly lawful.

<summary>Rumi interprets the story of the cow as a metaphor for the struggle between the intellect and the carnal soul, explaining that spiritual miracles and true sustenance require the sacrifice of the ego's material attachments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual interpretation of the "Story of the Cow" from the previous section. Having established that the "cow" represents the carnal soul (ego), the text now contrasts human rational thought with Divine Certainty and discusses the necessity of a spiritual guide to overcome the ego’s deceptions.</meta>

**2530.** When the human intellect <note>original: *'aql*; here referring to the individual, rational mind</note>—which is merely the outer husk—offers a hundred pieces of evidence, how could the Universal Intellect <note>The Divine Mind or Logos that governs the cosmos</note> take a single step without having absolute, intuitive certainty?
The individual intellect fills entire books with black ink; but the Intellect of intellects <note>The source of all wisdom</note> keeps the entire universe filled with light from the Moon of Reality.
It is free from the limitations of "black and white" <note>Referring both to ink on paper and the world of dualities/opposites</note>: the light of its moon rises and shines directly upon the heart and soul.
If these "black and white" writings have any power or value, it is only because they reflect the Night of Power <note>original: *Laylat al-Qadr*; the night the Qur'an was first revealed, signifying a moment of intense divine grace</note> that shone forth like a star.
The value of a scroll or a purse comes from the gold within it; without the gold, the scroll and the purse are worthless and discarded.

**2535.** Just as the worth of the body is derived from the soul, the worth of the soul itself is derived from the radiance of the Soul of souls <note>A poetic title for God, the animating force behind the spirit</note>.
If the soul could truly be alive without that divine radiance, would God have ever called the unbelievers "dead"?
Come, speak, my soul! For the <term>Logos</term> <note>original: *nutq*; the creative Word or Speech of God</note> is digging a channel so that the water of wisdom may reach the generations that come after us.
Although every generation has its own messenger who brings the Word of God, the sayings of those who came before remain helpful and illuminating.
Is it not true, O thankful one, that the Pentateuch <note>original: *Tawrat*; the Torah</note>, the Gospel <note>original: *Injil*</note>, and the Psalms <note>original: *Zabur*</note> have all borne witness to the truth of the *Qur’an*?

**2540.** Seek a spiritual livelihood that is won without physical toil and without human reckoning, so that the Archangel Gabriel may bring you apples from Paradise;
Better yet, seek a livelihood directly from the Lord of Paradise, without the headache of a gardener or the labor of sowing seeds.
Since the true nourishment in that spiritual bread is a gift from God, He can give you that benefit directly, without needing the "husk" of physical matter to deliver it.
The true flavor is hidden; the outward form of the bread is merely like a tablecloth. The "bread without a tablecloth" is the special portion reserved for the saints.
How will you ever gain this spiritual livelihood, despite all your effort and searching, except through the justice of the <term>Shaykh</term> <note>A spiritual master or elder</note> who acts as your "David"? <note>Referring to King David's role as a judge in the story mentioned in the previous pages</note>

**2545.** When the fleshly soul <note>original: *nafs*; the lower ego or carnal self</note> sees that your steps are joined with those of the <term>Shaykh</term>, it will become submissive to you whether it wants to or not.
In our story, the owner of the cow only became submissive when he was made aware of the inspired words of David.
The intellect can only prevail over your "currish" fleshly soul during its hunt for spiritual truth when the <term>Shaykh</term> is its helper.
The fleshly soul is a dragon with a hundredfold strength and cunning; the face of the <term>Shaykh</term> is the emerald <note>According to ancient lore, the sight of a pure emerald would blind a dragon or snake</note> that plucks out the dragon's eye.
If you wish to humble the owner of the "cows" <note>the ego's material desires</note>, O stubborn man, drive him in that direction as you would drive a pack-animal!

**2550.** When a person approaches a saint who is near to God, their boastful tongue—though it be a hundred yards long—is suddenly shortened.
The ego has a hundred tongues, and each of those tongues speaks a hundred languages; its fraud and guile are beyond description.
The one claiming the cow—the fleshly soul—is incredibly eloquent and brings forward hundreds of thousands of false excuses.
It can deceive everyone in the city except for the King; it cannot ambush the wise and sagacious King.
The fleshly soul may have the praise of God on its tongue and the *Qur’an* in its right hand, but in its sleeve, it hides a dagger and a sword.

He warns that the carnal soul is a deceptive "dragon" that uses religious outwardness to hide its inner malice, and can only be subdued through spiritual authority.</summary>

**2555.** Do not trust its recitation of the **Holy Scripture** <note>original: *Qur’an*</note> and its hypocritical displays of piety; do not make yourself its confidant or its companion. 
It will lead you to the water tank to perform the **ritual washing** <note>original: *wudu*; the purification before prayer</note>, only to cast you into the depths of the water. 
The intellect is filled with light and seeks what is good; why then does the dark **fleshly soul** <note>original: *nafs*; the lower self or ego that demands gratification</note> prevail over it? 
It prevails because the soul is at home here, while your intellect is a stranger; even a dog is as fierce as a lion when standing at its own door. 
Wait until the true lions return to the jungle; then you will see these blind dogs realize their own weakness.

**2560.** The common people of the city do not recognize the deceits of the fleshly soul and the body; it cannot be subdued except by divine inspiration within the heart. 
Everyone who shares its lower nature becomes its friend—except, of course, the **David** <note>The Prophet David is often invoked as a symbol of the perfect spiritual guide who can "soften iron" (the heart)</note> who serves as your **Spiritual Master** <note>original: *Shaykh*</note>. 
For he has been transformed, and whoever God has settled in the dwelling of the heart is no longer of the same nature as the physical body. 
All other people are made weak by the spiritual traps lying in ambush within them; it is certain that weakness seeks out the company of weakness. 
Every worthless person pretends to be a "David"; and everyone who lacks **discernment** <note>The spiritual ability to distinguish truth from falsehood</note> clings to them.

**2565.** Such a person hears the call of a bird from a hunter and, like a foolish bird, flies straight toward that sound. 
He cannot distinguish reality from imitation; he is lost. Come, flee from such a man, even if he appears to be spiritual. 
To him, what has grown naturally and what has been artificially tied on look exactly the same; though he may claim to have **intuitive certainty** <note>original: *yaqin*; absolute spiritual knowledge</note>, he is actually lost in deep doubt. 
Even if such a person is clever in worldly matters, if he lacks this spiritual discernment, he is a fool. 
Listen: flee from him as a deer flees from a lion! Do not rush toward him so boldly, O wise one!

### ***How Jesus, on whom be peace, fled to the top of a mountain to escape from the fools.***

**2570.** **Jesus** <note>original: *‘Isa*</note>, the son of Mary, was seen fleeing toward a mountain; you would have thought a lion was trying to shed his blood. 
A man ran after him and called out, “Is everything well? No one is chasing you; why do you flee like a bird?” 
But Jesus kept running with such haste that he did not even answer the man. 
The man continued the pursuit for the distance of a field or two, then called out to Jesus with great earnestness, 
Saying, “For the sake of God’s pleasure, stop for a moment! I am confused by your flight.

**2575.** From whom are you running in this direction, O noble one? There is no lion behind you, no enemy, and there is no visible fear or danger.” 
Jesus replied, “I am fleeing from the fool. Go away! I am saving myself. Do not hinder me!” 
“But,” the man said, “are you not the **Messiah** <note>The "Anointed One" capable of performing miracles</note> by whom the blind and the deaf are healed?” 
Jesus answered, “Indeed, I am.” The man asked, “Are you not that King in whom the mysteries of the **Hidden Realm** <note>original: *‘alam-i ghayb*; the spiritual world beyond physical perception</note> reside?”

<summary>This passage warns against the deceptions of the ego and false spiritual leaders, introducing a parable where Jesus flees from a fool to demonstrate that spiritual ignorance is a more dangerous "disease" than physical ailments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the famous narrative of Jesus fleeing from a fool. Having previously established the dangers of the lower self (nafs), the text now explains why spiritual miracles fail to cure the "disease" of folly, concluding with the introduction to the parable of the people of Sabá.</meta>

(I do this so that) when you recite those spells over a dead man, he springs up rejoicing, like a lion that has caught its prey.”

2580. Jesus said, “Yes, I am he.” The other asked, “Are you not the one who fashions living birds out of clay, O beautiful one?”
He replied, “Yes.” The other said, “Then, O **Pure Spirit**, you can do whatever you wish. Of whom could you possibly be afraid?
With such miraculous evidence, who in the world would not be one of the devoted servants to you?”
Jesus said, “By the holy **Essence** <note>The inner reality or 'Being' of God (Dhat)</note> of God, the Maker of the body and the Creator of the soul in eternity;
By the sanctity of the pure Essence and His Attributes, for whose sake the collar of Heaven is torn open—

2585. I swear that the spells and the **Most Great Name** <note>original: *Ism al-A’zam*; a secret, supreme name of God which, in Islamic tradition, allows the speaker to perform miracles</note> which I pronounced over the deaf and the blind produced good results.
I pronounced them over the stony mountain: it was split apart and tore its mantle down to its very center.
I pronounced them over a corpse: it came to life. I pronounced them over non-existence: it became existence.
I pronounced them lovingly over the heart of the fool hundreds of thousands of times, and there was no cure for his folly.
He became like hard rock and did not change from that disposition; he became like sand from which no harvest can grow.”

2590. The other asked, “What is the reason that the **Name of God** succeeded there, while it had no benefit here?
That physical infirmity is a disease, and this folly is also a disease: why did the Name not become a cure for this, since it cured the other?”
Jesus said, “The disease of folly is the result of the **Wrath of God**; physical disease and blindness are not the result of Divine Wrath—they are a **probation** <note>A spiritual trial or test (ibtilá) meant to refine the soul</note>.
Probation is a disease that brings Divine Mercy in its wake; folly is a disease that brings Divine Rejection.
That which is branded upon the fool, God has **sealed** <note>A reference to the Qur'anic concept of God 'sealing' the hearts of those who remain willfully ignorant</note>: no hand can apply a remedy to it.”

2595. Flee from the foolish, seeing that even Jesus fled from them! How much blood has been shed by the companionship of fools!
Just as the air slowly absorbs water, the fool steals away religion from you.
He steals away your spiritual heat and gives you coldness, like someone who puts a stone under your seat.
The flight of Jesus was not caused by fear—for he is safe from any mischief—it was for the purpose of teaching others.
Even if intense frost filled the world from end to end, what harm could it do to the radiant sun?

### ***The story of the people of Sabá and their folly, and how the admonition of the prophets produces no effect upon the foolish.***

2600. I am reminded of the story of the people of **Sabá** <note>The ancient kingdom of Sheba in Yemen, used here as a parable for a society that turned from gratitude to ruin</note>—how their balmy breeze was turned into a pestilence by the words of the foolish.
That kingdom of Sabá resembles the great, legendary city which you may hear of from children in their tales.
Children relate tales, but in their stories many a mystery and moral lesson is enfolded.

(Though) in (their) tales they say (many) ridiculous things, (yet) in all ruined places do thou ever seek the treasure. <note>A recurring Sufi motif: truth and spiritual wealth are often hidden in "ruined" or humble places, just as God is said to dwell in "broken hearts."</note>
(Once) there was a city very huge and great, but its size was the size of a saucer, no more (than that).

❦**2605.** (It was) very huge and very broad and very long, ever so big, as big as an onion.
The people of ten cities were assembled within it, but the whole (amounted to) three fellows with unwashed (dirty) faces.
Within it there were numberless people and folk, but the whole of them (amounted to) three beggarly fools.
The soul that has not made haste towards the **Beloved** <note>The "Beloved" refers to God or the spiritual Guide; Rumi suggests that without this orientation, the soul remains incomplete.</note>— (even) if it is thousands, (yet) it is (only) half a body.

❦**2620.** A dried-up dead fowl, and its bones through being pecked at by crows had become bare like threads.
They were eating thereof as a lion (eats) of his prey: each of them (became) surfeited, like an elephant, with eating it.
All the three ate thereof and grew exceedingly fat: they became like three very great and big elephants,
In such wise that each young man, because of fatness, was too stout to be contained in the world.
Notwithstanding such bigness and seven stout limbs, they sprang forth through a chink in the door and departed.

❦**2625.** The way of **creaturely death** <note>The physical process of dying common to all living beings.</note> is an invisible way: it comes not into sight: ‘tis a marvellous place of exit.
Lo, the **caravans** <note>A metaphor for the endless generations of souls passing from this life to the next.</note> are following one after another through this chink which is hidden (from view) in the door.
If you look on the door for that chink, you will not find it: (it is) extremely unapparent, though (there are) so many processions through it.

### ***Explaining (what is signified by) the far-sighted blind man, the deaf man who is sharp of hearing, and the naked man with the long skirts.***

<summary>Rumi uses a surreal parable of three companions—blind to God but keen for trifles, deaf to truth but sharp for gossip, and naked but fearful for their "skirts"—to illustrate the delusions of the worldly ego. Their eventual escape through a hidden chink serves as a metaphor for the mystery of death and the transition to the unseen world.</summary>

Know that **Hope** is the deaf man who has often heard of our dying, but has not heard of his own death or considered his own passing. <note>In Sufi psychology, "long hope" (tul al-amal) is the delusion that one has endless time, leading to the neglect of spiritual preparation.</note>
The blind man is **Greed**: he sees other people's faults, hair by hair, and gossips about them from street to street.

**2630.** But his blind eyes do not perceive even a single mote of his own faults, even though he is a professional fault-finder.
The naked man is afraid that his "skirt" will be cut off—but how could anyone cut the hem of a man who is already naked? <note>The "skirt" or "hem" represents a person's worldly status, honor, or possessions. Rumi mocks the man who has no spiritual merit yet remains terrified of losing his social standing.</note>
The worldly man is destitute and terrified; he possesses nothing of eternal value, yet he lives in constant dread of thieves.
Bare he came into this world and naked he leaves it, and all the while his heart is bleeding with anxiety because of the "thief." <note>The "thief" represents anything that might take away worldly goods, including time, taxes, or competitors.</note>
At the hour of death, when a hundred lamentations are being made around him, his spirit finally begins to laugh at its own former fears.

**2635.** At that moment, the rich man realizes he has no true gold; the clever man, too, realizes he is utterly devoid of real talent.
It is like a child whose lap is filled with **potsherds**; he trembles for them as if he were a master of great riches. <note>Potsherds are broken pieces of ceramic or pottery. Rumi uses this to show how adults value worldly objects that are, in the eyes of the enlightened, worthless junk.</note>
If you take a piece away, he begins to weep; and if you give the piece back to him, he begins to laugh.
Since the child is not endowed with true knowledge, his weeping and laughter are of no real importance.
Because the powerful man regarded what was only a "loan" as his own property, he spent his life quivering with anxiety for that false wealth.

**2640.** He dreams that he possesses wealth and fears the thief who might carry off his sack of gold.
When **Death** pulls his ear and startles him awake from his slumber, he falls to mocking his own previous fears.
Such is the trembling of these learned scholars who possess only the intelligence and knowledge of this material world.
Regarding these "accomplished" and "intelligent" men, God said in the *Qur'án*: *They do not know*. <note>Original: "Lā ya‘lamūn." This phrase appears frequently in the Qur'an (e.g., 6:37, 7:187) to describe those who are experts in worldly life but ignorant of the Hereafter.</note>
Each of them is afraid of someone stealing his time; he fancies that he possesses a great store of knowledge.

**2645.** He says, "They are wasting my time," but in truth, he has no time that is profitable for his soul.
He says, "The people have taken me away from my work," but his soul is actually plunged in idleness up to the throat.
Like the naked man, he is frightened and says, "I am trailing a long skirt; how shall I save my hem from their clutches?"
He knows a hundred thousand superfluous details connected to the various sciences, yet that unjust man does not know his own soul.
He knows the special properties of every chemical substance, but in explaining his own <term>Substance</term> (essence), he is as ignorant as a donkey. <note>"Substance" (jawhar) here refers to the eternal, spiritual core of a human being as opposed to the "accidents" of the physical body.</note>

**2650.** He says, "I know what is <term>permissible</term> and what is <term>unpermissible</term>." But you do not even know if you yourself are permissible or unpermissible. <note>He refers to the study of *Halal* (permitted) and *Haram* (forbidden) in Islamic Law. Rumi argues that legalistic knowledge is useless if one has not determined if their own soul is acceptable to God.</note>
You know this legal thing and that illegal thing, but are *you* legal or illegal? Consider this well!
You know the market value of every article of merchandise; but if you do not know the value of your own self, it is pure folly.

Rumi argues that focusing on external faults, worldly wealth, or academic trivia is a distraction from the only essential knowledge: the value and state of one's own soul.</summary>

<meta>Following the description of the "Three Companions" (Deafness/Hope, Blindness/Greed, and Nakedness/Destitution), Rumi continues his critique of those who focus on external knowledge while neglecting the state of their own souls. This page transitions from the psychological profile of the "naked man" to a historical-parabolic account of the people of Sabá (Sheba) to illustrate how material abundance without spiritual gratitude leads to ruin.</meta>

You have become familiar with the fortunate and inauspicious stars; yet you do not look to see whether you yourself are fortunate or spiritually foul and ill-favored. This—and only this—is the soul of all the sciences: that you should know who you shall be on the Day of Judgment.

❧ **2655.** You are acquainted with the <term>usúl (fundamentals)</term> <note>The *usul* refers to the foundational principles of Islamic jurisprudence and theology.</note> of religion, but look upon your own <term>asl (essence)</term> <note>The word *asl* means "root" or "origin"; Rumi is playing on the word *usul* (the plural of *asl*) to suggest that one's own character is the true "root" of religion.</note> and see whether it is good. Your own essential nature is more important for you than those two formal fundamentals; you must know your own essence, O great man.

### *Description of the luxuriance of the city of the Sabaeans and their ingratitude.*

Their essential nature was corrupt: those inhabitants of Sabá <note>Sabá, or Sheba, was an ancient kingdom in modern-day Yemen, famously mentioned in the Quran and the Bible for its wealth and eventual destruction.</note> were recoiling from the means that lead to meeting with God. Yet, He gave them so many estates, orchards, and meadowlands on both the left hand and the right, intended for their leisure and diversion. Because the fruit was falling to the ground in such abundance, there was no room for anyone to pass on the road.

❧ **2660.** The scattered bounty of fruit would block the way; the traveler would stand in amazement at such plenty. In their groves, simply by the dropping of the fruit, a basket carried on the head would be filled without any effort. The breeze would scatter the fruit, rather than any human hand; by that fruit, a multitude of skirts would be filled. Huge clusters, hanging low, would brush against the head and face of the wayfarer. Because gold was so plentiful, even a bath-stoker <note>A *hammami*, or bath-stoker, held one of the lowliest jobs in medieval society, working in the soot and heat of the furnace. His wearing a golden belt signifies extreme, inverted social wealth.</note> might have tied a golden belt around his waist.

❧ **2665.** The dogs would trample fine buns underfoot; even the desert wolf would suffer from indigestion because of the rich food. Both town and village had become safe from robbers and predators; the goat felt no fear even in the presence of the fierce wolf. If I were to explain all the blessings bestowed upon these people—blessings which increased day by day—it would hinder me from speaking of more important matters. The prophets brought the Divine command to the Sabaeans, saying: "Therefore, be righteous."

### *How the prophets came from God to admonish the people of Sabá.*

Thirteen prophets came there; all of them were ready to guide those who had lost the way,

❧ **2670.** Saying, "Come, the benefits have increased—where is the thanksgiving? If the steed of gratitude has lain down, set it in motion. In the view of reason, it is necessary to give thanks to the Benefactor; otherwise, the door of everlasting wrath will be opened. Listen, behold the loving-kindness of God! Would anyone but God do this—be content with a single act of thanks for such immense benefits? He bestows a head and asks for only one bow in return; He bestows feet and asks for only one moment of sitting in devotion." But the people replied, "A <term>ghoul</term> <note>In folklore, a desert spirit that leads travelers off the path; here it represents a spiritual distraction or delusion.</note> has carried off our gratitude. We have become weary of giving thanks and receiving benefits.

❧ **2675.** We have become so disgusted by this bounty that neither piety nor sin pleases us anymore."

<summary>Rumi argues that self-knowledge is the most vital science, using the story of the Sabaeans (Sheba) to illustrate how extreme material wealth and a lack of gratitude lead to spiritual boredom and the rejection of divine guidance.</summary>

“We do not desire these benefits or orchards; we do not desire the means for enjoyment or leisure.”

The prophets replied, “In your hearts is a malady that has produced a <term>canker</term> <note>A 'canker' refers to a persistent, spreading sore or a source of corruption; here, it signifies a spiritual rot that prevents one from feeling gratitude.</note> in your ability to acknowledge your obligations. Because of this, every benefit is turned entirely into a disease. How can food provide strength to someone who is already sick? O persistent sinner, think of how many sweet things have come to you, yet they all lost their sweetness and their purity became clouded!”

❧ **2680.** “You have become an enemy to these sweetnesses: whatever you lay your hand upon becomes bitter. Anyone who truly became your close companion or friend soon became despicable and lowly in your eyes; and yet, anyone who is actually a stranger to you seems, in your opinion, very grand and worthy of respect. This false opinion is also an effect produced by your sickness—its poison infects everyone you associate with. You must quickly remove that malady, for as long as you have that disease, even sugar will seem like filth.”

❧ **2685.** “Every sweet thing that comes to you turns bitter. If the <term>Water of Life</term> <note>original: "Āb-i Hayāt." In Persian mythology, this is a legendary spring located in the Land of Darkness that grants immortality to whoever drinks from it.</note> were to arrive, it would turn into fire in your presence. That morbid quality is the <term>elixir</term> <note>original: "iksīr." While an elixir usually turns lead to gold, Rumi uses it here ironically to describe a substance that turns life into death.</note> of death and woe: because of it, your spiritual life is eventually turned into death. There was many a food by which your spirit was once revived, but when it entered your body, it became foul. There is many a dear person you once hunted with charms; yet when they became your ‘prey,’ they became cheap in your eyes. When friendship between two intellects arises from true sincerity, their devotion increases every moment;”

❧ **2690.** “(But) know for certain that the friendship between one <term>carnal soul</term> <note>original: "nafs." The *nafs* is the lower self or ego that is driven by animalistic desires and impulses.</note> and another base soul is diminished every moment, because the carnal soul hovers around disease and quickly corrupts any friendship. If you do not wish your friend to turn away from you tomorrow, choose a friendship with the intelligent and with the intellect. Inasmuch as you are sick from the <term>simoom</term> <note>original: "samūm." A scorching, suffocating, and often poisonous desert wind.</note> of the carnal soul, you act as the instrument for infecting everything you touch with disease. If you take a jewel, it becomes a common stone; if you receive kindness of heart, it turns into hatred;”

❧ **2695.** “And if you hear a fine, original saying, once you have grasped it, it becomes tasteless and crude to you—

> ‘I have heard this many times; it has grown old. Tell me something else besides this, O trustworthy friend.’

Suppose that something else, fresh and new, is said to you; by tomorrow, you will again be bored and repelled by it. Remove the disease! When the disease is eradicated, every old tale will become new to you, so that the old story will bring forth new leaves—the old tale will cause a hundred clusters of flowers to blossom even from a ditch.”

❧ **2700.** “We are the spiritual physicians, the disciples of God: the <term>Red Sea</term> <note>original: "Bahr-i Qulzum." This refers to the miraculous parting of the sea for Moses, symbolizing the power of those aligned with the Divine.</note> beheld us and was split open. Those natural physicians who treat the body are different, for they look into the heart only by feeling the pulse. We look directly into the heart without any intermediary, for through our <term>clairvoyance</term> <note>original: "nazar" or "basīrat." This refers to spiritual insight or the "eye of the heart" that sees beyond physical appearances.</note> we stand upon a high <term>belvedere</term>.” <note>A 'belvedere' is an architectural structure, like a turret or gallery, built specifically to provide a grand, elevated view.</note>

<summary>The Prophets explain that the people's unhappiness stems from a spiritual sickness (the carnal soul) that corrupts all beauty and friendship. They identify themselves as spiritual physicians who can see into the heart to heal this internal rot.</summary>
