“Those others are physicians who prescribe food and fruit; through them, the animal soul remains strong. We, however, are physicians of deeds and words: we are inspired by the rays of light from the <term>Divine Majesty</term> <note>original: "Jalāl." This refers to the awe-inspiring and powerful aspect of God's presence.</note>.

**2705.** We are given the insight to know that a specific deed will benefit you, while another will cut you off from the Way. We know that certain words will lead you toward grace, while others will only bring you anguish. To those other physicians, a sample of urine provides evidence of health or sickness, but our evidence is the inspiration of the Almighty.

We do not desire a fee from anyone; our reward comes from a Holy Place. Listen! Come here for the incurable disease! We, each of us, are a medicine for the spiritually sick.”

### How the people of Sabá demanded miracles from the prophets.

**2710.** The people replied, 
> “O you company of impostors! Where is the proof of your knowledge of medicine or your usefulness?
Since you are in bondage to the same sleep and food as we are—pasturing in this same country—since you are trapped by this water and earth, how can you possibly be hunters of the <term>Simurgh</term> <note>original: "Sīmurgh." A benevolent, mythical bird in Persian mythology, often used in Sufi poetry to represent the Divine or the soaring human soul.</note> of the heart?
It is only the love of power and dominion that induces a man to count himself among the prophets. We will not let such vain boasts and lies enter our ears and fall into your deception.”

**2715.** The prophets replied, 
> “This disbelief arises from your own malady: the original blindness of your hearts is the screen that prevents you from seeing the truth.
You have heard our call, yet you do not see this jewel in our hands. This jewel is a test for the people: we move it before their eyes.
Whosoever asks, ‘Where is the evidence?’ proves by his own words that he does not see the jewel and is a slave to blindness.”

Imagine a sun that could speak and said, 
> “Arise! The day has dawned; jump up and do not argue!”

**2720.** And imagine if you replied, 
> “O Sun, where is the evidence?” 
It would say to you, 
> “O blind one, pray to God to give you an eye.”

If anyone searches for a lamp in the middle of a bright day, the very act of searching announces his blindness. And if you cannot see the daylight, but have only formed an opinion that it is dawn and you are behind a veil, do not announce your blindness with these words; stay silent and wait for Divine grace. To ask “Where is the day?” in the middle of the day is only to expose your own condition, O seeker of the day.

**2725.** Patience and silence attract Divine mercy, whereas demanding a sign is a sign of your own weakness. Accept the command to <term>be silent</term> <note>original: "Ansitū" (Arabic). A reference to the Quranic injunction to listen in silence to the divine word.</note> so that the reward for your silence may reach your soul from the Beloved.

If you do not wish to suffer a relapse in the presence of this Physician, throw down your <term>gold</term> <note>original: "zar."</note> and your <term>head</term> <note>original: "sar."</note> <note>In Sufi poetry, "throwing down one's head" signifies the surrender of the ego and intellectual pride.</note>, O man of understanding. Sell your unnecessary talk and buy the sacrifice of life, the sacrifice of status, and the sacrifice of gold. Do this so that the grace of <term>Him</term> <note>original: "Hū." A common Sufi term for God, literally meaning "He."</note> may praise you, and even Heaven will envy your high estate.”

**2730.** When you show regard for the hearts of the physicians <note>The "physicians" here are the prophets, who offer healing for the soul rather than the body.</note>, you will see your true selves and become ashamed of your conduct.
It is not within the power of created beings to remove this spiritual blindness, but your act of honoring these physicians is a sign of Divine guidance.

### ***How the people doubted the prophets.***

The people said, “All this is nothing but fraud and deceit. Why would God make a representative out of <term>Zayd or Bakr</term>? <note>original: "Zayd and Bakr." These are common names used in Arabic and Persian literature as placeholders for "any ordinary person," similar to "John Doe" or "everyman."</note>
Every king’s messenger must be of the same kind as the king himself. What comparison can there be between water and clay and the Creator of the heavens?

**2735.** Have we eaten ass’s brains <note>A Persian idiom meaning to be foolish or to have lost one's mind.</note> that we, like you, should believe a tiny gnat could be the confidant of the <term>Humá</term>? <note>original: "humá." A legendary bird of Persian myth that lives in the high heavens and never touches the ground; it represents the highest spiritual authority and royalty.</note>
Where is a gnat compared to the <term>Humá</term>? Where is the earth compared to God? What relation does a speck of dust have to the sun in the sky?
What kind of resemblance or connection is this? How could such a thing even enter a rational mind or brain?”

### ***The story of the hares who sent one of their own as an ambassador to the elephant, telling him, 'I come to you as the envoy of the Moon in heaven to warn you to stay away from this spring,' as told in the Book of Kalila and Dimna.***

“This claim of yours resembles the story of a certain hare who said, ‘I am the ambassador of the Moon and the Moon's companion.’
For all the wild animals were in misery because a herd of elephants had settled beside a clear spring;

**2740.** They were all deprived of water and kept away from the spring by fear. Since their physical strength was less than the elephants’, they devised a plan.
From the mountain top, an old hare cried out to the elephants on the first night of the new moon:
‘Come on the fourteenth night, O King Elephant, so that you may find the proof of my words within the spring itself.
O King Elephant, I am an ambassador in your presence. Stop! Ambassadors should not be subjected to imprisonment, violence, or anger.
The Moon says: "O elephants, leave! This spring is mine; turn away from it.

**2745.** And if you do not leave, I will strike you blind. I have declared the wrong you are doing and am no longer responsible for what happens if you continue to trespass.
Leave this spring and depart, so that you may be safe from the blows of the Moon's sword."
Indeed, the proof of my truthfulness is this: the Moon reflected in the spring will be disturbed the moment the water-craving elephant touches it.
Come and be present on the appointed night, O King Elephant, so that you may see the proof of this claim within the spring.’
When fifteen nights of the month had passed, the King Elephant came to drink from the spring.

**2750.** When the elephant put his trunk into the water that night, the surface was disturbed, and the reflection of the Moon appeared to tremble in distress.”

### ***How the prophets answered their sneers and uttered parables unto them.***

Oh, alas that in the case of your disease the remedy has become for you the poison of soul-wringing Divine vengeance. <note>The prophets lament that their message, intended to heal, is instead causing the listeners to harden their hearts further, leading to spiritual ruin.</note>

❧**2755.** This lamp of spiritual admonition has increased the darkness of that diseased eye, since God has set over it the veil of wrath.
What dominion shall we crave from you? For our dominion is greater than the sky."
What glory should the sea of pearls acquire from the ship—especially a ship that has been filled with dung? <note>The prophets argue that they do not need the validation or wealth of the people, as their spiritual "sea" is far more vast than the "filthy" material world.</note>

❧**2760.** The devilish eye showed—or rather, saw—his Adam's spring as winter: it moved in the direction where its original home was.
Oh, many a fortune that comes now and then to the unfortunate one, and he turns away from it!
Oh, many a beloved who comes unbeknown to an ill-starred one, and he knows not how to make love!
This that misleads the eye is our original damnation, and this that turns the heart from seeing the truth is our evil destiny.
Since to you the idol of stone has become an object of adoration, the curse of God and blindness have overshadowed you.

❧**2765.** When your stone is a fitting partner for God, how are not intellect and spirit fitting confidants of God? <note>The prophets point out the hypocrisy: the people worship inanimate stones as gods, yet refuse to believe that a living, breathing human can be a messenger of God.</note>
The dead gnat has become the consort of the <term>humá</term> <note>original: "humá." A legendary bird of Persian myth that represents royalty and spiritual grace; it is said that its shadow brings good fortune.</note>: how then is the living one not fit to be the confidant of the King?
Or, maybe, it is because the dead one is fashioned by you, whereas the living gnat is fashioned by God.
Ye are in love with yourselves and the thing manufactured by yourselves: to serpents' tails the serpent's head is a law.
In that tail there is no fortune or happiness; in that head there is no pleasure or delight.

❧**2770.** That serpent's tail is circling around the head: both those friends are fit and suited to each other.

Limbs and bodies are congruous; qualities are congruous with souls.
Unquestionably the quality of every soul has congruity with the soul; for God fashions it accordingly.

❧**2775.** Inasmuch as He hath joined the quality to the soul, know that it is congruous, like eyes and face.

<meta>This page continues the prophets' response to the people of Sabá. After the people used a fable to mock the prophets' warnings, the prophets now explain that human hearts are merely instruments in the hands of the Divine. They warn that interpreting God's actions through worldly parables is a dangerous path taken by those who fell from grace, like Iblis and Korah.</meta>

Good and evil qualities match the good and evil souls they inhabit; they are the very letters that God has written.
The eye and the heart are held between two fingers like a pen in the hand of a writer, O Husayn. <note>In Sufi tradition, the "two fingers of God" represent the alternating states of the human heart, swinging between different spiritual emotions.</note>
These are the fingers of Grace and Wrath, and between them the pen—the heart—is either in distress or at ease because of these fingers.
O pen, if you are one that truly magnifies God, consider whose fingers you are held between!

**2780.** All your will and movement are controlled by this finger; your very head stands at the crossroads of the great assembly.
These letters, which symbolize your various states of being, are of His writing: your forming a purpose and then changing it comes directly from His own forming and changing of purpose.
There is no path forward but through supplication and humility; not every pen is aware of this subjection to Divine control.
The pen knows this control, but only according to its pre-ordained capacity; it shows its measure of knowledge through its good and evil actions.
As for that fable which they applied to the hare and the elephant, they confused the eternal decrees of God with mere tricks. <note>This refers to the previous page where the people of Sabá used a story about a clever hare tricking an elephant to suggest they could outsmart the prophets' warnings.</note>

### [Explaining that it is not seemly for every one to adduce parables, especially concerning Divine actions.]

**2785.** How is it appropriate for you to create these comparisons and hurl them at that Holy Court?
The use of parables belongs to the Lord, for He is the sole authority with knowledge of both the hidden and the manifest.
What do you know of the hidden nature of anything, that you—a mere baldpate—should use a lock of hair or a cheek as a comparison?
Moses saw a piece of wood and thought it a rod, but it was not; it was a dragon. Its hidden nature was revealed when it opened its jaws.
Since even a spiritual king like Moses did not know the hidden nature of a piece of wood, how should you know the hidden nature of this spiritual snare and bait?

**2790.** Since the eye of Moses was mistaken in its initial comparison, how should a meddling mouse find a way to perceive the truth?
God will turn that comparison of yours into a dragon, so that it may tear you to pieces in response.
The accursed <term>Iblís</term> <note>The primary name for the Devil in Islam, who fell from grace because he arrogantly compared himself to Adam.</note> used this kind of comparison, and so he fell under God's curse until the Day of Judgement.
<term>Qárún</term> <note>Known in the Bible as Korah; a figure of immense wealth who was swallowed by the earth for his arrogance and refusal to listen to Moses.</note> used this kind of comparison out of spite, and so he sank into the earth along with his throne and crown.
Know that your comparisons are like the cries of crows and owls, by which a hundred households are brought to ruin.

### *Story of the thief who was asked, "What are you doing at the bottom of this wall at midnight?" and replied, "I am beating a drum."*

Hear this parable—how a wicked thief was digging a hole at the foundation of a wall.

**2800.** A man who was ill and half-awake heard the soft tapping of the thief’s tool.
He went onto the roof, leaned over, and said to him, "What are you doing, father?
I hope all is well. What are you doing here at midnight? Who are you?" The thief replied, "I am a drummer, O honorable sir."

Understand that the true nature of that "hare" is the arrogant Devil, who has come as an ambassador to your soul,

What is a mere elephant? For three small birds crushed the bones of those wretched elephants. <note>A reference to the 'Year of the Elephant' in Islamic history, where an invading army with elephants was defeated by birds.</note>

The Spirit defeated them and threw them headlong into the sea: the water shattered them into pieces.
Who has not heard what happened to the tribe of **Thamúd**, or how the <term>sarsar</term><note>original: "sarsar" — a violent, freezing, and roaring wind.</note> wind swept the **'Ádites** away?
Open your eyes for once and look upon these true "Elephants"—the mighty prophets—who were the slayers of tyrants in every war.
Such arrogant kings and "elephants" are always exiled from grace, living under the wrath of the prophet’s heart.

### ***The meaning of prudence, and a parable of the prudent man.***

Either reflect on what happened to the peoples of the past, or fly with great **prudence** toward your final end.
What is prudence? It is taking precaution when faced with two choices: of the two, you choose the path that is furthest from madness.
One person may say, "On this road there is no water for seven days, only sand that will scorch your feet."
Another may say, "This is a lie: push forward, for you will find a flowing spring every night."

❦**2845.** Prudence dictates that you carry your own water, so that you are safe from terror and remain on the right side of things.
If it turns out there is water on the road, you can simply pour out your supply; but if there is none, woe to the stubborn man who brought nothing!
O children of the **Vicegerent** <note>A reference to Adam, who according to Islamic tradition was appointed as God's representative or "Khalifa" on Earth.</note>, act with justice: practice prudence for the sake of the **Day of Meeting** <note>The Day of Resurrection or Judgment when the soul meets its Creator.</note>.
That enemy <note>Satan (Iblis).</note> who took revenge upon your father Adam and dragged him from the **Highest Heavens** <note>original: "'Illiyyín." The loftiest part of Paradise where the records of the righteous are kept.</note> to this earthly prison,
Who checkmated that king of the spiritual chessboard and cast him out from Paradise to be a servant to hardships—

❦**2850.** How often in battle did the enemy seize him by trickery, trying to wrestle him down and throw him to the ground in shame!
This is what he did to that great hero Adam: do not look upon that enemy with contempt, O you who follow!
That envious one nimbly snatched away the crown and jewels of our mother and father.
He left them naked, wretched, and humbled: for many years Adam wept bitter tears,
So much so that sweet herbs grew from the tears of his eyes, as he wondered why his name was written in the **scroll of negation** <note>original: "lá." Meaning "No" or "None." In Sufi thought, this refers to the first part of the testimony of faith ("There is no god..."), representing the annihilation of the ego or a state of spiritual exile.</note>.

❦**2855.** Judge the Devil's shameless cheating by the fact that he made such a prince as Adam tear his beard in grief.
Beware, O worshippers of the material world, of his malice: strike the sword of **"There is no power but in God"** <note>original: "lá hawl." A shortened form of the Arabic prayer "Lā hawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh," used to ward off evil or temptation.</note> upon his head!
For he watches you from a hidden place where you cannot see him. Take care!
The bird-catcher scatters grain constantly: the grain is easy to see, but the trap is hidden.
Wherever you see the grain of worldly desire, beware, lest the trap snap shut on your wings,

❦**2860.** Because the bird that can walk away from the bait is the one that eats the true grain from the **vast field of Reality** which is free of all deception.
With that spiritual grain it is satisfied, and so it escapes the snare: no trap can ever confine its wings.

### *Story of the vow made by the dogs every winter that when next summer comes they will build a house for the winter.*

❦ **2885.** In winter the bones of the dog are drawn together: the blows of the frost make him so
small
That he says, 
> "Having such a little body, I must build a stone house."
"When summer comes, I will build with my claws a stone house against the cold."
But when summer comes, his bones expand from the relief which he feels, and his skin grows
sleek,
And, when he sees himself stout, he says, 
> "In what house should I find room, O noble sir?"

2890. He grows fat and slinks away into a shady spot—a lazy, well-fed, cowardly, and self-important creature!

2895. Giving thanks for a blessing is actually sweeter than the blessing itself: why would someone who is addicted to thanksgiving ever turn his attention only to the gift?

### ***How the unbelievers stopped the prophets, on whom be peace, from giving admonition and brought forward Necessitarian arguments.***

2900. The people <note>original: "Sabá." Referring to the inhabitants of the ancient kingdom of Sheba, who in Islamic tradition are cited as a people who rejected their prophets and were subsequently punished.</note> said, “O preachers, what you have said is enough, if there is anyone in this village who can hear you.

The Artist has painted our picture in this way: this design will not be changed by mere talk.
For a hundred years you might tell a pebble to become a ruby, or tell the old to become new again;
You might tell the earth to take on the qualities of water, or tell water to become honey or milk—

2905. (But it is all in vain): He is the Creator of the heavens and the heavenly beings, the Creator of water and earth and all earthly creatures.
To the heaven He gave its constant circling motion and its purity; to the mixture of water and earth He gave its dark appearance and its power to grow things.
How can the heaven choose to be murky? How can the mixture of earth and water buy purity?
To every person He has assigned a specific path: how could a mountain, even with all its effort, ever become as light as a straw?”

### ***The answer of the prophets, on whom be peace, to the Necessitarians.***

<term>Necessitarians: Those who believe in absolute predestination (Jabr), arguing that humans have no free will and are compelled to act as they do by divine decree.</term>

The prophets said, “Yes, He has indeed created some qualities from which it is impossible to escape,

2910. But He has also created qualities that are merely 'accidental' <note>In traditional philosophy, an 'accidental' quality is one that is not essential to a thing's nature and can therefore be changed or removed.</note>, so that a person who is currently disliked can become acceptable.
If you ask a stone to become gold, that is a futile request; but if you ask copper to become gold, the path for that transformation exists.
If you ask sand to become clay, it is unable to do so; but if you ask dry earth to become clay by adding water, that is possible.
He has indeed ordained certain illnesses for which there is no remedy, such as lameness, a flat nose, or blindness;

<summary>This passage contrasts the spiritual laziness brought on by physical comfort with the transformative power of gratitude. It then introduces a debate between the people of Sabá, who argue that their characters are fixed by fate, and the prophets, who explain that while some traits are innate, the soul's character can be transformed through spiritual alchemy.</summary>

God has provided illnesses for which there are remedies, such as paralysis or a headache.

❦**2915.** He created these medicines to restore harmony: these ailments and their cures are not created in vain.

### *How the unbelievers repeated the arguments of predestination.*

The people said, “O assembly of prophets, this spiritual sickness of ours is not the kind that can be cured.
For years you have recited spells and warnings of this sort, but through them, our internal chains have only grown tighter.
If this disease could be healed, at least some small part of it would have been removed by now.

❦**2920.** When a person suffers from a liver ailment <note>The original refers to 'hepatitis' or 'dropsy,' where the body fails to process water correctly.</note>, water cannot properly enter the liver. Even if he drank the entire sea, the water would only go elsewhere;
As a result, his hands and feet swell up, and his drinking does not quench the thirst.”

### *How the prophets (peace be upon them) answered them once more.*

The prophets replied, “Despair is an evil thing; the grace and mercy of the Creator are infinite.
It is not right to lose hope in such a Benefactor; cling tightly to the harness of His mercy.
Oh, many a situation seemed impossible at the start, but later it was eased and the hardship passed away.

❦**2925.** After despair, many hopes arise; after darkness, many suns appear.
I admit that you have become like stone and have locked your ears and your hearts;
But our task has nothing to do with whether you accept us or not. Our business is simply to surrender to God and carry out His command.
He has commanded us to perform this service; we did not take this office of the prophet <note>The word used is 'proclaimer' or 'messenger.'</note> upon ourselves.
We live only to fulfill God's command: if He tells us to sow seeds in a desert of sand, we sow.

❦**2930.** A prophet’s soul has no friend but God; he is unconcerned with whether the people accept or reject his message.
The reward for delivering His message comes from Him alone. We have become targets of hate and appear as enemies to you only for the sake of the Beloved.
We do not grow weary at this Divine Gate; we do not stop just because the road ahead seems long.
The only one who is truly heavy-hearted and weary is the one who is imprisoned by being separated from the Friend.
But the Heart-Ravisher <note>A poetic term for God, who captures or 'steals' the heart of the seeker.</note> and the One we desire is right here with us; amidst the gifts of His mercy, our souls are constantly giving thanks.

❦**2935.** Within our hearts is a field of anemones and a garden of roses; there is no way for old age or decay to enter here.
We are always fresh, young, and graceful—vibrant, sweet, laughing, and radiant.
To us, a hundred years are the same as a single hour, because the concepts of 'long' and 'short' time are things separated from our reality.
That sense of length and shortness exists only in physical bodies; how can such measurements apply to the soul?”

<summary>In this passage, Rumi depicts a debate between unbelievers, who argue that their spiritual state is unchangeable (predestination), and prophets, who insist that God's mercy is infinite and that their duty is to preach regardless of the outcome.</summary>
<keywords>predestination, free will, spiritual healing, hopelessness, prophetic duty, eternal youth of the soul, Divine Mercy</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the prophets have been arguing against the people’s fatalistic view that their "spiritual sickness" is incurable. The prophets now illustrate how the soul, when immersed in the Divine, loses its sense of time and worldly suffering, using the story of the Men of the Cave as a metaphor for spiritual peace.</meta>

The three hundred and nine years that the Men of the Cave <note>This refers to the "Seven Sleepers," a story found in the Quran and Christian tradition where a group of youths flee persecution and sleep in a cave for centuries, protected by God.</note> slept seemed to them like only a single day that passed without any grief or pain.

❦**2940.** It was only when their spirits returned from the realm of non-existence back into their bodies that it felt like a day had even passed.
When there is no day, night, month, or year, how could there be hunger, old age, or exhaustion?
Since we find a state of selflessness in the garden of non-existence <note>In Sufi philosophy, "non-existence" (adam) refers to the spiritual realm where the ego is absent, allowing for union with the Divine.</note>, we are filled with the ecstasy of God’s grace.
Anyone who has not tasted this cannot understand: "He who has not tasted, does not know" <note>original: *Man lam yadhuq lam yadri*—a famous Arabic proverb in Sufi literature regarding direct experiential knowledge.</note>. How could a dung-beetle ever imagine the fragrance of a rose?
It is impossible to imagine; if it could be imagined, it would be a mere mental concept and would vanish like all other worldly thoughts.

❦**2945.** How could Hell conceive of Paradise? Does a beautiful face ever emerge from the snout of an ugly pig?
Listen, do not sabotage your own soul! Pay attention, you who feel worthless, now that such a spiritual feast has been placed before you.
We have finished the difficult parts of the journey; we have made the path easy for our followers.”

### ***How the people of Sabá resisted the prophets’ message and turned against them.***

The people of Sabá <note>Sabá (Sheba) was an ancient kingdom in modern-day Yemen. In the Quran, they are described as a people who were given great prosperity but turned away from God's prophets.</note> said, “If you bring good luck to yourselves, you are nothing but a bad omen to us; we reject you and your message.
Our souls were once free from worry, but you have plunged us into sorrow and hardship.

❦**2950.** Because of your 'evil eye' and your talk of doom, the harmony and peace we once enjoyed has been shattered into a hundred pieces.”

### **How the prophets, peace be upon them, answered them once once more.**

**2955.** The prophets replied: “The foul and evil omen you perceive is actually supported by what is inside your own souls. 
If you were sleeping in a dangerous place and a dragon <term>dragon: in Sufi literature, the dragon often symbolizes the 'nafs' or the greedy, lower self that threatens to consume the soul</term> was creeping toward you from nearby, 
And a kind person woke you up, saying, ‘Jump up quickly, or the dragon will devour you!’— 
Would you say, ‘Why are you giving me such a bad omen?’ He would answer: ‘What bad omen? Just wake up and look for yourself in the light of day. 
I am the one trying to rescue you from the bad omen and take you safely home.’

**2960.** A prophet is someone who makes you aware of hidden things, seeing what the people of this world cannot see. 
If a doctor tells you, ‘Do not eat those unripe grapes, for they will cause a sickness that brings great trouble,’ 
And you reply, ‘Why are you giving me a bad omen?’ then you are making your sincere advisor look like the guilty one. 
If an astrologer says to you, ‘Do not start this task today,’ 
Even if you have seen the astrologer be wrong a hundred times, if he is right once or twice, you are still eager to trust him.

**2965.** Our 'stars' <note>This refers to the divine insight of the prophets, which they contrast with the speculative and often inaccurate predictions of worldly astrologers.</note> never conflict with the truth; how is it that their truth remains hidden from you? 
The doctor and the astrologer speak from their own opinions, but we speak from direct spiritual sight. 
We can see the smoke and fire of destruction rushing from afar toward those who refuse to believe. 
You say, ‘Be quiet and stop saying these things, for your bad omens hurt us.’ 
But O you who refuse to hear the warning of those who advise you, the evil omen stays with you wherever you go.

**2970.** A viper is crawling on your back. An advisor sees it from a rooftop and warns you; 
You tell him, ‘Hush! Do not annoy me.’ He says, ‘Fine, be happy! The warning has already been spoken.’ 
But when the viper sinks its teeth into your neck, all your desire for happiness will turn to bitterness. 
Then you will say to him, ‘O friend, was that all the warning you gave? Why didn’t you tear your shirt and scream? 
Why didn't you throw a stone at me from the roof to make me see this great calamity clearly?’

**2975.** He will answer, ‘I didn't do more because you were getting annoyed.’ Then you will say sarcastically, ‘Well, you certainly made me very happy!’ 
He says, ‘I gave my advice freely and generously, hoping to rescue you from this useless and profitable bondage.’”

<meta>This page continues the prophets' discourse on the nature of the human soul. They explain that some spirits respond to kindness, while others only recognize the truth through hardship. “Because of your base nature, you felt no sense of duty or gratitude for that generosity; instead, you turned it into a source of harm and arrogance.”
This is the way of those with a low nature: they return your goodness with evil.
As for the <term>fleshly soul: the 'nafs' or ego, which Sufi tradition views as an internal obstacle to spiritual growth</term>, you must humble it through self-denial; it is base by nature, and kindness does not improve it.

❧ **2980.** If you show kindness to a noble person, it is well-placed: they will return seven hundred blessings for every one you give.
But be firm with the ignoble: when you treat a person of low character with severity, they become a most faithful servant to you.
The ungrateful sow the seeds of cruelty when they are prosperous; but later, in Hell, their only cry is “O Lord, deliver us!”

### ***The wisdom of God having created Hell in the world to come and the prison of tribulation in this present world, so that they may serve as places of worship for the arrogant: “Come ye willingly or unwillingly.”*** <note>original: "a-tiyā taw‘an aw karhan." This is a reference to Quran 41:11, where God commands the Heavens and Earth to submit.</note>

For it is through suffering and severity that the base are purified; when they receive nothing but kindness, they themselves become the oppressors.
Therefore, Hell is the “mosque” where they finally perform their devotions: for a wild bird, a trap is the only thing that acts as a tether.

❧ **2985.** Prison is the monastery for the thief and the villain; it is only there that they are constantly mindful of God.
Since the worship of the Divine was the ultimate purpose for the creation of mankind, Hellfire was established as the place of worship for the rebellious.
A human being has the power to act in many ways, but this service to God has always been the final goal for them.
“I did not create the <term>Jinn: supernatural beings made of fire who, like humans, have the choice to follow or reject God's guidance</term> and mankind except that they might serve Me.” <note>Quran 51:56</note> Recite this text! The final purpose of the world is nothing but Divine worship.
Even though the purpose of a book is the knowledge it contains, if you use it as a pillow to rest your head, it will serve that purpose too;

❧ **2990.** But acting as a pillow was never its true intent: its goal was learning, knowledge, right guidance, and spiritual profit.
If you use a sword as a tent-peg, you have chosen defeat over victory.
Although the goal of every person is to know God and to find the right path in religion, every person has a specific “place of worship” suited to their soul.
The place where the noble man worships is through your kindness toward him; the place where the base man worships is through your severity toward him.
Strike the base so that they may bow their heads; give to the noble so that they may bear good fruit.

❧ **2995.** Out of necessity, God has created a sanctuary for both—Hell for the former, and an increase of bounty for the latter.
Moses built the <term>Báb-i Saghír: the 'Small Gate' in Jerusalem. Tradition says it was built low so that people had to bow their heads to enter, symbolizing humility</term> in Jerusalem so that those tormented by their own arrogance would be forced to lower their heads.
He did this because they were insolent and prideful. Hell is like that Small Gate: a place of necessary humiliation.

<summary>Rumi explains that different souls require different treatments: the noble thrive on kindness, while the arrogant require the "prison" of hardship or Hell to turn toward God. He uses the analogy of a book used as a pillow to illustrate how humans often miss their primary purpose—Divine worship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of humbling the "nafs" or fleshly soul. Having established that the base-natured person only turns to God through suffering, the text now illustrates this through the historical-religious metaphor of the "Small Gate" and the misplaced devotion people show to worldly power.</meta>

...be peace, built the **Small Gate** <note>original: Báb-i Saghír</note> in the wall of Jerusalem in order that the insolent and wicked men among the Israelites might bow low when they entered in, according to the text: "Enter the gate, prostrating yourselves, and say, 'May our sins be forgiven.'" <note>original: "hittatun." This refers to a Quranic account where the Israelites were commanded to enter a gate in humility to receive pardon.</note>

Likewise, God has built a **Small Gate** from the flesh and bones of kings. Take heed!
The people of this world prostrate themselves before these kings, because they are opposed to bowing before the Divine Majesty.

❧ **3000.** God has made a little dunghill their <term>mihráb: the prayer niche in a mosque that indicates the direction of prayer</term>: the name of that prayer niche is "prince" and "hero."
You worldlings are not fit for this holy Presence: holy men are like sugarcane; you are like an empty reed.
These vile wretches grovel before those curs; but it is a disgrace to the lion that they should be so submissive to him.
The cat is the dreaded overseer of every mouse-like soul: what is a mouse that it should even be afraid of lions?
Their fear is only for the curs of God: how could they ever have fear for the Sun of God?

❧ **3005.** The prayer of those venerable ones is "My Lord the Most High"; <note>original: "Subhána Rabbiyal-A'lá," a phrase recited during prostration in Islamic prayer.</note> but "my lord the most low" is more suitable for these fools.
How should the mouse fear the lions of the spiritual battlefield? No, those who fear the lions are those who possess the speed and the musk-bag of the deer. <note>In Persian poetry, the deer represents the refined seeker who possesses the "musk" of spiritual scent.</note>
O licker of pots, go to him who licks basins and write him down as your lord and benefactor!
Enough! If I give a long and far-reaching explanation, the worldly prince will be angered; and besides, he already knows deep down that his case is exactly as I have described.
The conclusion is this: "O noble man, treat the vile with severity, so that the villain may humble his neck before you."

❧ **3010.** When the noble man deals kindly with a villain, that wicked fleshly soul shows only ingratitude.
It was for this reason that the afflicted are often thankful, while those who are fortunate and wealthy are often rebellious and deceitful.
The lord with his gold-embroidered coat is rebellious; the distressed wearer of a coarse woollen cloak <note>original: "‘abá," the simple garment of a dervish or poor man.</note> is thankful.
How should thankfulness grow from mere possessions and riches? True thankfulness grows from tribulation and sickness.

### ***Story of the Sufi who fell in love with an empty food-wallet.***

One day a <term>Sufi: a practitioner of the mystical path of Islam, seeking direct inward experience of God</term> caught sight of a food-wallet hanging on a nail: he began to whirl in a dance and tear his garments in ecstasy,

❧ **3015.** Crying out, "Look! Here is the food of the foodless! Look! Here is the remedy for famine and the pangs of hunger!"
When his excitement and the "smoke" of his passion grew great, every other Sufi present joined him in his behavior.
They were shouting and shrieking; several were becoming intoxicated and losing themselves in the moment.
An idle busybody said to the Sufi, "What is the matter? It is only a food-wallet hanging on a nail, and it is completely empty of bread!"
The Sufi replied, "Go away, go away! You are merely a form without a spirit. You seek physical existence, but you are no lover of the Truth; for the lover sees what is hidden within non-existence."

<summary>Rumi explains that worldly power acts as a "Small Gate" where the arrogant are forced to bow, though their devotion is misplaced. He concludes with the start of a parable about a Sufi whose spiritual perception allows him to find divine nourishment in an empty bag.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of worldly pride and the "Small Gate" of humility to the nature of spiritual perception. **3020.** The lover’s nourishment is their love for the bread, even without the bread itself; no one who is truly sincere in their love is a slave to material existence.

That <term>dervish: a member of a Muslim religious order, often known for vows of poverty and austerity</term> who perceived Reality used to weave baskets even though his hand had been cut off. <note>This refers to a traditional story of a saintly man whose spiritual power allowed him to perform physical tasks despite his disability.</note>

How shall a human being perceive the Jinní's scent, when human nature is the very opposite of theirs?
That scent-inhaling spirit gains a great delight from a smell, a delight you would not find even in a hundred <term>maunds: an ancient unit of weight varying by region, often around 80 pounds</term> of sweet dainties.
To the Egyptian <term>Copt: an inhabitant of Egypt; in this context, the followers of Pharaoh</term>, the water of the Nile is blood; but to the righteous Israelite, it is pure water. <note>This references the plague in Egypt where the Nile turned to blood for the Egyptians but remained water for the Israelites.</note>

### *How Jacob, peace be upon him, was privileged to taste the cup of God from the face of Joseph, and inhale the scent of God from the scent of Joseph; and the exclusion of Joseph's brothers and others from both these privileges.*

**3030.** That which Jacob experienced from beholding the face of Joseph was unique to him; when did such delight ever reach Joseph's brothers?
Jacob, out of love for Joseph, would put himself in the pit, while the brother digs a pit for Joseph out of hatred.
In the eyes of the brother, Joseph's food-bag is empty of bread; but in the eyes of Jacob, it is full, for he is filled with eager desire.
No one with an unwashed face can behold the faces of the <term>houris: beautiful celestial companions in Paradise</term>; as the Prophet said: "There is no ritual prayer without the ablution." <note>original: "La salāta illā bi-tuhūrin." A foundational Islamic principle stating that physical and spiritual purity are required for prayer.</note>
Love is the meat and drink of souls; and in this sense, hunger is the true food of the spirit.

**3035.** Jacob hungered for Joseph; therefore, the scent of the "bread" reached him from a great distance.
The one who carried Joseph's shirt was hurrying on his way but did not smell the shirt’s scent,
While Jacob, who was a hundred leagues away from that place, was already smelling the perfume because he was Jacob.
Oh, there is many a learned person who gains no profit from their knowledge; such a person is one who merely commits facts to memory, rather than one who truly loves knowledge.
The listener may perceive the scent of that knowledge, even if the listener is just an ordinary person,

**3040.** Because the knowledge in the hand of that "learned" man is a borrowed thing, like a slave-girl in the hands of a merchant.
The slave-girl is of no use to the dealer; she is only in his hands for the sake of the person who will eventually buy her.
God's providence is a distribution of allotted portions; no one’s portion can be taken by another.
A beautiful imagination becomes a garden of Paradise for a blessed man, while an ugly imagination waylays the unblessed man and leads him to ruin.

# ***The Story of the Master and his Slave who was Devoted to Prayer and Found Great Joy in Communing with God.***

❀**3055.** At daybreak, the <term>Amír: a high-ranking official or commander</term> wanted to go to the bathhouse. He shouted, "Hey, Sunqur, wake up!"
"Get the washbasin, the towel, and the cleaning clay from Altún <note>Sunqur and Altún are Turkish names common for attendants in this period.</note> so we can go to the bathhouse, my indispensable servant."
Immediately, Sunqur took the basin and a fine towel and set out with him—the two of them together.
There was a <term>mosque: a Muslim place of worship</term> along the road, and the call to prayer reached Sunqur’s ears.
Sunqur was very fond of the <term>ritual prayer: the formal Islamic prayer (Salah) performed five times daily</term>. He said, "O my Master, O kind sir,"

❀**3060.** "Wait patiently for a moment on this bench so I may perform my required prayers and recite the <term>Sūra: a chapter of the Quran</term> beginning with the words '*They were not...*' <note>original: "lam yakun." Then he called out, "Sunqur, why don't you come out?" He replied, "This artful One will not let me go!"
"Be patient! Look, I’m coming, light of my eyes! I haven't forgotten you; your voice is in my ear."

❀**3065.** Seven times the Master waited and then shouted—until at last he was driven to despair by Sunqur's delay.
Sunqur's answer was always the same: "He will not let me come out yet, honored Master."
The Master said, "But there is no one left in the mosque! Who is holding you there? Who has made you stay?"
Sunqur replied, "The One who has chained you outside the mosque has chained me inside of it."
"He who will not let you come in will not let me come out."

### ***How the prophets lost hope of being accepted and approved by the unbelievers, as God has said: "Until, when the messengers despaired..."*** <note>original: "Hattá idhá istay’asa ’l-rusul" — a reference to Quran 12:110, describing the moment when prophets feel their message is being entirely rejected by their people.</note>

The prophets said to their own hearts, “How long shall we continue giving warnings and advice to this person and that person?
How long shall we fruitlessly beat a piece of cold iron? <note>A metaphor for trying to change someone whose heart is hardened and unresponsive.</note> Listen, how long shall we continue to breathe into a cage?”
The movement and actions of created beings are caused by Divine destiny and appointment: the sharpness of the teeth is caused by the burning hunger of the stomach.

**3080.** The <term>First Soul: also known as the Universal Intellect, the first emanation of Divine wisdom</term> acted upon the second soul: a fish stinks from the head, not from the tail. <note>This proverb suggests that the state of the "head" (the spiritual or governing origin) determines the state of the "tail" (the individual or the followers).</note>
But, while recognizing this, still speed forward like an arrow: since God has said, “Deliver the message,” there is no escaping that duty. <note>original: "Balligh" — the Quranic command to the Prophet Muhammad to deliver the Divine revelation regardless of the response.</note>
You do not know which of these two types you are: therefore, strive for as long as necessary so that you may eventually discern what you are.
When you put cargo on board a ship, you are making that venture based on trust.
For you do not know which of the two you are—whether you are destined to be drowned on the voyage or saved from death.

**3085.** If you say, “Until I know which one I am, I will not hurry to embark on the ship and the ocean;
Reveal to me which party I belong to: the saved or the drowned.
I will not start this voyage with doubt and idle hope, like the others”—
Then no business will ever be done by you, because the secret of these two possibilities lies in the <term>Unseen: 'al-Ghayb,' the spiritual realm hidden from human senses</term>.
The merchant of a timid disposition and frail spirit neither gains nor loses in his quest;

**3090.** Indeed, he suffers a loss, for he is deprived of fortune and remains lowly: only the one who is an "eater of flames"—ardent and courageous in their search—will find the light.
Inasmuch as all affairs in life turn upon hope, the work of religion is the most worthy of all to inspire hope, for by this means you may win salvation.
Here it is not permitted to knock at the door with demanding persistence; nothing but hope is allowed: God knows the right course best.

### The story of Anas, may God be pleased with him: how he cast a napkin into a fiery oven, and it was not burnt.

❦**3110.** It has come down to us concerning <term>Anas son of Málik</term> <note>A well-known companion of the Prophet Muhammad who served him for many years.</note> that a certain person became his guest. ❦**3115.** After a short time, she took it out of the oven, clean, white, and purged of all that filth.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on absolute trust in the Divine and those close to God. The party of guests asked, "O venerable Companion of the Prophet <note>This likely refers to Anas ibn Malik, a well-known companion of Mohammed, who in traditional stories possessed a napkin that could be cleaned by fire.</note>, how is it that the cloth did not burn? ### *Story of the Prophet—on whom be peace—coming to the aid of a caravan of Arabs who had been brought to a desperate state by thirst and lack of water and had resigned themselves to death: both the camels and the people of the caravan were so exhausted that their tongues hung from their mouths.*

The tongues of their camels were hanging out, and the people were strewn everywhere across the desert sands.

❧**3135.** He took pity on them and said, "Listen! Some of your comrades must go at once and run toward those sandhills. Those seeking help approached the sandhills, and after a short while, they saw that it was exactly as he had said: a black slave was traveling with a camel, carrying a water-skin filled with water like one bearing a precious gift.

❧**3140.** Then they said to him, "The Pride of Mankind, the Best of Created Beings, invites you to come in this direction."

He replied, "I do not know him; who is he?"

The spokesman answered, "He is that moon-faced, sweet-natured one."

The slave’s eyes filled with tears; he forgot both his master and his home.

**3170.** "Now is not the time for being lost in wonder; that state lies ahead of you. For now, move forward on your path with speed and vigor."
The slave took the hands of <term>Mustafá</term> <note>A title for the Prophet Muhammad meaning "The Chosen One."</note> and pressed them to his face, kissing them with deep love.
Then the Prophet rubbed his blessed hand over the slave's face, bringing him great fortune.
That <term>Abyssinian</term> <note>A historical term for a person from Ethiopia or the surrounding regions of East Africa.</note> man became as bright as the full moon; his dark night was transformed into a radiant day.
He became like <term>Joseph</term> <note>The Prophet Yusuf, who in Persian tradition is the ultimate symbol of physical beauty and spiritual purity.</note> in his beauty and grace. The Prophet said to him, "Now, return home and tell what has happened to you."

**3175.** He walked on, losing all sense of himself, intoxicated by divine ecstasy; in his state, he could not distinguish his feet from his hands.
He hurried back from the caravan’s vicinity to his master, carrying the two full water-skins.

### ***How the master saw his slave transformed and white, failed to recognize him, and said, "You have killed my slave; your crime has been discovered, and God has delivered you into my hands."***

The master saw him from a distance and was struck with confusion; in his amazement, he called out to the people of the village.
"This is my water-skin and my camel," he said, "but where has my dark-skinned slave gone?
This man approaching from afar is like a full moon; the light from his face outshines the very daylight.

**3180.** Where is my slave? Perhaps he lost his way, or a wolf attacked and killed him."
When the slave stood before him, the master asked, "Who are you? Are you a native of <term>Yemen</term> or a <term>Turcoman</term> <note>The master is guessing the man's ethnicity based on his new, lighter complexion.</note>?
Tell me, what have you done to my slave? Speak the truth! If you have killed him, confess it! Do not try to make excuses."
The slave replied, "If I had killed him, why would I come to you? Why would I walk on my own feet into the scene of a murder?"
The master asked again, "Where is my slave?" The slave answered, "I am he! The hand of God’s grace has made me radiant."

**3185.** "What are you saying? Where is my slave? Listen, you will not escape me unless you tell the truth."
The slave said, "I will recount every one of your secret dealings with that slave, one by one.
I will tell you everything that happened from the moment you bought me until this very hour,
So that you may know I am the same person in spirit, even though a bright dawn has broken through my dark body.
The color has changed, but the pure spirit is free from color, free from the <term>four elements</term> <note>The classical elements of earth, air, fire, and water which were believed to compose the physical body.</note>, and free from the dust of the earth."

### *How the unbelieving woman came to the <term>Mustafá</term> <note>Original: "Mustafá," meaning "The Chosen One," a title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note> (Muhammad), on whom be peace, with a nursing babe, and how it spoke, like Jesus, of the miracles of the Prophet—may God bless and save him!*

**3220.** A woman of that same village, one of those who did not believe, ran to the Prophet for the sake of testing him.

### ***How an eagle seized the boot of the Prophet, on whom be peace, and carried it into the air and turned it upside down, and how a black serpent dropped down from the boot.***

They were thus engaged, when <term>Mustafá</term> <note>Original: "Mustafá," meaning "The Chosen One," a common title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note> heard from aloft the call to the ritual prayer.
He asked for water and renewed the <term>ablution</term> <note>Original: "wudu," the ritual washing of hands, face, and feet performed by Muslims before prayer.</note>: he washed his hands and face with that cold water.

**3240.** He washed both his feet and gave attention to—was about to take—his boot: a boot-snatcher carried off the boot.
That man of sweet address moved his hand towards the boot: an eagle snatched the boot from his hand,
And bore it away into the air, swift as the wind; then she turned it upside down, and a serpent dropped from it.
From the boot dropped a black serpent: on account of that Divine care for the Prophet, the eagle became his benevolent friend.
Then the eagle brought back the boot and said, “Come, take it and go to prayers.

**3245.** I did this presumptuous act from necessity: I am abashed by my feeling of reverence for thee.
Woe to him that behaves presumptuously without necessity and only because vain desire authorizes him!”
Then the Prophet thanked her and said, “I deemed this act of thine rudeness, but it really was kindness.
Thou didst carry off the boot, and I was perturbed: thou tookest away my grief, and I was aggrieved.
Although God has shown to me every unseen thing, at that moment my heart was occupied with myself.”

**3250.** She, the eagle, said, “Far be it from thee that forgetfulness grew up in thee: my seeing that invisible thing is from thy <term>reflection</term> <note>In Sufi thought, the "reflection" (aks) of a saint or prophet can enlighten those around them, granting them temporary access to divine vision.</note>.
If I, in the air, see the serpent in the boot, it is not of myself, it is thy reflection, O Mustafá.”
The reflection of the man of light is wholly resplendent; the reflection of the man of darkness is wholly like a <term>bath-stove</term> <note>Original: "gulkhan," the furnace or ash-pit of a public bath; used here as a metaphor for the dark, soot-covered state of a soul turned away from God.</note>.
The reflection of the servant of God is wholly luminous; the reflection of the stranger to God is wholly blindness.
Know every one's reflection: see it plainly, O my soul. Then ever sit beside the <term>congener</term> <note>Original: "jins," meaning those of the same spiritual nature or genus.</note> whom thou desirest.

### ***The right way of taking a lesson from this story and knowing with certainty that “verily, together with hardship there is ease.”***

**3255.** That tale is a lesson to thee, O my soul, to the end that thou mayst acquiesce in the decree of God;
So that thou wilt be quick to understand and wilt have good thoughts of God when thou seest a calamity befall thee of a sudden.
While others turn pale from dread of it, thou wilt be laughing in the hour of gain or loss, like the rose.
Because the rose, though thou tear it petal by petal, does not leave off laughing and does not become bent with grief.

### ***How a certain man demanded of Moses that he should teach him the language of the beasts and birds.***

A young man said to Moses, "Teach me the language of the animals, so that perhaps from the voices of animals and wild beasts I may learn a lesson regarding my religion.
Since the languages of the sons of Adam are used entirely for the sake of acquiring food, water, and fame,

**3270.** "Go away," said Moses. "Abandon this empty desire, for this wish involves much danger both before and behind you.

## **How Revelation came from God most High to Moses, instructing him to teach the man what he demanded, or at least a part of it.**

God said, "Grant his request; let him have a free hand to choose between good and evil."
Choice—the exercise of free will—is the very "salt" of devotion. Without it, there would be no merit. The celestial spheres revolve involuntarily;
Therefore, their rotation earns neither reward nor punishment. Free will is what is measured at the time of the <term>Reckoning</term> <note>The final judgment where actions are weighed.</note>.
While all created beings truly glorify God, a forced glorification earns no spiritual "wage."

❧ **3290.** "Put a sword in his hand and pull him away from his inability to choose, so that he may become either a holy warrior or a brigand.

❧ **3295.** Those inspired by God are the fountain of life; those lured by the attractions of sensuality are the poison of death.

## ***How the cock foretold the death of the Khwája.***

“But tomorrow he will certainly die; his heir, in mourning for him, will slaughter a cow. The owner of the house will die and depart from this world; look, tomorrow a great deal of food will reach you.

**3345.** People of all ranks, high and low, will find pieces of bread, dainty morsels, and fine foods in the middle of the street. The meat of the sacrificed cow and thin loaves of bread will be scattered quickly over the dogs and the beggars.”

The deaths of the horse, the mule, and the slave were intended to avert the doom of this foolish, deluded man. He fled from the loss of wealth and the grief it causes; in doing so, he increased his wealth but shed his own blood <note>By selling the animals and the slave, the man avoided the "sacrifices" that might have satisfied his destiny; as a result, the "death" meant for his property finally fell upon him</note>.

These austerities of <term>dervishes</term> <note>original: "darvishán"; Muslim mystics who often practice poverty and self-discipline</note>—what are they for? The reason is that the tribulation imposed on the body is, in truth, the everlasting life of the spirit.

**3350.** Unless a mystic traveler gains the everlasting life of his spiritual self, why would he make his body a sick and perishing thing? How should he move his hand to acts of altruism and devotional work unless he sees the salvation of his soul in exchange for what he gives?

That one who gives without any expectation of gain—that one is God, is God, is God, or the friend of God—the saint—who has taken on the nature of God, has become luminous, and has received the <term>Absolute Radiance</term> <note>The pure, unmanifested light of the Divine</note>; for He is rich, while all except Him are poor. How should a poor man say “Take” without expecting compensation?

**3355.** Until a child sees that the apple is there, it will not let go of the stinking onion in its hand. All these market-folk, for the sake of worldly objects, sit on their shop benches in the hope of receiving payment. They offer a hundred fine articles of merchandise, but within their hearts, they are intent on compensation.

O man of the true Religion, you will not hear a single <term>salaam</term> <note>original: "salám"; a greeting meaning "peace"</note> whose end will not eventually pluck at your sleeve and demand something from you. I have never heard a disinterested greeting from anyone, high or low, O brother—and I give this greeting to you—

**3360.** Except for the greeting of God. Come, seek that peace from house to house, from place to place, and from street to street! From the mouth of the person who has a "good scent" <note>A metaphor for someone with spiritual insight or purity</note>, I heard both the message and the peace of God; and in the hope of that divine greeting, I listen to the greetings of everyone else as though they were sweeter than life.

The saint's greeting has become the greeting of God because he has set fire to the household of the "self." He has died to his ego and become living through the Lord; therefore, the mysteries of God are on his lips.

<summary>The cock reveals that the master's attempts to avoid financial loss have led to his own imminent death, illustrating the spiritual danger of greed. Rumi explains that true giving is only possible for God and His saints, who have surrendered their egos.</summary>

### ***How that person ran to Moses for protection when he heard from the cock the announcement of his death.***

When he heard these things, he began running in a panicked rush: he went to the door of Moses, the <term>Kalím</term> <note>original: "Kalím-Allāh"; an honorific for Moses meaning "The one who conversed with God"</note>.

**3370.** Go and throw the loss upon the true believers! Make your purses and traveling bags twice as large!

> “O you who possess such beautiful qualities, do not beat me over the head now; do not rub my sins into my face. 
> That sin came from me because I was unworthy; please, offer a good response to my unworthy action.”

But I will pray for God's gracious decree—that you may at least take your Faith with you when you depart from this world.
When you carry your Faith with you, you are truly alive; when you depart with Faith, you are enduring forever.”
At that very moment, the <term>Khwája</term> <note>original: "khwāja"; a title of respect for a master or merchant</note> became ill; he felt a sudden nausea, and they brought a basin to him.
This is the nausea of death, not simple indigestion: how could vomiting help you now, you foolish and unfortunate man?

**3380.** Four men carried him back to his house: his legs were rubbing against each other in his final throes.
If you do not listen to the counsel of a Moses and show such disrespect, you will find yourself dashing against a sword of steel.
The sword feels no shame or hesitation in taking your life: this is your own doing, brother, your own doing.

### ***How Moses prayed for that person, that he might depart from the world (die) in the Faith.***

At the break of dawn, Moses began his <term>orison</term> <note>original: "niyāz"; a humble prayer or supplication</note>, saying: 
> “O God, do not take the Faith away from him, do not let it be lost!
> Act in Your royal majesty and forgive him, for he has erred, acted with impudence, and overstepped all bounds.

**3385.** I told him, ‘This knowledge is not suitable for you,’ but he viewed my words as a mere attempt to thwart his desires and as something empty.”
Only the man whose hand can turn a wooden rod into a dragon should ever lay hands on a real dragon.
To learn the secrets of the <term>Unseen</term> <note>original: "ghayb"; the hidden, spiritual realm known only to God</note> is appropriate only for the one who can seal his lips and refrain from speaking of what he knows.

### *The story of the woman whose children always died young, and how God answered her lament: "This loss replaces the spiritual discipline you never practiced; it is your version of the self-mortification others choose for themselves."*

That woman used to give birth to a son every year, but the child never lived longer than six months;

**3400.** Within three or four months, the child would perish. The woman wailed, crying, "Alas, O God!
For nine months I carry the burden of pregnancy, and for only three months do I have joy; my happiness vanishes faster than a rainbow."
Because of the terrifying anguish she suffered, that woman used to offer this sorrowful outcry before the men of God.
In this way, twenty of her children went to the grave; a fire of destruction fell swiftly upon their young lives,
Until one night, she was shown a vision of a garden—everlasting, lush, delightful, and limitless.

**3405.** I have called this <term>Absolute Grace</term> <note>original: "fayḍ-i bī-chūn"; literally 'bounty without a "how"' or unconditioned grace</note> a "garden" because it is the source of all blessings and the gathering place of all beauty;
Otherwise, it is something no eye has ever truly seen—how can we even call it a garden? Yet the term is used because God Himself called the Light of the Unseen a "lamp" <note>A reference to the 'Verse of Light' (Surah An-Nur 24:35) in the Quran, where God's light is compared to a lamp in a niche</note>.
This is not a direct comparison, but a parable, used so that those who are bewildered might catch a scent of the ultimate reality.
In short, the woman saw that Divine Grace and became intoxicated by it; at that revelation, the fragile creature fell into a spiritual <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "ḥāl"; a state of rapture or direct spiritual experience</note>.

### *How Hamza, may God be well-pleased with him, went into battle without a coat of mail*

Beyond the realm of the senses, I behold the camp of the Divine King thronged with the army of the Light of God,

<image-desc>floral decorative symbol</image-desc>**3435.** And that one to whom death is the opening of the gate—for him in the <term>Allocution</term> <note>original: "Khitab"; referring here to the Qur'án as the direct speech or address of God.</note> there is the command, *“Vie ye with each other in hastening”* <note>Qur'án 3:133, encouraging believers to race toward forgiveness and Paradise.</note>.

<meta>The previous page concluded the story of Hamza, who viewed death not as an end, but as a gateway to a beautiful reality. When a man has sown the seed of a prostration in prayer or a humble bow, in that other world his prayer blossoms into Paradise.

**3460.** When altruism and charity have grown from your hands, those generous acts transform on the other side into date-palms and fresh greenery.

**3480.** Your anger is the very seed of Hell-fire: take heed, and extinguish this Hell of yours now, for it is a trap.

### ***The means of preventing oneself from being swindled in sale and purchase.***

A certain friend said to the Prophet, “I am always being swindled in business.

❦**3495.** The trickery of everyone who sells or buys acts like magic on me and leads me astray.”
The Prophet replied, “When you are afraid of being cheated in a deal, make a condition for yourself that you have three days to decide.
For deliberation comes from the Merciful God, while haste comes from the accursed Devil.”
When you throw a piece of bread to a dog, he first smells it and then he eats, O careful observer.
He smells with his nose; we, who are gifted with wisdom, must "smell" the matter with a purified intelligence.

❦**3500.** This earth and the heavenly spheres were brought into existence by God with a deliberation extending over six days;
Otherwise, He was fully able—merely by saying "Be, and it is" <note>original: "Kun fa-yakun." This is a recurring phrase in the Qur’an describing God's absolute creative power.</note>—to bring forth a hundred earths and heavens from non-existence.
Little by little, until the age of forty, the Almighty makes a human being into a complete man;
Though He was able in a single moment to raise up fifty people from nothingness.
Jesus was able to make the dead spring back to life without delay by means of a single prayer:

❦**3505.** Is the Creator of Jesus then unable to bring full-grown men into existence one after another without delay?
This slow deliberation is for the purpose of teaching you: you must seek God patiently and without stopping.
A little stream that moves continually never becomes stagnant or foul-smelling.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual discernment. From this deliberation <note>The term used here refers to patient, spiritual reflection rather than mere intellectual thought.</note> are born felicity and joy: this deliberation is the egg, and fortune is like the birds hatched from that egg.
How should the bird resemble the egg, O obstinate one, even though it is produced from the egg?

❧**3510.** Wait until your limbs, like eggs, hatch birds at the very end <note>A reference to the Resurrection, where the true nature of the soul is revealed.</note>!

### *How Bilál, may God be well-pleased with him, died rejoicing.*

When <term>Bilál</term> <note>Bilal ibn Rabah was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the first Muezzin (caller to prayer) in Islam. He was formerly enslaved and was known for his deep devotion and beautiful voice.</note> became thin as the new moon from weakness, the hue of death fell upon Bilál's face.
His wife saw him in this state and cried, "Oh, sorrow!" Then Bilál said to her, "Nay, nay! Say instead, 'Oh, joy!'" <note>original: "Wā tarabā." This reflects Bilal's transition from the "sorrow" of earthly separation to the "joy" of meeting the Divine.</note>
"Until now I have been in sorrow from living: how should you know how delightful death is, and what it truly is in reality?"

❧**3520.** He was saying this, and at the very moment of saying it, his countenance was blooming with narcissi, rose-leaves, and red anemones.
The glow of his face and his eye full of radiance were giving testimony to the truth of his words.
Every black-hearted person regarded him only as black and despised him; but why is the <term>Man of the eye</term> <note>This is a play on the term "Insān al-ʿAyn," which literally means "the man of the eye" but refers to the pupil. Rumi suggests that just as the pupil is black yet is the source of sight, Bilal's outward appearance hid a profound spiritual vision.</note> black?
The person who is spiritually blind is "black-faced" (shamed), but the Man of the inward eye—the Seer—is the mirror for the Moon of Truth.
Who in the world, indeed, sees the man of your inward eye except the Man of piercing spiritual sight?

❧**3525.** Since none but the Man of the eye beheld it, who, then, but he attained to knowledge of its essential color?
Therefore, all except the Seer are merely imitators—lacking immediate knowledge—regarding the attributes of the sublime man of the eye.
His wife said to him, "This is the parting, O man of goodly qualities." "Nay, nay," said he, "it is the union, the union with God."
The wife said, "Tonight you will go to a strange country; you will be absent from your family and kindred."
"Nay, nay," he replied; "on the contrary, tonight my spirit is truly coming home from a strange country."

❧**3530.** She said, "Where shall we see your face?" He answered, "In God's chosen circle."
His chosen circle adjoins you, if you look upward with the spirit, not downward with the ego.
In that circle, the Light from the Lord of created beings is gleaming like the precious stone in the circle of a signet ring.

<summary>Rumi explains that while bodies appear similar, souls differ based on their inner "fruit," culminating in the story of Bilal, who welcomes death as a joyful homecoming and union with the Divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scene of Bilal's deathbed. His wife laments the "ruin" of their home—referring both to their domestic life and his physical body—but Bilal corrects her. He explains that death is not a destruction but a necessary demolition to build a grander spiritual palace. "Alas," she said, "this house has been ruined." 
"Look at the moon," he replied, "do not look at the cloud. He has ruined it so that He may make it more flourishing; my kinsfolk were many and the house was too small."

### ***The Divine wisdom in ruining the body through death.***

❀3535 "Formerly, like <term>Adam</term> <note>The first man, who in the mystical tradition represents the soul's exile from Paradise into the 'grief' of the material world.</note>, I was imprisoned in sorrow; now the East and the West are filled with my spirit's progeny. I was a beggar in this dungeon-like house; now I have become a king: a palace is needed for a king." 

Truly, palaces are the place for spiritual kings to take their pleasure; for one who is spiritually dead, a grave is a sufficient house and dwelling. To the prophets, this world seemed narrow; like kings, they departed into the realm of <term>spacelessness</term> <note>original: "la-makan". A Sufi concept referring to the divine dimension that exists beyond the physical constraints of time and space.</note>. To the spiritually dead, this world appears splendid; its exterior seems large, but in reality, it is a narrow place.

❀3540 If it were not narrow, why would there be this constant lamenting? Why has everyone become more bowed down with affliction the longer they live in it? When the spirit is freed from this world during sleep, see how it rejoices in that place where it goes! Even the wicked man is delivered from his own nature's malice, and the prisoner escapes the thoughts of his cell. 

This vast earth and heaven become exceedingly small at the time of lying down to sleep. The world is like an eye-bandage <note>A metaphor for a magic spell or a distraction that prevents one from seeing the true nature of reality.</note>: it appears wide but is truly narrow; its laughter is actually weeping, and its glory is entirely shame.

### ***Comparison of this world—which is wide in appearance but narrow in reality—to a hot bathhouse, and the next world to the release of sleep.***

❀3545 This world is like a bathhouse that is kept too hot, so that you are distressed and your soul is melted with anguish. Although the bathhouse is broad and long, your soul is exhausted by the heat. Your heart finds no relief until you come out; what advantage, then, is the size of the room to you? 

Or it is as if you should put on tight shoes, O misguided one, and walk into a wide desert. The vastness of the desert becomes a source of distress; that open plain becomes a prison to you.

❀3550 Whoever sees you from a distance says, "He blooms like a fresh anemone <note>A common poetic image for someone looking cheerful and healthy.</note> in that desert"; they do not know that you, like the wicked, are outwardly in a rose garden while your soul is crying out in pain. 

Your sleep is the taking off of those tight shoes, for then your soul is free from the body for a while. To the saints, O reader, sleep is a kingdom, just as it was for the <term>Men of the Cave</term> <note>Also known as the Seven Sleepers, these were youths who fled religious persecution and were preserved by God in a miraculous sleep for centuries. Here, they symbolize the soul's protection from the world's 'heat' during spiritual rest.</note> in this world. They sleep and dream, yet no physical sleep is there; they enter into <term>nonexistence</term> <note>In Sufi terms, 'nonexistence' (fana) is not a void, but the state of being lost in God’s presence, free from the limitations of the ego and the material world.</note>, yet no material door is required.

❀3555 "The body is a narrow house, and the soul within is cramped: God ruined it so that He might build a royal palace."

<summary>Bilal uses several metaphors—including a cramped house, tight shoes in a desert, and a hot bathhouse—to explain that the physical world is a spiritual prison. He argues that death and sleep are forms of liberation that allow the soul to expand into its true, royal nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Bilal on his deathbed. Having previously explained to his wife that his death is a "flourishing" rather than a ruin, he now expands on the metaphor of birth. "I am cramped like the <term>embryo</term> <note>In this mystical context, the soul is compared to an unborn child; the physical world is the dark, limited womb that it must eventually leave to truly live.</note> in the womb: I have reached nine months of age: this migration has become urgent.
Unless the throes of childbirth overtake my mother (what else can I do?): in this prison, I am surrounded by fire.
My mother—namely, my physical nature—is giving birth to my spirit as a result of these death-throes, so that the lamb of my soul may be released from the ewe of the body,
So that the lamb may graze in the green fields of the divine. Come, open your womb, for this lamb has grown too big for it."

❧**3560.** If the pain of childbirth is grievous to the pregnant woman, for the embryo, it is the breaking of its prison.
The pregnant woman weeps during labor, crying, “Where is my refuge?”—but the embryo laughs, saying, “My deliverance has appeared.”
Whatever "mothers" exist under the sky—whether they be mineral, animal, or vegetable—

❧**3565.** What the <term>man of heart</term> <note>original: "sahib-dil." A Sufi term for a clairvoyant mystic whose inner "eye" is open to spiritual realities.</note> knows of your inner condition, you do not even know of yourself, O seeker.

### ***Setting forth that whatever is denoted by the terms "heedlessness," "anxiety," "indolence," and "darkness" is entirely derived from the body, which belongs to the earth and the lower world.***

Heedlessness was derived from the body; when the body is transformed into spirit, it inevitably beholds the <term>mysteries of the Unseen</term> <note>The hidden spiritual truths (Ghayb) that are normally veiled from human perception by physical distractions.</note>.
When the earth’s shadow is removed from the celestial atmosphere, there is no longer night, nor shade, nor sunset.
Wherever shade, night, or a shadowy place exists, it is caused by the earth, not by the heavens or the moon.
Likewise, it is from the damp faggots that smoke always arises, never from the pure and resplendent fires.

❧**3570.** The imagination falls into error and mistake, but the intellect is engaged only in acts of true perception.
Every state of heaviness, sloth, or indolence is derived from the body; the spirit, by its very lightness and subtlety, is always on the wing.
The face appears red from the predominance of blood; the face turns yellow from the movement of the <term>yellow bile</term>.
The face is white from the power of the <term>phlegm</term>; and it is from the <term>black bile</term> <note>These refer to the "Four Humors" of medieval Galenic medicine—blood, yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile. Mystics used these physical states to explain how bodily imbalances affect the soul's "weather."</note> that the face becomes swarthy.
In reality, God is the Creator of all effects, but the <term>formalists</term> <note>original: "followers of the husk." Those who only look at the outward, physical causes of things rather than the divine reality behind them.</note> see nothing but secondary causes.

❧**3575.** The kernel of the intellect that remains trapped in the husks of the world has no way to escape from the doctor or the disease;
But when a son of man is <term>born twice</term> <note>A reference to spiritual rebirth. Just as a child is born from the mother into the world, the mystic is "born" from the world into the spirit.</note>, he plants his foot upon the head of all secondary causes.
The <term>First Cause</term> <note>God, the ultimate origin of all things.</note> is his only religion; the secondary, material causes can do him no harm and bear him no enmity.
He flies like the sun across the spiritual horizon with his bride, Sincerity; for him, material form is merely a veil.
Nay, he exists beyond horizons and skies; he is without locality, dwelling like pure spirits and celestial intelligences.

<summary>Rumi uses the metaphor of childbirth to describe death as a liberation of the soul from the "womb" of the body. He explains that all spiritual darkness and sloth stem from our physical nature, whereas the enlightened "twice-born" soul transcends material causes to reach the divine.</summary>

**3580.** Indeed, our intellects are but His shadows; they fall, like shadows, at His feet.
