### *Comparison between Divine Decree and Human Analogy*

Know for certain that the divine decree is the revelation of the Holy Spirit, and the analogy formed by the individual intellect is subordinate to it.
The intellect receives its perception and enlightenment from the Spirit; how then should the Spirit be subject to the intellect's oversight?

**3585.** Yet the Spirit leaves an impression upon the intellect, and by virtue of that impression, the intellect exercises a kind of authority.
If the Spirit has inspired faith within you, as it did in Noah, where is the Sea, the Ark, and the Flood of Noah? <note>This suggests that the internal spiritual experience of a saint contains the reality of the historical events; the "Flood" is within.</note>
The intellect mistakes the impression for the Spirit itself, but the light of the sun is a far cry from the actual orb of the sun.
Thus, a <term>spiritual wayfarer</term> <note>original: "salik." A seeker traveling the path toward God.</note> is content with a small disk of light, so that by its radiance he may be guided toward the Divine Orb. <note>The original Persian uses the word "qurs," which means both a round loaf of bread and the solar disk. Rumi is playing on the idea of being sustained by a "loaf" of light while seeking the Sun itself.</note>
For this light here below is not permanent; it sets and fades with every day and night,

**3590.** While he whose home and dwelling is within the Divine Orb is perpetually immersed in that Light.
No cloud obstructs him, nor does the sun ever set; he is freed from the agonizing pain of separation.
Such a person originated from the heavens—or if he was of the earth, he has been transformed,
Because an earthly creature cannot endure the sun's beams striking it perpetually.
If the sun’s radiance struck the earth without ceasing, the earth would be so scorched that no fruit could grow from it.

**3595.** The life of a fish is always in the water; how could a snake have the power to follow its path?
Yet in the mountains, there are clever snakes who mimic the actions of fish within this Sea. <note>A metaphor for those who use logic or imitation to pretend they are at home in the "Ocean" of divinity, though their nature remains "earthly" or "mountainous."</note>

<summary>Rumi argues that human intellect and logic (analogy) are merely reflections of the Divine Spirit (Revelation). He uses the metaphor of the sun and its light to explain that while the intellect is guided by spiritual impressions, it is not the source itself, and only a "transmuted" soul can live permanently in the Divine Light.</summary>

### ***Rules for listeners and disciples when wisdom flows from the tongue of the Shaykh.***

To those who are tired, this is merely repetition; but to my eyes, it is the gift of life renewed.
A candle burns brighter with every flash of the flame; earth turns to gold through repeated heat.
If there are thousands of eager seekers and only one who is bored or disgusted, the Messenger will hold back the message.

**3605.** These messengers who speak the secrets of the Hidden Mind require a listener with the nature of <term>Isráfíl</term> <note>The archangel who blows the trumpet to resurrect souls; here, it refers to a listener who can bring the words to life within themselves.</note>.
They possess a dignity and pride like that of kings: they require devotion from the people of the world.
Until you show them the proper respect, how will you benefit from their words?
How can they give you that sacred trust until you have bowed low before them?
Why should they accept just any kind of service?—for they have come from the Sublime Palace of God.

**3610.** They are not beggars who should be grateful to you, you pretender, for every little service.
Yet, O you who are the very heart of God's awareness, despite the lack of desire in the audience, scatter the <term>Sultan’s</term> <note>The King or Sovereign (referring here to God's authority).</note> charity: do not hold it back!
O heavenly Messenger, ignore those who are weary and let your horse gallop forward!
Blessed is the <term>Turcoman</term> <note>Historically a nomadic warrior; here used as a metaphor for a bold and swift spiritual seeker.</note> who leaves arguments aside and whose horse leaps into the moat of fire—
Who drives his horse so hard in the race that it tries to reach the very peak of the sky;

**3615.** Who has closed his eyes to everything but God and to jealousy; who, like fire, has consumed both the dry and the wet <note>A common Persian idiom meaning "to consume everything indiscriminately" or "to be all-encompassing."</note>.
If his own repentance tries to find fault with him, he burns that repentance away first.
Truly, repentance does not even appear out of nothingness when it sees the passion of one whose presence brings good fortune.

### ***How every animal recognizes the scent of its enemy and takes precautions. The foolishness and ruin of the person who is an enemy of the One against whom no precaution, flight, or resistance is possible.***

The horse, though only an animal, recognizes the roar and scent of the lion, except in rare cases;
Indeed, every animal knows its own enemy by some sign or mark.

**3620.** The tiny bat does not dare to fly in the light of day: it comes out at night, like a thief, to find its food.

### ***The difference between knowing a thing by comparison and convention and knowing the essence of that thing.***

**3635.** The effects and the fruit of His mercy are visible to everyone, but how could anyone except Him know its <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "mahiyyat." The inner essence or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>? 
No one knows the true essence of the attributes of Divine Perfection except through their effects and by using comparisons. 
A child does not know the essence of <term>sexual intimacy</term> <note>original: "concubitus." The Latin term for the physical act of marriage.</note>, except when you tell him, "It is like sweet candy to you." 
How could the actual pleasure of intimacy be anything like the sweetness of candy, master? 
But, since you are still "childish" in your understanding, that wise man offered you an analogy using sweetness,

**3640.** So that the child might understand it by comparison, even though he does not know the <term>quiddity</term> or the true essence of the matter. 
Therefore, if you say "I know," it is not far from the truth; but if you say, "I do not know," it is also not a lie. 
If someone asks you, "Do you know Noah, the Messenger of God and the Light of the Spirit?"— 
And if you reply, "How could I not know him? For that spiritual Moon is more famous than the sun and moon in the sky: 
The little children at school and all the <term>Imáms</term> <note>Leaders of prayer in a mosque.</note> in the mosques

**3645.** Recite his name clearly in the <term>Qur’án</term> <note>The holy book of Islam.</note> and tell his story plainly as it has come down from the past"—

The visions which are now revealed to you—was it not the case that at first they seemed impossible to you?

### ***How the negation and affirmation of one and the same thing may be combined and reconciled through perspective and difference of aspect.***

It is possible to both deny and affirm the same thing: when the point of view is different, the relationship is twofold.
The scripture which says *you did not throw when you threw* <note>original: "wa ma ramayta idh ramayta." A reference to Quran 8:17. During the Battle of Badr, the Prophet Muhammad threw a handful of sand at the enemy; the verse explains that while he physically threw it, it was God who truly "threw" it to make it effective.</note> is a matter of perspective: it is both a negation and an affirmation, and both are correct.

❦**3660.** You threw that gravel, since it was in your hand; yet you did not throw it, for it was God who manifested His power.
The strength of one born of Adam has a limit: how else could a mere handful of earth cause the retreat of an entire army?
God said, “O Muhammad, the handful is your handful, but the throwing is from Me.” Because of these two perspectives, both the denial and the affirmation of the act are right.
The prophets are known by their enemies just as clearly as parents know their own children.
The unbelievers know the prophets, as they know their own children, by a hundred indications and a hundred signs,

❦**3665.** But, out of jealousy and envy, they hide their knowledge and addict themselves to saying, “I do not know.”
Then, since God has said, “The unbeliever knows,” why has He said in another place, “None knows them except Me, so stop seeking to know them;
Truly, they are hidden beneath My tents” <note>original: "Awliya'i tahta qibabi." A famous Divine Saying (Hadith Qudsi): "My saints are beneath My domes; no one knows them but Me."</note>? None knows them by immediate, personal experience except God.
Regard this subject—that you both know and do not know Noah—as something that can be explained through this same relationship of perspectives.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual perception and the nature of the "Perfected Human." Here, the text explores the Sufi concept of "annihilation" (fana), where the seeker’s individual attributes are consumed by the Divine presence, and begins a narrative illustration involving a disgraced minister in Bukhara.</meta>

The speaker said, “There is no such thing as a dervish <note>A dervish is a Sufi seeker or ascetic. The word literally means "one who stands at the door," representing a person at the threshold of the Divine.</note> in this world; and if a dervish does exist, that dervish is effectively non-existent.”

3670. He exists in terms of his physical essence, but his individual qualities have been completely dissolved into the attributes of God. 
He is like the flame of a candle in the presence of the sun: in a technical sense, the flame is still there, but in practical reality, it is gone. 
The essence of the flame exists—if you put a piece of cotton on it, the sparks will still burn it— 
But it is truly "non-existent" in that it gives you no light; the brilliance of the sun has overwhelmed it. 
It is like throwing an ounce of vinegar into two hundred <term>maunds</term> <note>original: *man*. A traditional unit of weight; in this context, roughly 3 kilograms or a significant bulk.</note> of sugar; when it dissolves,

3675. The taste of the vinegar is gone when you eat the sugar, even though that ounce remains as extra weight when you put the sugar on a scale. 
In the presence of a lion, a deer becomes paralyzed with fear; her own existence becomes nothing more than a veil for the lion's presence. 
These comparisons made by imperfect men regarding the actions of the Lord come from the heat of love; they are not meant as a sign of disrespect. 
A lover’s pulse might beat wildly and without formal etiquette as he weighs himself against the King. 
On the surface, no one seems more irreverent than the lover; yet in his heart, no one is more deeply respectful.

3680. Understand, O chosen one, that these two opposites—"respect" and "disrespect"—are reconciled through their relationship to the Beloved. 
The lover seems disrespectful from the outside because his claim of love implies he is an equal to the Beloved; 
But when you look at his inner state, where is the "claim"? He and his claims are completely vanished in the presence of that King. 
Consider the phrase "Zayd died" <note>original: *Māta Zaydun*. This is a classic example used in Arabic grammar to explain sentence structure.</note>: even though Zayd is the grammatical "agent" (the subject of the verb), he is not actually "acting" because he is dead. 
He is the agent only in the way we speak; in reality, he is the one who has been acted upon, and Death is his conqueror.

3685. How can he be called an "agent" when he has been so overpowered and every quality of a person who acts has been taken from him?

### ***The Story of the Minister of the Chief of the World, who fell under suspicion and fled from Bukhara in fear for his life; then love drew him back irresistibly, for life itself is of little value to lovers.***

In the city of Bukhara, a servant of the <term>Sadr-i Jahán</term> <note>Literally "Chief of the World," a title for a high-ranking ruler or religious leader.</note> fell under suspicion and went into hiding from his master. 
For ten years, he wandered in a daze—now in Khurásán, now in the mountains, now in the desert. 
After ten years, his longing became so great that he could no longer endure the days of separation from his beloved master. 
He said, “From now on, I cannot bear to be apart any longer. How can patience ever heal the state of one who has been cast away?”

3690. Without the Beloved, even the richest soil becomes barren, and fresh water turns yellow, foul-smelling, and dark.

<summary>This passage uses the metaphors of a candle in the sun and grammatical subjects to explain 'fana'—the mystical annihilation of the self in God. It introduces the story of a minister who, despite fearing for his life, is drawn back to his master by the overwhelming power of love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discourse on spiritual "annihilation" (fana), where the seeker's identity is dissolved into the Divine. Having discussed how the seeker becomes like a candle flame in the sun, the text now shifts to the theme of separation (firaq) and introduces a narrative illustration: the encounter between the Virgin Mary and the Archangel Gabriel, serving as a metaphor for the soul's encounter with the Divine Spirit.</meta>

The very air that gives us life can turn foul and diseased; a fire that burns bright eventually turns to cold ash and dust.
The garden that once looked like Paradise becomes a place of sickness, its leaves turning yellow and falling away in decay.
The sharpest mind, when cut off from its spiritual companions, becomes like an archer whose bow has snapped in two. 
It is this separation that makes Hell burn so fiercely; it is this separation that makes the elderly tremble with frailty.

⚜**3695.** If I were to speak of the agony of separation—which is like a shower of sparks—until the Day of Resurrection, I would have described only one part out of a hundred thousand. 
Therefore, do not even try to speak of its burning; simply say, "Lord, save me! Lord, save me!" 
In every moment of worldly joy, remember the inevitable parting that follows. 
Many people have been delighted by the same things that make you glad, but in the end, those things slipped away from them and vanished like the wind. 
They will escape from you as well; do not tether your heart to them. You must find a way to let go of the world before the world lets go of you.

### ***The appearance of the Holy Spirit (Gabriel) in the shape of a man to Mary when she was undressed and washing herself, and how she took refuge with God.***

⚜**3700.** Before your earthly possessions slip away, say to the fleeting forms of this world—just as Mary did—"I take refuge from you with the Merciful God." 
While in her private chamber, Mary saw a form that seemed to radiate life—a beautiful, heart-stealing presence. 
That "Trusted Spirit" <note>original: *Rūḥ al-Amīn*. This is a title for the Archangel Gabriel (Jibra'il) in Islamic tradition.</note> rose up before her from the earth, shining like the sun and the moon. 
Beauty itself stood unveiled before her, rising from the ground as brilliantly as the sun rises in the East. 
A tremor ran through Mary’s body, for she was unclothed and feared the presence of evil.

⚜**3705.** The form was so beautiful that if Joseph <note>In Sufi literature, the Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) represents the pinnacle of human physical and spiritual beauty. This refers to the Quranic story where women were so distracted by Joseph's beauty that they accidentally cut their hands.</note> had seen it clearly, he would have cut his own hands in amazement, just as the Egyptian women once did. 
It bloomed from the earth like a rose before her—like a vision that rises up from the depths of the heart. 
Mary lost all sense of herself, and in her state of "selflessness" <note>This "selflessness" or "ecstasy" refers to a state where the ego is silenced, allowing the soul to perceive the Divine directly.</note> she cried out, "I will leap into God’s protection!" 
For that pure-hearted woman had made it her habit to flee from the visible world toward the Unseen. 
Because she saw this world as a kingdom that would not last, she wisely built a fortress within the Divine Presence.

⚜**3710.** She did this so that at the hour of her death, she would have a stronghold that the Enemy <note>The "Enemy" here refers to Iblis (Satan) or the base ego (nafs) that tries to distract the soul at the moment of death.</note> could never hope to attack. 
She saw no better fortress than God's protection; she chose to live her life near that spiritual castle. 
She looked upon those loving, soul-shattering gazes that pierce the heart like arrows— 
Kingly armies are captivated by Him; even the masters of worldly intelligence are left witless in His presence. 
Hundreds of thousands of kings are held in His service; hundreds of thousands of "full moons" <note>A poetic metaphor for beautiful and enlightened people.</note> has He consumed with the fever of love.

⚜**3715.** Even Zuhra <note>original: *Zuhrah*. The planet Venus, personified in Persian poetry as a celestial musician or the symbol of ultimate beauty; here, she is silenced by the Archangel's presence.</note> does not have the courage to speak; even Universal Reason <term>Universal Reason</term> <note>original: *‘Aql-i Kull*. In Sufi philosophy, this is the first manifestation of the Divine Intellect, the blueprint of the cosmos. Even this highest intellect is humbled before the Divine Spirit.</note>, when it sees Him, humbles itself in his presence.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of the Divine and the human soul’s journey. Previously, the text explored the concept of "separation" through the story of Mary and the Archangel Gabriel. Now, the narrator reflects on the limitations of human perception and the necessity of spiritual "seasons"—the alternating states of sorrow and joy that refine the soul.</meta>

What can I say? For He has placed a seal upon my lips; His furnace has consumed the very channel of my breath. 
“I am the smoke of that fire, I am the evidence for it”—may that King be far removed from such false interpretations! 
In truth, there is no evidence for the existence of a sun except for the light of the high sun itself. 
What is a shadow that it should serve as evidence for Him? It is enough for the shadow that it should be humbled and laid low before Him.

**3720.** This divine <term>Majesty [Kibriya]</term> <note>original: "Kibriya" refers to the overwhelming greatness and pride of God that transcends human logic.</note> which I have attributed to Him speaks the truth: all human perceptions fall behind Him; He is always outstripping them. 
All perceptions are like riders on lame donkeys, while He is mounted on a wind that flies as swift as an arrow. 
If He chooses to flee, none can even find the dust of the King; and if they try to flee from Him, He is already there, barring the way ahead. 
All our faculties are restless; this is a time for the struggle of battle, not for the ease of the festal cup. 
One perceptive faculty flies like a falcon, while another, swift as an arrow, tears through its own path;

**3725.** Another is like a ship with spreading sails, and yet another turns back in retreat every moment. 
When a spiritual goal appears to them from afar, all these "birds"—our perceptions—speed up their pursuit. 
But when it vanishes from their sight, they become lost; like owls, they wander into every wilderness, 
Waiting with one eye closed and the other open, hoping that the delicious prey might appear again. 
When it stays hidden for long, they grow weary and say, "We wonder if that was a real prize or just a phantom."

**3730.** The right course is for them to rest for a short while, to gather their strength and vigor. 
If there were no night, people would consume themselves in the heat of their own greed and pursuit. 
Out of a desperate desire to amass gain, everyone would give their very bodies to be consumed by effort. 
Night appears like a treasure-house of mercy, so that they may be delivered from their greed for a short time. 
When a feeling of spiritual <term>Contraction [Qabd]</term> <note>Qabd is a Sufi term for a state of spiritual "tightness" or melancholy, often seen as a necessary period of internal focus.</note> comes over you, O traveller, it is for your own good: do not let your heart catch fire with grief.

**3735.** For in that opposite state of <term>Expansion [Bast]</term> <note>Bast is the state of spiritual "opening" or joy. Rumi argues that one cannot exist without the other.</note> and delight, you are spending your spiritual energy; that expenditure requires an "income" of preparation and inward pain to balance it. 
If it were always the season of summer, the blazing heat of the sun would penetrate the garden 
And burn the soil to its very roots, so that the withered plants would never become fresh again. 
If December appears sour-faced, it is actually being kind; summer is laughing, but it is also destroying. 
When spiritual contraction comes, look for the expansion hidden within it: stay fresh and do not let wrinkles mark your brow.

**3740.** Children are always laughing, but the wise are "sour-faced" or solemn: sorrow belongs to the liver <note>In medieval physiology, the liver was the seat of heavy emotions, while the lungs were associated with lightness and joy.</note>, and joy arises from the lungs. 
The eye of the child, like that of a donkey, is fixed only on the feeding stall; the eye of the wise man is busy calculating the final outcome. 
The child sees only the rich fodder in the stall, while the wise man sees the ultimate end: death at the hand of the Butcher. 
That fodder is bitter in the end, for it was the Butcher who provided it; He has set up a pair of scales to weigh our flesh. 
Go, and instead eat the fodder of wisdom, which God has given to us freely out of His pure bounty.

<summary>Rumi explains that human intellect cannot grasp the Divine essence, comparing our perceptions to slow animals chasing a swift wind. He further describes the spiritual necessity of 'contraction' (sorrow) and 'expansion' (joy), using the metaphor of winter preparing the ground for summer.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the spiritual encounter between Mary and the Archangel Gabriel into a broader philosophical discourse on the nature of suffering, joy, and the necessity of spiritual "contraction." Rumi uses the teachings of his predecessor, Sanai (the Sage of Ghazna), to explain that spiritual growth often requires the "eating of sorrow" to reach a higher state of wisdom.</meta>

**3745.** O servant of your own desires, you have understood "bread" to be the only meaning when God tells you, *“Eat of His provision.”* 
<note>original: "Eat of His provision" refers to Quran 67:15, which Rumi reinterprets here as a call to consume spiritual wisdom rather than just physical food.</note>
In this stage of your existence, God’s true provision is wisdom—a food that will not cause you to choke when you face the end of your life in the world to come.
If you close this physical mouth, another mouth will open; one that feeds on the morsels of <term>spiritual mysteries</term>.
If you can wean your body from the "milk" of the Devil—the pleasures of the lower self—you will find great happiness.
I have given only a partial and imperfect explanation of this, like meat that is barely boiled; hear the full truth from the **Sage of Ghazna**. 
<note>The "Sage of Ghazna" refers to Hakim Sanai (d. 1131), a highly influential Sufi poet whom Rumi deeply admired.</note>

**3750.** In his book, the <term>Iláhí-náma</term> <note>original: "The Book of the Divine," one of Sanai’s masterpieces of mystical poetry.</note>, that master of hidden truths explains it this way:
"Consume sorrow," he says, "and do not eat the bread of those who only increase your future grief. For the wise man 'eats' sorrow while the child only seeks 'sugar' or superficial joy."
The sweetness of joy in the hereafter is the fruit of the garden of sorrow grown here. This worldly joy is like a wound, while spiritual sorrow is the healing plaster.
When you encounter spiritual sorrow, embrace it with passion. It is like looking down upon the beauty of Damascus from the heights of **Rubwa**. 
<note>Rubwa is a hill near Damascus famous for its panoramic, beautiful views. Rumi uses it to illustrate how a high perspective transforms a difficult climb into a magnificent vision.</note>
The wise man sees the wine while looking at the grape; the lover of God sees the reality of a thing even when it does not yet exist.

**3755.** Just the day before yesterday, I saw porters arguing and shouting: "Let me carry the load! Let me lift it like a lion!"
Because they saw the profit to be gained from that hard work, they were trying to snatch the heavy burden from one another.
What comparison can there be between a reward from God and a reward from a lowly creature? The latter gives you a mere coin, but the former gives you a treasure.
God gives you a golden treasure that stays with you even when you lie buried under the sand; it is not a heritage you must leave behind.
It runs ahead of your funeral procession and becomes your companion in the grave—that place where everything else feels foreign.

**3760.** For the sake of your final day, be "dead" to your ego now, so that you may be united with **Everlasting Love**, my fellow servant.
Through the veil of this inner struggle, renunciation sees the "face" of the Beloved—bright as a pomegranate flower—and the "tresses" of the One we desire.
Sorrow acts as a mirror for the spiritual warrior; it is through this "opposite" that the face of the other "opposite"—joy—becomes visible.
After the pain of one state, its opposite—gladness and victory—will show its face.
Observe these two qualities of <term>contraction and expansion</term> in your own hand: surely, after the fist is closed, it must open again. 
<note>In Sufi psychology, "Qabd" (contraction/sorrow) and "Bast" (expansion/joy) are two necessary alternating states of the heart, much like the beating of a pulse.</note>

**3765.** If the fingers were always clenched or always open, the owner would be considered disabled.
A person's work and life are regulated by these two states; they are as vital to a human as wings are to a bird.
Consider Mary: she was suddenly filled with dismay, gasping like a fish out of water.

❧**3785.** Such Divine grace flows like the river Nile—but because we act like Pharaohs <note>In the Quranic story, the Nile turned to blood for the Egyptians (the "Pharaohs") but remained fresh water for the Israelites.</note>, it becomes like blood.

Do you not see that even a long-suffering friend appears like a snake when you have grown hostile toward him? 
His true nature remains unchanged; it is only in appearance that he has become so evil to you.

## **How the Deputy, moved by love, made up his mind to return to Bukhara recklessly.**

Leave the candle of Mary lit, for that ardent lover is now going to **Bukhara**, 

❧**3790.** Driven by great impatience and the blazing furnace of love. Now, let us transition to the story of the **Chief of the World** <note>original: "Şadr-i Jahān," a title for a high-ranking religious or political leader.</note>.

In the presence of a **Shaykh** <note>A spiritual master or elder.</note> you are essentially in "**Bukhara**" <note>original: "Bukhara." It is the home of my Friend and the city of my King: in the eyes of the lover, this is the true meaning of 'love for one's homeland.'"

### ***How a loved one asked her lover who had traveled in foreign countries, "Which city did you find the most beautiful, most crowded, most magnificent, rich, and charming?"***

A loved one said to her lover, "O youth, you have seen many cities abroad. 
Which of them is the most beautiful?" He replied, "The city where my sweetheart lives."

❦**3810.** Wherever the carpet is spread for our King, that place is a vast plain, even if it is as narrow as the eye of a needle. 
Wherever a **Joseph** <note>In Persian poetry, Prophet Joseph is the ultimate archetype of physical and spiritual beauty.</note> as beautiful as the moon may be, that place is Paradise, even if it is the bottom of a well.

### ***How his friends tried to stop him from returning to Bukhara and threatened him, and how he said, "I do not care."***

A sincere adviser said to him, "O reckless man, think of the consequences, if you have any sense at all. 
Consider the future and the past with reason: do not let yourself be burnt like a moth in the flame. 
How can you go to Bukhara? You are mad; you are only fit for chains and the prison-house.

❦**3815.** The Master is champing at the bit in his wrath against you; he is searching for you with twenty eyes. 
He is sharpening the knife for you: he is like a starving dog, and you are like a bag of flour."

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the narrative follows the "Wakíl" (the Deputy), who is so overwhelmed by his longing for the presence of his master in Bukhara that he disregards all warnings of the danger and potential execution awaiting him there. After you have escaped and God has given you an open road, why are you returning to prison? What is wrong with you?
Had there been ten types of guards over you, you would have needed all your wits just to get free of them.

### *How the lover, driven by love, told the person who counselled and scolded him, "I don't care."*

**3830.** He said, "O counsellor, be silent! How long, how long will you scold?
Do not give me advice, for the chains upon me are incredibly heavy.
My bonds are more painful than your advice; the doctor who taught you knew nothing of love.
In that school where love was increasing my pain, **Bú Hanífa** <term>Bú Hanífa (Abu Hanifa): The 8th-century founder of the Hanafi school of Islamic law.</term> and **Sháfi'í** <term>Sháfi'í: The 9th-century founder of the Shafi‘i school of Islamic law. Do not threaten me with being killed, for I am deathly thirsty for my own blood."
For lovers, there is a death at every moment; truly, the death of lovers is not of just one kind.

**3835.** The lover has two hundred lives from the **Soul of Guidance**, and those two hundred he sacrifices at every instant.
For every life he gives, he receives ten as its price: read from the **Quran** <note>original: "ten like unto them." This refers to the Quranic verse (6:160) promising a tenfold reward for good deeds.</note>.
"If that Beloved with the beautiful face sheds my blood, I will dance in triumph as I pour out my life for Him.
I have tested it: my death is actually my life. When I escape from this life, it is to live forever.
Kill me, kill me, O trusted friends! Truly, in my being killed is life upon life." <note>original: "Iqtuluni ya thiqati..." A famous Arabic phrase attributed to the mystic Al-Hallaj, expressing the desire for the ego to die so the soul can live in God.</note>

**3840.** O You who make the face shine, O Eternal Spirit, draw my spirit to Yourself and generously grant me a meeting with You.
I have a Beloved whose love burns my very heart; if He wished to walk upon my eyes, He would be welcome.
Speak in **Persian**, even though **Arabic** <note>While Arabic was the language of formal theology, Rumi often preferred Persian for the intimate expression of mystical love.</note> is sweeter; for Love has a hundred other tongues besides these two.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the narrative follows the "Wakíl" (the Deputy), who is so overwhelmed by his longing for the presence of his master in Bukhara that he disregards all warnings of the danger and potential execution awaiting him there. **3845.** Since the lover has repented <note>In this context, 'repenting' means the lover has turned away from his fear and intellectual excuses to return to the path of love.</note>, now be careful of misunderstanding, for he will give his lecture like the masters of mystical love—even if it is from the gallows.
Although this lover is going to Bukhárá, he is not going there to attend academic lectures or to learn from a worldly teacher.
For lovers, the only lecturer is the beauty of the Beloved; their only book, lecture, and lesson is His face.
They are silent on the outside, but the shrill sound of their inner repetition is rising up to the throne and the high-seat of their Friend.
Their only lesson is enthusiasm, the whirling dance, and the trembling of spiritual agitation; it is not the *Ziyádát* <term>Ziyádát: A famous technical book on Islamic law; here it symbolizes dry, formal education.</term> or the chapter on "the chain" <note>original: "al-silsila"; this refers to a logical or legal sequence of arguments, which Rumi compares to the 'chains' of the Beloved's hair.</note>.

**3850.** The "chain" of these people—the lovers of God—is the musk-scented curls of the Beloved; they do have a question about "the circle," but it is the circle of the Friend's presence.
If anyone asks you about the legal question of "the purse" <note>A reference to financial laws or disputes.</note>, tell them that God’s treasure cannot be contained in any purse.
If there is talk of *khul’* and *mubárá* <term>Khul’ and mubárá: Types of divorce or mutual release in Islamic law; Rumi uses these technical terms to rhyme with 'Bukhárá,' suggesting the lover has 'divorced' the world.</term> among them, do not judge: inwardly, they are only speaking of "Bukhárá."
The mention or recollection of anything produces a specific spiritual effect, just as every quality has its own essential nature.
In Bukhárá you reach the peak of the sciences; but when you turn toward lowliness <note>original: "ba-khwárí"; a pun on the name Bukhárá. Rumi suggests that true spiritual knowledge is found through "lowliness" or humility.</note>, you are finally freed from them.

**3855.** That man of Bukhárá did not suffer the frustration of academic knowledge: he was fixing his eyes on the "sun of vision."
No one who has found the way to direct spiritual vision in solitude will seek power through different types of book-learning.
When one has become a companion to the beauty of the Soul, they will feel a deep dislike for traditional, secondhand learning.
Vision is far superior to knowledge: this is why the physical world dominates the minds of the common people,
Because they see this world as "ready money" (immediate), while they think of the next world as a "debt" (far off).

### *How that loving servant turned his face towards Bukhárá.*

**3860.** With a throbbing heart, the lover—who shed tears mixed with blood—set out for Bukhárá in a great hurry.
The desert sands of Ámún <note>The desert region near the Oxus River.</note> felt like soft silk to him, and the great Oxus River seemed like a tiny pond.
To him, that wilderness was like a rose-garden: he was falling on his back with laughter, like a rose in full bloom.
Physical candy is found in Samarcand; but his lips found a spiritual sweetness from "Bukhárá," and that sweetness became his entire faith.
"O Bukhárá, you have increased the intellect of others, but you have robbed me of both my intellect and my formal religion.

**3865.** I am searching for the Full Moon: that is why I have become thin as a crescent moon. I am searching for the Prince in this 'shoe-row' <term>Shoe-row: The humble entrance where people leave their shoes; the lover is willing to take the lowest place just to be near the master.</term>."

### *How the reckless lover entered Bukhárá, and how his friends deterred him from showing himself.*

Joyously he entered Bukhárá near his beloved and him who was the abode of his security,
Like the man intoxicated with love who in his imagination flies to heaven: the Moon embraces him and says, “Embrace me!”
Every one that saw him in Bukhárá said to him, “Arise and go before showing thyself! Do not sit still! Flee!

**3875.** For that Prince is seeking thee in anger, that he may wreak a ten years' vengeance on thy life.
By God, by God, do not plunge in thine own blood, do not rely on thy artful words and wiles.
Thou wert the <term>Sadr-i Jahán: A title meaning "Chief of the World," referring here to the high-ranking religious and political ruler of Bukhara.</term>'s constable and a noble; thou wert the trusted agent and master-engineer in his affairs.
Then thou didst act treacherously and flee from punishment: thou hadst escaped: how hast thou let thyself be caught again?
With a hundred devices thou didst flee from tribulation: has folly brought thee hither or thy fate?

**3880.** O thou whose intellect jeers at Mercury <note>In medieval astrology, Mercury (Utārid) was the "Celestial Scribe" and the planet associated with the highest human intellect and calculation.</note>, Destiny makes a fool of intellect and the intelligent.
Luckless is the hare that seeks to encounter the lion: where is thy cleverness and intelligence and quick-wittedness?
The wiles of Destiny are a hundred times as many as thine: the Prophet has said, ‘When Destiny comes, the wide field is straitened’ <note>original: "idha jā'a al-qadar daqa al-fadā"; an Arabic proverb meaning that when God's decree arrives, even the vastest escape route feels narrow.</note>.
There are a hundred ways and places of refuge on left and right, but they are barred by Destiny, for it is a dragon.”

### *How the lover answered those who scolded and threatened him.*

He said, “I am <term>dropsical: Suffering from dropsy (edema), a condition where the body swells with fluid. In Sufi poetry, this is a classic metaphor for the spiritual "thirst" that increases the more one drinks from the Divine source.</term>: the water draws me, though I know that the water too will kill me.

**3885.** None afflicted with dropsy will flee from the water, even if it checkmate and ruin him two hundred times.
If my hands and belly become swollen, yet the passionate desire for the water will not abate and depart from me.
At the time when they ask me of my inward state, I say, ‘Would that the Sea were flowing within me!’
Let the water-skin, my belly, be burst by the waves of the water: if I die, my death is acceptable.

Wherever I see the water of a stream, jealousy comes over me—I wish that I might be in its place, flowing toward the source.

**3890.** With hands swollen like a tambourine and a belly like a drum, I am proclaiming my love for the water, just as the rose does by opening its petals to the rain. 
If that Trusty Spirit <note>The "Trusty Spirit" usually refers to the Archangel Gabriel (Rūḥ al-Amīn), acting here as the divine executioner or messenger.</note> spills my blood, I will drink draught after draught of that blood, just as the earth soaks up the rain.
I am a drinker of blood, like the earth and like the embryo in the womb; ever since I became a lover, this has been my trade.
During the night I boil on the fire of passion, like a kettle; all day until nightfall, I drink blood like the thirsty sand.
I repent that I ever set any clever plan in motion to escape, or that I fled from the path of his divine anger.

**3895.** Let him drive his anger against my intoxicated soul without restraint! He is the Feast of the Sacrifice <term>Eid al-Adha: the festival commemorating the willingness of Abraham to sacrifice his son; here, it represents the beloved's power over the lover.</term>, and the lover is the buffalo prepared for the altar.
Whether the buffalo sleeps or eats, the master only fattens it for the Feast and the eventual slaughter.
Consider me to be like the cow of Moses <note>In the Quranic and Biblical tradition, the sacrifice of a specific cow was used to identify a murderer. When the dead man was struck with a piece of the sacrificed cow, he temporarily returned to life to name his killer.</note> that brought life back to the dead; every limb of mine is a means of raising the spiritually dead back to life.
The cow of Moses was a sacrifice; even her smallest limb brought a murdered man back to life.
At its touch, the murdered man sprang up from his place—at the words spoken by God: *Strike the body with part of the sacrificed cow.*

**3900.** O my noble friends, slaughter this "cow" which is the fleshly soul, if you desire to bring the spirits of true insight back to life!
I died as a mineral and became a plant; I died as a plant and rose to the animal kingdom.
I died from the animal state and became a human; why then should I fear? When have I ever become "less" by dying?
At the next stage of my journey, I shall die to the human state, so that I may soar and lift my head among the angels.
And I must escape even the state of the angel, for as the scripture says: *Everything is perishing except His Face.* <note>original: "kullu shay’in hālikun illā wajhahu." This is a quote from the Quran (28:88), emphasizing that only the Divine Essence is eternal.</note>

**3905.** Once more, I shall be sacrificed and die to the angelic state; I shall become that which cannot even be imagined.
Then I shall become non-existence; and non-existence says to me, in tones as loud as an organ: *Verily, unto Him shall we return.* <note>original: "Innā ilayhi rāji'ūn." A common phrase (Quran 2:156) recited during times of death or loss.</note>
Understand death to be the thing the community is agreed upon: that the Water of Life <term>The "Water of Life" (Āb-e Hayāt) is a legendary spring found in the "Land of Darkness," often associated with the prophet Khidr.</term> is hidden within the Land of Darkness.
Grow from this riverbank like a water-lily—greedy for the water and craving death as one who suffers from dropsy. <note>Dropsy (edema) was historically associated with an unquenchable thirst; the more the sufferer drinks, the more the illness worsens, yet they cannot stop.</note>
The water is death to the sufferer, and yet he seeks the water and drinks it—and God knows the right course best.

**3910.** Oh, how cold is the lover who is draped in the felt garment of shame, fleeing from the Beloved out of fear for his own life!
O you who are a disgrace even to the weak-hearted, behold hundreds of thousands of souls clapping their hands as they rush toward the sword of His love!
You have seen the river, so empty your small jug into it. Why would the water try to flee from its own source?
When the water inside the jug enters the river, it disappears within it and *becomes* the river.

### ***How the lover reached his Beloved after he surrendered his life.***

Prostrating himself on his face and head, rolling like a ball, he approached the Prince <term>Sadr: A high-ranking official or religious leader; here, it refers to the Beloved who holds the power of life and death.</term> with tearful eyes.
The crowds were waiting, their heads craned, watching to see if the Prince would burn him or hang him.

Like a moth, this lover mistook the lethal sparks for a welcoming light; in his foolishness, he fell in and was cut off from life.”

**3920.** But the candle of Love is not like a physical candle: it is radiance upon radiance upon radiance.
It is the opposite of a fire that consumes; it may look like a flame, but in reality, it is pure sweetness.

### ***A description of the mosque that kills its guests, and the fearless seeker who stayed there.***

Listen closely to this story, O seeker of wisdom! There was once a mosque on the outskirts of the city of Rayy <term>Rayy: An ancient and major city located near modern-day Tehran, Iran.</term>.
No one ever spent the night there without dying of terror by morning, leaving their children orphans.
Many a destitute stranger entered its doors at sunset only to be carried to the grave at dawn, vanishing like the fading stars.

**3925.** Pay close attention to this tale! The dawn of understanding has come, so shake off your slumber.
People used to say that fierce Jinnís <term>Jinní: Supernatural creatures in Islamic tradition, often translated as 'genies,' made of smokeless fire and capable of interacting with humans.</term> lived inside, killing guests with invisible, blunt swords.
Others claimed it was the result of magic and a talisman <note>original: "talisman"—a charmed object or inscription intended to protect a place or exert a magical influence.</note>, an enchantment that acted as a mortal enemy to all life.
Some suggested, “Post a clear warning on the door: 'O guest, do not stay here.
Do not sleep here if you value your life; otherwise, death will spring an ambush for you in this place.'”

**3930.** And others would say, “Bolt the door at night so that no heedless traveler can wander in by mistake.”

### ***How the guest entered the mosque.***

The situation continued this way until a guest arrived at nightfall who had heard these marvelous rumors.
He was determined to put the legend to the test, for he was incredibly brave and had grown weary of his earthly life.
He said to himself, “I care very little for my physical body; what does it matter if one small grain is lost from the great treasure of the spirit?
Let this bodily form perish—who am I in truth? Does the physical figure matter at all when my soul is eternal?

**3935.** Since the Divine Spirit was breathed into me by the grace of God, I am the very Breath of God, temporarily held apart from the body's windpipe.”

### How the people of the city warned the lover-guest against sleeping in the mosque and threatened him with death.

You are a stranger here and do not realize that anyone who spends the night in this place perishes.”

We have seen this not just once, but a hundred times; we didn’t hear it second-hand, we saw it with our own eyes.
The Prophet said, ‘The religion is sincerity (<term>nasíhat: good advice or sincere loyalty to others</term>)’; that sincerity is the opposite of betrayal (<term>ghulúl: unfaithfulness or embezzlement</term>).

### The lover's reply to those who scolded him.

He replied, “O sincere advisors, I have become utterly weary of this worldly life.
I am a restless vagabond, seeking and even inviting blows; do not expect a wanderer to take the safe path.
I am not the kind of beggar who looks for scraps of food; I am the reckless seeker who hunts for death itself.
I am not the traveler who seeks a few coins in his palm, but the swift traveler who wishes to cross the bridge into the next world—

<image-desc>floral fleuron</image-desc> **3950.** I am not the one who clings to every shop in the marketplace; rather, I am the one who leaps away from physical existence to strike gold in the mine of reality.
Death and the migration from this earthly home have become as sweet to me as leaving a cage and flying away is to a captive bird.
Imagine a cage placed in the middle of a lush garden, where the bird can see the rose-beds and the trees through the bars,
While outside, a chorus of free birds sings beautiful tales of liberty.
At the sight of that green paradise, the caged bird loses its appetite for seed; it no longer has patience or any desire for rest.

<image-desc>floral fleuron</image-desc> **3955.** It pokes its head through every gap in the wire, hoping to tear the shackles from its legs.
If its heart and soul are already outside like that, imagine its joy when you finally open the door!
But this is not the case for a bird caged by worldly anxieties, with hungry cats circling its enclosure.
How could a bird in such dread and sorrow ever wish to leave its cage?
It would wish for a hundred more cages to be built around its current one, just to save its feathers from being plucked by the enemy.”

<meta>Continuing from the story of the traveler who bravely entered the Guest-Killing Mosque, the text now pivots to a philosophical critique of those who cling to physical life out of a lack of spiritual vision. The translator uses Galen, the famous Greek physician, as a symbol for worldly knowledge that fears the transition of death.</meta>

The love of **Galen** <note>original: "Jālīnūs," the 2nd-century Greek physician whose medical theories were foundational in the Islamic world.</note> is only for this present life, for his medical art is only useful here; he has not practiced any art that is worth anything in the marketplace of the afterlife. In that realm, he finds himself no different from the most unlearned commoner.

❧**3960.** This is just as the wise Galen said, driven by his passion for this world and his desires within it—

> “I would be content if only half of my **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit: in medieval medicine, the life-force or 'pneuma' that animated the physical body</term> remained, so that I might continue to see the world, even if only through the backside of a mule.”

He sees "cats" <note>symbolizing death or predatory fate</note> all around him in troops, and so the bird of his soul has lost all hope of flying. Or perhaps he has judged everything outside of this physical world to be non-existence, failing to perceive the hidden resurrection that dwells within that seeming void. He is like an embryo that the Divine Bounty is trying to draw out into the world, yet it clings and flees back toward the safety of the mother's belly.

❧**3965.** Divine Grace is turning the embryo's face toward the exit, while the embryo tries to make its permanent home in the mother's loins,

> Saying, “Oh, I wonder, if I fall outside of this city and this place of pleasure, will I ever see this dwelling-place with my own eyes again?
> Would there be a door in that strange, noisy city so that I might look back into the womb?
> Or would there be a path for me, as narrow as the eye of a needle, so that the womb might remain visible to me from the outside?”

That embryo is entirely unaware of the vast world outside; it is a stranger to it, just like Galen.

❧**3970.** It does not know that the **humours** <term>humours: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term> which sustain it in the womb are actually supplied from the world outside. Even the four elements of our world <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note> receive a hundred forms of support from the **City beyond space** <note>original: "Lā-makān," the "Placeless" or spiritual dimension beyond physical coordinates.</note>. If a bird finds water and seeds inside its cage, those things have surely been brought there from a garden or a wide field. The spirits of the prophets behold that Garden from within the cage of the body at the time they are being freed and transported; hence they are free from the fears of Galen and the world, shining like the moon in the heavens.

❧**3975.** And if this saying attributed to Galen is merely a legend, then my answer is not directed at Galen himself, but to whoever first said it, for a luminous heart has never been their companion. The bird of such a person's spirit became like a mouse seeking a hole the moment it heard the "cats" of death cry out, “Halt!” Because of that fear, his spirit—like a mouse—deemed its true home and shelter to be in this "hole" of a world. Within this hole, he began to build and acquired a knowledge suited only for living in a dark burrow;

❧**3980.** He chose the trades that would benefit him there, things that would be of use only in such a cramped space. Because he turned his heart away from the idea of going outside, the path to deliverance from the body was barred to him. If a spider had the nature of the **'Anqá** <term>'Anqá: a mythical bird of immense size and wisdom, similar to the Phoenix, representing the high-soaring human soul</term>, why would it spend its life weaving a tent of flimsy gossamer? The "cat" of death has thrust its claws into the cage of the body; the names of those claws are pain, delirium, and sickness. The cat is Death itself, and its claws are diseases: it strikes at the bird of the soul and its feathers.

❧**3985.** The sick man darts like a panicked bird from corner to corner, seeking a remedy. In this scene, Death is like the **cadi** <term>cadi: a judge (original: "qādī")</term>, and the disease is the witness testifying against you. This witness arrives like the judge’s bailiff, summoning you to the place of judgment. As you try to flee your fate, you beg him for a respite: if he agrees, you are granted a little more time; otherwise, he simply says, “Arise and come with me.”

<meta>Continuing from the philosophical critique of Galen—who feared the loss of physical life—the narrative returns to the traveler in the "Guest-Killing Mosque." The focus shifts from the general fear of death to the specific warnings given by the townspeople to the guest, and Rumi’s subsequent teaching on the difference between true spiritual courage and empty bravado.</meta>

The seeking of a respite consists in remedies and cures, that you may patch thereby the tattered cloak—the body. At last, one morning, **Death** comes angrily, saying, “How long will this respite be? Now, prithee, be ashamed!”

❧**3990.** O envious man, ask your pardon of the King before such a day as that arrives. For he who rides his horse into the darkness and altogether removes his heart from the Light is fleeing from the witness and his own purpose; for that witness is calling him to judgement.

### How the people of the mosque blamed the guest once more for his intention of sleeping in the mosque by night.

The people said to him, “Do not act with foolhardiness; depart, lest your bodily vesture and your soul become in pawn to Death.” From afar it seems easy, but look well! For in the end, the passage is grievous.

❧**3995.** Many a man has hanged himself and broke his neck, and at the moment of agony sought something for his hand to cling to. Before the battle, the fancy of good or evil is slight and makes no deep impression in a man’s heart; but when he enters into the fray, then to that person the matter becomes woeful.

Since you are not a lion, beware, do not step forward, for that **Doom** is a wolf, and your soul is the sheep; but if you are one of the **Abdal** <term>Abdal: literally 'the Substitutes,' a high rank of saints in Sufi cosmology who are said to be the spiritual pillars of the world</term> and your sheep has become a lion, come on securely, for your death has been overthrown.

❧**4000.** Who is the **Abdal**? He that becomes transmuted; he whose "wine" <note>symbolizing worldly passions or the lower self</note> is turned into "vinegar" <note>symbolizing spiritual sobriety or preservation</note> by Divine transmutation. But you are drunken with pride and from mere opinion think yourself to be a lion: Beware, do not advance!

God has said of the unrighteous **Hypocrites** <note>original: "Munafiqun," those who feigned faith in the time of the Prophet Muhammad</note>, “*Their valour amongst themselves is a great valour.*” <note>A reference to the Quran 59:14, describing those who appear strong but are internally divided and fearful.</note> Amongst one another they are manly, but in a warlike expedition they are as the women of the house.

The **Prophet** <note>Muhammad</note>, the commander-in-chief of the things unseen, said, “There is no bravery, O youth, before the battles.”

❧**4005.** The drunken make a froth when there is talk of war, but when war is raging they are as useless as froth. At the time when war is spoken of, his scimitar is long and extended; at the time of combat, his sword is sheathed like an onion <note>implying it is layered in excuses or entirely absent</note>.

At the time of premeditation, his heart is eager for wounds; then, in action, his bag is emptied of air by a single needle. I marvel at the seeker of purity who, at the time of polishing, shrinks from being handled roughly. **Love** is like a lawsuit; to suffer harsh treatment is the evidence. When you have no evidence, the lawsuit is lost.

❧**4010.** Do not be aggrieved when this **Judge** <note>God</note> demands your evidence: kiss the snake in order that you may gain the treasure. That harshness is not directed towards you, O son; nay, it is towards the evil qualities within you.

The blows of the stick with which a man beats a rug he inflicts not on the rug, but on the dust in the rug. If that vindictive fellow lashes the horse, he directs the blows not at the horse, but at its stumbling.

He critiques those who boast of courage but lack the "evidence" of endurance and suffering required for true spiritual love.</summary>

In order that it may be delivered from the vice of stumbling and may move well: you must imprison the grape juice in the vat in order that it may become **wine**. <note>Rumi uses wine as a common Sufi metaphor for spiritual ecstasy and divine love, which only matures through the "confinement" of discipline.</note>

❧ **4015.** Someone once asked, “You have struck that little orphan so many blows; were you not afraid of the Divine wrath?”
The striker replied, “O dear soul and friend, when did I strike him? I was striking at the **devil** <note>original: "shaitan"</note> that lives within him.”
If your mother says to you, “May you die!” she is wishing for the death of your evil nature and the death of your iniquity.
Those people who flee from such correction have dishonored their own manhood and the company of true men.
The mockers drove them back from the spiritual war, and so they remained infamous and weak.

❧ **4020. Do not listen to the boasting and roaring of those who talk idly: do not go into the battle-line with such fellows.**
Since *they would have added to you naught but corruption*, <note>This is a reference to the Quran, Surah At-Tawbah 9:47, regarding those who lack true faith joining a military expedition.</note> God said: “Turn away from companions who lack courage.”
For if they go along with you, the true warriors will become weak, like hollow straw.
They place themselves in the line with you on the field of battle; then they flee, and their cowardice breaks the heart of the formation.
Therefore, it is better to have a small army without such people than to be reinforced by **Hypocrites**. <note>In the Islamic tradition, "Hypocrites" (Munafiqun) refers specifically to those who outwardly professed Islam but worked against the community from within.</note>

❧ **4025. A few well-sifted almonds are better than a great many sweet ones mixed with bitter ones.**
The bitter and the sweet may sound the same when they are poured out and rattle against each other; the defect only appears because they are not the same at their core.
The faithless person has a timid heart because he lives in a state of doubt regarding the next world.
He travels along the road but does not know any of the stages; one whose heart is blind always steps with fear.
When a traveler does not know the way, how can he proceed? He goes with many hesitations, while his heart is full of anguish.

❧ **4030. If anyone shouts, “Hey! This is not the way!” he will halt right there and stand still in terror.**
But if the traveler’s wise heart truly knows the way, how could every "hey" and "ho" affect his ears?
Therefore, do not journey with these "camel-hearted" <note>A Persian idiom for a coward or someone who is easily spooked.</note> ones, for in the hour of distress and danger, they are the ones who will fail you.
Then they flee and leave you alone, even though in their boasting they claimed to possess the magic of **Babylon**. <note>Babylon was traditionally associated with powerful sorcery and illusions.</note>
Beware! Do not ask those who love luxury to fight; do not ask **peacocks** to join the hunt and the chase.
The **carnal nature** <term>carnal nature: "nafs" in Persian/Arabic, refers to the lower ego or animal soul that seeks comfort and worldly status</term> is like a peacock: it tempts you and speaks empty words just to lure you away from your spiritual post.

### *How Satan said to the Quraysh, “Go to war with Ahmad (Mohammed), for I will aid you and call my tribe to help”; and how, when the two battle-lines confronted each other, he fled.*

As an example, **Satan** became the "hundred-and-first" <note>meaning an extra, unexpected addition</note> in the army of the **Quraysh** <note>The powerful merchant tribe of Mecca that opposed the Prophet Muhammad.</note> and spoke deceptive words, saying, “Truly, I am your protector.”
When the Quraysh had assembled at his command and the two armies faced one another, Satan suddenly saw a host of **angels** on the road beside the ranks of the Faithful.

**4040.** Turning on his heel, he began to retreat, saying, “I behold a marvellous host”—

The **fleshly soul** <note>original: "nafs"</note> and the **Devil** both have (ever) been one person (essentially); (but) they have manifested themselves in two forms,

**4055.** You have such an enemy as this in your inward part: he is the preventer of the intellect, and the adversary of the spirit and of religion.
At one moment he dashes forward like the Libyan lizard; <note>The poet refers to the "dhabb" or spiny-tailed lizard, known for its quick movements and habit of retreating into burrows.</note> then (again) in flight he darts away into a hole.
Just now he has (many) holes in the (human) heart, and from every hole he is putting out his head.
The name that denotes the Devil’s becoming hidden from (men’s) souls and going into that hole is <term>khunús</term> (slinking back),
For his *khunús* is like the *khunús* of the hedgehog: like the head of the hedgehog, he pops in and out;

**4060.** For God hath called the Devil <term>Khannás</term> (the slinker), <note>This term appears in the final chapter of the Quran, "The People" (Surah An-Nas), describing the "whisperer who slinks away."</note> because he resembles the head of the little hedgehog.
The head of the hedgehog is continually being hidden because of its fear of the cruel hunter,
Until, when it has found an opportunity, it puts out its head: by such a stratagem the snake becomes its prey.
If the **fleshly soul** had not waylaid you from within, how would the brigands have any power to lay a hand upon you?
On account of the exigent myrmidon, who is **Lust**, the heart is captive to greed and cupidity and bane.

❦ **4070.** Through trickery, magic can make a mere straw appear as a mountain; or conversely, it can weave a mountain to look like a straw.

The essence of magic is this: it breathes incantations and, with every moment, transforms the way we perceive reality.

❦ **4075.** But in this world where such dark arts exist, there are also spiritual magicians <note>Referring to the Prophets and Saints who possess "lawful magic" (divine wisdom) to counter the ego's deceptions.</note> who can defeat such sorcery.
In the same field where this potent poison grows, the antidote has also sprung up, my friend.
The antidote says to you, “Seek protection from me, for I am closer to you than the poison itself.”
The soul's words are a dark magic leading to your ruin; my words are a holy magic, acting as the counter-spell to her enchantments.

### ***How the critics repeated their warnings to the guest of the mosque where visitors were known to perish.***

The Prophet said, “Truly, there is a kind of magic in eloquent speech”; <note>original: 'Inna min al-bayāni la-siḥran'. A famous saying of the Prophet Muhammad suggesting that beautiful speech has a power similar to enchantment.</note> and that noble hero spoke the truth.

❦ **4080.** “Hey, do not do something so reckless! Depart, O generous man, and do not bring suspicion upon us or this mosque.
For an enemy will speak out of malice, and tomorrow a villain will stir up a fire of suspicion against us,
Saying, ‘Some criminal strangled him, knowing he would be safe from suspicion under the cover of the mosque.’
They will say this so they can blame the murder on the mosque and, because the mosque already has a bad reputation, the real killer might escape.”
Do not bring this shadow of doubt upon us, O man of brave spirit, for we are not safe from the schemes of our enemies.

❦ **4085.** “Come now, leave! Do not be so daring; do not cling to such a vain desire, for it is as impossible as trying to measure the planet Saturn with a yardstick.”
Many people like you have bragged about their luck, and in the end, they were left in such despair that they tore out their beards, hair by hair.

### ***How the guest replied to them, using the parable of the field-watchman who tried to scare off a camel with a small drum, even though the camel was already carrying the Great Sultan’s massive war-drums.***

❦ **4090.** The birds, hearing the rattle of that little drum, would fly away in fear, leaving the field safe from their hunger. 
But then the Sultan, the noble King Mahmud, <note>Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998–1030), a famous ruler often used in Persian poetry to represent the "Divine King" or absolute authority.</note> passed by that way and pitched his great imperial tent nearby.

❦ **4095.** This camel wandered into the cornfield, and the boy began beating his little drum to protect the grain.

Truly, your threats are like that boy's toy drum compared to the awesome sights these eyes of mine have witnessed.

❦ **4100.** O comrades, I am not an inexperienced traveler who would halt his journey because of idle fears or fancies.

The Prophet has taught us that whoever is certain of their reward will give generously and in advance.
Whoever truly sees the hundredfold compensation for their gift will immediately surrender what they have in order to reach that goal.

❦ **4105.** In the <term>bazaar</term> <note>A marketplace, used here as a metaphor for the world of commerce and human endeavor.</note> of this world, everyone is tied to their business, waiting for the moment they can trade their money for a profit.
With gold held tight in their purses, they sit expectantly, hoping for a gain that will make them eager to spend what they have saved.
When a merchant sees merchandise that promises a profit far exceeding his own, his affection for his current stock grows cold;
He only remained enamored with his own goods because he had not yet seen any advantage superior to them.
It is the same with knowledge, accomplishments, and trades: a person is only consumed by them because they have not yet seen a greater excellence.

❦ **4110.** While we know of nothing better than this life, life seems precious to us; but when something better appears, the very name of "life" becomes a slippery, empty thing.
A lifeless doll is as dear as life itself to a child, until that child grows into a man.
This world’s imagination and fancy are like that doll: as long as you are a spiritual child, you have need of them;
But when the spirit escapes the limits of childhood, it enters into Union with the Divine: it is finished with the toys of physical perception, imagination, and fancy.

<summary>Rumi uses the parable of a camel carrying a royal drum to explain that a soul transformed by Divine experience is unmoved by worldly threats. **4115.** The goods of this world and the physical body are like snow melting away to nothing; yet God is their purchaser, for it is written that **God has purchased** the lives and possessions of the faithful. <note>original: "Inna Allāha ishtarā" — A reference to Quran 9:111, which describes a spiritual contract where God "buys" the believer's soul and wealth in exchange for Paradise.</note>

**4120.** For in the tested spiritual Way, knowledge is inferior to certainty, yet it sits high above mere opinion.

Knowledge leads eventually to vision, O knowing one: if their knowledge became intuitive certainty, they would see the "Hell" of their own worldly desires even now.
Vision is born immediately from certainty, just as fancy and delusion are born from mere opinion.

**4125.** See in that same Chapter, **Abundance**, the explanation of this: namely, how the "knowledge of certainty" transforms into the "intuition of certainty." <note>The poet is distinguishing between *Ilm al-yaqin* (knowledge by inference) and *Ayn al-yaqin* (knowledge by seeing/experience).</note>

That which God said to the rose to cause it to laugh in full-blown beauty, He said also to my heart, making it a hundred times more beautiful.

**4130.** He bestowed on my heart that same touch that reached the cypress and made its stature straight, and that of which the narcissus and the wild-rose partook.
He gave that which made sweet the soul and heart of the sugar-cane, and that from which the lowly creature of earth gained the exquisite form of a beauty from **Chigil**. <term>Chigil</term> <note>A city in Central Asia (modern Uzbekistan/Turkestan) legendary in Persian poetry for the extraordinary beauty of its inhabitants.</note>

### ***Comparison of the true believer's flight from tribulation and his impatience in affliction to the agitation and restlessness of chickpeas and other vegetables when boiling in the pot, and to their running upwards in order to jump out.***

Look at a chickpea in the pot, and how it leaps up when it is subjected to the fire.

❦ **4160.** At the moment it begins to boil, the chickpea rises continually to the top of the pot and raises a hundred cries,
Saying, "Why are you setting this fire under me? Since you bought and chose me, why are you turning me upside down?"
The housewife continues hitting it with her ladle. "No!" she says: "Boil nicely and do not jump away from the one who tends the fire.
I do not boil you because I hate you; rather, it is so that you may gain taste and flavor,
So that you may become nourishment and mingle with the **vital spirit**: <note>original: "Jān" — the soul or life-force.</note> this affliction of yours is not because you are despised."

<summary>This passage explores the necessity of divine "affliction" as a tool for spiritual refinement, comparing the suffering of a believer to a chickpea being boiled to become nourishment. It emphasizes that prophets and saints endure trials not because they are abandoned, but because they are being prepared for union with the Divine.</summary>

### The Boiling of the Soul: The Chickpea in the Pot

❦ **4165.** “You, when you were green and fresh, were drinking water in the garden; that drinking of water was for the sake of this fire.”
**God’s mercy** <note>original: "Rahmat" — Divine compassion.</note> precedes **His wrath**, so that through that mercy, the afflicted person might have the strength to suffer trial.
His mercy eternally came before His wrath so that the **stock-in-trade** <note>the fundamental assets or "capital" of a being.</note>—which is existence—could be acquired;
For without pleasure, flesh and skin do not grow; and unless they grow, what would the love of the **Friend** <note>original: "Dost" — referring to God as the Beloved.</note> have to consume?
If, because of that divine requirement, acts of wrath occur, it is so that you may eventually give up that earthly stock-in-trade.

❦ **4170.** Afterward, **Grace** will come again to offer an excuse for the suffering, saying, “Now you have washed yourself clean and have leaped forth from the river of tribulation.”
The housewife says, “O chickpea, you fed in the springtime; now **Pain** has become your guest—entertain him well,
So that the guest may return home giving thanks for your hospitality, and may speak of your generosity in the presence of the **King**,
So that the **Bestower of Favor** <note>God, the source of all blessings.</note> may come to you instead of just the favor itself, and so that all other favors may envy you.
I am <term>Khalíl</term> <note>original: "Khalíl-Allāh" — The Friend of God, a title for the Prophet Abraham.</note>, and you are my son: lay your head before the knife, for *lo, I see in a dream* that I must sacrifice you.”

❦ **4175.** Lay your head before my wrath with a heart unmoved, so that I may cut your throat like that of <term>Ismá’íl</term> <note>original: "Ismá’íl" — Ishmael, who in Islamic tradition is the son Abraham was commanded to sacrifice as a test of faith.</note>.
I will cut off your head, but this head is one that is immune to being truly cut or dying;
Yet your willingness to give yourself up is the goal of God's eternal purpose: O <term>one who submits</term> <note>original: "Moslem" — one who has surrendered their will to God.</note>, you must seek this self-surrender.
Continue, O **chickpea**, to boil in tribulation, so that neither your "existence" nor your "self" remains within you.
If you formerly laughed in that earthly garden, you are now the rose of the garden of the spirit and the spiritual eye.

❦ **4180.** If you have been parted from the garden of water and earth, you have now become food in the mouth and have entered into the world of the living.
Become nourishment, and strength, and thoughts! Formerly you were merely milk-sap; now, be a lion in the jungles!
By God, you grew from His attributes in the beginning; now go back nimbly and swiftly into those same attributes.
You came from the cloud, the sun, and the sky; then you became diverse attributes and began to ascend back to heaven.
You came in the form of rain and heat; now you shall enter into the goodly **Divine attributes**.

❦ **4185.** You were once a part of the sun, the cloud, and the stars; you became soul, action, speech, and thoughts.
The existence of the animal arose from the "death" of the plant; therefore, the command “<term>slay me, O trusty friends</term>” <note>original: "Uqtuluni ya thiqati" — A famous ecstatic cry attributed to the mystic Al-Hallaj, suggesting that the death of the ego is the beginning of true life.</note> is right.
Since such a victory awaits us after the checkmate of death, the words “verily, in my being slain there is a life” are true.
Action, speech, and sincerity become the food of the **angel**, so that by means of this ladder, the soul mounts to heaven,
Just as when a morsel of food becomes the nourishment of a human, it rises from its inanimate state and becomes possessed of a soul.

### How the housewife apologized to the chickpea, and the wise purpose in keeping the chickpea on the boil.

The mistress says to it, “In the past, I—like you—was a part of the earth.

### **_Commentary on the tradition of Muhammad, the Chosen One <note>original: "Mustafá"</note>, peace be upon him, regarding the principle that the Scripture has an outer meaning and an inner meaning, and that its inner meaning contains further inner meanings, up to seven levels of depth._**

Know that the words of the Scripture have an outer sense, and beneath that outer sense lies an inner meaning that is exceedingly overpowering;

4245. And beneath that inner meaning lies a third interior layer, where all human intellects lose their way.
The fourth inner meaning of the Scripture has been perceived by no one at all, except for God, the peerless and incomparable.
In the Scripture, my son, do not look only at the outward form: remember that the Devil <note>A reference to the story of Iblis (Satan), who refused to bow to Adam because he only saw Adam's physical form of clay, failing to see the divine spirit within.</note> regarded Adam as nothing but clay.
The outer meaning of the Scripture is like a person’s physical body: the features are visible, while the spirit is hidden.
A man's own uncles might see him for a hundred years and yet never see even the tip of a hair of his true inner state.

### **_An explanation that the retreat of the prophets and the saints, peace be upon them, to mountains and caves is not for the purpose of hiding themselves out of fear of being disturbed by people, but for the purpose of guiding people to the right way and encouraging them to abandon the material world as much as possible._**

4250. As for the claim that the saints dwell in the mountains so that they may be hidden from the eyes of men:
In reality, they are more prominent in the sight of the people than a hundred mountains, and they plant their footsteps upon the Seventh Heaven.
Why, then, should one who has traveled beyond a hundred seas and mountains need to hide or seek refuge in a physical mountain?
He has no need to flee to the hills—he is the one in pursuit of whom the "colt" of the Heavens has worn out a hundred horseshoes.
The celestial sphere has revolved for ages and never even glimpsed the dust of the spirit; for this reason, the Heavens wear the dark colors of mourning.

4255. If, outwardly, the spirit-being <term>Peri: In Persian mythology, a winged, supernatural spirit known for being hidden from human sight.</term> is hidden, then a human being is a hundred times more hidden than the spirits.
In the view of the intelligent, a human is indeed a hundred times more concealed than the spirit who is hidden.
Since, in the view of the intelligent, an ordinary human is hidden, how much more hidden must be the "Adam" <note>Referring here to the "Perfect Man" or the chosen spiritual guide.</note> who is pure and chosen by God in the unseen world!

### **_A comparison of the outward form of the saints and the form of their speech to the rod of Moses and the life-giving breath of Jesus, peace be upon them both!_**

The true human is like the rod of Moses <note>Which appeared to be a simple wooden staff but possessed the power to transform and perform miracles.</note>; the true human is like the life-giving breath <note>original: "incantation"</note> of Jesus.
For the sake of justice and proper decorum, the heart of the true believer is held in the hand of God, between His "two fingers" <note>A reference to a famous prophetic tradition (Hadith): "The hearts of all the children of Adam are between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful." ### ***Parable of the foal's refusing to drink the water because of the shouting of the grooms.***

As he <note>Sanai</note> has said in his discourse, a foal and its mother were drinking water.

❦**4295.** Its mother asked, “O foal, why are you always refusing to drink this water?”

❦**4305.** Carry the water-skin down to the river—the skin that longs for water—so that you may

## *Commentary on the verse of the Qur’án: “And raise the battle-cry against them with your horsemen and men on foot.”* <note>original: Qur'an 17:64. In this context, it refers to the psychological warfare the Devil wages against the soul.</note>

4330. Saying, “I have tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. I will walk the Way of religion later; I still have plenty of time.”

Because the falcon does not hunt flies: only spiders catch flies.
The spider, which is the **Devil**, has power over flies like you, not over the partridge and the eagle.
The cry of the devils is the driver of the damned; the cry of the Lord is the guardian of the blessed saints,
To the end that, because these two cries are so far apart, not a single drop of the **sweet sea** may mingle with the **briny sea** <note>This refers to the Quranic metaphor of the two seas—one fresh and one salt—that meet but do not mix, representing the separation between the spiritual and the worldly.</note>.

### **_How the magical cry came at midnight to the ears of the guest in the mosque_**

❧**4345.** Now hear the tale of the terrible cry, by which that fortunate man was not dismayed.
He said, "How should I fear? For this is the drum of the **Festival** <note>The "Festival" (Eid) represents spiritual liberation or the Resurrection.</note>. Let the drum fear, since blows belong to it!
