Now hear how, when this drum boomed, he cooks the pot containing the broth of felicity.

❧**4350.** When that man of insight heard the drum, he said, "How should my heart be afraid of the drum of the Festival?"

The time has come for me, like **Haydar** <note>Haydar, meaning "The Lion," is a title for ‘Alí ibn Abí Tálib, famous for his extraordinary bravery in battle.</note>, to seize a kingdom or to leave this body."

❧**4355.** So much gold poured down that the youth feared that its abundance might block the doorway.

<summary>Rumi uses a story about a guest in a haunted mosque to illustrate that the terrifying "cries" of the Devil are illusions. When the seeker bravely confronts these fears, the magical illusions shatter, revealing a treasury of spiritual gold.</summary>

❧**4360.** In the same way, children break bits of pottery and call them "gold," gathering the fragments in their skirts.

❧**4370.** You reach that conclusion because of your own state; that human nature is in you, not him. The "fire" and "thorns" of false opinion belong to your side of the world.

❧**4375.** The first is like a flattering friend who eventually burns you, while the other illuminates the heart at the moment of spiritual union.

### **The Meeting of the Lover with the Chief of the World**
<note>original: *Şadr-ı Jahān*—literally "Chief of the World," a title for a high-ranking official, used here as a metaphor for the Divine Beloved.</note>

<meta>Continuing from the previous passage where Rumi explored the hidden connections between hearts—illustrated by the lover's journey to the Sadr-i Jahan in Bukhara—the text now expands this principle of attraction to the entire physical and spiritual cosmos. The desire implanted in the female for the male is so that they may complete each other's work.

### How each element attracts its fellow-kind <term>Congener: A person or thing of the same type or origin.</term> that has been imprisoned in the human body by the surrounding, dissimilar elements.

The Earth says to the earth within the body, "Return! Leave the spirit behind and come back to me like dust. **4425.** The upper air <note>original: "aether," referring here to the element of fire or heat.</note> calls to the heat of the body, saying, "You are made of fire; follow the path back to your origin." There are seventy-two diseases <note>In medieval Islamic medicine, seventy-two was a traditional number representing the variety of ailments caused by the imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note> in the body, caused by the elements pulling at the body without needing a rope. These elements are like four birds with their legs tied together: death, sickness, and disease are what loosen those ties.

When death has released their legs from one another, every "bird-element" surely flies away to its own home.

**4430.** The tension between these original sources and their derivatives <note>The physical parts of the body derived from the universal elements of earth, water, air, and fire.</note> constantly creates pain in our bodies, so that it may tear these physical mixtures apart and allow each part, like a bird, to fly back to its home. But Divine Providence <term>Divine Providence: God's intervention and guidance in the universe; the sustaining power that keeps the soul and body together.</term> prevents them from rushing away and keeps them together in health until the set time of death.

God says, "O parts, your time is not yet known to you; it is useless for you to try to fly away before your term is up." Since every physical part of the body seeks support, imagine the state of the soul—a stranger here—in its separation from its true home!

### How the soul is likewise drawn to the world of spirits, and how it longs for its home, becoming separated from the physical parts that act as a chain on the leg of the spiritual falcon.

**4435.** The soul says, "O my lowly earthly parts, my exile is even more bitter than yours, for I am celestial." The soul's desire is for wisdom and the sciences; the body's desire is for orchards, meadows, and vineyards.

<summary>Rumi explains that all existence is governed by a "law of attraction" where parts long to return to their origins. <meta>Continuing from the previous discussion of elemental attraction, where the earth and water within the human body long to return to their origins, Rumi now elevates this principle to the spiritual realm. The desire of the soul is to ascend to the heights; the desire of the body is for worldly gain and the means to find its fodder.

❧**4440.** That divine exaltedness also feels desire and love for the soul; from this fact, you can understand the meaning of the verse: *He loves them and they love Him.* <note>original: "Yuhibbuhum wa yuhibbunahu" (Quran 5:54). ❧**4445.** However, the desire of the lovers makes them grow thin and frail, while the desire of the "loved ones" makes them fair and beautiful.

❧**4455.** Who is it that pulls you, O restless seeker? It is He who does not even allow you to finish this word.

He filled your heart with a hundred passionate desires, then disappointed you and broke your heart.

❧**4460.** Since He broke the wings of your first intention, how could the existence of the "Wing-breaker" not be perfectly clear to your mind?

### ***Commentary on the Tradition that Mustafá (the Chosen One), peace be upon him, said: "Do not declare me to be more excellent than Jonah, son of Amittai."***

The Prophet said, “No preference should be given to my ascension as being superior to the ascension of Jonah <note>original: "Yúnus ibn Mattá"</note>.
Mine was an ascent up to heaven, and his was a descent down into the belly of the Great Fish, because nearness to God is beyond any physical calculation.”
To be near to God is not to go up or down; to be near to God is to escape from the prison of your own existence.

❧ **4515.** What room does non-existence <term>fana: the mystical state where the self is extinguished in the Divine</term> have for "up" or "down"? Non-existence has no "soon," "far," or "late."
The workshop and the treasury of God are found in non-existence. You are deluded by your physical existence; how could you truly know what non-existence is?
The heart of the matter is that this "defeat" of theirs, my friend, does not look like our worldly defeats at all.
They rejoice in being humbled and destroyed, just as we rejoice in hours of success and honor.
The provision of having no provisions is the only inheritance assigned to the Prophet; poverty and lowliness are his true pride and glory.

❧ **4520.** One of the captives said, “If our adversary is truly as you describe, then why did he laugh when he saw us bound in chains?
Since you claim he has been transformed, and that his joy is not caused by this worldly prison or his own freedom from it,
Then how could he rejoice at the subjection of his enemies? How could he be puffed up by this victory and conquest?
His soul rejoiced because he easily gained God's help and the upper hand over fierce lions like us.
From this, we know that he is not truly free from the desires of the flesh; it is only because of this world that he is happy and glad at heart.”

❧ **4525.** “Otherwise, how could he laugh at us? For those who live for the other world are compassionate and kind to both the evil and the good.”
Thus did those captives whisper to each other as they discussed the matter, saying, “Be careful, lest the guard hear us and rush to tell those words to that spiritual King.”

### ***How the Prophet, peace be upon him, became aware of their criticism regarding his joy.***

Although the guard did not hear those words, they reached the ear that hears directly from the presence of God.
The scent of Joseph’s spirit was not noticed by his own jailer, but his father Jacob inhaled it from far away. <note>A reference to the Quranic story of Joseph; Jacob could smell his son's scent on a shirt sent from Egypt, despite being hundreds of miles away, due to his spiritual connection.</note>

<summary>Rumi explains that spiritual closeness to God is not about physical height or worldly victory, using the comparison between Muhammad’s heavenly ascent and Jonah’s descent into the whale. He then presents a challenge from the Prophet's captives, who mistake his spiritual joy for worldly pride.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion where the Prophet explains that nearness to God is not about physical distance or height, but about the extinction of the self, the text now transitions to the Prophet’s unique spiritual vision and his true motivation for conflict—not for worldly gain, but for the salvation of souls.</meta>

❧ **4530.** The devils at the high threshold of Heaven cannot overhear the secrets of the mystery-knowing Tablet <term>The Preserved Tablet: the celestial record of all human destiny</term>;
Yet when Muhammad went to sleep and reclined on his bed, the secret came to him and circled around him.
He whose heart is open receives the spiritual gifts, not merely he who reaches out with long fingers.
The gleaming star became a watchman and drove the devils away, saying, “Cease your theft and receive the true secret from Ahmad.” <note>original: "Ahmad" – another name for the Prophet Muhammad</note>
O you whose eyes are turned toward your shop from early morning, listen: go to the mosque instead and seek the portion of grace allotted by God.

❧ **4535.** The Prophet then understood their private thoughts and said, “That laughter of mine did not come from a place of malice.
These captives are already spiritually dead and decayed; in my view, it is not the act of a true man to kill those who are already dead.
Who are they, truly? For even the moon is split <note>A reference to the 'Splitting of the Moon,' a miracle attributed to Muhammad</note> when I set foot upon the battlefield.
Back when you were free and powerful, I already saw you bound in chains just like this.
O you who pride yourself on your wealth and family, in the eyes of the wise, you are as precarious as a camel perched upon a narrow water-spout.”

❧ **4540.** “Ever since the bowl of my physical form fell from the roof <note>A Persian idiom meaning a secret has been revealed or a great change has occurred; here, the falling away of the ego</note>, the reality that 'everything destined to come is already here' has rolled before my inner eye.
I look at the sour, unripe grape and I clearly see the finished wine; I look at nothingness, and I see the reality of existence.
I look into the deepest consciousness and see a hidden universe, even before Adam and Eve had emerged into this world.
I saw you all, shackled and humbled, at the moment when all mankind were gathered like tiny ants on the Day of Alast <term>The Day of Alast: the primordial moment before creation when God asked the souls of humanity, 'Am I not your Lord?'</term>.
My knowledge was not increased by the creation of the heavens that stand without pillars.

❧ **4545.** I have always seen you fallen headlong, even before I was formed from water and clay.
I saw nothing new today that would cause me to gloat; I saw this same fate even during your time of worldly prosperity.
While you were bound in the invisible chains of Divine Wrath—and what a terrifying Wrath it is!—you were eating sugar that contained a hidden poison.
If your enemy delighted in eating such poisoned sugar, would you truly feel envy toward him?
You were eating that poison with joy, while Death had already secretly seized you both by the ears.

❧ **4550.** I did not wage war to gain victory or to conquer the world,
For this world is merely a carcass and vile carrion; why would I hunger for such a thing?
I am not a dog that would fight over the remains of the dead; I am like Jesus: I come to bring the dead back to life.
I was breaking through the ranks of battle for the sole purpose of delivering you from certain destruction.
I do not cut men’s throats so that I may have power, glory, or a great following;

❧ **4555.** Rather, I cut some throats so that the entire world might be liberated from the tyranny of those throats.
For in your ignorance, you make a habit of rushing toward the flames like moths,
While I, like a man intoxicated by God, desperately drive you away with both hands to save you from falling into the fire.”

<summary>In these verses, the Prophet Muhammad explains that his spiritual vision transcends time, seeing the ultimate fate of his enemies long before their physical defeat. He clarifies that his battles are not for worldly power, which he views as worthless carrion, but are acts of spiritual mercy intended to save souls from their own destructive ignorance.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the Prophet Muhammad explains that his apparent military conquest is not born of a desire for power, but is a divine instrument for the salvation of his enemies. He refutes the idea that their previous worldly successes were true victories.</meta>

That which you deemed victories for yourselves—thereby you were sowing the seed of your damnation.
You were calling one another most earnestly to fight against me, and by doing so, you were riding your horses towards the dragon.

❧ **4560.** You were overpowering me, whilst in the very act of overpowering, you yourselves were being overpowered by the lion of Time. <note>The "lion of Time" refers to the inescapable decree of God that governs human history.</note>

### *Showing that the rebellious sinner, in the very act of overpowering, is overpowered; and in the very moment of victory, is made captive.*

The robber overpowered and murdered the merchant and carried off the gold; he was just engaged in that business when the magistrate arrived.
If at that time he had fled from the merchant, how should the magistrate have set the police on him?
The robber's overpowering of the merchant was in reality his being overpowered and punished, because his act of violence cost him his life.
His prevailing over the merchant becomes a trap for him, in order that the magistrate may arrive and take retaliation on the murderer.

❧ **4565.** O you that have become mighty over the people and are steeped in warfare and victory,
That One—God—has purposely caused them to be routed, so that while drawing you on, He may at last bring you into the net.
Beware, draw the reins! Do not push on in pursuit of this fugitive, lest you have your nostrils pierced with a nose-ring like a beast of burden.
When by this device He has drawn you into the trap, after that you will see the onset of the people pressing in crowds upon you.
When did the intellect ever rejoice in this kind of victory, inasmuch as in this victory it saw ruin?

❧ **4570.** The intellect is keen-eyed and possessed of foresight, for God has powdered it with His own collyrium. <term>Collyrium: a medicinal powder or salve used for the eyes, used here as a metaphor for divine insight that allows one to see the spiritual reality behind physical appearances.</term>
The Prophet said that the folk destined for Paradise are often those who seem feeble or worsted in quarrels, because of their noble accomplishments—
This is because of the perfection of their prudence and their habit of thinking ill of their own egos, not from any deficiency of intellect, cowardice, or weakness of religious faith.
In giving the advantage to their enemies, they have hearkened in secret to the wisdom of the scripture: *Had there not been true-believing men...* <note>original: "Law lā rijālun mu'minūna" – A reference to Quran 48:25, explaining that God stayed the hands of the Muslims at Mecca to protect the secret believers living among the pagans.</note>
To keep their hands off the accursed infidels became a duty for the sake of delivering those true believers.

❧ **4575.** Read the story of the covenant of Hudaybiya: *It was He who restrained your hands from them.* <term>Hudaybiya: A 7th-century peace treaty where Muhammad chose a diplomatic retreat over a bloody victory, demonstrating that spiritual restraint is superior to worldly triumph.</term> From that saying, perceive the meaning of the whole story.
Even in victory, the Prophet deemed himself subdued by the snare of Divine Majesty.
“It is not because I suddenly marched against you before dawn and took you captive that I laugh at your chains;
I laugh because I am dragging you in chains and shackles toward the cypress garden and the roses of Paradise.
O wonder! We are bringing you in bonds from the merciless fire to the place abounding in verdure;

❧ **4580.** With heavy chains, I am dragging you from the direction of Hell toward the everlasting Paradise.”

<summary>Rumi explains that worldly victory is often a spiritual trap, using the analogy of a robber caught by the law. He concludes by showing that the Prophet's "conquest" is actually a paradoxical act of mercy, forcibly pulling souls away from destruction toward salvation.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page where the Prophet Muhammad explains that his military actions are actually a form of divine mercy, this section explores the psychology of the spiritual path. It describes how God draws different types of souls—the fearful and the loving—back to Himself.</meta>

Every person who follows blindly on this Way, whether they are good or evil, is being led by God, bound as they are, into His Presence.
All travel this Way in the chains of fear and suffering, except for the saints.
Others are dragged along this Path reluctantly, except for those who are familiar with the mysteries of the Divine action.
Strive so that your inner light becomes radiant, so that your journey of devotion and service to God may become effortless.

4585. You take children to school by force because they are blind to the benefits of knowledge;
But when the child becomes aware of those benefits, he runs to school—his soul expands with joy at the thought of going.
A child goes to school in great distress because he has not yet seen the rewards for his labor;
But when he earns even a single <term>dáng</term> <note>original: "dáng"; a small Persian coin or fraction of a currency, symbolizing even the smallest tangible reward.</note> from his handiwork and puts it in his purse, he stays awake at night with excitement, like a thief.
Strive until the rewards for your obedience to God arrive; then, you will be the one others envy for your devotion.

4590. The command "come against your will" <note>A reference to a Quranic verse where God commands the heavens and earth to obey; here it represents the person who obeys out of duty or fear.</note> is for the one who has become a blind follower of religion; "come willingly" is for the one who is shaped by sincerity.
The former loves God for the sake of some secondary cause <note>Such as the promise of Paradise or the fear of Hell.</note>, while the latter possesses a pure, selfless love.
The former loves the Nurse for the sake of the milk, while the latter has given his heart for the sake of this <term>Veiled One</term> <note>A metaphor for the Divine Essence, which remains hidden from those who only seek material or spiritual rewards.</note>.
The child—the blind follower—has no knowledge of Her beauty; he has no desire in his heart for Her except for the milk,
While the other is truly the lover of the Nurse; he is selfless and single-minded in his passionate love.

4595. Therefore, he who loves God out of hope and fear reads the book of religious conformity with great effort,
While he who loves God for God's sake—where is he? For he is beyond self-interest and secondary causes.
Whether he is like this or like that, as long as he is a seeker of God, God’s attraction is pulling him toward the Divine.
Whether he loves God for some benefit other than Him, so that he may continually receive His goodness, 
Or whether he loves God for His very Self and nothing else, out of fear of being separated from Him—

4600. The searching and seeking of both these lovers come from that one Source; this captivation of the heart is caused by that <term>Heart-ravisher</term> <note>A common Sufi term for God, describing the way Divine Beauty "captures" or "steals" the human heart.</note>.

### ***How the Beloved attracts the lover in such a way that the lover neither knows it nor expects it, nor does it even cross his mind; no sign of that attraction appears in the lover except for a fear mixed with despair, yet he still persists in his search.***

We returned to this point in the story: if the attraction of that lover had not been hidden within the <term>Sadr-i Jahán</term> <note>original: "Sadr-i Jahán"; literally "Pillar of the World." In Rumi’s story, this is a title for the high official or spiritual master who is the object of the lover's intense devotion.</note>,
How would the lover have been so restless in separation, and how would he have come running back to his home?
The desire of the "loved ones" is hidden and veiled, while the desire of the lover is announced with a hundred drums and trumpets.

<summary>Rumi explains that while some people follow God out of fear or hope for reward (like a child forced to school), others follow out of pure, selfless love. Ultimately, both types of seekers are being pulled toward the Divine by God's own hidden attraction.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page where the poet discusses those who love God out of duty versus those who love Him with pure, selfless sincerity. The text now transitions from the philosophical benefits of devotion to the specific story of a lover from Bukhara and the concept of "dying before one dies."</meta>

Here is a story worthy of deep consideration, but the man from Bukhárá <note>A historic city in modern-day Uzbekistan, often used in Persian literature as a center of culture and spirituality.</note> has grown weary from waiting in expectation;

4605. So we shall omit it, for he is occupied in searching and seeking, hoping that before death arrives he may see the face of his beloved.
His goal is to escape death and find true deliverance, because the sight of the beloved is the Water of Life <note>A legendary spring that grants eternal life; in Sufism, this represents divine knowledge or the presence of the Beloved.</note>.
Anyone whose presence does not push back the fear of death is not the true beloved, for such a person has neither fruit nor leaf to offer the soul.
The essential point, O intoxicated and longing lover, is that true love is found in that state where death itself becomes sweet to you.
O youth, the true sign of sincere faith is finding sweetness in the moment of death.

4610. If your faith, dear soul, is not yet like this, it is not perfect; go then, and seek to make your religion complete.
Whenever someone has become "death-loving" for your sake—desiring your ego to die so you may truly live—without it being hateful to your heart, that person is your true beloved.
When that inner dislike of death is gone, it is no longer "death" in the traditional sense; it is merely the appearance of death, while in reality, it is a migration to a higher state.
When the fear is gone, dying becomes beneficial; thus, it is true that death is repelled by the presence of the Beloved.
The true Beloved is God, and those to whom He has said, "Thou art Mine and I am thine."

4615. Now listen, for the lover is approaching—the one whom Love has bound *with a cord of palm-fibre* <note>original: "bi-hablin min masad"; a Quranic reference (111:5) used here to describe being bound by the inescapable pull of Divine Love.</note>.
When he finally beheld the face of the <term>Sadr-i Jahán</term> <note>original: "Sadr-i Jahán"; literally "Chief of the World," a title for a high-ranking official or spiritual leader. Here, it represents the manifestation of the Divine.</note>, you might say the bird of his spirit flew right out of his body.
His physical form fell like a piece of dry wood; his vital spirit turned cold from the crown of his head to his toes.
Whatever incense or rose-water they applied to revive him, he neither moved nor spoke.
When the King saw the lover’s saffron-colored <note>A poetic way to describe a pale or pallid face, often associated with the "illness" of longing.</note> face, he dismounted from his horse and came toward him.

4620. He said, "The lover seeks the beloved with heat and passion; but when the beloved actually appears, the lover vanishes."
You are a lover of God, and God is of such a nature that when He arrives, not a single hair of your "self" remains.
At that divine look, a hundred people like you would vanish; it seems to me, sir, that you are in love with self-naughting <note>The Sufi concept of *fana*, or the annihilation of the individual ego in the presence of the Divine.</note>.
You are like a shadow in love with the sun; when the sun arrives, the shadow is quickly made into nothing.

### ***How, in the presence of Solomon—on whom be peace—the gnat appealed for justice against the Wind.***

A gnat came from the garden and the grass, and it began to demand justice from Solomon <note>In Islamic and Near Eastern tradition, King Solomon was given power over all creatures, the wind, and the Jinn, and could understand the speech of animals.</note>,

4625. Saying, "O Solomon, you deal out justice to the devils, to the children of Adam, and to the <term>Jinn</term> <note>Spiritual beings mentioned in the Quran, often translated as 'genies'.</note>.
The birds of the air and the fish of the sea are under the protection of your justice; who is so lost that your bounty has not found them?
Give justice to us, for we are truly miserable; we are being kept away from the orchards and the rose-gardens."
Solomon replied, "The difficulties of every weak creature are solved by me; indeed, the gnat is the very symbol of weakness."

We are famous for being weak and fragile, while you are famous for your kindness and your care for the lowly.

❧ **4635.** When we were born, injustice died on that very day; who, then, has committed an act of injustice in our time?
When the light dawned, the darkness vanished; for darkness is the very source and support of injustice.
Look, some of the devils are performing work and service for us, while the others are bound in shackles and bonds.

❧ **4640.** So that burning sighs may not soar upward; so that the sky and the stars may not be shaken;
So that the highest heaven <term>Empyrean: the Arsh, or the throne of God</term> may not tremble at an orphan’s wail; and so that no living soul may be ruined by violence.
We have established a law of justice throughout the kingdoms of the earth, so that no cry of “O Lord!” <note>original: "Ya Rabb!"</note> should need to ascend to the skies.
O oppressed one, do not look to Heaven for help, for you have a heavenly king right here in the physical world.”

❧ **4645.** Through his oppression we are in great distress; with closed lips, we are suffering great torment because of him.”

### ***How Solomon (peace be upon him) commanded the plaintiff gnat to bring its adversary to the court of judgment.***

Then Solomon said, “O you with the beautiful voice, it is necessary for you to listen with your whole soul to the command of God.
God has said to me: ‘Beware, O Judge! Do not hear one side of a dispute without the other side being present.’
Until both parties come into the presence of the court, the truth does not come to light before the judge.
Even if one party alone raises a hundred cries of protest, beware! Do not accept his word without hearing his opponent.”

❧ **4650.** I dare not turn my face away from the Divine command. Go, and bring your adversary before me.”
The gnat said, “Your words are a sound and conclusive argument. My adversary is the Wind, and he is under your jurisdiction.”
The King then shouted, “O East-wind! The gnat complains of your injustice. Come!
Listen, come face-to-face with your opponent; reply to him and defend yourself.”
When the Wind heard the summons, he arrived very rapidly; but the gnat immediately took flight.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, King Solomon has offered to judge the dispute between the gnat and its oppressor, the Wind. This section transitions from the literal story into a profound Sufi meditation on the relationship between the human ego and the Divine Presence.</meta>

4655. Then Solomon said, “O gnat, where are you going? Stop, so that I may pass judgment on you both.”
The gnat answered, “O King, my death comes from his very existence; truly, my day is turned black by his smoke.
Since he has arrived, where shall I find rest? For he wrings the very breath of life out of my body.”
The seeker of God’s Court is just like this: when God appears, the seeker is made into nothing.
Although that union with the Divine is immortality upon immortality, at first that immortality <term>Baqá: The state of "subsistence" or eternal life in God.</term> consists of dying to the self <term>Faná: The spiritual concept of "annihilation," where the ego dissolves in the presence of the Divine.</term>.

4660. The reflections that seek the Light are made naught when His Light finally appears.
How should human reason remain when He commands it to go? *Everything is perishing except His Face* <note>original: "Kullu shay’in hālikun illā wajhah" — A famous verse from the Quran (28:88) emphasizing that only God is eternal.</note>.
Before His Face, both the existent and the non-existent perish; to find true existence within such non-existence is a marvelous thing indeed!
In this place of His presence, all minds are lost and beyond control; when the pen of the poet reaches this point, it breaks.

## **How the Beloved caressed the senseless lover, that he might return to his senses.**

The Sadr-i Jahán <note>Literally "Chief of the World," the title of the high-ranking official who serves as the "Beloved" in this particular story within the Masnavi.</note>, out of kindness, was gradually drawing the lover back from his state of fainting into a capacity for clear speech.

4665. The Prince cried into his ear, “O beggar, I bring gold to scatter over you; spread out your skirt!
Your spirit, which was trembling with distress because we were apart—now that I have come to protect it, why has it fled?
O you who have suffered through heat and cold while separated from me, come back to yourself from this selflessness and return!”
A domestic hen, acting like a host, foolishly brings a camel into her tiny house.
But when the camel set foot inside the hen’s house, the house was destroyed and the roof fell in.

4670. The hen’s house is our weak human intelligence and understanding; the "good intelligence" is one that seeks God’s she-camel <note>A reference to the miraculous She-Camel of the Prophet Salih, symbolizing a divine sign that requires space and respect.</note>.
When that she-camel put her head into this "water and clay" (the human body), neither the clay remained nor the soul and heart.
A sense of pre-eminence in love made Man overweening; because of this desire for more, he is *very unjust and very ignorant* <note>original: "Zhalūman jahūlā" — A reference to Quran 33:72, which describes Man as being "unjust and ignorant" for taking on the Divine Trust that the heavens and mountains refused.</note>.
He is ignorant, and in this difficult hunt, the hare is trying to clasp a lion in his arms.
How would he ever dare to clasp the lion if he truly knew and saw what the lion was?

4675. He is "unjust" to himself and his own soul—but behold, this is an "injustice" that wins the prize over all forms of justice!
His "ignorance" has become the teacher to all forms of knowledge; his "injustice" has become the right way for all justices.
The Beloved took the lover’s hand, saying, “This man whose breath has departed will only come back to life when I give him my own spiritual breath.
When this man whose body is dead becomes 'I' through 'Me,' then it will be My spirit that turns its face toward Me.
By means of this spirit, I make him a person of high estate; only the spirit that I give is capable of experiencing My bounty.”

4680. The spirit that remains a stranger to God cannot see the face of the Beloved; none sees it except the spirit whose origin is from His own dwelling-place.

<summary>Rumi explains that the human ego (the gnat/the hen) cannot survive the direct presence of the Divine (the wind/the camel). He reinterprets the Quranic description of Man as "unjust and ignorant" as a hidden compliment to Man's unique capacity for Divine Love.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the Sadr-i Jahán (the Prince of Bukhara, acting as a symbol for the Divine Beloved) has been gently coaxing his lover back to consciousness after the man fainted from the overwhelming power of the Divine presence.</meta>

“Like a butcher, I breathe into this dear friend, so that his noble inner spirit may be released from the skin.” <note>Butchers would traditionally blow air under the skin of a slaughtered animal to make it easier to peel; here, it is a metaphor for the Divine Breath separating the soul from the ego.</note>

❦**4685.** I speak to you silently because those physical lips shrink from this Breath; it is breathed forth on the bank of the hidden River.
At this moment, open the ‘ear of earlessness’ to hear the mystery of *God does whatever He wills* <note>original: "Yaf‘alu-llāhu mā yashā’" — A Quranic phrase emphasizing that Divine actions are beyond human questioning.</note>.”
When he began to hear the call to union, little by little, the ‘dead’ man began to stir.
He, the lover of God, is no less than the earth which, at the gentle touch of the spring breeze, puts on a garment of green and lifts its head from the death of winter;
He is no less than the seminal drop from which, at the Divine command, Josephs with faces like the sun are born; <note>Joseph is the traditional Islamic archetype of ultimate physical and spiritual beauty.</note>

❦**4690.** He is no less than a wind from which, at the command “Be!”, peacocks and sweet-voiced birds came into being within the egg.
He is no less than the mountain of rock which, through a miraculous birth, brought forth the she-camel that in turn gave birth to a foal. <note>A reference to the miracle of the Prophet Salih, where a living camel was brought forth from a solid rock.</note>
Leave all this behind. Did not the substance of non-existence bring forth, and does it not continually bring forth, an entire Universe?
The man of Bukhárá sprang up and quivered; he whirled in dance once or twice with great joy, then fell down in worship.

## ***How the senseless lover came to himself and turned his face in praise and thanksgiving to the Beloved.***

He said, “O <term>‘Anqa: A mythical, benevolent bird (similar to the Phoenix or Simurgh) representing the Divine or the perfected soul.</term> of God, you who are the destination of the spirit’s circling flight, I give thanks that you have returned from the distant <term>Mountain of Qaf: The legendary emerald mountain that circles the earth, where the mythical 'Anqa bird resides.</term>.

❦**4695.** O <term>Seraphiel: The angel Israfil, who blows the trumpet to signal the Day of Resurrection; here, he represents the awakening of the heart.</term> of Love’s resurrection-place, O Love of love and O Heart’s-desire of love,
I desire, as the first gift of honor you grant me, that you lay your ear against my window.
Although through your purity you already know my feelings, lend an ear to my words, O nurturer of your servant.
Hundreds of thousands of times, O unique Prince, my wits flew away in longing for your ear—
For that hearing of yours, that listening of yours, and those life-quickening smiles of yours;

❦**4700.** For your hearkening to my small and great matters, and even to the deceptions of my suspicious soul.
Then my ‘false coins’ <note>The lover’s imperfect spiritual state or insincere thoughts.</note>, which are well-known to you, you accepted as if they were genuine money;
This you did for the sake of the boldness of one who was impudent and deluded, O you beside whose mercy all other mercies are but a speck of dust!
Firstly, hear that when I abandoned your net, the ‘first and the last’ <note>This world and the hereafter.</note> vanished from before me;
Secondly, hear, O loving Prince, that I searched long, but there was no second to you;

❦**4705.** Thirdly, since I have been away from you, it is as though I have said, ‘*the third of three*’; <note>original: "thālithu thalāthah" — An allusion to the concept of the Trinity/polytheism; here it means that being separated from the Beloved is a state of spiritual division rather than Divine Unity.</note>
Fourthly, because my cornfield is burnt up, I can no longer tell the fifth finger from the fourth.” <note>A metaphor for being so overwhelmed by love that one loses the ability to perform basic distinctions or calculations.</note>

<summary>The Beloved (the Prince) revives the lover from his faint using the "Divine Breath," leading the lover to regain consciousness and perform a joyful dance. The lover then offers a poetic prayer of gratitude, acknowledging that the Beloved's presence has dissolved his concerns for both this world and the next.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the Sadr-i Jahán (the Prince of Bukhara, acting as a symbol for the Divine Beloved) has been gently coaxing his lover back to consciousness after the man fainted from the overwhelming power of the Divine presence.</meta>

Wherever you find blood upon the soil, if you look closely, you will see it comes from my own eyes.
My words are like thunder, and this storm of moaning commands the clouds to rain upon the earth.
Caught between words and tears, I hesitate: should I weep or should I speak? What is the right way?

❦**4710.** If I speak, my weeping is silenced; but if I weep, how can I offer my songs of praise?
“Heart’s blood is falling from my eyes, O King! See what has become of me!”
The thin, exhausted man said this and began to weep so violently that everyone, from the lowest beggar to the highest noble, wept with him.
So many cries of spiritual ecstasy rose from his heart that the people of Bukhara <note>A historic city in modern-day Uzbekistan, representing the "abode of the heart" in this context.</note> formed a great circle around him.
He was speaking like one possessed, weeping like a madman, laughing like a madman—men and women, children and elders, all stood in total bewilderment.

❦**4715.** The entire city shed tears alongside him; men and women gathered as if it were the Day of Resurrection.
In that moment, the Heavens said to the Earth, “If you have never seen the Resurrection, look upon it now!”
The human intellect was stunned, saying, “What is this love? What is this ecstasy? I cannot tell which is more miraculous: being separated from Him or being united with Him.”
The sky read the announcement of this Resurrection and was so overwhelmed that it tore its own garment all the way to the Milky Way.
Love is a stranger to both this world and the next; within it are seventy-two different types of madness. <note>original: "haftād u dū dīvānagī" — A reference to the traditional "seventy-two sects" of Islam; Rumi suggests Love transcends all religious divisions and human categories.</note>

❦**4720.** Love is deeply hidden, yet its bewilderment is plain for all to see; the souls of even the greatest spiritual leaders long for it.
Its religion is different from the seventy-two sects; compared to it, the thrones of kings are nothing more than a temporary bandage on a broken limb.
During the <term>Sama</term> <note>A Sufi practice of "spiritual listening" involving music, poetry, and often whirling to reach a state of divine ecstasy.</note>, Love’s musician plays this tune: “Being a servant is a chain; being a lord is a headache.”
What then is Love? It is the Sea of Non-existence; there, the legs of the intellect are broken.
The roles of servant and king are well-known; but the state of being a lover is hidden behind these two veils.

❦**4725.** Would that Existence itself had a tongue, so that it might pull back the veils from all living things!
O breath of physical existence, whatever words you speak, know that you are only wrapping another veil around the mystery.
That speech and that physical state are the enemies of true spiritual perception; trying to explain the Divine with human words is like trying to wash away blood with more blood—it is completely absurd.
Since I am a friend to those who have been driven mad by Him, I spend my days and nights breathing out the secrets of Love from this cage of physical life.
You are profoundly drunk, senseless, and distracted—tell me, my soul, where did you wander last night?

❦**4730.** Careful, be careful! Do not let out a single breath! First, rise up and find a friend you can truly trust.
You are a lover, you are intoxicated, and your tongue is running wild!
By God! By God! You are like the ‘camel on the water-spout’! <note>A Persian idiom for something that is impossible to hide; a camel standing on a high roof-gutter would be visible to everyone in the city.</note>
When the tongue tries to tell of His mystery and His beauty, Heaven itself begins to pray: “O God, You who are so good at covering our faults, hide this secret!”
But what can be covered? It is like fire in a bale of cotton—the more you try to hide it, the more it shows itself.

<summary>The lover’s intense emotional outburst causes a spiritual "resurrection" in the city of Bukhara, illustrating how divine love transcends the intellect, religious sects, and the limitations of language.</summary>

<meta>This section continues from the previous page, where the Sadr-i Jahán (the Prince of Bukhara) was comforting his lover. When I endeavour to hide Love’s secret, He lifts up His head like a banner, crying out, "Look, here I am!"

**4735.** Even against my will, He seizes me by both ears and says, “O scatter-brain, how do you expect to cover this? Cover it if you can!”
I say to Him, “Begone! Though You have boiled over with passion, You are both manifest and hidden, just like the soul.”
He replies, “This body of mine is imprisoned in the jar like unfermented juice, but like finished wine, I am clapping my hands in joy at the banquet.”
I say to Him, “Go, before You are taken as a pledge <note>In this context, being 'put in pawn' refers to being confined or restricted by the physical world or social expectations.</note>, lest the sickness of intoxication falls upon You.”

**4740.** When evening comes and tries to steal my cup, I will say to it: ‘Give it back! For my true evening has not yet arrived.’”
This is why the Arabs applied the word <term>mudam</term> <note>original: "mudām" — A term meaning both "wine" and "that which is perpetual or enduring."</note> to wine, because the one who drinks it is never truly sated.
Love causes the wine of spiritual realization to bubble; He is the secret Cup-bearer to the <term>şiddiq</term> <note>original: "ṣiddīq" — A person of absolute truthfulness and sincerity; in Sufism, one who has reached a high station of devotion.</note>.
When you seek the ultimate reality with God’s help, the essence of the spirit is the wine, and the physical body is merely the flagon that holds it.
When He increases the wine of His divine assistance, the sheer potency of that wine bursts the flagon.

**4745.** The spirit then becomes the Cup-bearer, and the spirit also becomes the drunken man. Do not ask how this can be! God knows the truth best.
It is the radiance of the Divine Cup-bearer that entered the grape-juice; the juice bubbled up, began to dance, and grew strong in spirit.
On this matter, ask the skeptic: “When did you ever see ordinary grape-juice act like this?”
To anyone with true knowledge, it is self-evident and requires no deep reflection: wherever you see a person in a state of holy disturbance, there must be a Divine Disturber present.

### ***Story of the lover who had been long separated from his beloved and had suffered much tribulation.***

There was once a certain youth who was madly enamoured of a woman, but the good fortune of being united with her was not granted to him.

**4750.** Love tortured him terribly upon the earth; why, in truth, does Love seem to carry such hatred toward the lover from the very beginning?
Why is Love so murderous at the start, so that any outsider is frightened away?
Whenever this youth sent a messenger to the woman, the messenger—consumed by his own jealousy—would become a highwayman, blocking the path of the message.
And if his secretary wrote a letter to be sent to the woman, his representative would read the letter to her with <term>tashíf</term> <note>original: "tashḥīf" — A linguistic term for misreading or miswriting dots on Arabic letters, which can completely change a word's meaning. Here, it suggests the messenger intentionally distorted the lover's words.</note>.
Even if, in good faith, he tried to make the morning breeze his envoy, that breeze would be choked and darkened by a cloud of dust.

**4755.** If he sewed his letter to the wing of a bird, the bird's wing would be scorched by the sheer heat of the longing written in the letter.
Divine jealousy barred every possible path of human cleverness and broke the banners of the army of his own thought.
At first, the hope of expectation was the only friend to his sorrow; but in the end, it was that very same expectation that broke him.
Sometimes he would cry out, “This is an incurable affliction!” and other times he would say, “No, this pain is the very life of my spirit.”

<summary>Rumi explores the irrepressible and intoxicating nature of Divine Love, comparing the spirit to wine that eventually bursts the vessel of the body. He then introduces a new narrative about a lover whose every attempt to reach his beloved is thwarted by Divine jealousy and misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Love, wine metaphor, spirit and body, şiddiq, mudam, tashíf, spiritual trial, Sufi poetry, Rumi</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Rumi’s philosophical diversion regarding the hidden nature of the soul and the contrast between outward appearance and inner reality. Having previously discussed the "wine" of divine love, he now reflects on how spiritual seekers must look beyond the physical world (represented by the "dust" of the graveyard and the "pot" with a lid) to find the truth, before returning to the narrative of the lover from Bukhara who has spent seven years in search of his beloved.</meta>

Sometimes self-awareness would manifest in him; other times he would taste the fruit of self-annihilation <note>The text contrasts "existence" (ego) with "non-existence" (fana), the Sufi concept of the passing away of the self in God.</note>.

**4760.** When his physical nature grew cold and weary, the fountain of spiritual union began to boil with heat.
When he accepted the destitution of exile, the riches of that very "nothingness" rushed toward him.
The grain of his thoughts was cleared of the husks of distraction; he became, like the moon, a guide for those traveling through the dark night.
Oh, there is many a parrot that speaks even when silent; oh, there is many a sweet-spirited soul whose outer expression appears sour.
Go to the cemetery, sit for a moment in the silence, and witness those eloquent silent ones;

**4765.** Though you see their dust is all the same color, their spiritual states are not the same.
The flesh and fat of the living looks uniform, yet one person is sorrowful and another is joyful.
Until you hear their words, how can you know their feelings, since their inner state is hidden from you?
You may hear their cries—"Hay! Huy!" <note>original: "hāy, hūy" — Ecstatic cries often associated with Sufi dhikr or intense emotional outbursts.</note>—but how could you grasp an inner state that has a hundred layers?
Our physical forms are similar, yet they hold opposing qualities; likewise, their dust is uniform, but their spirits are diverse.

**4770.** Similarly, voices may sound the same in tone, yet one carries grief and another carries charm.
On the battlefield, you hear the cry of horses; in a stroll through a garden, you hear the song of birds.
One voice springs from hatred, another from harmony; one from pain, and another from joy.
To someone ignorant of these inner states, the voices all sound the same.
One tree is stirred by the strikes of an axe, while another tree is moved by the breeze of dawn.

**4775.** I was greatly deceived by the lowly pot, because the lid was on while it boiled.
The intensity and flavor of every person calls out to you, "Come!"—the intensity of true sincerity and the intensity of false hypocrisy.
If you do not have the spiritual discernment <note>Literally "the scent," referring to the ability to smell the "fragrance" of Truth.</note> to recognize the true face of reality, go and seek the spiritual insight that can catch the scent.
The insight that lingers in that divine Rose-garden—it is this which brightens the eyes of all who wait like Jacob <note>A reference to the Quranic story where the Prophet Jacob’s blindness was cured by the scent of his son Joseph’s shirt.</note>.
Come now, let us return to what happened to that heartsick youth, for we have left the man of Bukhara far behind, O son.

### ***How the lover found his beloved; and a discourse showing that the seeker is a finder, for he who shall do as much good as the weight of an ant shall see it in the end.*** <note>The second half of this heading is a paraphrase of Quran 99:7.</note>

**4780.** For seven years that young man was engaged in searching and seeking; from clinging to the vision of union, he became thin as a ghost.
If the protection of God is over a servant’s head, the seeker will eventually become a finder.
The Prophet said that when you knock on a door, eventually a head will peer out from that door.
When you wait on someone’s path, eventually you will see their face.
When you dig the earth for a well every day, eventually you will reach pure water.

<meta>This page continues Rumi’s philosophical discourse on divine providence and the folly of focusing on rare exceptions to universal spiritual laws. Having previously discussed the hidden diverse natures of human souls, he now addresses the skeptic who uses rare spiritual failures as an excuse for inaction or lack of faith.</meta>

❧ **4785.** Even if you may not believe it, everyone knows this: one day you will reap exactly what you are sowing. 
You strike flint against steel and the fire does not flash out? This simply cannot be; or if it does happen, it is extremely rare.
The person to whom happiness and salvation are not granted by God—his mind focuses on nothing but those rare exceptions.
He says, "So-and-so sowed seeds and had no crop," or "That other man pulled an oyster from the sea, and the shell held no pearl."
He points to <term>Bal'am son of Bā`ūr<gloss>A figure in Islamic and Judeo-Christian tradition (Balaam) who possessed spiritual knowledge but fell from grace due to ego.</gloss></term> and the accursed <term>Iblīs<gloss>The primary name for Satan in Islamic tradition.</gloss></term>, arguing that their acts of worship and their religion did not save them.

❧ **4790.** The hundreds of thousands of prophets and travelers on **the Way** <note>original: "rah" — the spiritual path of Sufism leading to divine truth.</note> never enter the mind of that cynical man.
He chooses these two examples which produce only spiritual darkness. How could his ill fate put anything else in his heart?
Oh, there is many a person who eats bread with a joyful heart, yet it becomes the death of him: it gets stuck in his throat.
Go then, you unfortunate man—do not eat bread at all, lest you fall into misery like him!
Yet hundreds of thousands of people are eating bread, gaining strength, and nourishing their vital spirits.

❧ **4795.** How have you fallen into such a rare calamity, unless you are deprived of blessings or were born a fool?
The unfortunate man has turned away from this world full of sunshine and moonlight and has shoved his head into a pit,
Saying, "If it is true, then where is the light?" Lift up your head from the pit and look, you miserable wretch!
The whole world, east and west, is filled with that light, but while you are in the pit, it will not shine upon you.
Leave the pit; go to the palace and the vineyards. Do not argue here, for you must know that quarreling brings bad luck.

❧ **4800.** Beware! Do not say, "Look, so-and-so sowed seed, and in such-and-such a year the locusts devoured everything.
Why, then, should I sow? For there is danger in this. Why should I throw this grain away from my hand?"
Meanwhile, the one who did not neglect to sow and labor is filling his barn with grain, much to your embarrassment.
Because the lover was patiently knocking at the door, at last, one day, he was granted a private meeting.
Out of fear of the **night-patrol** <note>The "night-patrol" (pasban) represents the external hardships or "scourges" of life that can inadvertently drive a person toward a better path.</note>, he leaped into the orchard by night: there he found his beloved, radiant as a candle and a lamp.

❧ **4805.** At that moment, he said to the Maker of the circumstances, "O God, have mercy on the night-patrol!
Without me knowing, You created the means: from the very gates of Hell, You have brought me to Paradise.
You made this terrifying situation a means to an end, so that I may never again hold even a single thorn in contempt."
In exchange for a broken leg, God bestows a wing; likewise, from the very depths of a pit, He opens a door of escape.

<summary>Rumi argues against spiritual cynicism, using analogies of farming and the story of a lover to show that while failure is possible, it is the exception to the rule of divine reward. He concludes that even seemingly "bad" events, like the threat of a night patrol, are often the hidden "means" God uses to lead a soul to its beloved.</summary>

# BOOK IV

->In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.<-

This is the Fourth Journey toward the best of dwellings and the greatest of benefits. By reading these words, the hearts of the <term>gnostics<gloss>Those who possess direct, experiential knowledge of Divine Truth.</gloss></term> will rejoice, just as the meadows bloom under a heavy downpour and as the eyes find delight in the sweetness of sleep. Within these pages is comfort for the spirit and healing for the body. It is what the sincere seekers—those devoted entirely to God—crave and love, and it is what the <term>travellers<gloss>A term for Sufi disciples (salikin) who are actively walking the spiritual path toward God.</gloss></term> seek and desire. It is a refreshment to the eyes and a joy to the soul; the sweetest of fruits for those who gather them, and the most sublime of all things hoped for. It brings the sick man to his physician and guides the lover to his beloved. 

To God be all praise, for this work is the grandest of gifts and the most precious of prizes. It renews the ancient covenant of friendship with the Divine and eases the burdens of those in distress. Its study will increase the longing of those who feel estranged from God, while increasing the joy and gratitude of those who are blessed. Its heart holds a wealth of spiritual finery far beyond the jewels worn by young ladies; it serves as a reward for those who follow both the theory and the practical discipline of the spiritual path. It is like a full moon that has risen or a lost fortune that has finally returned, exceeding the highest hopes and providing nourishment for those who do good works. 

This book raises our spirits after a time of <term>depression<gloss>Referring to "qabd," a spiritual state of contraction or internal heaviness.</gloss></term> and expands our hope after a period of <term>contraction<gloss>Referring to "bast," the spiritual state of openness and joy that follows hardship.</gloss></term>—it is like the sun shining radiantly after the clouds have scattered. It is a light for our friends and a treasure for those who follow in our spiritual footsteps.

We ask God to help us give Him proper thanks, for indeed, gratitude is the means of securing the blessings we already hold and the secret to capturing even more—though nothing truly happens except what He intends.

> "One of the things that stirred my heart to longing was when I was sleeping, distracted from my sorrow by the cool, sweet breeze, 
> Until a grey dove in the thick branches of a grove called out, singing beautifully with long, sobbing notes. 
> And if I had wept from my passion for <term>Su'dá<gloss>A traditional name used in Arabic poetry to represent the Beloved.</gloss></term> before she began her sobbing, I would have healed my soul of its pain before I had cause to regret my delay." <note>original: these verses are in Arabic, often used by Rumi to invoke the classical tradition of longing for the Divine Beloved.</note>

<summary>This page concludes Book III and opens Book IV with a poetic preface. Rumi describes his work as a spiritual medicine and a guide that leads the seeker from "contraction" (sorrow) to "expansion" (divine joy).</summary>
<keywords>Book IV, Preface, Gnostics, Spiritual Path, Gratitude, Contraction and Expansion, The Beloved</keywords>

# BOOK IV

O **Radiance of Truth** <gloss>Ziyá’u ‘l-Haqq</gloss>, **Sword of the Religion** <gloss>Husámu’ddín</gloss>, you are the one through whose light the *Mathnawí* <term>Mathnawí<gloss>Literally meaning "rhyming couplets," this is Rumi's six-volume masterpiece of spiritual teaching.</gloss></term> has surpassed even the moon in its brilliance.
O you in whom all hopes are placed, your lofty spiritual aspiration is drawing this poem—God knows to what heights.
You have taken hold of the neck of this *Mathnawí*: you are pulling it in the direction only you know.
The *Mathnawí* is running forward, but the one drawing it is unseen—unseen, at least, by the ignorant who lack spiritual insight.

❦**5.** Because you were the very origin of this poem, if it grows in size, it is you who have caused it to increase.
Since you wish it to be so, God wishes it so: for God grants the desires of those who are truly devoted to Him.
In the past, you belonged entirely to God, so that now, in return, it is as if “God belongs to him.” <note>This refers to a famous sacred tradition (Hadith Qudsi): "Whoever is for God, God is for him."</note>
On your account, the *Mathnawí* had thousands of thanksgivings to offer: it lifted up its hands in prayer and gratitude.
God saw the thanks to you on its lips and in its hands: therefore He showed grace and bestowed even more favor and growth;

❦**10.** For to the one who gives thanks, more is promised, just as drawing close to God is the reward for the <term>prostration<gloss>The act of bowing to the ground during ritual prayer (Sajdah).</gloss></term>.
Our God has said, “**And prostrate yourself and come near to Me**”: <note>original: "Wasjud waqtarib" (Quran 96:19)</note> the prostration of our physical bodies becomes the spiritual closeness of the soul to God.
If this poem is expanding, it is for this reason; it is not for the sake of empty pride or making noise.
We are as glad for you as a vineyard is glad for the summer heat: you have the authority: come, pull us forward, so that we may always be following your lead.
Lead this caravan happily toward the spiritual Pilgrimage, O Commander of the truth that “Patience is the key to joy.”

❦**15.** The formal Pilgrimage consists of visiting a physical House, but the true Pilgrimage—to the Lord of the House—is the only journey worthy of a true man.
I called you **Radiance** <gloss>Ziyá</gloss> and **Sword of the Religion** <gloss>Husámu’ddín</gloss> because you are like the Sun, and these two words describe the sun’s qualities;
For, you see, this "sword" and this "radiance" are one and the same: the sun’s beam is like a sword made of light.
**Reflected light** <gloss>Núr</gloss> belongs to the moon, but this **essential radiance** <gloss>ziyá</gloss> belongs to the sun: you can read this distinction in the *Qur’án*. <note>The Quran (10:5) describes the sun as a "radiance" (diya) and the moon as a "light" (nur), implying the sun is the source and the moon is the reflection.</note>

<summary>This page marks the grand opening of the Fourth Book of the Mathnawi, where Rumi credits his disciple Husamuddin as the spiritual "sun" and driving force behind the poem's continued creation.</summary>
<keywords>Husamuddin, Mathnawi, Divine Light, Prostration, Quranic imagery, spiritual pilgrimage, gratitude, radiance</keywords>

--- Page 201 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the prose introduction of Book IV into the opening verses. The text shifts from a series of prayers and blessings into a poetic exploration of spiritual light, addressing Rumi's companion and scribe, Husamuddin (Ziyá'u 'l-Haqq), and resuming a narrative left unfinished in the previous volume.</meta>

The Qur'án has called the sun **radiance** <gloss>ziyá</gloss>, O father, and it has called the moon **light** <gloss>núr</gloss>. Consider this!

❦**20.** Since the sun is more exalted even than the moon, know, then, that **radiance** <gloss>ziyá</gloss> is superior to **light** <gloss>núr</gloss> in dignity. <note>In Quranic terminology, *ziyá* refers to an essential, self-originating brilliance (like the sun), while *núr* refers to a reflected or secondary light (like the moon).</note>
Many a one did not see the way in the moonlight, (but) it became visible as soon as the sun rose.
The sun displayed (all) objects of exchange perfectly: of necessity, markets were (held) in the daytime,
In order that the false coin and the good money might come into view, and that he (the merchant) might be far (immune) from swindling and trickery.
(The sun rose) until its light came to perfection on the earth, **a universal mercy** <note>original: "rahmatan li’l-’álamín"—a Quranic title for the Prophet Muhammad, here applied to the sun as a metaphor for divine guidance.</note> to the traders;

❦**25.** But to the false coiner it is hateful and grievous, because by it his money and wares are made unsaleable.
Hence the false coin is the mortal foe of the money-changer: who is the enemy of the dervish <term>Dervish<gloss>A member of a Muslim (specifically Sufi) religious order who has taken vows of poverty and austerity.</gloss></term> but the dog?
The prophets contend with their enemies; then the angels utter cries of "Save (them), O Lord,"
Saying, "Keep this Lamp, which is light-disseminating, far from the puffs and breaths of thieves."
Only the thief and the coiner are adversaries of the light: succour (us) from these twain, O Succourer!

❦**30.** Shed light upon the Fourth Book, for the sun rose from the Fourth Heaven. <note>In medieval Islamic cosmology, the Fourth Heaven or Sphere is the station of the Sun.</note>

70. Consider this same point, O person of experience: how one thing can be many different things to a thousand different people.
**Zayd** <note>original: "Zayd"—a common name used in Arabic and Persian literature as a placeholder, similar to "John Doe" or "any man."</note>, in the eyes of one person, may seem like a devil; yet to another, he may appear as a benevolent **sultan**.

## ***The Story of the preacher who began every sermon by praying for the cruel, the hard-hearted, and the faithless.***

There was a certain preacher who, whenever he stood upon the pulpit, would begin by praying for highway robbers—those who rob and mistreat the righteous.
He would raise his hands and cry out, 
> "O Lord, let your mercy fall upon the wicked, the corrupt, and the arrogant sinners!
> Have mercy on all who mock the good, on those whose hearts are closed to faith, and even those who dwell in the <note>original: "Dayr-i Nasara"—the Christian monastery, used here by the poet to signify those outside the preacher's own faith community.</note> monastery."
He would not pray for the pure of heart; he would offer prayers for no one but the wicked.

85. People said to him, 
> "This is unheard of! It is no act of kindness to pray for people of such wickedness."
He replied, 
> "I have experienced goodness from these very people; for this reason, I have chosen to pray for them.
> They committed so much evil, injustice, and oppression against me that they eventually drove me out of my own darkness and into the light of goodness.
> Every time I turned my face toward the distractions of this world, I suffered blows and beatings from them,
> And so I took refuge from their blows in the Divine: those 'wolves' were always pushing me back onto the right Path.
> 
> 90. Since they were the means of my spiritual well-being, it is only right that I pray for them, O wise one."

A servant of God may complain to the Creator about their pain and suffering, making a hundred grievances about their hurt.
But God says, 
> "In the end, this grief and pain have made you humble, prayerful, and righteous.
> You should instead complain about the worldly 'blessings' that distract you, for they take you far from My door and turn you into an outcast."

In reality, every enemy you face is actually your medicine: they are an <term>elixir<gloss>In alchemy, an elixir was a substance believed to turn base metals into gold; here, it refers to a spiritual transformation.</gloss></term>, a benefit, and a secret seeker of your heart's ultimate good.

<summary>Rumi explains that our perception of people and events depends on our perspective, and even our enemies or hardships are "medicine" that drive us back toward God.</summary>

### ***How they asked Jesus, on whom be peace, saying, "O Spirit of God, what is the hardest thing to bear of all the hard things in existence?"***

A sober-minded man said to **Jesus** <note>In Islam, Jesus (Isa) is a major prophet often associated with deep spiritual wisdom, asceticism, and the "Spirit of God."</note>, "What is the hardest to bear of all things in existence?"
He replied, "O my dear soul, the hardest is God's anger, on account of which Hell is trembling even as we are."

**115.** The man said, "What is the security against this anger of God?" Jesus said, "To abandon your own anger at once."
Therefore, as the policeman became a mine for this anger, his ugly rage surpassed even that of a wild beast.
What hope is there for him of Divine mercy, unless perchance that graceless man should turn back from that vile quality?
Although the world cannot do without such people, this statement is a means of casting those who hear it into error.
The world cannot do without urine either, but that urine is not *clear running water* <note>original: "ma'īn"—a Quranic term for the pure, flowing water of Paradise.</note>.

# *The lover’s attempted betrayal, and how the beloved scolded him.*

❦ **120.** When that foolish man found her alone, he immediately tried to embrace and kiss her.

❦ **125.** You saw the wind moving, but you must know that the **Mover of the wind** is here, the One who drives the wind along.”
The "fan"—meaning the direction of the wind's course by God’s command—strikes this air and keeps it constantly in motion.
The air that is within our control does not stir until you move a fan.
Without you and without the fan, the movement of that air does not happen, O simpleton.
The movement of the wind of the breath, which is on the lips, follows the path directed by the spirit and the body.

❦ **130.** At one time you make your breath a song of praise and a kind message; at another time you make your breath a mocking insult and foul speech.
Understand, then, from this small example the nature of all other winds; for the intellect perceives the whole through its parts.
God sometimes makes the wind like spring; but in December, He strips away this kindness.
He makes the wind a <term>şarşar<gloss>A violent, intensely cold, and screaming wind.</gloss></term> for the people of <term>’Ad<gloss>An ancient, powerful Arabian tribe mentioned in the Quran who were destroyed by a great storm after rejecting their prophet.</gloss></term>; yet, He makes it fragrant and balmy for the prophet <term>Hud<gloss>The prophet sent to the people of ’Ad; in the tradition, the wind that destroyed his enemies was gentle and pleasant to him.</gloss></term>.
One wind He makes as deadly as the poison of the <term>simoom<gloss>A hot, dry, suffocating desert wind.</gloss></term>; yet He also makes the arrival of the east-wind delightful.

❦ **135.** He has established the "wind" of the breath within you so that you may judge every other wind by its example.
The breath does not become speech without taking on a quality of gentleness or harshness; it is honey for one group of people and poison for another.
A fan is moved for the benefit of a person, and to drive away every fly and gnat.
Why then should the "fan" of <term>Divine fore-ordainment<gloss>The concept that God has pre-destined the course of all events.</gloss></term> not be filled with trials and tests through good and evil?
Inasmuch as the part—namely, the wind of the breath or the fan—is nothing but a cause of either harm or benefit,

❦ **140.** How could the north wind, the east wind, and the west wind be far from showing favor or granting blessings?
Look at a handful of wheat from a granary and understand that the whole harvest will be just like that one handful.
How could the wind rush out from the heavens without being driven by the "fan" of the One who guides the wind?
Is it not true that at <term>winnowing-time<gloss>The agricultural process of tossing harvested grain into the air so the wind blows away the lighter chaff (straw), leaving the heavy seeds behind.</gloss></term> the laborers on the threshing-floor pray to God for wind,
So that the straw may be separated from the wheat, allowing the grain to be gathered into the granaries or pits?

### *Story of the Súfí who caught his wife with a strange man.*

A <term>Súfí<gloss>A practitioner of Islamic mysticism (Sufism), often characterized by a focus on the internal search for God.</gloss></term> came back to his house in the daytime: the house had only one door, and his wife was with a cobbler.
The wife was joined with her servant lover in that one room because of the lust of the flesh. <note>original Latin: "Uxor copulata erat cum servo (amatore) suo in illo uno cubiculo propter corporis libidinem."</note>

❦**160.** When in the forenoon the Súfí knocked on the door with all his might, both the lovers were at a loss; there was neither device nor way of escape.
It was never known—it was unprecedented—for him to return home from the shop at that time,
But on that day the alarmed man purposely returned to his house at an unseasonable hour, because of a suspicion.
The wife's confidence was based on the fact that he had never come home from his work at this time.
By Divine destiny, her reasoning did not turn out to be right: though He, God, is the <term>Coverer<gloss>From the Arabic "al-Sattar," referring to God's attribute of concealing the sins of His servants to allow them a chance to repent.</gloss></term> of sins, still He will impose the penalty.

❦**165.** When you have done evil, be afraid; do not feel secure, since the evil is a seed, and God will cause it to grow.

The thief cried out, saying, “O Prince of the land, this is my first offense. Mercy!”
“God forfend,” said 'Umar, “that God should inflict severe punishment the first time.”

The wife replied, 'I too have repeated it and have explained our lack of household goods;
But her resolution is firmer than a mountain, for she is not discouraged by a hundred instances of poverty.
She keeps saying, "What I want is chastity: what is sought from your family is sincerity and high-mindedness."'

❧**205.** The Súfí said, 'In truth, she has seen and continues to see our household goods and possessions, both the visible and the hidden—
A narrow house, a dwelling-place meant for a single person, where even a needle could not remain hidden. <note>The Sufi is pointing out that his house is so small and bare that the "lady visitor" (who is actually a cover for the lover) must surely see there is no room for secrets—including the lover hiding there.</note>
Moreover, in her innocence, she knows better than we do what modesty, purity, renunciation, and virtue are.
She knows better than we all the aspects of modesty: the front, the back, the head, and the tail of it.
Evidently our daughter is without household goods or servants, and the lady herself is well-acquainted with virtue and modesty.

❧**210.** It is not required of a father to speak at length on his daughter's modesty, when in her it is as obvious as a bright day.'
I have told this story so that you may not weave idle talk when your offense is glaring.
O you who are likewise excessive in your pretensions, in your case too there has been this same hypocritical effort and vain belief.
You have been unfaithful, just like the Súfí's wife: you have opened the snare of cunning in fraud,
For you are ashamed before every dirty braggart, but not before your God.

### *The purpose for which God is called the Hearing (Samí‘) and the Seeing (Basír).*

❧**215.** God has called Himself <term>the Seeing One<gloss>Arabic: *Basír*</gloss></term>, in order that the knowledge that He sees you may at every moment be a deterrent against sin.
God has called Himself <term>the Hearing One<gloss>Arabic: *Samí‘*</gloss></term>, in order that you may close your lips and refrain from foul speech.
God has called Himself <term>the All-Knowing<gloss>Arabic: *‘Alím*</gloss></term>, in order that you may fear to even think of a wicked deed.
These are not merely labels or proper names applied to God; for names are often just designations—even a dark-skinned person might be given the name <term>Camphor<gloss>Arabic/Persian: *Káfúr*; a white, translucent substance. Rumi is explaining that while humans give names that might contradict reality, God’s names are essential truths of His nature.</gloss></term>.

<summary>The Sufi continues to challenge his wife's elaborate lies about a wealthy visitor, using her own logic to highlight the impossibility of her excuses. The narrative then shifts to a moral lesson, reminding the reader that God's attributes of Seeing, Hearing, and Knowing are active realities meant to guide human behavior.</summary>

The Names of God are rooted in His essence and represent His Eternal Attributes; they are not empty or hollow like the philosophical concept of the **First Cause** <note>Rumi argues that God is a personal, active being with real qualities, rather than the cold, distant "Unmoved Mover" described by some philosophers.</note>.

220. Otherwise, it would be nothing but a joke, a mockery, and a lie—like calling a deaf man **"The Hearer"** <note>original: *Samí'*</note> or calling those who are blind **"Radiance"** <note>original: *Ziyá*</note>;
Or as if **"Modest"** <note>original: *Hayí*</note> should be the proper name for a shameless person, or **"Beautiful"** <note>original: *Sabíh*</note> the name of someone hideous.
You might give a newborn child the title of **"Pilgrim"** <note>original: *Hájjí*</note> or **"Holy Warrior"** <note>original: *Ghází*</note> just to honor their family line;
But if these titles are used to praise the person, they are incorrect unless that person actually possesses that specific quality.
Otherwise, it is a mockery or madness: God is far above and untouched by what *the unrighteous say*.

225. I knew, even before we met, that you were fair to look at but foul in your nature;
I knew, even before we stood face to face, that your stubbornness had left you trapped in damnation.
When my eye is red with <term>ophthalmia<gloss>A historical term for severe inflammation or redness of the eye.</gloss></term>, I know it is diseased even if I cannot see the redness myself.
You thought of me as a lamb without a shepherd; you thought I had no one watching over me.
The reason lovers have groaned in grief is that they have looked at things the wrong way <note>Literally "rubbed their eyes at the wrong time," implying their spiritual vision was distorted or misplaced.</note>.

230. They looked upon that **Gazelle** <note>A metaphor for the Beloved or the spiritual seeker protected by God.</note> as if it had no shepherd; they looked at that **Captive** as someone who could be taken without cost,
Until suddenly an arrow from the gaze of **Divine jealousy** <note>The concept that God protects the honor and "secrets" of His friends from the prying eyes of the unworthy.</note> strikes the heart, as if to say, "I am the Guardian: do not look with lust."
Am I lower than a lamb or a goat, that I should have no protector behind me?
I have a Guardian who is fit to rule: He knows every wind that blows upon me.
Whether that wind is cold or hot, that All-Knowing One is never unaware and never absent, O weak man.

235. The <term>appetitive soul<gloss>In Sufism, the 'nafs' or the lower, ego-driven self that seeks worldly and sensory gratification.</gloss></term> is deaf and blind to God. With my heart, I could see your blindness from a distance.
For eight years I did not ask after you at all, because I saw you were filled with layer upon layer of ignorance.
Why indeed should I ask after someone who is in the **furnace** of lust? Why say "How are you?" to someone who is drowning in their own physical senses?

### **_Comparison of this world to a bath-furnace and of piety to the bath._**

The lust of this world is like the **bath-furnace** <note>original: *gulkhan* — the room where the fire is stoked to heat the water for a public bathhouse.</note> which makes the bath of piety shine;
But the pious man's only interest in this furnace is the purity it creates, because he stays inside the hot bath in cleanliness.

240. The wealthy are like those who carry dung to fuel the bath-keeper’s fire.
God has planted greed within them so that the bath may stay hot and well-supplied <note>This striking metaphor suggests that worldly people, through their labor and obsession with material things, inadvertently provide the infrastructure for spiritual life to exist.</note>.
Leave this furnace and go into the hot bath: know that leaving the furnace behind is the very heart of the bath itself.
Anyone who stays in the furnace-room is merely a servant to the person who is self-denying and watchful.
When someone has truly entered the bath, the evidence is visible on their beautiful and bright face.

<summary>Rumi explains that God’s attributes are real and protective, warning that the "appetitive soul" is blind to the Divine Guardian. He uses the metaphor of a public bath to show that worldly greed is merely the "fuel" that heats the spiritual life of the pious.</summary>
