**❧245.** The marks of the **stokers** <note>Rumi uses the "stoker"—someone who feeds a bathhouse furnace with dry dung—as a metaphor for those consumed by the "filth" of worldly greed.</note> are plain to see, both in their clothing and in the soot and dust that blacken them.
And if you cannot see his face, then use your nose; smell is like a walking stick for everyone who is blind.
If you lack a sense of smell, then draw him into conversation; from his current talk, you will learn his old secrets.
Then, a gold-seeking stoker will say, "I have hauled twenty baskets of filth from dawn until nightfall."
Your greed is like a fire in this physical world: every flaming tongue of it has opened a hundred mouths to swallow dirty money.

**❧250.** In the eyes of **Reason**, this gold is as foul as dung, even though, like dung, it is what keeps the fire of desire blazing.
The sun, which rivals the fire, dries the moist filth to make it fit for the furnace.
The sun also turned stone into gold <note>A reference to the medieval scientific belief that sunlight, over long periods, matured base minerals into gold deep within the earth.</note> so that a hundred sparks might fly into the stove of greed.
When a man says, "I have gathered riches," what does it really mean? It means, "I have collected all this filth."
Even though this is a shameful thing to say, the stokers actually brag about it.

**❧255.** One of them says: "You only carried six baskets before dark; I carried twenty without any trouble!"
For one who was born in the furnace and has never known purity, the scent of musk actually has a painful effect.

## **The Story of the tanner who fainted and became ill upon smelling perfume and musk in the perfumers' bazaar**

A certain man fell senseless and curled up the moment he entered the bazaar of the perfumers.
The fragrance of the perfume drifting from the shops of the goodly perfumers struck him, so that his head reeled and he collapsed on the spot.
He lay there unconscious, like a corpse, at high noon in the middle of the busy road.

**❧260.** A crowd gathered around him, everyone crying out, "**There is no power but in God!**" <note>original: *Lá hawl*. A common Arabic phrase used in times of distress or to ward off evil.</note> and trying various remedies.
One man placed his hand over the tanner's heart, while another splashed rose-water upon him—
For he did not realize that it was the scent of rose-water from the meadow that had caused this calamity to overtake him.
One person was massaging his hands and head, while another brought wet clay mixed with straw to use as a cold plaster.
One prepared an incense of aloe-wood and sugar, while another began removing some of his clothes.

**❧265.** Another felt his pulse to see how it was beating; another smelled his mouth,
To see if he had been drinking wine or eating <term>henbane<gloss>original: *beng*. A plant used historically as an intoxicant or sedative.</gloss></term> or **hashish**; the people were left in despair by his total lack of consciousness.
So they hurried to bring the news to his family: "Your relative is lying there in a state of collapse!"
"No one knows how he was struck with this **seizure** <note>original: *catalepsy*. A medical condition characterized by a trance-like state and rigid muscles.</note>, or what led to this public scene."

<summary>Rumi uses the metaphor of "stokers" feeding a fire with dung to illustrate how worldly greed consumes and blackens the soul. This leads into a famous parable about a tanner—accustomed to the foul smells of his trade—who faints from the "overwhelming" purity and sweetness of a perfume bazaar.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative following the description of the "stokers"—those who spend their lives gathering the "filth" of worldly wealth. It moves into the specific story of the tanner who fainted in the perfume-sellers' bazaar because he was so accustomed to foul odors that the sweet scent of musk overwhelmed him. His brother now arrives to "save" him using the only thing the tanner knows.</meta>

That stout tanner had a brother, who was both cunning and sagacious; he came at once in hot haste.

❧**270.** With a small quantity of dog's dung hidden in his sleeve, he pushed his way through the crowd and approached the senseless man with cries of grief.
“I know,” he said, “where his illness comes from. When you know the cause of a disease, the means of curing it becomes clear.
When the cause is unknown, the remedy is difficult to find, and there are a hundred different reasons to which it might be blamed.
But when you have identified the cause, the task becomes easy; for knowledge of causes is the very means of banishing ignorance.”
He said to himself, “The smell of that dog's dung is woven into his brain and his veins.

❧**275.** Up to his waist in filth, he is absorbed in the tanner's craft until nightfall, seeking his livelihood.
Thus the great **Galen** <note>original: "Jālīnūs"—the famous Greek physician whose medical theories dominated Islamic science for centuries.</note> said: ‘Give the patient that to which he was accustomed before his illness.’
For his illness arises from doing the opposite of his usual habit; therefore, seek the remedy for his illness in that which is habitual to him.”
The tanner, from carrying dung, has become like a **dung-beetle** <note>The dung-beetle is Rumi's favorite metaphor for a soul so accustomed to the "filth" of the world that it finds the "perfume" of spiritual truth or virtue deadly.</note>; and the dung-beetle is made unconscious by the scent of rose-water.
The remedy for him consists in that same dog's dung to which he is accustomed and habituated.

❧**280.** Recite the scripture: *The wicked women are for the wicked men* <note>A reference to the Quran, Surah An-Nur 24:26, suggesting that things—and people—naturally gravitate toward those of a similar nature.</note>; recognize both the front and the back of this saying.
Sincere mentors might prepare medicine for a wicked man using ambergris or rose-water to open the door of **Divine Mercy**;
But sweet words will not work for the wicked; such things are not fitting or suitable for them, O ye trusty ones!
When the wicked infidels encountered the perfume of **Revelation**, they became disordered in mind and lost in error; their cry was: “*We see an evil omen in you.*” <note>Referencing how the messengers of God were often treated as bringers of bad luck by those who preferred their own ignorance.</note>
They said, “This discourse of yours is an illness and a sickness to us; your exhortation is not a good sign for us.

❧**285.** If you begin to advise us openly even once, we will stone you at that very instant.
We have grown fat on frivolity and distraction; we have never steeped ourselves in your warnings.
Our food is falsehood, idle boasts, and jests; our stomachs turn at the delivery of this message.
You are making our illness a hundred times worse; you are drugging our intelligence with **opium** <note>Here used metaphorically to mean something that dulls the senses or confuses the mind.</note>.”

### *How the tanner's brother sought to cure him secretly with the smell of dung.*

The youth kept driving the people away from the tanner, so that they would not see the "medicine" he was using on the sick man.

❧**290.** He brought his head close to his brother’s ear, like someone whispering a secret; then he held the substance he had in his hand to the tanner's nose.
He had rubbed the dog's dung on his palm; he deemed it the only remedy for a brain polluted by foul work.
A short while passed, and the man began to move. The people said, “This was a wonderful **charm**! <term>charm: (Persian: afsún) An incantation or prayer used for healing.</term>
For this youth recited charms and breathed them into his ear; the man was dead, and the charms came to rescue him.”
The movement of iniquitous folk is always toward the quarter where there is forbidden desire, wandering eyes, and flirtation.

## *How the lover begged to be excused for his sin, yet with duplicity and pretense; and how the beloved perceived that as well.*

> The lover said, “I only made that test—please do not take offense—so that I might see whether you were a <term>hetaera</term> <note>A high-class courtesan or prostitute; here the lover makes the insulting claim that he was "testing" her virtue.</note> or a modest woman. I already knew the truth without the test, but how can merely hearing something be the same as seeing it for oneself?
> You are like the sun: your name is famous and known to everyone; what harm is there if I have tested your brilliance?
> You are my very self: every day I test myself in matters of profit and loss, good and evil.
> 
> 310. Even the prophets were put to the test by their enemies, which resulted in their miracles being displayed to the world.
> I only tested my own eyes using your light—O you, may the evil eye be far from your beauty!
> This world is like a ruin, and you are the treasure buried within it; if I have searched for your treasure, do not be aggrieved.
> I recklessly committed such an indiscretion so that I might always boast of your virtue to your enemies;
> So that, when my tongue speaks your name, my eyes can provide witness to the truth of what I have seen.
> 
> 315. If I have actually sought to rob you of your honor, then I come before you, O Moon of Beauty, with a sword and a burial shroud.
> Do not cut off my feet or my head except with your own hand, for I belong to this hand, and to no other.
> You are speaking of separation again: do whatever you wish to me, but do not do that!”

The path is now open to enter the realm of <term>Discourse</term> <note>original: "Maqāl"—formal spiritual exposition or speech.</note>; but it is impossible to speak on the subject now, as there is no time.
We have described the husks (the external stories), but the kernel (the inner meaning) remains buried; if we remain alive, this meaning will not stay hidden as it is now.

## ***How the beloved rejected the excuses of the lover and rubbed his duplicity into him***

> ⚜️**320.** The beloved opened her lips to answer him, saying, “On my side it is day, and on your side it is night.
Why do you bring forward dark evasions in an argument before those who see the truth so plainly?
To us, all the deceit and pretenses you hold in your heart are as manifest and clear as the day.
If we, out of kindness to our servant, cover up your faults, why do you push your shamelessness beyond all limits?
Learn from your Father <note>A reference to Adam, the first man in Islamic and Judeo-Christian tradition.</note>; for in the hour of his sin, Adam came down willingly to the vestibule of repentance.
> 
> ⚜️**325.** When he beheld the Knower of Secrets <note>A traditional title for God.</note>, he stood upon his feet to ask for forgiveness.
He seated himself on the ashes of contrition: he did not jump from one branch of idle pleading to another.
He said only, ‘O Lord, truly we have done wrong,’ <note>original: "Rabbana zalamna anfusana" — a direct quote from the Quran (7:23) regarding Adam and Eve's repentance.</note> when he saw the angelic life-guards in front and behind.
He saw the life-guards who are invisible, just as the spirit is—each one’s mace reaching to the sky—
Saying, ‘Pay attention! Be like the ant before Solomon, lest this mace strike you asunder.’ <note>A reference to the Quranic story (27:18) where an ant warns its colony to be humble and hide so that King Solomon’s passing army does not accidentally crush them.</note>
> 
> ⚜️**330.** Do not for one moment stand anywhere but in the place of truth: a man has no guardian like his own seeing eye.
Even if a blind man is purified by a warning, he continually becomes polluted again.
O Adam, you are not blind of vision, but when Divine Destiny <note>The concept of "Qadar," or the divine decree that sometimes overrides human reason or physical senses.</note> arrives, even the sharpest sight becomes blind.”

Lifetimes are needed—and it happens only rarely—for a man with vision to fall into a pit because of destiny.
But for the blind man, this destiny is his constant companion on the path; for it is his very nature and disposition to fall.

⚜️**335.** He falls into the filth and does not know what the smell is; he asks himself, “Is this smell from me, or is it because I have been polluted by something else?”
Likewise, if someone sprinkles <term>musk</term> <note>A highly valued, sweet-smelling perfume used here as a metaphor for spiritual grace.</note> over him, he thinks the sweetness comes from himself and not from the kindness of his friend.
Therefore, to you, O man of vision, two clear eyes are worth more than a hundred mothers and a hundred fathers;
Especially the eye of the heart—the spiritual eye—which is seventy times more powerful, and of which these two physical eyes are only the gatherers of scraps.
Oh, alas, the highwaymen are waiting for me: they have tied a hundred knots beneath my tongue.

⚜️**340.** How can a smooth-paced horse move well when its leg is tied? This is a very heavy chain: I ask you to excuse me!
These words of mine are coming out brokenly, O heart; for these words are pearls, and the Divine Jealousy is the millstone that breaks them.
But, even though the pearls are broken into small fragments, they become <term>tutty</term> <note>Also known as <term>collyrium</term>, a medicinal powder or ointment used in ancient times to treat eye ailments and sharpen the vision of the spirit.</note> for the sore eye of the spirit.
O pearl, do not beat your head in grief because you are broken, for through being broken you will become radiant light.
The word must be uttered thus—brokenly and in bandages: God, who is Self-sufficient, will make it whole at last.

**345.** If wheat is broken and torn apart in the mill, it eventually appears in the baker’s shop, as if saying, "Look! Now I am a perfect loaf!"
You too, O lover—since your fault has become plain—abandon your attempts to smooth things over with "water and oil" <note>A metaphor for using specious or superficial excuses to varnish over a mistake.</note> and allow yourself to be broken in contrition.
Those who are the noble children of Adam sigh forth the confession: "*Truly, we have done wrong.*" <note>original: "Rabbana zalamna" — a reference to the Quranic prayer of Adam and Eve (7:23) after their fall.</note>

**350.** Abu Jahl <note>Literally "Father of Ignorance," a nickname given to one of the Prophet Muhammad's most stubborn opponents.</note>, acting like a vengeful Ghuzz Turcoman <note>A reference to a Turkic tribal group known in Rumi's time for their fierce and sometimes relentless nature.</note>, demanded a miracle from the Prophet;
But that *Siddíq* of God <note>original: "Siddíq" — The Truthful, the title given to Abu Bakr, the Prophet’s closest companion.</note> did not crave a miracle: he simply said, "Truly, this face speaks nothing but the truth."
How could it be fitting for someone like you, out of sheer egoism, to put a beloved like me to the test?

## *How the Jew said to 'Alí, may God honour him: "If you have confidence in God's protection, cast yourself down from the top of this pavilion"; and how the Prince of the Faithful answered him.*

One day a rebellious man, who was ignorant of the reverence due to God, said to Murtazá <note>original: "Murtazá" — The Chosen/Pleasing One, a common title for 'Alí ibn Abí Tálib, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet.</note>,
While they were on the roof of an exceedingly high terrace or pavilion: "Are you truly aware of God's protection, O wise man?"

**355.** "Yes," 'Alí replied; "He is the Protector and the Self-sufficient One who has preserved my existence since the time of my infancy and conception."
The Jew said, "Then come, cast yourself down from this roof! Put your entire confidence in God’s protection,
So that your certain faith and your beautiful, proven conviction may become clear to me."
Then the Prince of the Faithful said to him, "Be silent! Go, lest your soul be forfeited for this boldness."
How is it right for a servant of God to venture on an experiment with God by putting Him to a test?

**360.** How should a servant have the arrogance to put Him to the test, you mad fool?
That right belongs to God alone, who brings forward a test for His servants at every moment,
In order that He may show us plainly to ourselves, revealing what secret beliefs we truly hold.
Did Adam ever say to God, "I tested You by committing this sin and trespass,
Just so I could see the furthest limit of Your mercy, O King"? Ah, who would be capable of such a thing?

**365.** Because your understanding is confused, your excuse is even worse than your crime.
How can you try to test the One who raised the high vault of heaven?
O you who have not yet learned to distinguish good from evil, first test yourself, and then test others.
When you have truly examined yourself, you will be too occupied to bother testing anyone else.
When you come to know that you are a grain of sugar, then you will know that you belong in the sugar-house.

**370.** Know then, without any need for a trial, that if you are "sugar," God will not send you to the wrong place.
Without testing, know this of God’s knowledge: when you are a spiritual leader, He will not leave you waiting in the outer hallway.

<summary>Through the story of 'Ali and a skeptical challenger, Rumi argues that while God tests humanity to reveal their inner nature, it is an act of spiritual arrogance for a human to "test" God. The text emphasizes that self-knowledge and humility are the keys to finding one's rightful place in the divine order.</summary>

Does any intelligent man let a precious pearl fall into the midst of a privy <note>A toilet or latrine.</note> full of ordure <note>Excrement or filth.</note>?
Inasmuch as a sagacious and attentive man will nowise send wheat to a straw-barn,
If a novice has made trial of the Spiritual Master <note>original: "Shaykh"</note> who is the spiritual leader and guide, he is an ass.

<image-desc>ornamental floral flourish</image-desc> **375.** If you make trial of him in the way of religion, *you will be tried* by tribulation, O man without faith.
Your audacity and ignorance will become naked and exposed to view: how should he be made naked by that scrutiny?
If the mote <note>A tiny speck of dust.</note> comes and tries to weigh the mountain, its scales will be shattered by the mountain, O youth;
For the novice applies the scales of his own judgment and puts the man of God in those scales;
But since the Master is not contained by the scales of intellect, he consequently shatters the scales of intellect.

<image-desc>ornamental floral flourish</image-desc> **380.** Know that to make trial of him is like exercising authority over him: do not seek to exercise authority over such a spiritual king.
What authority should the pictures—the phenomenal forms—desire to exercise over such an Artist for the purpose of testing Him?
If the picture has known and experienced any trial, is it not the case that the Artist brought that trial upon it?
Indeed, this form that He fashioned—what is it worth in comparison with the forms which are in His knowledge?
When the temptation to make this trial has come to you, know that ill fortune has come and smitten your neck.

<image-desc>ornamental floral flourish</image-desc> **385.** When you feel such a temptation, at once, at once turn unto God and begin the prostration in prayer.
Make the place of prostration wet with flowing tears and say, “O God, do Thou deliver me from this doubt!”
At the time when it is your object to make trial of God, the mosque—namely, your religion—becomes filled with <term>kharrúb</term> <note>The carob tree. In Islamic tradition, a carob tree grew in Solomon's Temple as a sign of its impending ruin and his approaching death. Here, it symbolizes the desolation of one’s spiritual life caused by doubt.</note>.

### *Story of the Farther Mosque <note>original: "Masjid al-Aqsa," the holy site in Jerusalem.</note> and the carob and how, before the reign of Solomon, on whom be peace, David, on whom be peace, resolved on building that Mosque.*

When David's resolve that he would build the Farther Mosque with stone came to sore straits, God made a Revelation to him, saying, “Proclaim the abandonment of this enterprise, for the building of this place will not be achieved by thy hand.

<image-desc>ornamental floral flourish</image-desc> **390.** It is not in Our fore-ordainment that thou shouldst raise this Farther Mosque, O chosen one.”
He said, “O Knower of the secret, what is my crime, that Thou forbiddest me to construct the Mosque?”
He (God) said, “Without committing a crime, thou hast wrought much bloodshed: thou art responsible for the blood of many persons who have suffered injustice;
For from hearing thy voice a countless multitude gave up the ghost and fell a prey to thy voice <note>In Sufi lore, David’s voice was so beautiful and powerful that people and animals would fall into such ecstasies that they would literally die of longing or wonder.</note>.
Much blood is chargeable to thy voice, to thy beautiful soul-ravishing song.”

<image-desc-desc>ornamental floral flourish</image-desc> **395.** David said, “I was overpowered by Thee, drunken with Thee: my power was tied up by Thy hand."

<summary>Rumi warns that the human intellect cannot "test" a spiritual master without being shattered, much like a tiny scale trying to weigh a mountain. This leads into the story of David, who was forbidden from building the Temple in Jerusalem because his divinely beautiful voice caused the deaths of many who heard it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of spiritual authority and the limitations of the ego. Following the previous discussion on the futility of a novice attempting to "test" a spiritual master, Rumi now explores the state of spiritual "extinction" (faná), where the seeker's will is entirely absorbed into the Divine will, leading into a discussion on the essential unity of all prophets and believers.</meta>

Was not every one that was overpowered by the King <note>Referring to God as the ultimate Sovereign.</note> the object of His mercy? Was not he excused on the ground that "The overpowered is like the non-existent"? <note>original: "al-maghlūb ka’l-ma‘dūm." A legal and philosophical principle suggesting that one who has lost their agency to a higher power is no longer a separate, accountable entity.</note>

He (God) said, "This overpowered man is that non-existent one who is only relatively non-existent. Have sure faith!

Such a non-existent one who hath gone from himself—becoming selfless—is the best of beings, and the great one among them.

He hath passed away <term>faná (spiritual extinction)</term> in relation to the passing away of his own attributes into the Divine attributes, but in that passing away from selfhood, he really possesses the life everlasting <term>baqá (spiritual subsistence)</term>.

❧**400.** All spirits are under his governance; all bodies too are in his control.

He that is overpowered and overwhelmed in Our grace is not compelled; nay, he is one who freely chooses devotion to Us."

In truth, the ultimate goal of free will is that his free will should be lost here.

The free agent would feel no spiritual delight if, at last, he did not become entirely purged of egoism.

If there is delicious food and drink in the world, yet his pleasure in them is only a branch derived from the extinction of worldly pleasure.

❧**405.** Although he was unaffected by worldly pleasures, yet he was a man of spiritual pleasure and became the recipient of that true pleasure.

->**Explanation of the saying: "Verily, the Faithful are brothers, and the 'ulamá <note>original: "learned divines" or "scholars of religion."</note> are as one soul"; in particular, the oneness of David, Solomon, and all the other prophets, on whom be peace: if you disbelieve in one of them, your faith in any prophet will not be perfect; and this is the sign of their oneness, that if you destroy a single one of those thousands of houses, all the rest will be destroyed, and not a single wall will be left standing; for "We make no distinction between any of them <note>Referring to the prophets; a reference to Quran 2:285.</note>." Indication is sufficient for him that hath intelligence: this goes even beyond indication.**<-

(God said to David), "Although it will not be accomplished by thy labour and strength, yet the Mosque <note>The Temple in Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis).</note> will be erected by thy son, Solomon.

His deed is thy deed, O man of wisdom: know that between the Faithful there is an ancient union."

The Faithful are numerous, but the Faith is one: their bodies are numerous, but their soul is one.

Besides the understanding and soul which is in the ox and the ass, Man has another intelligence and soul;

❧**410.** Again, in the owner of that Divine breath, there is a soul other than the human soul and intelligence.

The animal soul does not possess oneness: seek not thou this oneness from the airy, vital spirit.

If this one eats bread, that one is not filled; and if this one bears a load, that one does not become laden;

Nay, but this one rejoices at the death of that one, and dies of envy when he sees that one's prosperity.

The souls of wolves and dogs are separate, every one; but the souls of the Lions of God <note>A term for the spiritually enlightened and courageous saints.</note> are united.

❧**415.** I have spoken of their souls nominally in the plural, for that single soul is like a hundred in relation to the body,

Just as the single light of the sun in heaven is a hundred in relation to the courtyards of the houses on which it shines,

But when you remove the walls of the houses, all the lights falling on them are revealed as one.

When the bodily houses have no foundation remaining, the Faithful remain as one soul.

<summary>Rumi explains the concept of faná (spiritual extinction), where the individual's will is lost in God's will, and emphasizes the essential unity of all prophets and believers, using the metaphor of sunlight divided by the walls of different houses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of spiritual "extinction" (faná), clarifying that the seeker's disappearance into the Divine is not a total loss of being, but a transformation—much like a star "vanishing" in the glare of the daylight. Rumi uses various sensory metaphors, from courageous lions to lamps and hornets, to explain how the individual ego is superseded and absorbed by a greater Reality.</meta>

Differences and difficulties arise from this saying, because this is not a (complete) similitude: it is (only) a comparison.

☿420. Endless are the differences between the corporeal figure of a lion and the figure of a courageous son of man;
But at the moment of (making) the comparison consider, O thou who hast good insight, their oneness in respect of hazarding their lives;
For, after all, the courageous man did resemble the lion, (though) he is not like the lion in all points of the definition. <note>Rumi warns the reader not to take metaphors too literally; a man is called a "lion" because of his bravery, not because he has paws or a mane.</note>
This abode (the world) does not contain any form (that is) one (with any other form), so that I might show forth to thee a (complete) similitude.
Still, I will bring to hand an imperfect comparison, that I may redeem thy mind from confusion.

☿425. At night a lamp is placed in every house, in order that by its light they (the inmates) may be delivered from darkness.
That lamp is (like) this body, its light like the <term>animal soul</term> <note>The "animal soul" (nafs) refers to the biological life force and basic instincts that animate the physical body.</note>; it requires a wick and this and that.
That lamp with six wicks, namely, these <term>senses</term> <note>The five physical senses plus the "common sense" or internal perception.</note>, is based entirely upon sleep and food.
Without food and sleep it would not live half a moment; nor even with food and sleep does it live either.
Without wick and oil it has no duration, and with wick and oil it is also faithless (transient),

☿430. Inasmuch as its light, (being) related to (secondary) causes, is seeking death: how should it live when bright day is the death of it?
Likewise all the human senses are impermanent, because they are naught in the presence of the Day of Resurrection.
The light of the senses and spirits of our fathers is not wholly perishable and naught, like the grass;
But, like the stars and moonbeams, they all vanish in the radiance of the Sun.
‘Tis just as the smart and pain of the flea’s bite disappears when the snake comes in to you (and bites you). <note>This striking metaphor suggests that the overwhelming presence of the Divine (the "snake") makes the minor irritations and sensations of worldly existence (the "flea") completely unnoticeable.</note>

☿435. ‘Tis just as the naked man jumped into the water, that in the water he might escape from the sting of the hornets:
The hornets circle above (him), and when he puts out his head they do not spare him.
The water is recollection (<term>dhikr</term>) <note>original: "dhikr." The practice of the rhythmic repetition of the names of God or religious formulas.</note> of God, and the hornet is the remembrance, during this time, of such-and-such a woman or such-and-such a man.
Swallow (hold) your breath in the water of recollection and show fortitude, that you may be freed from the old thought and temptation.
After that, you yourself will assume the nature of that pure water entirely from head to foot.

☿440. As the noxious hornet flees from the water, so will it be afraid of (approaching) you.
After that, be far from the water, if you wish; for in your inmost soul you are of the same nature as the water, O fellow-servant.
Those persons, then, who have passed from the world are not naught (nonexistent), but they are steeped in the (Divine) Attributes.
All their attributes are (absorbed) in the Attributes of God, even as the star is (left) without trace in the presence of the sun.
If you demand a citation from the <term>Qur’án</term>, O recalcitrant, recite "all of them shall be brought into Our presence." <note>original: "jami'un ladayna muhdarun." A reference to the Qur'an, Surah Ya-Sin (36:53), emphasizing that those who return to God are "brought forth" and present, rather than extinguished into nothingness.</note>

☿445. (The person denoted by the word) <term>muhdarún</term> (brought into the presence) is not non-existent (<term>ma’dúm</term>). Consider (this) well, that you may gain certain knowledge of the everlasting life (<term>baqá</term>) <note>original: "baqá." The Sufi concept of "subsistence" or "abiding" in God after the ego has been extinguished.</note> of the spirits.

<summary>Rumi uses metaphors of light, water, and predatory animals to explain that spiritual "extinction" is not the end of existence, but an absorption into Divine Attributes where the individual spirit persists in a higher state. He emphasizes that while the physical senses are transient, the spirit finds "everlasting life" (baqá) by immersing itself in the "water" of Divine remembrance (dhikr).</summary>

<meta>This section continues Rumi’s discourse on the distinction between the physical senses and the divine spirit. Having previously compared the seeker’s ego to a star vanishing in the sun, he now contrasts the "animal soul" (the individual lamp) with the "divine soul" (the universal sun) to explain why spiritual masters are in harmony while ordinary people are in conflict.</meta>

The spirit barred from everlasting life is in great agony; the spirit joined with God in eternal life is free from every obstacle.
I have explained the purpose of this "lamp" of <term>animal sense-perception</term> <note>original: "hiss-i hayvānī"; the basic sensory awareness shared by all living creatures.</note>. Be careful not to let your soul become identical to it.
O friend, make your spirit join quickly with the holy spirits of the <term>Travellers</term> <note>original: "sālikān"; those on the mystical path toward God.</note>.
Your hundred lamps, whether they go out or remain burning, are separate from one another and are not a single light.

❦**450.** Because of this, these companions of ours are all in conflict. Yet, no one has ever heard of war among the prophets.
This is because the light of the prophets was the Sun, while the light of our physical senses is merely a lamp, a candle, and smoke.
One lamp dies out, another lasts until dawn; one is dim, another is bright.
The <term>animal soul</term> is kept alive by food; no matter how good or bad its condition, it will eventually die.
If this lamp dies and is put out, why should the neighbor’s house become dark?

❦**455.** Since the light in that house continues even without this lamp, it follows that the lamp of physical perception is different in every "house" (every person).
This is a parable for the animal soul, not for the divine soul.
Furthermore, when the moon is born from the <term>Hindu</term> <note>In classical Persian poetry, "Hindu" is often used as a metaphor for "black" or "darkness," here representing the Night.</note> of Night, its light shines into every window.
Count the light of those hundred houses as one, because the light of one house cannot exist without the light of the other.
As long as the sun shines on the horizon, its light is a guest in every house.

❦**460.** But when the spiritual Sun sets, the light disappears from every house.
This is only a comparison of the Light, not a perfect likeness; for you, it is a true guide, but for the enemy of the Light, it is a thief on the road.
That person of evil nature is like a spider: he weaves foul veils.
Out of his own thin gossamer, he made a veil over the Light; he made the eye of his own understanding blind.
If one grabs a horse by the neck, he gains an advantage; but if he grabs its leg, he gets a kick.

❦**465.** Do not ride a stubborn horse without a bridle: let Reason and Religion be your leaders, and then you are safe.
Do not look at this spiritual quest with scorn or contempt, for on this Path, there is a need for self-denial and deep suffering of the soul.

### ***The rest of the Story of the building of the Farther Mosque.***

When Solomon began the building—as holy as the <term>Ka'ba</term> <note>original: "Ka'ba"; the sacred cube-shaped sanctuary in Mecca.</note> and as majestic as <term>Miná</term> <note>original: "Miná"; a sacred valley near Mecca where pilgrims perform rituals.</note>—
Splendor and greatness were seen in his construction. It was not cold and lifeless like other buildings.
From the start, every stone in the building—every piece broken from the mountain—was clearly saying, "Take me along!"

❦**470.** Just as light shone from the earth and water of the body of <term>Adam</term> <note>Refers to the Quranic tradition of God breathing spirit into the clay of the first man.</note>, light shone forth from the pieces of mortar.
The stones moved without anyone carrying them; those doors and walls had become alive.
God says that the wall of Paradise is not lifeless and ugly like ordinary walls.
Like the door and wall of the human body, it is endowed with intelligence. The house of Paradise is living because it belongs to the King of kings.

<summary>Rumi contrasts the individual, animalistic soul with the unified divine spirit of the prophets and describes the miraculous, sentient construction of Solomon's Temple.</summary>
<keywords>animal soul, divine soul, spiritual sun, Solomon, Al-Aqsa, Ka'ba, living stones, unity of prophets, mysticism</keywords>

<meta>This section continues Rumi’s exploration of the spiritual reality versus physical appearance. Following the previous page’s discussion on the "animal soul" (sensory perception) versus the "divine soul," the text now describes the nature of Paradise and the power of deeds over words, illustrated through the figures of Solomon and the Caliph ‘Uthmán.</meta>

Both the trees, the fruits, and the clear waters converse and discourse with the inhabitants of Paradise.

⚜**475.** This is because Paradise has not been constructed from physical building materials; rather, it has been fashioned out of good deeds and pure intentions.
This earthly building is made of dead water and earth, while that heavenly building has arisen from living piety.
This physical structure resembles its foundation, which is full of flaws, while that spiritual structure resembles its own foundation: knowledge and action.
The throne, the palace, the crown, and the robes all engage in a dialogue of question and answer with the inhabitant of Paradise.
The carpets there are spread without the need for a <term>farrash</term> <note>original: "farrāsh"; a servant or carpet-spreader responsible for preparing a house.</note>, and the house of Paradise is kept clean without a broom.

⚜**480.** Look at the house of the heart: it was once cluttered with worldly anxieties, yet it was swept clean by a vow of repentance without the need for a sweeper.
The heart's throne moves without a carrier; its door-ring and the door itself become like a musician and a singer, making sweet music.
The life of the <term>Everlasting Abode</term> <note>original: "dār-i baqā"; a common term for Paradise or the eternal realm beyond death.</note> exists within the heart; since it cannot be fully expressed by my tongue, what is the use of trying to describe it?
When Solomon went into the Mosque every morning to guide the servants of God onto the right path,
he would offer exhortation—sometimes through speech, melody, and harmony, and sometimes through action, by which I mean a bow or the service of prayer.

⚜**485.** An exhortation made through action draws people more powerfully, for it reaches the soul of everyone who can hear, as well as those who are deaf.
In that kind of teaching through action, the pride of leadership is less apparent; therefore, the impression it makes upon followers is much stronger.

### ***The Story of the beginning of the Caliphate of ‘Uthmán, may God be pleased with him, and his sermon explaining that the one who exhorts through deeds is better than the speaker who exhorts through words.***

The story is told that when <term>‘Uthmán</term> <note>The third Caliph (leader) of the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad.</note> attained the <term>Caliphate</term>, he hurried to mount the pulpit.
It was the pulpit of the <term>Chief</term> <note>The Prophet Muhammad.</note>, which had three steps. <term>Abú Bakr</term> <note>The first Caliph.</note> had seated himself on the second step.
<term>‘Umar</term> <note>The second Caliph.</note>, during his reign, sat on the third (lowest) step out of reverence for Islam and the true religion.

⚜**490.** When the reign of ‘Uthmán began, that man of blessed fortune went up to the very top of the pulpit and seated himself.
Then, a person prone to idle interference questioned him, saying, “Those two predecessors did not sit in the Prophet’s own place.
How is it that you have sought a seat higher than theirs, when you are lower than them in rank?”
He replied, “If I were to step onto the third step, people might imagine that I am trying to resemble ‘Umar.
And if I sought a seat on the second step, you would say, ‘That is the seat of Abú Bakr, and this man is trying to be like him.’

⚜**495.** This top step is the place of <term>Mustafá</term> <note>original: "Mustafā"; "The Chosen One," a title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note>. No one will ever imagine that I am like that spiritual King.”

<summary>Rumi explains that Paradise is built from deeds rather than matter, and uses the Caliph ‘Uthmán’s choice of seating on the Prophet's pulpit to illustrate the importance of distinguishing oneself through humility and action rather than imitation.</summary>
<keywords>Paradise, intentions, heart, Solomon, preaching, ‘Uthmán, Caliphate, Abú Bakr, ‘Umar, Mustafá, deeds vs words</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, where Rumi used the figure of Solomon to illustrate how pure intention and spiritual presence speak louder than words, the text now transitions to the Caliph ‘Uthmán (referred to as "that loving man"). He sits in silent meditation on the pulpit, demonstrating that the presence of a saint radiates a divine influence that transcends verbal preaching.</meta>

Afterwards, seated in the preaching-place, that loving man <note>A reference to the third Caliph, ‘Uthmán ibn ‘Affán, who was known for his modesty and deep spiritual state.</note> kept silence until near the time of the afternoon prayer.
None dared to say, “Come now, preach!” or to go forth from the mosque during that time.
An awe had settled and descended on high and low alike: the court and roof of the mosque had become filled with the Light of God.
Whoever possessed vision was beholding His Light; the blind man too was being heated by that Sun.

❧ **500.** Hence, by reason of the heat, the blind man’s eye was perceiving that there had arisen a Sun whose strength never fails.
But this heat—unlike the heat of the physical sun—opens the inward eye <note>The "inward eye" refers to the spiritual heart capable of perceiving metaphysical truths.</note>, so that it may see the very substance of everything it has only heard about.
Its heat causes a grievous agitation and emotion, but from that glow there comes to the heart a joyous sense of freedom and expansion.
When the blind man is heated by the Light of Eternity, he says out of gladness, “I have become seeing.”
Thou art mightily well drunken, but, O Bu ’l-Hasan <note>original: "Bu ’l-Ḥasan"; likely an address to a spiritual seeker or a specific contemporary of the poet.</note>, there is still a bit of the way to be traversed before thou truly attain to seeing.

❧ **505.** This is the blind man’s portion from the Sun, and a hundred such portions; and God best knows what is right.
And as for he who has a vision of that Light—how could the explanation of his state be a task within the capacity of Bú Síná? <note>original: "Bū Sīnā"; known in the West as Avicenna (d. 1037), the preeminent philosopher and physician who represents the limits of human reason and logic.</note>
Even if it were a hundred times more capable, what is this tongue that it should move with its hand the veil of mystical clairvoyance?
Woe to the tongue if it touch the veil! The Divine sword severs its hand.
What of the hand? The sword rends off even the tongue's head—the head that, out of ignorance, puts forth many a "head" of pride and self-conceit.

❧ **510.** I have said this to you, speaking hypothetically; otherwise, indeed, how far is its hand from being able to do that!
If my maternal aunt had the organs of a man, she would be my uncle <note>original: "Materterae si testiculi essent, ea avunculus esset"; a Latin proverb used to illustrate a purely hypothetical or impossible condition.</note>: this is hypothetical—an "if there were."
If I say that between the tongue and the eye that is free from doubt there is a hundred thousand years’ journey, it is little in comparison with the reality.
Now come, do not despair! When God wills, light arrives from heaven in a single moment.
At every instant His power causes a hundred influences from the stars to reach the subterranean mines <note>Medieval science believed that the influence of planets and stars transformed earth and minerals into precious metals like gold over long periods of time.</note>.

❧ **515.** The star of heaven deletes the darkness; the star of God is fixed in His Attributes.
O thou that seekest help, the celestial sphere, though at a distance of five hundred years’ journey, is in effect close to the earth.
It is a journey of three thousand five hundred years to Saturn; yet his special property acts incessantly upon the earth.
God rolls the soul up like a shadow at the return of the sun: in the presence of the Sun, what is the length of the shadow?
And from the pure "stars" that are the souls of the saints, replenishment is ever coming to the physical stars of heaven.

❧ **520.** The outward aspect of those stars is our ruler, but our inward essence has become the ruler of the sky.

### ***Explaining that while philosophers say that Man is the microcosm, theosophists say that Man is the macrocosm, the reason being that philosophy is confined to the*** <note>The text concludes on the next page, likely explaining that philosophy is limited to the physical realm while mysticism explores the spiritual vastness within.</note>

He concludes by asserting that while humans seem small (microcosm) to the eye, their spiritual essence is the true "macrocosm" that governs the heavens.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the poet Rumi concludes the story of the Caliph ‘Uthmán’s silent sermon, transitioning into a deeper philosophical meditation on the relationship between the human form and the divine essence. He argues that while humans appear small, they contain the entirety of the universe within them.</meta>

### ***The external form of Man, whereas spiritual wisdom is connected with the essential truth of his true nature.***

Therefore, in your outer form, you are the <term>microcosm<note>The "small world"—the idea that a human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note></term>; however, in your spiritual reality, you are the <term>macrocosm<note>The "great world"—the totality of the universe. Rumi suggests the human soul is vaster than the physical cosmos.</note></term>.
Outwardly, the branch is what produces the fruit; but inwardly, the branch only exists for the sake of the fruit.
If the gardener had no desire or hope for the fruit, why would he have ever planted the root of the tree?
Therefore, in reality, the tree was born from the fruit, even if it appears that the fruit was produced by the tree.

❦**525.** For this reason, <term>Mustafá<note>original: "Muṣṭafá"; a title for the Prophet Muhammad meaning "The Chosen One."</note></term> said, "Adam and the other prophets follow behind me, under my banner."
It is for this reason that the master of all knowledge uttered the cryptic saying: "We are the last and the foremost."
This means: "Though I was born from Adam in appearance, in reality, I am the forefather of every ancestor."
Since the angels bowed to Adam only for my sake, and he ascended to the <term>Seventh Heaven<note>The highest celestial sphere in traditional cosmology, signifying the utmost proximity to the Divine.</note></term> because of me.
Therefore, in reality, the Father (Adam) was born from me; in reality, the tree was born from the fruit.

❦**530.** The thought or idea, which comes first in the mind, is the last thing to be physically realized—especially the eternal thought of God.
In short, in a single moment, the spiritual caravan travels from Heaven to this world and back again.
This road is not long for such a caravan: why should the desert seem terrifying to one whom God has granted success?
The heart (the spirit) travels to the <term>Ka'ba<note>The spiritual center of the world; here used to represent the Divine Presence.</note></term> at every moment, and through Divine grace, the physical body begins to take on the nature of the spirit.
This concept of "long" or "short" distances applies only to the body; where God is present, what meaning do "long" and "short" have?

❦**535.** When God has transformed the body, He allows it to travel without needing leagues or miles.
There are a hundred hopes in this present moment. Step forward, O youth, like a true lover, and leave behind empty arguments.
Though you may close your eyes, you are like a passenger asleep on a ship, still moving safely toward your destination.

## ***An explanation of the Prophetic Tradition: "The likeness of my community is the likeness of the Ark of Noah: whoever clings to it is saved, and whoever stays behind is drowned."***

On this account, the Prophet said, "I am like the Ark in the Flood of Time.
I and my Companions are like the Ship of Noah: whoever holds fast to us will receive spiritual blessings."

❦**540.** When you are with the <term>Shaykh<note>original: "Shaykh"; a spiritual guide or master who leads the seeker along the path of truth.</note></term>, you are far removed from evil; day and night, you are a traveler safe within a ship.
You are under the protection of a spirit that gives life; you are asleep in the boat, yet you continue on the way.
Do not break your connection with the prophet of your time; do not rely on your own cleverness or your own footsteps.
Even if you are a lion, you are merely arrogant and lost if you attempt this journey without a guide.
Take heed! Do not try to fly except with the wings of the Master, so that you may receive the help of the Master's spiritual armies.

❦**545.** At one time, the wave of His mercy is your wing; at another moment, the fire of His wrath is what carries you.

This is not like the physical ascent of a piece of earth to the moon; no, it is like the transformation of a stalk of cane into sugar.
It is not like a vapor rising to the sky; no, it is like an embryo’s ascent into the realm of reason.

With no need for physical hands or feet, travel toward Eternity in the same way that spirits once sped out of non-existence.
If there were no dullness or inattention in the listener’s ear, the veil of logical reasoning would have been torn apart by this discourse.

❦**560.** O Heaven, shower pearls upon the Shaykh's <term>wisdom<note>original: "rede"; his counsel or speech.</note></term>! O World, be humbled by his world!
If you shower these pearls, your very substance will increase a hundredfold: your unfeeling matter will become seeing and speaking.
Therefore, you will have scattered this gift for your own sake, since every part of your being will be multiplied ten times over.

### *Story of Bilqís sending a gift from the city of Sabá to Solomon, on whom be peace.*

The gift of <term>Bilqís<note>The Queen of Sheba (Sabá).</note></term> consisted of forty mules: their entire load was made of bricks of gold.
When her envoy reached the open plain belonging to <term>Solomon<note>The Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), who in Islamic tradition was given kingship over humans, jinn, animals, and the wind.</note></term>, he saw that the very ground was carpeted entirely with solid gold.

❦**565.** The envoy rode upon gold for the distance of forty stages, until gold no longer had any value in his eyes.
Many times the travelers said, "Let us take the gold back to the treasury: what a useless quest we are on!
A vast land where the soil itself is pure gold—to bring gold here as a gift is absolute folly."
O you who have brought your human intelligence to God as a gift, in that Divine Presence, intelligence is worth less than the dust of the road.
When the worthlessness of their gift became clear there in Solomon’s kingdom, shame began to pull them back toward Bilqís;

❀**590.** You will deem the physical sun base, lowly, and temporary once strength has come to your inward eye from the Creator."

# The miraculous gifts and illumination of Shaykh 'Abdullah Maghribi, may God sanctify his spirit.

Shaykh 'Abdullah Maghribī said, "During sixty years I never perceived in night the quality of night. During sixty years I never experienced any darkness, neither by day nor by night nor from infirmity." <note>Shaykh 'Abdullah Maghribi (d. 903 CE) was a famous ascetic of the North African (Maghribi) school of Sufism, known for his intense spiritual discipline.</note>

❦ **600.** The <term>Súfís<note>Followers of the mystical branch of Islam who seek a direct personal experience of God.</note></term> declared his words to be true: "During the night we would follow him
Into deserts filled with thorns and ditches, he going in front of us like the full moon.
Without looking behind him, he would say, (though it was) at night-time, 'Hark! here is a ditch: turn to the left!'
Then, after a little while, he would say, 'Turn to the right, because a thorn is before your feet.'
Day would break: we would come to kiss his foot, and his foot would be like the feet of a bride,

❦ **605.** No trace of earth or mud on it, none of scratch from thorns or bruise from stones."
God made the <term>Maghribí<note>original: "Maghribī"; meaning "the Westerner" or "one from the place of sunset."</note></term> a <term>Mashriqí<note>original: "Mashriqī"; meaning "the Easterner" or "one from the place of sunrise."</note></term>: He made the place of sunset light-producing like the place of sunrise. <note>This is a play on words: though his name means "the Westerner/Sunset," his soul has become the "East/Sunrise" where the sun of God's light rises.</note>
The light of this one who belongs to the Sun of suns is riding in majesty: by day he is guarding high and low.
How should that glorious light, which brings thousands of suns into view, not be a guardian?
By his light do thou walk always in safety amidst dragons and scorpions.

❦ **610.** That holy light is going in front of thee and tearing every highwayman to pieces.
Know aright the meaning of the scripture: *On the Day when He will not put the Prophet to shame; their light shall run before them.* <note>A reference to Quran 66:8, describing the light of the believers on the Day of Resurrection.</note>
Although that light will be increased at the Resurrection, beg of God to grant thee a trial of it here;
For He bestows spiritual light both on cloud and mist, and God best knoweth how to impart it.

## *How Solomon, on whom be peace, bade the envoys of <term>Bilqis<note>The Islamic name for the Queen of Sheba.</note></term> return to her with the gifts which they had brought; and how he called Bilqis to accept the Faith and to abandon sun-worship.*

## ***Story of the druggist whose balance-weight was clay for washing the head; and how a customer, who was a clay-eater, stole some of that clay covertly and secretly, whilst sugar was being weighed.***

**625.** A certain clay-eater went to a druggist to buy a quantity of fine hard sugar-loaf. <note>Eating certain types of mineral-rich clay was a known habit/addiction in the medieval East, often used for medicinal purposes or as a hair-wash.</note>
Now, at the druggist's—who was a crafty and vigilant man—in place of a proper metal balance-weight, there was only a piece of clay.
He said, "If you want to buy sugar, be aware that my balance-weight is made of clay."
The customer said, "I need sugar for an urgent matter; let the balance-weight be whatever you wish."
To himself he thought, "What does the material of the weight matter to one who loves to eat clay? Indeed, to me, clay is better than gold!"

**630.** He was like the <term>dallála<note>original: "dallāla"; a professional matchmaker or go-between.</note></term> who said, "O son, I have found a very beautiful new bride for you.
She is exceedingly pretty, but there is just one thing: the lady is a confectioner's daughter."
"All the better!" said the man. "If it is indeed so, his daughter will be even fatter and sweeter."
The customer thought, "If you have no proper weight and your weight is made of clay, this is better and better; clay is the very fruit my heart desires."
The druggist placed the clay weight—because it was ready at hand—in one scale of the balance;

**635.** Then, for the other scale, he began breaking off pieces of sugar with his hand to match the weight.
Since he had no pick-axe, the process took a long time and he made the customer sit and wait.
While the druggist's face was turned toward the sugar, the clay-eater, unable to restrain his craving, began secretly to steal bits of clay from the weight scale.
He was terribly frightened lest the druggist's eye should fall upon him suddenly to test his honesty.
The druggist saw exactly what was happening, but he kept himself busy, thinking: "Go on, steal more, O pale-faced one!

**640.** If you want to be a thief and take my clay, keep going, for you are only eating from your own side. <note>This is a metaphor for self-sabotage: because the scale-weight was becoming lighter, the customer was ultimately receiving less sugar for his money.</note>
You are afraid of me, but only because you are a foolish ass; I am actually afraid that you will eat too little!
Though I seem occupied, I am not such a fool as to let you get too much of my precious sugar-cane.
When you see by experience the actual amount of sugar you have bought, then you will know who was truly foolish and careless."
The bird looks happily at the bait, yet the bait—even from a distance—is leading it to its doom.

**645.** If you are deriving pleasure from the greed of your eyes, are you not simply eating the roast-meat of your own flesh?
Looking at forbidden things from a distance is like poisoned arrows; your passion increases while your self-restraint is destroyed.
Worldly riches are a trap for weak birds; the "kingdom of the next world" is a trap for the noble birds,
To the end that by means of this "kingdom"—which is a much deeper trap—even the greatest souls might be tested and ensnared. <note>Rumi suggests that even the desire for "spiritual status" or "heavenly kingdoms" can be a subtle trap if it isn't pure devotion to God.</note>
Solomon said: "I do not desire your earthly kingdom; rather, I will deliver you from every path of destruction."

Solomon's rejection of the Queen's gifts serves as the ultimate example of choosing spiritual wealth over material traps.</summary>

### ***How a dervish saw a group of Shaykhs in a dream and begged for a daily portion of lawful food—to be received without the labor that hinders spiritual service—and how they guided him, and how the sour mountain fruit became sweet to him through the bounty of those Shaykhs.***

A certain <term>dervish<note>A practitioner of the Sufi path, often associated with poverty and asceticism.</note></term> said during a night-gathering, “I saw those saints associated with <term>Khizr<note>A mystical figure in Islamic tradition known as the 'Green Man,' who guides seekers and possesses immortal wisdom.</note></term> in a dream.
I said to them, ‘Where shall I find my daily portion of lawful food that will not cause me harm?’

**680.** They led me toward the mountains; they were shaking down the fruit from the trees in the forest,
Saying, ‘God has made the fruit taste sweet in your mouth because of our blessings.
Come, eat food that is pure and lawful, free of accounting, without the trouble of traveling or the toil of searching.’
Then, from that daily provision, a gift of speech appeared in me; the spiritual flavor of my words began to carry away the minds of the people.
I said, ‘This is a temptation! O Lord of the world, bestow on me a gift that is hidden from all Your creatures!’

**685.** Speech then left me, and I gained a joyful heart; I was bursting with rapture, like a ripe pomegranate.
I said, ‘If there is nothing else in Paradise for me but this delight which I have within my soul,
I would desire no other blessing; I would not be distracted from this joy by the <term>houris<note>Celestial beings of beauty in Paradise.</note></term> or the sweetness of heaven.’
Of my former earnings, only one or two small coins remained with me, sewn into the sleeve of my *jubba*. <note>original: "jubba" — a long, open-fronted robe with wide sleeves, typically worn by scholars or religious men.</note>

### ***How he intended to give this money to a woodcutter, since he had obtained his daily provision through the miraculous gifts of the Shaykhs; and how the woodcutter was offended by his secret thought and intention.***

A poor man was carrying firewood; he approached me from the forest, looking weary and exhausted.

**690.** I said to myself, ‘I am now independent of earning my bread; from now on I have no anxiety for my daily portion.
The bitter fruit has become sweet to me; a special provision for my body has been provided.
Since I have been freed from the demands of the stomach, I will give these small pieces of money to him.
I will give this money to this toil-worn man, so that for a few brief days he may be made happy by food.’
But the woodcutter knew my mind, because his inner hearing was illuminated by the candle of **Hú**. <note>original: "Hú" — Literally "He" (God), a term used in Sufi meditation to signify the Divine Presence.</note>

**695.** To him, the secret of every thought was as clear as a lamp within a glass.

No mental conception was hidden from him: he was a ruler over the very contents of men's hearts. Therefore, that wondrous man began muttering to himself under his breath in answer to my unspoken thoughts:

Immediately, those branches of gold turned back into firewood. My intellect and my sight were intoxicated—utterly amazed—at his miraculous work. After that, he took up the firewood and hurried away from me toward the town.

❧**710.** I wished to follow that spiritual king to ask him about my difficulties and hear his answers; but the awe he inspired kept me as if I were bound. The common people have no way of entering the presence of the elect. 

And if the way should become open to anyone, let him offer his very life in devotion, for that admission to their presence comes only from their mercy and their power of attraction. Therefore, when you gain companionship with the <term>siddíq<note>original: "صدیق" — A 'Truthful One,' representing the highest rank of sainthood and absolute sincerity.</note></term>, consider that Divine favor to be a precious opportunity. Do not be like the fool who wins the favor of the King and then carelessly falls away from the path of grace.

❧**715.** When more of the King's favor is bestowed upon such a fool, he says, “Surely this is just the thigh of an ox.”

It is not the thigh of an ox, O maker of lies! To you it appears as the thigh of an ox only because you are an ass <note>Rumi uses this metaphor to describe someone who is spiritually dull and perceives a divine miracle as something mundane or coarse.</note>. This is a royal gift, free from any corruption; this is pure generosity springing from a great mercy.

Even as in the spiritual warfare of love, King Solomon <note>In Islamic tradition, Solomon (Sulayman) is both a prophet and a king with power over winds, animals, and jinn.</note> drew the cavalry and foot-soldiers of Bilqis <note>The Queen of Sheba.</note> toward him, saying: 

“O honored men, come quickly, quickly, for the waves have risen from the sea of bounty!"

## *The cause of the migration of Ibrahim ibn Adham—may God sanctify his spirit—and his abandonment of the kingdom of Khurásán.*

Shatter the kingdom of this world as quickly as Ibrahim ibn Adham did, so that you, like him, may win the kingdom of eternal life.
One night, that king lay asleep on his throne, while the guards were patrolling the palace roof.
The king’s purpose in hiring guards was not to keep away thieves or troublemakers;
He knew that a ruler who is just is safe from attack and secure in his heart.

730. Justice is the true guardian of joy—not the men who beat their wooden rattles on the roofs at night.
Rather, his purpose in listening to the music of the <term>rebeck<note>A medieval bowed string instrument, similar to a fiddle.</note></term> was to recall—as true lovers of God do—the memory of that <term>Divine Address<note>Refers to the 'Day of Alast,' the primordial moment before creation when all human souls heard God's voice and swore a covenant with Him.</note></term>.
The shrill cry of the trumpet and the thunder of the drum bear some resemblance to that Great Trumpet of the Resurrection.
Because of this, philosophers have said that we learned these harmonies from the movement of the celestial spheres;
They say the melodies people sing with the lute and their own throats are echoes of those cosmic rotations.

735. But the true believers say that the beauty of Paradise makes even unpleasant sounds seem lovely.
We were all once part of Adam; we heard those same melodies in Paradise.
Though the "water and clay" of our physical bodies have caused us to doubt, some faint memory of those sounds still returns to us.
Yet, since it is now mixed with the "earth of sorrow," how can these high and low notes provide the same original delight?
When pure water is mixed with waste, its very nature becomes bitter and sour.

740. Even the small amount of water in a man's body—though it be mixed with impurities—can still extinguish a fire.
Even if the water is tainted, its essential property remains: by its very nature, it cools the fire of grief.
Therefore, <term>Sama‘<note>The Sufi practice of 'spiritual listening,' where music and poetry are used to induce a state of contemplation or ecstasy.</note></term> is the food of those who love God, for it contains the memory of inner composure.
Through these sounds and melodies, the images in the mind gain great strength; indeed, they take form in the imagination.
The fire of love is kindled by music, just like the excitement of the man who dropped walnuts into the water. <note>This refers to a previous parable where a thirsty man enjoyed the sound of walnuts splashing into a pool as much as the water itself, illustrating how the 'sound' of spiritual truth can sustain a seeker.</note>

### *Story of the thirsty man who dropped walnuts from the top of a walnut-tree into the water-brook that was in the hollow, without reaching the water (himself), in order that he might hear the sound made by the walnuts falling on the water, which thrilled him with joy as (though it were) sweet music.*

**745.** The water lay in a deep ravine: the thirsty man climbed the tree and scattered the walnuts one by one.
As the walnuts fell from the tree into the water, the splashing sound reached his ears, and he watched the bubbles rise.
A sensible person said to him, “Stop this, young man; losing these walnuts will only bring you regret and further thirst.
The more fruit falls into the water—since the water is so far below you—
The river's current will carry them away long before you can make the effort to climb down from the treetop.”

**750.** He replied, “My goal in scattering these is not to keep the walnuts; look more closely, do not settle for this superficial view.
My purpose is to hear the sound of the water, and to see those bubbles dancing on its surface.”
Indeed, what is a thirsty man's business in this world? To circle forever around the edge of the reservoir,
Around the stream, around the Water and the sound of the Water, like a pilgrim circumambulating the <term>Kaaba<note>The cube-shaped building in Mecca; Rumi uses it here as a metaphor for the ultimate spiritual Goal or Truth.</note></term> of Truth.
In the same way, in the composition of this <term>Masnavi<note>Rumi's monumental poem; the word literally means "rhyming couplets."</note></term>, it is you, O <term>Husamuddin<note>Literally "Sword of the Faith," Rumi’s favorite disciple and the inspiration for the poem.</note></term>, the Radiance of God, who are my true aim.

**755.** This entire *Masnavi*, in all its branches and roots, belongs to you; you are the one who has accepted it.
Kings accept both the good and the bad: once they accept something, it can no longer be called "rejected."
Since you are the one who planted this sapling, give it water. Since you have given it the freedom to grow, untie its knots.
In every expression, my goal is to reveal your mystery; in composing it, my goal is to hear your voice.
To me, your voice is the voice of God; Heaven forbid I should say the lover is ever separate from the Beloved.

**760.** There is a union beyond description or analogy between the Lord of Man and the spirit of Man.
But I said <term>*nas*<note>The Arabic word for "mankind" or "people."</note></term>, not <term>*nasnas*<note>A mythical, monstrous sub-human creature; Rumi uses it to describe those who have lost their spiritual essence.</note></term>; *nas* is nothing but the spirit that recognizes the Divine Spirit.
*Nas* is Man, but where is true Manhood? You have never even seen the head—the spiritual principle—of Man; you are merely a tail.
You have recited the verse *thou didst not throw when thou threwest*, <note>original: "wa-mā ramayta idh ramayta" — a reference to Quran 8:17, often used by Sufis to explain that God is the true actor behind human movements.</note> but you are still just a body; you remain trapped in the world of division.
Like <term>Bilqis<note>The Queen of Sheba.</note></term>, O foolish one, abandon the kingdom of your body for the sake of the prophet Solomon.

**765.** I am crying out, “*There is no power but in God*,” <note>original: "lā hawl" — a common Arabic formula used to repel evil or express that only God has true agency.</note> not because of my own words, but because of the false suggestions of those accustomed to thinking ill,
Who harbor vain fantasies about my words—fancies born from the doubts and disbelief of their own thoughts.
I am crying “*there is no help but in Him*,” because in your heart, you are contradicting me.
Since my words have stuck in your throat, I shall be silent; you go ahead and speak your own.

## *The continuation of the story of the people of Saba, and the guidance given by Solomon (peace be upon him) to the kinsfolk of Bilqis—how he provided each with the specific wisdom needed for their spiritual struggles, and how he lured every type of soul, like a bird, with the particular call and bait suited to its nature.*

## *How Bilqis was freed from her kingdom and became intoxicated with longing for the Faith, and how, at the moment of her spiritual migration, her desire was severed from her entire kingdom, except for her throne.*

**860.** Except, perhaps, for the "bird" that was without a soul or wings, or one that was born deaf and mute like a fish.

When Bilqis set out from Sabá with her whole heart and soul, she felt deep regret for the time she had wasted.

To her eyes, her beautiful servants and handmaidens now looked like rotten onions.

**865.** For the sake of divine love, her orchards, palaces, and flowing rivers seemed to her as worthless as a heap of refuse.

From afar, Solomon perceived that for her—who was otherwise following the path of surrender—it was a bitter thing to part with her throne.
If I were to explain the exact reason why she felt such love and attachment for her throne, the story would become too long.

❦**875.** Although a reed-pen is technically a lifeless thing and not of the same nature as the writer, it is still a close and familiar friend to him. Likewise, every tool of a craftsman, though it lacks a soul, is a familiar companion to the human spirit.
I would have explained this reason precisely if I didn't see a certain "moisture" <note>Metaphor for a lack of clarity or a "dimness" in perception.</note> in the eye of your understanding.
There was no physical way to transport the throne from the kingdom of Saba because its size exceeded all limits.
It was made of delicate filigree work, and there was a danger in taking it apart, as its pieces were joined together like the limbs of a body.

❦**880.** Therefore Solomon said, "Though in the end, her crown and throne will become cold and repulsive to her—"
(For when the spirit reveals itself from the state of <term>Unity<note>The Sufi concept of *Tawhid* or *Fana*, where the individual self dissolves into the Divine Oneness.</note> to which it has attained, the physical body has no splendor at all compared to the spirit's light;
When the flaming sun rises, who would choose the stars of Scorpio's tail <note>A constellation representing a much dimmer light than the sun.</note> as their resting place?)—
"—Yet, despite all this, we must find a way to transport her throne here anyway.

❦**885.** We do this so that she does not feel hurt when we meet, and so her wishes may be fulfilled, just as we satisfy the whims of children.
The throne is worthless to me, but it is incredibly precious to her. Let it be brought here, so that even the lowliest can be present at the banquet of the celestial spirits.
That throne of delight will become a lesson for her soul, just like the coarse shepherd’s coat and rustic shoes kept in the presence of Ayáz <note>Ayáz was the beloved servant of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni; he famously kept his old, poor clothes to remind himself of his humble origins so he would never become arrogant.</note>.
It is so the grieving one (Bilqis) may realize her former state and see the lowly place from which she has risen to such heights."
In the same way, God is always keeping our origins—the clay, the seed, and the embryo—before our eyes,

❦**890.** As if to say, "O human of ill-intent, where did I bring you from, that you now feel such disgust for your humble beginnings?
You were in love with that lowly state when you were in it; at that time, you were denying the very grace I have now given you."
Since this current blessing is the proof that refutes the denial you made while you were still just clay,
The fact that you were brought to life is the ultimate argument against those who deny the Resurrection. Yet you still deny it; your sick soul is only made worse by the very medicine that should cure it.

Where would mere clay get the power to imagine such a thing? How could a drop of semen conceive of opposition or denial?

**895.** Even though at that moment you were without a heart or spirit, your very act of denial now proves your capacity for reflection. Since your previous "denial" arose from a state of being inanimate and without reason, your present denial actually confirms the certainty of your resurrection.

### ***How Solomon, on whom be peace, devised a plan for bringing the throne of Bilqis from Saba.***

A certain ’Ifrit <term>’Ifrit: A powerful, often cunning or rebellious spirit or demon in Islamic tradition.</term> said, "By my craft, I will bring her throne here before you even rise from this council."

Asaf <term>Asaf: Asaf ibn Barkhiya, Solomon’s vizier, who is traditionally believed to have known the "Greatest Name of God," allowing him to perform miracles.</term> said, "By means of the Greatest Name of God, I will bring it here into your presence in a single moment."

**905.** Although the ’Ifrit was a master of magic, that miracle was actually displayed through the spiritual breath and power of Asaf. **910.** Both the worshipper and the object of worship are ignorant of the true Spirit; yet the worshipper has felt a slight movement and effect of that Spirit. He felt, at the moment he became lost in devotion and awe, that the stone spoke and made signs to him. 

When the wretched man directed his devotion to the wrong place and believed a stone lion to be a real lion, the real Lion <note>A metaphor for God.</note>, out of kindness, showed great generosity and immediately threw a bone to the dog. 

God said, "Even though the dog is not acting correctly, as far as I am concerned, the bone is a gift that all may share."

## ***A Parable: On how humanity is satisfied with worldly goods, their greed in seeking them, and their indifference to the high and blessed state of the spiritual ones—who are their true kin—who cry out, "Oh, would that my people only knew!"***

❧**1045.** A dog saw a blind beggar in the street; it rushed at him and began tearing at his cloak.
We have shared this story before, but we repeat it here to emphasize its message.
The blind man said to the dog, “Why attack me? At this very moment, your friends are hunting real prey on the mountain.
Your kinsfolk are catching wild animals in the hills, yet here you are in the streets, catching blind men.”
O stubborn <term>Shaykh</term><note>A spiritual teacher or leader.</note>, abandon this deception: you are like salty, undrinkable water that has gathered a few blind followers around you.

❧**1050.** It is as if you are saying, “These are my disciples,” but because you are salty water, they drink from you and only lose their sight.
Sweeten your "water" with the inner, spiritual Sea; do not use your foul water as a trap for these blind souls.
Arise, and look at the "Lions of God" who capture the wild spirit: how can you be like a dog, catching the blind through hypocrisy?
What "prey" do they seek? They are far from hunting anything but the Beloved. They are all lions, hunters of lions, and are drunk with the Light of God.
In their contemplation of the King’s own hunt, they have abandoned their own desires and have become lost in wonder.

❧**1055.** The Friend <note>A common Sufi term for God.</note> has taken them and made them like a "dead bird" <note>A decoy bird used by hunters to lure others of its kind.</note> so that He may use them to hunt down their own kind.
The decoy bird has no will of its own, whether it is joined to the flock or separated from it. You have likely read the <term>Hadith</term><note>A traditional account of the words or actions of the Prophet Muhammad.</note>: “The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the Merciful God.” <note>original: "al-qalbu bayna isba‘ayni min asābi‘ al-rahmān." This signifies that God has total control over the human heart.</note>
Everyone who is "caught" by God's decoy bird will realize, once they see the truth, that they have actually been captured by the King.
Whoever turns away from this "dead bird" will never be held in the hand of that Great Hunter.
The decoy bird says, “Do not look at the fact that I seem like a corpse; see instead the King’s love shown in how He preserves me.

❧**1060.** I am not truly dead; the King has 'killed' my ego, and so I only appear to be still.
My old way of moving was by my own wings; now my movement comes from the hand of the Divine Judge.
My temporary life has left my body; now my movement is everlasting, for it comes from Him.
If anyone acts wrongly in the presence of my movement, I will strike them down, even if they were the mighty <term>Simurgh</term>.<note>A legendary, benevolent bird in Persian mythology, often symbolizing the highest spiritual reach.</note>
Take heed! If you are spiritually alive, do not think of me as dead; if you are a devoted servant of God, see me as a tool in the King’s hand.”

<summary>Through the metaphors of the Queen of Sheba and hunting dogs, Rumi warns against the pursuit of worldly status and false spiritual teachers. He describes the true saint as a "decoy" who, having surrendered their ego to God, serves as a vessel to bring others to the Divine.</summary>
