<meta>This page continues the spiritual discourse, moving from the parable of the blind man and the dog to the nature of divine power manifested through prophets and the distinction between spiritual and worldly natures.</meta>

**1065.** Jesus, through His grace, brought the dead back to life; yet I am held in the hand of the Creator of Jesus.
How could I remain dead while in the grasp of God? Do not assume such a thing is possible for one in the "hand of Jesus."
I am "Jesus"; and anyone who has gained life from my breath will remain alive for eternity.
<note>In Sufi poetry, the "Breath of Jesus" (Dam-i 'Isá) is a common metaphor for the life-giving power of spiritual truth.</note>
The man in the miracle was made living by the historical Jesus, but he eventually died again. Truly happy is the one who gives his life to *this* spiritual "Jesus."
I am the staff in the hand of my "Moses": my "Moses" is hidden from view, while I am here, visible in his presence.

**1070.** For the true believers, I become a bridge across the sea; but for Pharaoh, I become a dragon.
<note>A reference to the staff of Moses, which parted the Red Sea for the Israelites but turned into a serpent to defeat Pharaoh’s sorcerers.</note>
O son, do not look at this staff as a mere stick, for the staff would have no such power without the hand of God.
The waves of the Great Flood were also like a staff which, out of divine grief, swallowed up the hollow pomp of those who practiced magic.
If I were to list all the "staves" of God, I would expose and shatter the hypocrisy of those who follow the path of Pharaoh;
But let them be. Let them graze on this sweet, poisonous grass for a few more days.

**1075.** If the power and dominion of Pharaoh did not exist, where would Hell find its nourishment?
Fatten him up and then slaughter him, O Butcher; for the dogs of Hell are starving.
If there were no adversary or enemy in this world, then the fire of anger within humanity would eventually die out.
That anger *is* Hell: it needs an opponent to stay alive; otherwise, Divine Mercy would extinguish it.
If that happened, clemency would exist without any need for justice or the overcoming of evil—and how then would the perfection of the Divine King be revealed?

**1080.** Those who disbelieve have mocked these parables and the clear teachings of the ones who glorify God.
Go ahead and mock them, if you wish: but how long will you live as a mere walking corpse?
Rejoice, O lovers of God, in your prayers at this very door, for it stands open today.
Every herb in the garden, whether it be garlic or capers, has its own specific garden bed.
Each kind is watered in its own bed so that it may grow and reach its own maturity.

**1085.** You, who are a field of saffron, be saffron! Do not mix yourself with the other plants.
Drink the water, O Saffron, so that you may reach your full potential; you are saffron, and you will eventually become part of that <term>Halwa</term><note>A traditional sweetmeat; here it symbolizes the "sweet" spiritual reward or the refined state of the soul.</note>.
Do not stick your muzzle into the patch of turnips, for the turnip does not share your nature or your habits.
You are planted in one bed, and the turnip in another, for God’s earth is vast.
This is especially true of that other Earth—the unseen world—where, because of its incredible breadth, even demons and spirits lose their way.

**1090.** In the attempt to measure those spiritual seas, deserts, and mountains, human imagination and fancy fail entirely.
Compared to those vast deserts, this material world is like a single hair lost in a deep sea.
Still water whose source is hidden is fresher and sweeter than any running brook,
For, like the vital spirit and the rational soul, it has a hidden path and a moving foot within itself.

<summary>Rumi uses the miracles of Jesus and Moses to explain that prophets are instruments of a single Divine power, and argues that the existence of "Pharaoh-like" enemies is necessary to manifest God's justice and mercy. He concludes by urging the seeker to remain true to their noble spiritual nature rather than mixing with worldly, "turnip-like" influences.</summary>

The listener has fallen asleep; bring the address to a close. O preacher, do not try to paint this image upon the surface of the water. <note>Painting on water is a metaphor for a futile effort or speaking to those who cannot retain the message.</note>

❧ **1095.** Arise, O Bilqís, for the spiritual market is busy and profitable. Flee from these wretched people who ruin the trade of the soul.
O Bilqís, <note>Bilqís is the traditional name for the Queen of Sheba. In Rumi's poetry, she often represents the human soul called to surrender to the Divine.</note> arise now of your own free will, before Death appears in his absolute power.
After that moment, Death will pull you by the ear with such force that you will come in agony, like a thief being dragged before a judge.
How long will you spend your life stealing shoes from donkeys? If you must steal, come and steal a precious ruby!

❧ **1105.** Make a journey through the heavens without wings or feathers, moving like the sun, the full moon, and the new moon.

The Great Leviathan of Pain will not strike your ship, nor will the ugliness of decay appear in you as you pass from this life.
You will be the sovereign, the army, and the throne all at once; you will be both the fortunate one and Fortune itself.
Even if you are currently a powerful monarch, your "Fortune" is something separate from you; one day, that Fortune will leave you,

❧ **1110.** And you will be left as destitute as a beggar. Instead, become your own Fortune, O chosen one!
When you have become your own Fortune, O person of Reality, how can you ever lose yourself?
How could you lose yourself, O person of noble qualities, when your very Essence has become your kingdom and your wealth?

## The rest of the story of Solomon, peace be upon him: how he built the Farther Mosque by instruction and inspiration from God, for wise purposes which He alone knows; and how angels, demons, genies, and men lent visible aid.

<note>The "Farther Mosque" (Masjid al-Aqṣā) refers here to the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem.</note>

God said, "O Solomon, build the Farther Mosque, for the army of Bilqís has now entered into the ritual of prayer."
When he laid the foundation of that Mosque, both <term>genies (spirits of fire)</term> and men came and devoted themselves to the work,

❧ **1115.** One group worked out of love, and another company worked unwillingly—just as all servants of God fulfill their roles in the path of obedience.
The people of this world are like those demons; their own desires are the chains dragging them to the shops and the fields.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding Bilqís and the spiritual kingdom. It shifts focus to the psychological "chains" of greed and worldly anxiety, contrasting the hollow efforts of the materialistic mind with the enduring, selfless foundations laid by prophets like Abraham.</meta>

This chain is the result of fearing poverty and being crazed with worldliness: do not think of these people as free.
It drags them toward labor and hunting; it drags them to the depths of mines and across the seas.
It drags them toward both good and evil deeds: as God has said, *“On her neck is a cord of palm-fiber.”* <note>original: "fī jīdihā hablun min masad" (Quran 111:5). In this context, Rumi uses this verse to describe how worldly attachments act as a noose or a leash that dictates a person's movements.</note>

❦**1120.** We have placed the yoke upon their necks: We have made this cord out of their own natural tendencies.
No one—whether they are corrupted or recovered from a foul disease—exists whose "fortune" is not bound to their own neck. <note>This refers to Quran 17:13: "Every man’s fate We have fastened on his own neck." It implies that our character and choices determine our destiny.</note>
Your greed for doing wrong is like a fire: the black coal of an evil deed is only made to look pleasing by the glowing hue of that fire.
The underlying blackness of the coal is hidden within the flames: once the fire of desire dies out, the blackness becomes plain to see.
By your greed, the black coal is made to glow; when the greed is gone, only that vicious, dark coal remains.

❦**1125.** In that moment of passion, the coal appeared to be alive and bright; that was not due to the goodness of your action, but rather the fire of your own greed.
Greed had decorated your action; once the greed departed, your action was left in its natural squalor.
Only a fool would think the *ghawla* <term>ghawla (a deceptive fruit or mirage associated with desert demons)</term> is ripe and sweet just because the ghouls describe it as attractive.
When the soul actually tries to eat it, its teeth are blunted by the reality of the experience.
Because of vain desire—which is the distorting influence of the "ghoul" of greed—the trap appeared to be a delicious berry, though in truth it was unripe and hard.

❦**1130.** Instead, seek to be eager in the practice of religion and in good works: these remain beautiful even when the initial fire of eagerness fades.
Good works are beautiful in their own essence, not because of a borrowed glow from something else; if the heat of passion is gone, the inner light of the good deed remains.
But when the glow of greed leaves a worldly pursuit, nothing is left of the red-hot coal but black ashes.
Folly excites a greed for amusement in children, so that in their lightheartedness, they ride a hobby-horse made of a stick.
But when that childish greed leaves him, the boy begins to laugh at the other children,

❦**1135.** Saying, “What was I doing? What did I see in this?” Because of the distortion of greed, even vinegar once appeared to be honey.
That foundation of the prophets was built without any self-interest; this is why the splendor of their renown has increased so steadily.
Many a mosque have noble people built, but "The Farther Mosque" <note>original: 'al-Masjid al-Aqsa'. While this refers to the site in Jerusalem, Rumi uses it here to distinguish between buildings made for vanity and those made for God.</note> is not their name.
The grandeur that grows every moment for the Ka’ba <note>The cube-shaped building in Mecca, considered the most sacred site in Islam.</note> was derived from the acts of pure devotion performed by Abraham.
The excellence of a mosque built by a prophet does not come from its earth and stone, but from the fact that there is no greed or hidden enmity in its builder.

❦**1140.** Their Books are not like the books of others, nor are their mosques, their livelihoods, or their homes.
Neither is their respect, their anger, their discipline, their sleep, their logic, or their speech.
To each of them belongs a unique glory: the "bird" of their spirit flies with a different kind of wing.
The heart trembles just at the mention of their high state: their actions are the *qibla* <term>qibla (the direction of prayer; a point of orientation)</term> toward which we turn our own actions.
The "eggs" laid by the bird of their spirit are golden: even in the middle of the night, their spirit has witnessed the dawn.

<summary>Rumi explains that worldly greed is a deceptive fire that makes ugly deeds look attractive, whereas the selfless work of the prophets, like Abraham, possesses an inherent, eternal beauty. He concludes that the lives and actions of the prophets serve as the ultimate spiritual compass for humanity.</summary>

The demon may also exercise the power of a "Solomon" for a time, but how could every common weaver produce fine satin?

❦**1155.** The common weaver moves his hands just like the master weaver, but there is a vast difference between the two results.

### ***Story of the poet and how the king gave him a reward and how the vizier, whose name was Bu ’l-Hasan, made it many times greater.***

A poet once brought a poem to a king, hoping for robes of honor, gifts, and a higher status.
The king was naturally generous: he ordered the poet to be given a thousand <term>dinars (gold coins)</term> of red gold, along with other bounties and gifts.
However, the <term>vizier (the king’s high minister)</term> said to him, "This is too little. Bestow a gift of ten thousand gold coins upon him, so that he may leave truly satisfied.
A poet like him possesses great intellect; and from you, whose hand is as generous as the ocean, the ten thousand coins I mentioned is a small sum."

❦**1160.** He argued and reasoned with the king until the "tithe on the threshed grain was made up out of the unthreshed ears" <note>This is a metaphor for making a sum complete or augmenting a gift until it reached a perfect, generous amount.</note>.
The king gave him the ten thousand coins and the robes of honor suited to his rank; the poet’s mind became a house of thanksgiving and praise.
Afterward, the poet inquired, "Whose doing was this? Who spoke of my merit to the king?"
They told him, "It was the Pillar of the Faith <note>original: *al-Dīn* (of the Religion/Faith)</note>, the vizier whose name is Hasan and whose character and heart are also *hasan*." <note>A wordplay on the name *Hasan*, which means "good" or "beautiful" in Arabic.</note>
The poet wrote a long poem in praise of the vizier and returned to his home.

❦**1165.** Even without tongues or lips, that bounty from the king and those ceremonial robes were themselves silent witnesses praising the king’s greatness.

### ***How after several years the poet came back in the hope of receiving the same reward, and how the king according to his custom ordered a thousand dinars to be given to him, and how the new vizier, who was also named Hasan, said to the king, "This is very much: we have great expenses and the treasury is empty, and I will satisfy him with a tenth of that sum."***

<summary>Rumi uses the imagery of Solomon’s mastery over demons to illustrate how a disciplined heart governs the ego, then begins a story about a poet's encounter with two different viziers to demonstrate how character defines the "wealth" of an individual.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the soul's journey. This serves as an allegory for the human soul's inherent dependency on the Divine.</meta>

After some years the poet, driven by poverty and extreme lack, found himself in desperate need of his daily bread and the means to live. 
He said, "In times of poverty and empty-handedness, it is best to seek out someone who has already been tested and proven. 
The court where I have already experienced such generosity—I will take my new request to that same place." 
The famous grammarian <term>Síbawayh</term> <note>Síbawayh (d. 796 AD) was a foundational scholar of Arabic grammar. His name is synonymous with linguistic authority.</note> taught that the meaning of the name *Allah* is that all worshippers take refuge <note>original: *yawlahúna*</note> in Him whenever they are in need.

**1170.** He said, "We have turned to You for help <note>original: *alihná*</note> in our moments of necessity; we have sought our needs and found their fulfillment only with You." 
In the hour of suffering, hundreds of thousands of intelligent people are all crying out for help before that unique Judge. 
Would any fool continue to beg from a miser who is incapable of giving? 
Unless the wise had experienced God’s kindness more than a thousand times, why would they keep turning back to Him? 
Indeed, all the fish in the waves of the sea, all the birds in the high reaches of the sky,

**1175.** The elephant, the wolf, and even the hunting lion; the great dragon, the tiny ant, and the snake;

The very heavens make an incessant plea to Him: "O God, do not forsake me for even a single moment! 
Your safeguarding and protection is my only support; my entire existence is held within the power of Your two Hands." 
And the earth says, "Preserve me, O You who have caused me to stay firm upon the waters."

**1180.** All beings have filled their purses from His treasury and have learned from Him how to satisfy the needs of others.

Even if you ask another person for help, it is truly God who gives; He is the one who places the spirit of generosity into the heart and the open hand of that person. 
If He can turn a person who ignores Him into a <term>Qárún</term> <note>Qárún (the biblical Korah) was legendary for his immense wealth and his eventual destruction due to pride.</note> out of gold, imagine what He will do for you if you turn your face toward Him in obedience!

**1185.** The poet, burning with a desire for this bounty, turned his face once more toward that generous King. 
What is a poet’s offering? A new poem. He brings it to his benefactor and offers it as his only stake. 
The generous, for their part, have already prepared their gold and are waiting for the poets with a hundred gifts, favors, and kindnesses. 
In their eyes, a poem <note>original: *shi’r*</note> is more precious than a hundred bales of silk robes <note>original: *sha’r* - a pun on the Persian words for "poetry" and "hair/silk"</note>, especially when it comes from a poet who can pull pearls of wisdom from the depths. 
At first, a person is greedy for bread, because food is the pillar of physical life.

**1190.** Because of this greed and expectation, a person takes every risk to earn a living—whether through hard work, violence, or a hundred different schemes. 
But on those rare occasions when he finally becomes independent of the need for bread, he finds himself in love with fame and the praise of poets.

<summary>This passage uses the metaphor of a poet returning to a generous patron to illustrate the universal dependency of all creation—from animals and elements to the heavens—upon God's sustenance. In order that they may give fruit to—and adorn—his root and his branch, and may set up a pulpit to declare his excellence,

<meta>This page continues the story of the poet seeking his reward from the king. Having discussed the spiritual necessity of praise, the narrative now shifts to the worldly obstacles created by corrupt officials. “Though he be able to fly from the **Pleiades** <note>A prominent star cluster; here used to represent the highest reaches of heaven or great spiritual height.</note> down to the earth, he will become humble and meek the moment he sees me.”

❧ **1225.** “This expectation has killed me: at least give me permission to leave, so that this wretched soul might be freed from its bondage.”
After that, the vizier gave him only a fortieth part of the original gift. The poet fell into a heavy, dark mood.
He thought, “That first gift was paid so promptly and was so large; this one, which blossomed so late, is nothing but a handful of thorns.”
Then the courtiers said to him, “That generous vizier has departed from this life; may God reward you!
For under him, those gifts were always multiplied; in those days, there was never any fault to be found with the donations.

❧ **1230.** But now, he is gone and has taken all beneficence away with him. He is not truly dead, but it is *beneficence* itself that has died in this world, truly.
The generous and upright minister has left us; a minister who flays the skin off the poor has arrived in his place.
Go, take this small amount and flee from here by night, lest this new minister picks a quarrel with you.
We only managed to get this much from him through a hundred different tricks—you have no idea how hard we exerted ourselves for you!”
The poet turned his face toward them and asked, “O kindly men, tell me: from where did this **myrmidon** <note>original: "shihna" - a term for a harsh police official or ruffian.</note> come?

❧ **1235.** What is the name of this vizier who tears the very clothes off the backs of the poor?”
The company of courtiers said to him, “His name is also **Hasan**.”
The poet cried out, “O Lord! How can the names of that first man and this one be the same? Alas, O Lord of the Day of Judgment!
That first Hasan was such a man that with a single stroke of his pen, a hundred other ministers were inspired to be generous.
But *this* Hasan is such a man that from his ugly beard you could weave a hundred ropes to hang a soul.”
When a king listens to such a minister, that minister disgraces both the king and his kingdom forever.

### ***How Qábíl (Cain) learned the trade of grave-digging from the crow, before knowledge of grave-digging and graves existed in the world.***

When was grave-digging—which was the humblest of all trades—ever acquired through mere thought, cunning, or meditation?

❧ **1305.** It came down from the air and began skillfully to dig a grave for the dead bird for the purpose of teaching him.

Qábíl cried, “Oh, shame on my intellect! For a crow is superior to me in skill.”
Concerning the **Universal Intellect**, God has said, “*The sight did not rove,*” but the particular intellect is looking distractedly in every direction. <note>original: *má zágh*; a reference to the Quran (53:17) describing the Prophet Muhammad’s focused spiritual vision. ❧ **1335.** If its disgrace and defects were made visible to you, your soul would flee from it as far as the distance between the east and the west.

The true orchards and greenery exist within the very essence of the soul: their reflection on the outside world is like a reflection in running water.

### *Story of the growing of the carob in a nook of the Farther Mosque, and how Solomon, on whom be peace, was grieved thereat, when it began to talk with him and told its characteristic property and its name*

Then Solomon <note>In Islamic tradition, Solomon (Sulayman) was a prophet-king gifted with the ability to speak the language of animals, birds, and even plants.</note> saw that a new plant had grown, like an ear of corn, in a corner of the Farther Mosque <note>original: *Masjid al-Aqsa* in Jerusalem.</note>.
He saw a very uncommon plant, green and fresh: its vibrant greenness was so bright it almost dazzled the eyes.

❦**1375.** Then that herb immediately saluted him: Solomon returned its greeting and marveled at its beauty.
He said, "What is your name? Speak without a mouth." It replied, "It is the carob, O king of the world."
He asked, "What special property resides in you?" It replied, "Wherever I grow, that place becomes desolate.
I, who am the carob <term>kharrūb: the Arabic word for the carob tree</term>, am the ruin <term>kharāb: the Arabic word for ruin or destruction</term> of the home: I am the destroyer of buildings made of water and clay."
At that moment, Solomon immediately understood that the appointed end of his life had come and that his departure from this world would soon appear.

❦**1380.** He said, "So long as I exist, this Mosque will surely not be damaged by the passing of time or the elements.
While I am here and my life continues, how could the Farther Mosque fall into decay or be riven with cracks?"
Know then, that without doubt, the ruin of our spiritual mosque only occurs after our death.
The mosque is the heart to which the body bows down: wherever that mosque is, a "bad companion" is like the carob tree.
When love for a bad companion has grown within you, beware! Flee from him and do not converse with him.

❦**1385.** Tear it up by the root, for if it is allowed to grow, it will demolish both you and your mosque <note>Rumi uses the mosque as a metaphor for the sanctified heart; the "carob" represents the destructive influence of worldly or negative company.</note>.
O lover, your carob is falseness: why do you creep, like a child, toward that which is false?

# On Humility, Free Will, and the Ship of Love

Recognize yourself as a sinner and call yourself a sinner—do not be afraid—so that the Master does not withhold the lesson from you out of your own pride.
When you say, "I am ignorant; please teach me," such honesty is far better than maintaining a false reputation for wisdom.
Take a lesson from your father <note>Referring to Adam, the first human.</note>, O man of clear vision: remember how he once said, "*O our Lord*" and "*We have done wrong.*" <note>original: *Rabbana* and *Zalamna*. These are the opening words of Adam’s prayer of repentance in the Quran (7:23).</note>

**1390.** He offered no excuses, nor did he invent falsehoods, nor did he raise the banner of deceit.
That **Iblis** <note>The name for the Devil in Islamic tradition, known for his prideful refusal to bow to Adam.</note>, on the other hand, began to argue, saying, "I was once honored and 'red-faced': You have now made me 'yellow' with disgrace.
This color is Your color: You are the one who dyed me; You are the source of my sin, my misfortune, and my brand of shame."
Be careful! When you recite the text saying *because You have seduced me*, <note>original: *bima aghwaytani*. A reference to Quran 7:16, where Iblis blames God for his fall.</note> take care that you do not become a <term>Necessitarian</term> <note>One who believes in absolute predestination, arguing that humans have no free will and therefore no responsibility for their sins.</note> and weave a web of lies.
How long will you hide in the branches of the tree of fatalism and cast your own <term>Free Will</term> aside?

**1395.** How long will you act like **Iblis** and his offspring, engaging in battles and arguments with God?
How can there be "compulsion" when you are dragging your robes into sin with such total satisfaction?
Does anyone truly under compulsion walk so complacently? Does anyone who has truly lost their way go dancing so gleefully?
You fought like twenty men to get your way in the very matters where others were giving you sound advice.
You said, "This is right, and this is the only way; how could anyone but a fool criticize me?"

**1400.** How could someone who is "compelled" speak like that? How could someone who has no choice argue with such vigor?
Whatever your physical desires want, you claim to have **free will**; but whatever your reason requires, you claim **necessity** as an excuse to reject it.
One who is blessed and understands spiritual mysteries knows that cleverness comes from **Iblis**, while love comes from **Adam**.
Cleverness is like swimming in the Great Sea: the swimmer is rarely saved; they are often drowned at the end of the day.
Stop your "swimming," let go of your pride and your grudges: this is not a mere river like the **Jayhun** <note>original: *Jayhun*. The historical Oxus River in Central Asia, used here as a metaphor for a manageable challenge.</note>; it is a boundless ocean.

**1405.** And more than that, it is the Deep Ocean that offers no refuge: it sweeps away the seven seas like they were mere straw.
**Love** is like a ship for the chosen ones: it is rarely met with disaster; for the most part, it leads to deliverance.
Sell your cleverness and buy "bewilderment" <note>A spiritual state of awe and wonder where the intellect stops trying to categorize God.</note>: cleverness is merely opinion, while bewilderment is direct vision.
Sacrifice your personal understanding in the presence of **Mustafa** <note>original: *Mustafa*. A title for the Prophet Muhammad, meaning "The Chosen One."</note> and say, "*God is enough for me.*" <note>original: *hasbiya 'llah*.</note>
Do not pull your head away from the Ship of Salvation like **Canaan** <note>In Islamic tradition, Canaan was a son of Noah who refused to board the Ark, believing he could save himself by climbing a mountain.</note>, whose own "intelligent" soul deceived him.

**1410.** He said, "I will climb to the top of the high mountain: why should I owe a debt of gratitude to **Noah**?"
How could you shrink from being grateful to him, O unrighteous one, when even God expresses gratitude toward him?
How should gratitude to him not be an obligation on our souls, when God Himself gives him words of thankful praise and honor?

<summary>This passage contrasts the humble repentance of Adam with the intellectual arrogance of Iblis, warning that using fatalism to excuse sin is a satanic trait. Rumi argues that while cleverness leads to "drowning" in the ocean of existence, the "ship" of love and spiritual bewilderment leads to salvation.</summary>

<keywords>Adam, Iblis, Free Will, Predestination, Repentance, Love vs. Intellect, Noah's Ark, Humility, Muhammad, Spiritual Vision</keywords>

<meta>Building on the previous page's contrast between Adam’s humility and Iblis’s intellectual pride, Rumi now addresses those who rely solely on their own cleverness and "swimming skills" rather than boarding the ark of spiritual guidance.</meta>

# The Folly of the Wise and the Wisdom of the Simple

What do you actually know about his exalted state, you who are like a sack full of envy? Even God expresses gratitude toward him. 
I wish that **Kan’án** <note>Also known as Canaan, the son of Noah who refused to enter the ark, believing he could save himself from the Great Flood by climbing a mountain.</note> had never learned to swim! Had he been unable to swim, he might have placed his hope in Noah and the safety of the ark.

**1415.** I wish that, like a child, he had remained ignorant of clever devices. Then, like a child, he might have clung to his mother for protection.
Or, I wish that he had not been so full of traditional, book-learned knowledge, but instead had received the direct, heart-revealed knowledge that comes from a **saint**. 
When you bring a mere book to compete with such divine light, your own soul—which is made of the same essence as inspiration—will reproach you. 
Know that compared to the breath and words of the **Qutb** <term>The "Spiritual Pole" or the supreme saint of the age who acts as a direct channel for divine grace.</term> of the time, traditional knowledge is like performing a ritual ablution with sand <note>original: *tayammum*. This is a symbolic cleansing allowed in Islamic law only when water is unavailable.</note> even though fresh water is standing right there.
Make yourself "foolish"—meaning simple and humble—and follow behind him. It is only through this holy simplicity that you will find your deliverance.

**1420.** For this reason, O seeker, the **Sultan of Mankind** <note>A title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note> has said, "Most of the people of Paradise are the simple-hearted." 
Since your clever intelligence only stirs up pride and vanity within you, become a "fool" so that your heart may remain healthy and sound.
I do not mean the fool who acts like a buffoon for laughs, but the "fool" who is so lost in wonder and bewilderment for God that the world falls away. 
These "fools" are like the women of Egypt who were so overwhelmed by the beauty of **Joseph** <note>Referring to the Quranic and Biblical story where the women of the city were so entranced by Joseph's divine beauty that they accidentally cut their own hands with their knives while peeling fruit, without even feeling the pain.</note> that they cut their own hands—they were "foolish" regarding their own safety, but they were wise enough to recognize the divine beauty before them.
Sacrifice your intellect in your love for the **Friend** <note>A common Sufi term for God.</note>. After all, every bit of intellect you possess originally came from the very place where He dwells.

**1425.** Those who are truly (spiritually) intelligent have sent their intellects back to that divine source; only the dullard remains stuck in this world where the Beloved is not found.
If your intellect leaves your head because of this holy bewilderment, do not fear: every single hair on your head will become a new organ of intelligence and perception.
In that divine realm, the burden of thinking does not weigh upon the brain, for there, the mind and the spirit spontaneously produce gardens and orchards of spiritual wisdom.
If you turn toward a field there, you will hear a subtle discourse from the grass itself; if you enter an orchard, your own spiritual "palm tree" will become fresh and fruitful.
In this **Way** <term>The *Tariqa* or spiritual path of the Sufis.</term>, abandon all show and ostentation. Do not take a single step unless your spiritual guide moves first.

**1430.** Anyone who moves without a "head" (a guide) is merely a "tail"—lowly and contemptible. His movement is like the erratic scuttling of a scorpion.
He moves crookedly, blind to the light, ugly and venomous; his only trade is wounding the pure souls of those who have left the world behind.
Strike the head of anyone whose inner spirit is like this, and whose permanent character is so poisonous.
Indeed, it is a mercy to strike such a "head," so that his miserable soul might be freed from the prison of that ill-fated body.
Take the weapons out of the hands of the madman! By doing so, you satisfy the requirements of Justice and Goodness.

**1435.** Since he possesses weapons but lacks the understanding to use them well, bind his hands; otherwise, he will cause a hundred tragedies.

<summary>Rumi warns that intellectual arrogance and "cleverness" can prevent a seeker from seeking divine help, using Noah's son as a cautionary tale. He advocates for a "holy folly"—a state of humble bewilderment and submission to a spiritual guide—as the only way to transcend the ego.</summary>
<keywords>Noah, Kan’an, intellectual pride, divine folly, Qutb, Joseph, spiritual guide, humility, Sufi path, Muhammad</keywords>

<meta>Building on the previous page's warning about the dangers of "cleverness" without spiritual guidance, Rumi now explains how worldly success—knowledge, wealth, and rank—only serves to amplify the destructive nature of a person who lacks inner virtue. This serves as a transition to the necessity of following a true spiritual guide like the Prophet.</meta>

## That Knowledge, Wealth, and Power in the Hands of the Wicked are but a Sword in the Hands of a Thief

To teach a person of evil nature knowledge and skill is like putting a sword into the hand of a bandit. 
It is better to put a sword in the hand of a drunken madman than to allow knowledge to fall into the possession of a worthless person. 
Knowledge, wealth, authority, and high status are a source of ruin when held by those with a corrupt nature. 
This is the true reason for the **Holy War** <note>original: *jihad*. In this context, Rumi interprets the struggle as a necessary action to disarm those who would use power to cause spiritual or physical harm to others.</note>; it is meant to take the spear out of the hands of the "madman."

<image-desc>small floral ornament</image-desc> **1440.** Such a man’s spirit is like the madman, and his body is like the sword: take the weapon away from the wicked! 
A hundred lions could not cause the level of shame that a high office inflicts upon the ignorant. 
His inner vices were hidden until he gained the "instrument" of power; then his snake, emerging from its hole, slithered across the plain. 
The entire world becomes infested with snakes and scorpions when an ignorant man is given command over others. 
The worthless person who gains wealth and office becomes the architect of his own public disgrace.

<image-desc>small floral ornament</image-desc> **1445.** He either acts with stinginess, hoarding his gifts, or he shows a false generosity, bestowing favors in the wrong places. 
He treats the King like a pawn on a chessboard <note>A metaphor for a complete reversal of the natural or spiritual order.</note>: such is the nature of the "gifts" a fool gives. 
When authority falls to one who has lost his way, he believes he has attained **high rank** <gloss>original: *jáh*</gloss>, but in reality, he has fallen into a **pit** <gloss>original: *cháh*</gloss>.
He does not know the path himself, yet he insists on acting as a guide; his wicked spirit sets the whole world on fire. 
When one who is merely a "child" in the spiritual life tries to play the part of an **Elder** <term>original: *Sheikh* or *Pir*. A spiritual director or master who has reached maturity in the path of Sufism.</term>, a spirit of misfortune seizes those who follow him.

<image-desc>small floral ornament</image-desc> **1450.** "Come," he says, "and I will show you the moon," yet that impure man has never seen the moon himself. 
How can you show the moon when, in all your life, you haven't even seen its reflection in the water, you half-baked dunce? 
Because such fools have become leaders, the truly wise have pulled their heads into their cloaks and hidden away in fear.

### Commentary on the Verse: "O thou that wrappest thyself."

For this reason, God called the Prophet **The Enwrapped One** <note>original: *Muzzammil*. This refers to the 73rd Surah of the Quran, where Muhammad is addressed while wrapped in his cloak during a moment of intense revelation.</note>, saying: "Come out from your cloak, O you who are inclined to hide! 
Do not pull your head into your garment and do not cover your face, for the world is like a body losing its balance, and you are its guiding Intelligence."

<image-desc>small floral ornament</image-desc> **1455.** Listen! Do not hide yourself because of the insults of your enemies, for you carry the brilliant candle of **Revelation**. 
Listen! **Stand up in prayer during the night** <note>A reference to the Quranic command to the Prophet to keep night vigils.</note>, for you are a candle, O Prince, and it is at night that a candle must stand and burn. 
Without your radiance, even the brightest day is as dark as night; without your protection, the lion is made a captive by the hare. 
Be the captain of the ship in this sea of spiritual purity, for you are a second Noah, O **Mustafá** <gloss>The Elect One (a title of the Prophet Muhammad)</gloss>.

<summary>Rumi warns that power and knowledge in the hands of the spiritually immature are dangerous tools that lead to self-destruction and social chaos. He concludes by urging the Prophet (and by extension, true spiritual guides) to emerge from seclusion and lead humanity through the darkness.</summary>
<keywords>authority, ignorance, spiritual guidance, Muzzammil, Mustafá, Noah, moral character, corruption of power</keywords>

--- Page 259 ---
<meta>Building on the previous page's warning that power and knowledge are dangerous tools in the hands of the wicked, Rumi now shifts the focus to the necessity of a true spiritual guide. Having described the "snakes" of the ego that emerge when an ignorant man gains office, the text now addresses the Prophet (or the perfected spiritual master) as the only one capable of leading the "blind" caravan of humanity safely through the dangers of the world.</meta>

An expert guide, endowed with understanding, is needed for every road, especially on the road of the journey across the waters <note>A common Sufi metaphor for the perilous spiritual journey or the transition from the material world to the divine.</note>.

<image-desc>Small decorative icon of a winged, dragon-like creature</image-desc> **1460.** Arise! Look upon the caravan that has been waylaid: everywhere a **ghoul** <note>A desert-dwelling demon in folklore known for misleading travelers; here, it represents false teachers or the ego.</note> has become the captain of the ship.
You are the **Khidr** <note>original: *Khizr*. A legendary figure in Islamic tradition known as the immortal, hidden guide who assists travelers and seekers of truth.</note> of this time and the Deliverer of every ship in distress: do not practice solitude like **Jesus** <note>original: *Ruhullah* or "Spirit of God," a traditional title for Jesus in Islamic thought.</note> did.
In the sight of this assembly of people, you are the candle of heaven: cease from severing yourself from them and adopting a life of seclusion.
It is not the time for seclusion; come into the assembly, O you who are like the **Humay** <note>A mythical bird of paradise in Persian lore; its shadow was said to confer kingship and good fortune.</note>, while your guidance of souls is as vast as **Mount Qaf** <note>A legendary mountain range encircling the world, often representing the boundary between the physical and spiritual realms.</note>.
The full moon moves across the high sky by night: it does not stop its journey because of the barking of dogs.

<image-desc>Small decorative icon of a winged, dragon-like creature</image-desc> **1465.** The scoffers keep crying out like dogs at your full moon from their lowly places toward your high station.
These dogs are deaf to the Divine command, "**Be silent**" <note>original: *Ansitu*, a reference to Quran 7:204, commanding the faithful to listen in silence when the truth is revealed.</note>; out of folly, they keep barking at your full moon.
Listen! O you who are the cure for the sick, do not let go of the staff of the blind simply because you are angry with the deaf.
Did you not say?—"He who leads a blind man on the right path gains a hundred rewards and blessings from God."
Whoever leads a blind man for even forty steps is pardoned and will find salvation.

<image-desc>Small decorative icon of a winged, dragon-like creature</image-desc> **1470.** Therefore, lead the multitude of the blind, rank upon rank, away from this fleeting world.
This is the work of a guide: you are the Guide, you are the joy that dispels the sorrow of the end of days.
Listen, O **Imam** <note>A leader or prayer-leader; here referring to the Prophet or the supreme spiritual authority.</note> of the God-fearing, cause those who think vain thoughts to travel onward until they reach the station of certainty.
Whoever devotes their heart to plotting against you, I shall strike his neck; therefore, go forward joyously.
I will pile more blindness upon his existing blindness; he will think it is sugar, but I will truly be giving him poison.

<image-desc>Small decorative icon of a winged, dragon-like creature</image-desc> **1475.** All intellects have been lit by My light; all plots have been learned from My own divine planning.
What indeed is a nomad’s tent of black felt <note>original: *Turcoman*. Referring to the simple, temporary dwellings of Turkic nomads, used here to represent the flimsy nature of human schemes.</note> when standing before the feet of the fierce elephants of this world?
Before My **Sarsar** wind <note>A cold, roaring, and destructive wind mentioned in the Quran that destroyed the ancient people of ‘Ad.</note>, what is that flickering lamp of his own making, O My greatest prophet?
Arise and blow upon the terrible trumpet <note>The trumpet of the Archangel, used to signal the end of the world and the resurrection of the dead.</note>, so that thousands of the dead may spring up from the earth.
Since you are the **Israfil** <note>original: *Isráfíl*. The archangel Seraphiel, who is tasked with blowing the trumpet to signal the Resurrection.</note> of this age, bring about a resurrection before the Great Resurrection occurs.

<image-desc>Small decorative icon of a winged, dragon-like creature</image-desc> **1480.** O beloved, if anyone asks, "Where is the Resurrection?" show yourself to them and say, "Behold, I am the Resurrection."
Look, O questioner who is burdened by trials, and see that from this very resurrection a hundred worlds have already grown!
And if the scoffer is not worthy of this praise and humble prayer, then, O spiritual Sultan, the proper reply to a fool is silence.
Silence comes as the reply from God’s Heaven when a prayer goes unanswered, O dear soul.
Oh, alas! It is harvest time, but by our ill fortune, the day has grown late <note>Rumi concludes this section with a poetic lament, suggesting that the opportunity for spiritual growth or the completion of his work is being cut short by time.</note>.

<summary>In this passage, the Divine voice encourages the spiritual guide (the Prophet) to engage with humanity rather than seeking seclusion, likening his role to the archangel Israfil who awakens the spiritually dead. The text emphasizes that the guide must remain steadfast in leading the "blind" despite the mockery of the ignorant.</summary>

--- Page 260 ---
<meta>Building on the previous page's discussion of the need for a spiritual guide (the Khidr of the age), Rumi now addresses the difficulty of teaching those who are "blind" or foolish. He explains that while the subject is vast, human understanding is often too narrow to grasp it, necessitating a shift in teaching style—moving from direct discourse to silence or illustrative parables.</meta>

1485. Time is pressing, and the magnitude of this subject is such that an eternal life would be too short for it.
To try and strike a target with a lance in these narrow alleyways only brings disgrace to the one who throws.
Time is limited, and the mind and understanding of the common people is a hundred times narrower than time itself, O youth.
Inasmuch as silence is the proper reply to a fool, why are you prolonging this discourse?
It is because God, from the perfection of His mercy and the waves of His bounty, bestows rain and moisture even on the most barren soil <note>Rumi suggests that even the "foolish" or spiritually "barren" deserve the rain of divine wisdom, even if they cannot fully grasp it.</note>.

### ->***Showing that the proverb, "Omission to reply is a reply," confirms the saying that silence is the proper response to a fool. The explanation of both these sayings is contained in the story which will now be related.***<-

1490. There was a king who had a servant; this servant was one whose reason was dead and whose animal desires were very much alive.
He would neglect the finer points of service to the king: he thought his own evil actions were good.
The monarch said, "Reduce his allowance, and if he complains, strike his name off the payroll entirely."
The servant’s reason was deficient, but his greed was excessive: when he saw his allowance reduced, he became violent and rebellious.
Had there been any wisdom in him, he would have looked inward and examined himself, so that he might see his own fault and seek forgiveness.

1495. When a tethered donkey becomes violent due to its own stupidity, its front legs must be shackled in addition to its tether.
Then the donkey will complain, "One rope was enough for me!"; but in truth, do not think that is so, for those extra shackles are the direct result of the creature's own foul behavior <note>The donkey is a frequent symbol in Persian literature for the *nafs*, or the lower, ego-driven self that requires discipline.</note>.

### ->***In exposition of the following prophetic tradition*** <note>original: *Hadíth*</note> ***of the Chosen One*** <note>original: *Mustafá*, an honorific for the Prophet Muhammad</note>***, peace be upon him: "Verily, the most High God created the angels and set reason in them, and He created the beasts and set lust in them, and He created the sons of Adam and set in them reason and lust; and he whose reason prevails over his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust prevails over his reason is lower than the beasts."***<-

It is related in the **prophetic tradition** <note>original: *Hadíth*</note> that God in His majesty created the creatures of the world in three kinds.
One class He made entirely of reason, knowledge, and generosity; that is the angel: they know nothing but bowing down in worship.
In their original nature there is no greed or sensuality: they are absolute light, living through their love for God.

1500. Another class is devoid of knowledge, like the animals who live only to grow fat from eating their fodder.
The animal sees nothing but the stable and its food: it is heedless of future misery or spiritual glory.
The third class is the descendant of **Adam** <note>The first human, representing all of humanity.</note>, the Human Being: half of him is made of the angel and half of him is made of the donkey.
The "donkey-half" inclines toward that which is low and base; the other half inclines toward that which is rational and divine.
Those first two classes (the angels and the beasts) are at peace from war and internal combat, while Man is engaged in a painful struggle with two internal adversaries.

1505. And, moreover, the race of Man has been divided through this trial: they all appear to have a human shape, but in truth, they have become three distinct communities.

<summary>Rumi explores the spiritual hierarchy of creation, contrasting the pure reason of angels and the pure impulse of animals with the dual nature of humanity. He uses the story of a rebellious servant to illustrate how the lower self (the "donkey") requires discipline when it lacks the reason to recognize its own faults.</summary>
<keywords>reason vs. lust, angels and animals, the dual nature of man, nafs (ego), silence as a reply, spiritual discipline, Rumi's parables</keywords>

--- Page 261 ---
<meta>Building on the previous page's discussion of the "foolish servant" whose animal desires outweighed his reason, Rumi now expands this into a broader classification of humanity. He transitions from a specific anecdote about a king’s servant to a metaphysical explanation of why some people rise to angelic heights while others sink below the level of beasts.</meta>

One group has become completely immersed in the Divine and, like Jesus, has attained the nature of an angel. 
Their outer form is that of a human <note>original: "Adam"</note>, but their inner reality is that of Gabriel <note>The archangel who acts as the messenger between God and prophets.</note>: such a person has been delivered from anger, sensual passion, and empty arguments. 
They have been freed from the need for harsh discipline, asceticism, and self-mortification; you might even say they were never truly born from the line of Adam.
The second type of people have descended to the level of donkeys: they have become nothing but pure anger and absolute lust.

❧ **1510.** The qualities of Gabriel once existed within them but have since departed. The "house" of their being was too narrow, and those angelic qualities were too magnificent to remain. 
A person deprived of the vital spirit becomes dead; when their spirit is deprived of those angelic qualities, they become a beast. 
This is because a spirit lacking those virtues is vile; this is a truth testified to by the <term>Sufi: A practitioner of the mystical path of Islam who seeks direct, personal experience of the Divine</term>. 
Such a person suffers more anxiety than actual animals, for they employ subtle and clever arts to navigate the world. 
The cunning and deception they are capable of spinning—that level of trickery is produced by no other creature.

❧ **1515.** Whether it is weaving gold-embroidered robes, diving for pearls at the bottom of the sea, 
the intricate calculations of geometry or astronomy, or even the sciences of medicine and philosophy— 
all of these are connected only to this material world. They offer no path to ascend to the Seventh Heaven <note>In traditional Islamic cosmology, the highest celestial sphere, closest to the Divine Presence.</note>. 
All of this is merely the science of "building the stable," which serves as the foundation for the existence of those who live like oxen or camels. 
For the sake of sustaining the animal body for a few short days, these misguided fools have given the name of "mysteries" to these worldly arts and sciences.

❧ **1520.** The knowledge of the Way to God and the knowledge of His dwelling place—that is known only to the "owner of the heart," or perhaps we should say, by the heart itself. 
God created humans in this composite fashion—as a "goodly animal"—and made them capable of knowledge. 
But those who remain in a bestial state He has named "like the cattle" <note>original: "kal-an'am," a reference to Qur'an 7:179, describing people who have hearts but do not understand.</note>; for what resemblance is there between being truly awake and being asleep? 
The animal spirit knows nothing but the "sleep" of ignorance; this class of men possesses senses that are inverted or upside-down. 
When true spiritual awakening comes, that animal sleep vanishes, and the enlightened person can read the former confusion of their senses as if from a clear tablet.

❧ **1525.** It is like the perceptions of someone caught in a dream: only when they wake up does the distorted nature of what they saw become clear. 
By necessity, the bestial man is the "lowest of the low." Leave him be, for "I love not those that set" <note>original: "la uhibbu 'l-afilin." A reference to Qur’an 6:76, where the Prophet Abraham rejects the stars and moon as gods because they fade or "sink" away.</note>.

### ***In explanation of the following Verse: "And as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it [each new chapter of the Qur’an] added to their uncleanness"; and of His Word: "By it He leads many astray, and by it He guides many aright."***

The bestial man is the "lowest of the low" because he once possessed the potential to transform himself and strive to escape his low state, but he chose to lose it.

<summary>Rumi categorizes humanity into three states—angelic, bestial, and those in between—and argues that worldly sciences like medicine and astronomy are merely "stable-building" compared to the true "science" of knowing God.</summary>
<keywords>Gabriel, Jesus, Sufism, worldly vs. spiritual knowledge, Seventh Heaven, Qur'anic commentary, spiritual awakening, animal nature</keywords>

--- Page 262 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the three types of souls, Rumi has just described the second group: those who have lost their angelic nature and become worse than beasts through their cunning and worldly deception.</meta>

Furthermore, because the animal does not possess the capacity for spiritual growth, its excuse for remaining in a bestial state is perfectly obvious. 
But when the capacity—which serves as the guide to salvation—is stripped from a human, every bit of nourishment they consume becomes like the "brain of a donkey" <note>A metaphorical expression suggesting that such food only increases one's stupidity or spiritual dullness.</note>.

❧ **1530.** If such a person consumes <term>anacardium: The marking-nut (balādur), used in medieval medicine to sharpen memory, but feared for causing madness or "apoplexy" if administered incorrectly</term>, it acts upon them like opium: their state of paralysis and dementia only increases. 
There remains a third class of men: those engaged in a constant internal warfare. They are half animal and half spiritually alive, yet they are endowed with the potential for right guidance. 
Day and night, they exist in a state of strife and mutual struggle; the "last" state of such a person <note>their higher, spiritual aspirations</note> battles with their "first" state <note>their lower, animalistic origins</note>.

->***The battle of the reason against the flesh is like the contention of Majnún with his she-camel: Majnún’s inclination is toward the noble woman Laylá, while the she-camel’s inclination is to go back toward her foal. As Majnún said in his verse: "My she-camel’s love is behind me, while my love is in front of me; and truly, she and I are in total disagreement."*** <note>original Arabic: "Hawā nāqatī khalfī wa-hawāya amāmī / wa-innī wa-iyyāhā la-mukhtalifāni." Majnún is the "Madman of Laylá," a symbol of the soul's absolute devotion to God.</note><-

Truly, the reason and the flesh are like Majnún and his she-camel: the former is pulling forward while the latter pulls backward in mutual enmity. 
Majnún’s desire is to speed into the presence of his beloved Laylá; the she-camel’s desire is to run back after her foal.

❧ **1535.** If Majnún forgot himself for even a single moment, the she-camel would turn around and head back. 
Because his being was so saturated with love and passion, he had no choice but to frequently lose consciousness and become "beside himself." 
Reason is that which remains regardful and cautious; however, the passion for Laylá would carry his reason away. 
But the she-camel was very alert and watchful: whenever she felt the <term>toggle: A wooden peg or fastener on the camel’s harness or nose-ring</term> go slack, 
She would immediately realize that he had become heedless and dazed, and she would turn her face back toward the foal without a moment's delay.

❧ **1540.** When Majnún eventually came to his senses, he would see that she had traveled back many leagues from the goal. 
Under these conditions, Majnún remained traveling back and forth for years on what should have been a journey of only three days. 
He cried out, “O camel! Since we are both lovers—one of the Beloved and one of the foal—we are two opposites and unsuitable traveling companions. 
Your affection and your nature are not in harmony with mine; it is necessary for me to choose to part from your company.” 
These two fellow travelers—the reason and the flesh—are like bandits waylaying each other: lost is the spirit that does not dismount from the body.

❧ **1545.** The spirit, because of its separation from the highest Heaven, is in a state of great longing; the body, because of its passion for the "thorn-shrub" <note>A metaphor for the fleeting and prickly pleasures of the material world.</note>, is like a stubborn she-camel. 
The spirit unfolds its wings to fly upward; the body has dug its claws deep into the earth. 
Majnún said to the camel: “So long as you are with me, you who are mortally enamored of your home, my spirit will remain far from Laylá. 
Because of these experiences, my lifetime has wasted away for many years, like the lives of the people of Israel in the desert.” <note>A reference to the forty years the Israelites spent wandering the wilderness, unable to reach the promised land.</note> 
“This journey to union was only a matter of two steps; yet because of your 'noose' <note>the pull of the body</note>, I have remained sixty years on the way.

❧ **1550.** The way is near, not far, but I have arrived very late: I have become sick of this riding—sick, sick!” 
Then Majnún threw himself headlong from the camel’s back. He said, “I am consumed with grief: how long must this go on? How long?”

<summary>This page describes the "third class" of humans who struggle between their spiritual intellect and their physical desires, illustrated by the famous story of Majnún and his camel. The camel’s constant turning back toward its foal serves as a metaphor for how the body’s worldly attachments delay the soul's journey toward Divine Union.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous passage, the poet continues the allegory of Majnún and his she-camel. Majnún represents the rational soul or spirit striving toward the Beloved (God/Laylá), while the camel represents the lower, animalistic self that constantly tries to turn back to worldly comforts (the foal).</meta>

The wide desert became too narrow for him in his distress: he flung himself down upon the stony ground.
He threw himself down so violently that the body of that courageous man was nearly shattered.
As he cast himself to the earth in this way, by Divine destiny, his leg was broken.

1555. He bound his leg and said, “I will become like a ball; I will go rolling along, guided by the curve of His polo-bat.” <note>In Sufi poetry, the 'ball and the bat' (guy-o-chawgan) is a common metaphor for the seeker's total submission to God's will; the ball has no feet or hands and moves only where the player strikes it.</note>
For this reason, the sweet-tongued Sage <note>Likely referring to the poet Sana’i, whom Rumi deeply admired</note> utters a curse upon the rider who refuses to dismount from the body.
How could love for the Lord be any less than the love for Laylá? <note>Laylá is the object of Majnún's intense, sacrificial love in classical Persian literature, symbolizing the Divine Beloved.</note> To become a ball for His sake is a far more worthy fate.
Become like a ball, turn toward the side of total sincerity, and go rolling, rolling in the curve of the bat of Love,
For from this point on, the journey is accomplished by the "pull" of God, whereas the former journey on the she-camel was merely our own progression made through our own meager efforts.

1560. Such is this extraordinary mode of travel, which transcends the utmost exertion of both the **Jinn** <term>Jinn: In Islamic theology, supernatural creatures made of smokeless fire, often possessing great strength but still subject to God's laws</term> and mankind.
Such is the Divine pull—not just any common attraction—to which **Ahmad** <note>original: "Ahmad," another name for the Prophet Mohammed</note> awarded the highest pre-eminence. And now, farewell to that story!

### ***How the slave wrote to the King a statement complaining of the reduction of his allowance***

Cut short this discourse to return to the story of the slave who wrote a message to the King.
He is sending the gracious King a statement filled with arguments, self-conceit, and hidden hatred.
The human body is like a letter: look into it and see whether its contents are worthy of the King before you deliver it.

1565. Go into a quiet corner, open the letter, and read it; see if its words are suitable for royalty.
If it is not suitable, tear it to pieces, write another, and fix the faults.
But do not think it is a simple thing to open the "letter" that is the body; if it were, everyone would clearly see the secrets of the heart.
How difficult it is to open this letter! It is a task for grown men, not for children playing with knuckles. <note>A reference to "knucklebones," an ancient game similar to jacks or dice, implying that spiritual self-examination is not a trivial game.</note>
We have all become satisfied with merely reading the "table of contents," because we are steeped in greed and vain desires.

1570. The table of contents is a snare for the common people, intended to make them think the actual text of the scroll is just like the summary.
Open the title page! Do not turn your head away from these words—and God knows the best path.
That title is like a declaration made by the tongue: you must examine the actual text of the scroll—namely, the "bosom" or your inner self—
And see whether it agrees with your outward declaration, so that your actions are not merely hypocritical.
When you are carrying a very heavy sack, you must not fail to look inside it,

1575. To see what "sour" and "sweet" things you have packed. If the contents are worth bringing along, then bring them;
Otherwise, empty your sack of the stones you have collected, and save yourself from this fruitless labor and public disgrace.
Put into your sack only that which is fit to be presented to righteous sultans and kings.

<summary>Rumi uses the conclusion of the Majnún story to illustrate the difference between human effort and Divine attraction, then transitions into an allegory comparing the human body and heart to a letter or sack that must be inspected for worthiness before God.</summary>

## **Story of the divine with a massive turban and the man who stole it, and how the divine shouted, "Unroll it and see what you are taking—then take it if you wish!"**

->A certain religious scholar had gathered some old rags and wound them into his turban,<-
->In order that it might look grand and impressive when he entered the assembly at the *Hatím* <term>Hatím: A semi-circular wall near the Kaaba in Mecca; here it refers to a prestigious gathering place for scholars and pilgrims</term>.<-

❧ **1580.** He had clipped scraps from various old garments and decorated the outside of the turban with them.
The exterior of the turban looked like a robe of Paradise, but it was shameful and ugly within—just like a hypocrite.
Shreds of *dalq* <term>dalq: A coarse, patched cloak traditionally worn by dervishes or monks</term>, bits of cotton, and fur were buried inside that turban.
He set off toward the college at dawn, hoping that by using this false dignity, he might receive material gifts or blessings.
A clothes-thief stood waiting on the dark road to practice his trade.

❧ **1585.** The thief snatched the turban from the scholar's head and started to run so he could finish his business.
The scholar shouted after him, "My son, unroll the turban first! Then take it away with you.
Even as you fly away as if you had four wings, unroll the 'gift' you are carrying.
Unroll it and feel it with your hand; then take it if you still like it. I give you my permission!"
When the fleeing thief unrolled it, a hundred thousand old rags dropped onto the road.

❧ **1590.** Of that grand, deceptive turban, only an <term>ell</term> <note>original: "araš" (a unit of length roughly from the elbow to the fingertip)</note> of old cloth remained in the thief's hand.
He threw the rag to the ground, saying, "O worthless man! By this fraud, you have wasted my time and kept me from my work!"

### **The World’s silent warning to those obsessed with it, and how it reveals its unfaithfulness to those who hope it will keep its promises.**

The scholar replied, "I may have defrauded you, but at the same time, I was telling you the truth of the matter as a warning."
Likewise, though the World blossoms delightfully to make a fair show, it simultaneously cries out and declares its own unfaithfulness.
In this realm of existence and decay, O master, "existence" is the fraud and that "decay" is the warning.

❧ **1595.** Existence says, "Come, I am delicious," but its decay says, "Go, I am nothing."
O you who bite your lip in admiration at the beauty of spring, look also at the coldness and paleness of autumn.
In the daytime, you thought the face of the sun was beautiful; remember its "death" at the moment of setting.
You saw the full moon in this lovely sky; observe also its disappearance during the <term>interlunar period</term> <note>The time between the old moon and the new moon when the moon is invisible from Earth</note>.
A boy, because of his beauty, became a leader of people; yet after the "tomorrow" of his life, he becomes senile and an object of mockery.

❧ **1600.** If the bodies of those in the fresh bloom of youth have captured you, look at those bodies in old age—bleached like a cotton field.
O you who have seen rich, delicious meals, go and see what remains of them in the latrine.

<summary>Through the story of a thief who steals a scholar's deceptively large turban made of rags, Rumi allegorically warns that the material world hides its inherent decay behind a beautiful facade. He urges the seeker to look beyond temporary physical beauty—like youth or the sun—to see the inevitable "autumn" or decline that follows.</summary>

Speak to the waste and say, “Where is that beauty of yours—the flavor, the excellence, and the sweet scent you possessed while still on the serving dish?”
It replies, “That beauty was merely the bait, and I was the trap. Now that you have fallen prey to it, the bait has vanished from sight.”
Think of the many fingers that were once the envy of master craftsmen for their skill and dexterity; see how, at the last, they have become trembling and weak.

❦ **1605.** The soul-like, intoxicating narcissus-eye <note>A traditional Persian poetic metaphor for the captivating eye of a beloved</note> of the beloved—see it dimmed at the end, with water trickling from it.
The lion-like hero who charges into the ranks of valiant foes—at last, he is conquered by a lowly mouse.
The sharp, far-seeing, and artful genius—behold it in the end, as senseless as an old donkey.
The curly lock of hair that once spread the fragrance of musk and stole away the senses—at last, it resembles the ugly white tail of a donkey.
Observe the existence of this World: at first, it appears pleasing and full of joy; then observe its shamefulness and corruption in the end.

❦ **1610.** For the World showed its snare plainly; it plucked out the fool’s mustache right in your presence.
Do not say then, “The World deceived me with its trickery; otherwise, my reason would have escaped its snare.”
Come now and see how the golden collar and the decorative shoulder-belt have become a heavy shackle, a leg-iron, and a chain.
Consider every particle of this World in this way: bring both its beginning and its end into your contemplation.
The more a person looks toward the end (<term>ákhir: the ultimate outcome or spiritual result</term>), the more blessed they are; the more a person looks toward the stable (<term>ákhur: a manger or trough; here representing base, animalistic needs</term>), the more they are cast out.

❦ **1615.** Look upon every face as if it were the glorious moon; but when you have seen the beginning, look also to the end,
Lest you become a person who is blind in one eye, like <term>Iblís: the primary name for Satan in Islamic tradition</term>. He, like one who is spiritually maimed, sees only one half of reality and not the other.
He saw the clay (<term>tín: physical matter or mud</term>) of Adam, but he did not see Adam’s spiritual obedience to God (<term>dín: faith or inner religious reality</term>). He saw only the physical form of this world and missed the spirit that gazes upon the world beyond.
The superiority of men over women, O brave one, is not based on physical strength, or the ability to make money, or the possession of vast estates;
Otherwise, the lion and the elephant, because of their superior strength, would be greater than any human being, O blind one.

❦ **1620.** The superiority of men over women, O seeker of the moment, exists because man is more capable of looking toward the end.
The person who is "crooked" or failing in their ability to see the ultimate outcome is, in spirit, like the metaphorical "woman"—inferior to those who are acquainted with the end.
Two opposing cries are rising from this World: consider carefully which one you are suited to hear.
One cry is the means of reviving the devout with spiritual life; the other cry is the means of flattering and deceiving those without grace.
The World says: “I am the blossom on the thorn, O sweet lover; the flower will soon drop away, and I shall remain nothing but a jagged thorn-branch.”

❦ **1625.** The cry of the World’s blossom is, “Here is the flower-seller!” The cry of its thorn is, “Do not try to move toward me.”
If you have responded to the alluring cry of the blossom, you remain unmoved by the warning of the thorn; for a lover is always deaf to anything that contradicts the object of their love.

<summary>Rumi warns that the physical world is a deceptive bait that hides eventual decay, urging the seeker to look past outward beauty toward the spiritual "end." He uses the figure of Iblis (Satan) to illustrate the danger of "one-eyed" sight—seeing only the material "clay" while missing the divine "spirit."</summary>

One cry is this: “Here am I, ready and waiting!” while the other cry is, “Behold my final end!”
My apparent readiness is like a deceptive lure or an ambush: look upon the image of the end within the mirror of the beginning.
Once you have crawled into one of these two sacks <note>The "sacks" refer to different spiritual states or worldly attachments</note>, you become the opposite of, and unsuited for, the other.

❦ **1630.** Oh, how happy is the person who, from the very start, heard that which the intellects and the spiritual ears of the holy have heard.
If the World finds the house of the heart empty and takes up residence there, everything else will appear distorted or strangely miraculous to the inhabitant.
Like a new clay pot that has absorbed the smell of filth: even pure water cannot easily wash that stench away.
Everything in this world exerts a pull: faithlessness draws the faithless, and righteousness draws the one who is guided rightly.
There exists both the <term>amber: kahruba (literally 'straw-stealer'), which attracts straw through static electricity</term> and the <term>magnet: the lodestone that attracts iron</term>; whether you are iron or straw, you will inevitably be pulled toward your match.

❦ **1635.** The magnet will carry you away if you are iron; if you are straw, you will find yourself stuck to the amber.
When a person does not keep company with the good, they inevitably become a neighbor to the wicked.
In the eyes of an Egyptian <note>Meaning those who followed Pharaoh</note>, Moses appears lowly; yet in the eyes of an Israelite, Hámán <note>Pharaoh’s arrogant minister</note> is utterly cursed.
The spirit of Hámán has pulled the Egyptian toward himself, while the spirit of Moses has sought out the Israelite.
The belly of a donkey draws in straw when it swallows; the belly of Adam—the true Human—is drawn toward the "wheat-broth" of spiritual wisdom.

❦ **1640.** If, because of the darkness of ignorance, you cannot recognize a person’s true nature, look closely at whom they have chosen as their <term>imam: a leader or spiritual guide</term>.

### **_Explaining that the gnostic—one who possesses direct spiritual knowledge—receives a special nourishment from the Light of God; for the Prophet said,_ “I spend the night with my Lord: He gives me meat and drink”; _and,_ “Hunger is the food of God by which He revives the bodies of the <term>siddíqs: the 'truthful ones' or those of utmost sincerity</term>,” _meaning that in the state of spiritual hunger, God’s nourishment reaches them._**

Every foal follows after its mother, and through that following, its true nature and kinship become clear.
The milk for a human child comes from the breast—the upper, noble part of the body—while the milk for a donkey comes from the lower part.
This is the Justice of the Great Dispenser; it is an act of divine distribution. The wonder is this: in this divine plan, there is neither forced compulsion nor injustice.
If there were only compulsion, how could there be repentance? If there were injustice, how could God be our protection?

❦ **1645.** The day has ended, and the rest of the lesson must wait until tomorrow; how could a single day of this life ever contain the full depth of our mystery?
O you who have placed such firm confidence in the empty words and flattery of a scoundrel,
You have built a tent out of bubbles; in the end, you will find that such a tent has incredibly weak ropes.
Hypocrisy is like a flash of lightning: in its momentary gleam, the traveler cannot truly see the path.
This material world and its people are ultimately worth nothing; both are united in their lack of true faithfulness.

<summary>Rumi discusses the law of spiritual affinity, explaining that a person's nature is revealed by what attracts them and whom they follow. He contrasts the temporary, "bubble-like" nature of worldly success with the divine nourishment provided to the sincere seeker.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discourse on the deceptive nature of the material world. Rumi previously explained that worldly beauty is a trap and that humans are naturally drawn to what matches their inner state—either the "magnet" of the spiritual or the "static amber" of the material.</meta>

**1650.** The person obsessed with this world—the worldling—is as unfaithful as the world itself. Even when they turn their face toward you, that face is effectively their back, for they are already turning away from truth.
The people of the spiritual world are like that realm: because of their integrity, they remain forever faithful to their promises and sacred oaths.
When have two true prophets ever opposed one another? When have they ever tried to steal spiritual authority or miracles <note>original: "mu'jizat" — evidential miracles performed by prophets to prove their mission</note> from each other?
How could the "fruit" of the spiritual world ever go stale? Spiritual joy never decays into sorrow.
The <term>fleshly soul: nafs, the lower ego or animal self</term> is bound by no sacred covenant; for this reason, it must be subdued. It is base, and the place where its desires lead is equally low.

**1655.** This worldly assembly is perfectly suited for such base souls—just as the grave and the shroud are perfectly suited for the dead.
Though the ego may be clever and sharp, if its <term>qibla: the direction of prayer; here meaning one's ultimate focus or goal</term> is only this world, then consider it spiritually dead.
But when the "water" of Divine inspiration reaches this dead soul, a living spirit rises from the tomb of the corpse.
Until that inspiration arrives, do not be deceived by the "rouge" of worldly vanity or the flattering wish of "May your life be long!"
Instead, seek the renown that never fades and the radiance of a sun that never sets.

**1660.** Complex academic arguments and empty debates are like the followers of Pharaoh, and Death is like the waters of the Nile that will eventually swallow them.
Even though their intellectual brilliance and worldly power drag people along by the scruff of the neck,
Know that all of it is merely the illusion of magicians. Know that Death is like the staff of Moses, which transformed into a dragon.
That staff swallowed all their sorceries in a single gulp. The world was filled with the "night" of illusion, and the dawn of truth devoured it.
The Light of God is not made larger or "greater" by this act of devouring the darkness; it remains exactly as it has always been.

**1665.** The *effect* of the Light increases in the world, but its essence does not. A true essence suffers neither increase nor decrease.
God was not "increased" by the act of creating the universe; He did not become something now that He was not before.
Rather, the "effect"—the world of created things—increased. There is a vast difference between these two types of increase.
The increase of the "effect" is simply God's manifestation, allowing His divine attributes and actions to be made visible to us.
If a thing’s actual *essence* were to increase, it would be proof that the thing is not eternal, but is instead created and subject to causes.

### **_Commentary on the verse: "Moses conceived a fear in his heart: We said, 'Fear not, surely you will be the superior.'"_** <note>A reference to Qur'an 20:67-68 regarding the contest between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians.</note>

**1670.** Moses thought, "Magic is also a bewildering thing. How should I act? For these people have no discernment to tell the difference between sorcery and a miracle."
God replied, "I will provide that discernment. I will make the minds of those who cannot see capable of perceiving the truth."
"Though the magicians have whipped up foam like the sea, you, O Moses, will triumph. Do not be afraid!"
