<meta>Continuity: This page transitions from the general unfaithfulness of the material world to the specific metaphor of the "touchstone" and the "fake coin." It contrasts the temporary power of magic with the eternal truth of miracles, warning that while a pretender may flourish now, the inevitability of Death—the ultimate tester of spiritual value—will reveal their true nature.</meta>

Magic was glorious in its own time; however, when the rod <note>A reference to the staff of Moses which turned into a dragon, swallowing the illusions of Pharaoh's magicians.</note> became a dragon, those magic arts were disgraced.
Every one pretends to excellence and elegance, but the "Stone of Death" is the ultimate <term>touchstone: a stone used to test the purity of gold; here, a metaphor for spiritual testing</term> for these claims of beauty.

* **1675.** Magic is gone, and the miracle of Moses has passed; for both, the "bowl has fallen from the roof" <note>An idiom meaning a secret has been revealed or a state of being has ended.</note>.
What has the sound of magic's fallen bowl left behind but curses? What has the sound of religion's bowl left behind but a sense of the sublime?
Since the touchstone is currently hidden from man and woman, O counterfeit coin, go ahead—step into the light and brag!
Now is your time to boast. Since the tester is absent, people will pass you from hand to hand with honor.
The counterfeit coin is always saying to me arrogantly, “O pure gold, how am I any less than you?”

* **1680.** The gold replies, “Indeed, O fellow-servant; but the touchstone is coming. Be ready.”
The death of the body is a gift to those who know the mystery; what harm can a pair of scissors <note>Used to clip or test the edges of coins.</note> do to pure gold?
If the counterfeit coin could have seen its own end, it would have turned black at the very beginning.
If it had turned black at first, it would have been far from the double-dealing and damnation that comes from pretending to be what it is not.
It would have sought the <term>elixir: a substance believed to turn base metals into gold; here, Divine grace</term>; its reason would have triumphed over its hypocrisy.

* **1685.** Since it would have been broken-hearted by its own lowly state, it would have found the One who heals the broken.
When it saw the end and became contrite, it was immediately mended by the Great Bone-setter <note>A metaphor for God as the healer of spiritual wounds.</note>.
Divine grace pulled the pieces of copper toward the elixir; however, the "gilt" coin—only covered in a thin layer of gold—remained deprived of that bounty.
O you who are merely gold-plated, do not make false claims; realize that your "purchaser" will not stay blind forever.
The light of the Great Gathering <note>original: "Mahshar" — the Day of Resurrection or Last Judgement</note> will open their eyes and expose your trickery.

* **1690.** Look at those who have seen the end: they are the wonder of all souls and the envy of every eye.
Look at those who only see the present: their inner selves are corrupt; they are spiritually cut off from the Truth.
To those who only see the present, trapped in ignorance and doubt, the true dawn and the false dawn <note>The "false dawn" is a transient light in the sky that appears before the actual sunrise.</note> look exactly the same.
That false dawn has led a hundred thousand caravans into the wasteland of destruction, O seeker.
There is no genuine currency that does not have a deceptive counterfeit; woe to the soul that does not possess its own touchstone and scissors!

### **_Warning the pretender to stop their posturing and urging them to follow the true guide._**

* **1695.** Musaylim <note>Known as Musaylimah the Liar, a contemporary of Muhammad who claimed to be a prophet.</note> said, “I am also Ahmad <note>original: "Ahmad" — another name for the Prophet Muhammad</note>; I have cleverly confused the followers of Ahmad’s religion.”
Say to Musaylim, “Do not be so bold; do not be deceived by how things began. Look toward the end.”

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the discussion on the "Stone of Death" and the inevitable exposure of counterfeit spiritual claims. Having warned that the "tester" (Death) will eventually distinguish the pure gold from the fake coin, the text now transitions into a warning against following false guides who act out of greed.</meta>

Do not act as a guide out of a desire to amass wealth or power. Instead, follow behind so that the Candle <note>The "Candle" represents the true spiritual guide or Divine light that illuminates the path for others.</note> may lead the way.
This Candle, like the moon, clearly reveals the traveler’s destination—showing whether the path leads toward the grain of spiritual success or the snare of ruin.
Whether you wish it or not, as long as you carry this Lantern, the true nature of the falcon and the crow <note>The falcon represents the noble soul, while the crow represents the base or deceptive person.</note> will become visible to you.

❧**1700.** Otherwise, beware: these "crows" have lit a lantern of fraud. They have learned to mimic the cry of the noble white falcons.
If a man learns to imitate the call of the hoopoe <note>In mystical tradition, the hoopoe is the messenger of King Solomon and a symbol of the spiritual guide who knows the path to the Divine.</note>, does he truly possess the mysteries of Sabá <term>Sabá: the biblical and Quranic Sheba, representing the kingdom of the soul or the destination of the spiritual quest</term> and its hidden messages?
You must learn to distinguish the natural cry from the artificial one; you must know the difference between the crown of a king and the crest of a hoopoe.
These shameless people have put the speech of dervishes <term>dervish: a member of a Sufi order, often associated with poverty and spiritual devotion</term> and the deep wisdom of gnostics <term>gnostic: one who possesses direct, experiential knowledge of Divine mysteries</term> upon their tongues to deceive.
Every historical destruction of an ancient people occurred because they mistook precious sandal-wood for common firewood.

❧**1705.** They possessed the discernment required to see the difference, but greed and cupidity made them blind and deaf.
Physical blindness is not far from Divine mercy; it is the blindness caused by greed that is truly inexcusable.
Suffering or "crucifixion" <note>Here used metaphorically to mean trials or tribulations sent by God.</note> inflicted by the King is not far from mercy, but the self-inflicted torment of envy is never forgiven.
O fish, look toward the end and not just at the hook! Your base appetite has blindfolded the eye that should see the final outcome.
Look at both the beginning and the end with both eyes; beware of being one-eyed like the accursed Iblís <term>Iblís: the primary name for the Devil in Islamic tradition, who fell from grace due to pride and a limited perspective</term>.

❧**1710.** The "one-eyed" person is someone who sees only the present moment—ignorant, like a beast, of what comes afterward.
In the law of damages, the two eyes of an ox are valued only as a single eye of a human—for the animal possesses no spiritual excellence.
The ox's two eyes are worth only half its total value, because your own human eye must act as the support and guide for its vision.
But if you destroy a single eye of a son of Adam <term>son of Adam: a human being</term>, by law you must pay half his total value <note>Under traditional legal codes, the "blood money" or compensation for one eye was half the total amount for a human life.</note>.
This is because the human eye is capable of working on its own, without needing the eyes of another to find its way.

❧**1715.** Since the eye of a donkey cannot see the ultimate end along with the beginning, it is considered "one-eyed" even if it has two physical eyes.
This topic is endless—and meanwhile, that foolish man continues to write his letter in the hope of receiving bread.

### *The continuation of the story regarding the servant writing a petition for his allowance.*

Before writing the letter, the servant went to the steward of the kitchen and said, "O miser of the generous king's kitchen,
It is beneath the King and his great magnanimity that such a small matter as my meager allowance should even be brought to his attention."
The steward replied, "The King has ordered this for a good reason, not because of any stinginess or greed."

<summary>This passage explores the danger of greed-driven leadership and the necessity of spiritual discernment. It contrasts the "one-eyed" perspective of those focused only on immediate gain with the "two-eyed" vision that perceives both the beginning and the ultimate spiritual end of all things.</summary>

### **_The Story of the Praiser who, out of concern for his reputation, was thanking the person he praised; however, the scent of his inner grief and the shabbiness of his clothes revealed that his gratitude was empty and false._**

He continued to recite words of gratitude and praise until he had taken his thanks beyond all reasonable bounds.

### *The reduction of the allowance of God’s food for the soul and heart of the Súfí.*

The physical matter <note>original: "fat"</note> of your eye weighs only a couple of coins <term>dirhems: A unit of weight and currency used in the Middle East.</term>, yet the light of the spirit within it reaches the highest points of the sky.

**1885.** In dreams, the inner light sees everything without the physical eye; without this spiritual light, what would the eye be but a useless ruin?
The spirit does not care for the outward appearance—the beard or mustache—of the body; without the spirit, the body is merely a vile carcass.
If such is the magnificence of the 'animal spirit' <note>The basic life force shared by all living creatures.</note>, then go further and behold the true human spirit.
Go beyond mere human logic and scholarly debate, and reach the shore of the sea of the spirit of Gabriel <note>The Archangel Gabriel, the messenger of Divine Revelation.</note>.
After that, the spirit of Ahmad <note>Ahmad is a name for the Prophet Mohammed, representing the highest spiritual station.</note> will embrace you with love, while Gabriel himself will pull back in awe of you,

**1890.** And Gabriel will say, “If I come even a bow's length <note>A reference to the *Qaba Qawsayn* (two bows' length), the intimate distance the Prophet reached during his Night Journey to God.</note> closer to you, I shall be instantly consumed by the Divine Light.”

### ***How the slave was indignant because no reply to his letter arrived from the king.***

Truly, this spiritual desert has no beginning or end. That youth, receiving no reply to his letter, feels deeply wounded.
He says, “How strange! How could the King give me no answer? Perhaps the messenger acted treacherously out of envy,
And hid the letter instead of showing it to the King; he must be a hypocrite—like a hidden current of water flowing beneath straw.
I will write another letter to test him, and I will seek a more skilled messenger this time.”

## *How the wind blew perversely against Solomon, on whom be peace, because of his lapse.*

The wind began to blow violently against Solomon’s throne. Solomon cried out, 
> "O wind, do not move against me so perversely!"

The wind replied, 
> "Do not you act perversely, O Solomon; for if you act wrongfully, do not be angry at my own crookedness. God has established these scales of justice so that we may all be treated fairly throughout eternity.
> **1900.** If you give short measure, I shall give short measure; as long as you are honest with me, I will remain honest with you."

In the same way, Solomon's tiara <note>original: "tiara," referring here to a royal cap or turban representing his authority</note> slipped to one side, making his bright day feel as dark as night. He said, 
> "O tiara, do not sit crookedly upon my head! O sun, do not decline from my east <note>original: "orient"</note>!"

He tried to straighten the tiara with his hand, but the headwear would immediately slip back into a crooked position. Eight times he straightened it, and eight times it became tilted again. He asked, 
> "What is the matter, O tiara? Why do you sag so stubbornly?"

**1905.** It replied, 
> "Even if you straighten me a hundred times, it is useless. I go crooked because you have gone crooked, O trusted one."

Then Solomon looked inward and corrected his own soul: he cooled his heart toward the worldly lusts it had harbored. Immediately, the tiara became straight and sat exactly as he wished. Afterward, he tried to tilt it on purpose, but the tiara would skip back into its correct position on his head. Eight times the prince tried to make it crooked, and eight times it righted itself automatically.

**1910.** The tiara then spoke, saying, 
> "O King, you may now take pride in your station. Since you have shaken your wings free from the mud of this world, you are free to soar. I have no permission to speak further or to tear away the veils covering this mystery. Place your hand over my mouth; keep me silent from speaking what is hidden."

Therefore, whenever grief befalls you, do not resentfully accuse others; look instead within yourself. Do not think ill of another, you who seek to please your own soul. Do not do what that foolish slave was contemplating—

**1915.** At one moment, he quarreled with the messenger and the steward; at the next, his anger was directed at the generous Emperor. You are behaving like Pharaoh, who ignored the Moses within his own house and went out to slaughter the infants of the town. The enemy <note>Moses, representing the spiritual truth Pharaoh feared.</note> was already inside the house of that blind-hearted man, yet he was outside cutting the throats of children. 

You, too, are cruel to others on the outside, while you have become far too comfortable with the "grievous self" <term>Nafs: the carnal soul or lower ego that demands satisfaction</term> within. It is your true enemy, yet you feed it candy while you blame everyone else in the world.

## *How Shaykh Abu 'l-Hasan, may God be well-pleased with him, heard Báyazíd's announcement of his coming into existence and of what should happen to him.*

**1925.** It happened exactly as Báyazíd <term>Báyazíd: Báyazíd Bastami (d. 874), one of the most famous early Persian Sufi masters.</term> had predicted. Abu 'l-Hasan heard those prophecies from the people: 
> "Hasan will be my disciple and my true follower <note>original: "umma," meaning a religious community or a devoted spiritual successor</note>, and he will receive his lessons from my tomb every morning at dawn."

Abu 'l-Hasan said, "I have also seen him in a dream and have heard this promise from the spirit of the Shaykh <term>Shaykh: a spiritual teacher or master</term>." 
Every dawn he would turn his face toward the grave and stand there in devoted attention until the forenoon. 
Either the spiritual form of the Shaykh would appear to him, or his inner difficulties would be solved without a single word being spoken.

**1930.** This continued until one day he arrived at the grave at an auspicious hour, only to find the burial ground covered in deep, new-fallen snow. 
He saw the snow piled in wreaths like flags, mound upon mound, and his soul felt a pang of grief. 
From the shrine of the spiritually living Shaykh, a cry reached him: "Listen! I am calling you so that you may run to me! 
Hey, come quickly in this direction, toward the sound of my voice. Even if the world is buried in snow, do not turn your face away from me." 
From that day forward, his spiritual state became sublime, and he began to experience those wondrous things which, at first, he had only known through hearsay.

## *How the slave wrote another letter to the king when he received no reply to the first letter.*

**1935.** That man of evil thoughts wrote another letter, full of insults, clamor, and loud complaints. 
He said, "I wrote a letter to the king; I wonder if it ever arrived or if it found its way to him at all." 
The beautiful king read this second letter as well, but just as before, he gave no reply and remained silent. 
The king withheld every sign of favor from him, yet the slave repeated his letter five times. 
"After all," the king’s chamberlain said, "he is your Majesty's slave. It would be fitting if you wrote him a reply.

**1940.** What harm could come to your sovereignty if you cast a glance of favor upon your humble servant?" 
The king replied, "To do so would be easy; but he is a fool. A foolish man is foul and rejected by God. 
Though I might pardon his sins and faults, his spiritual disease would infect me as well. 
From contact with one person who has the itch, a hundred others become itchy—especially in the case of this loathsome, unrepentant itch <note>The "itch" is used here as a metaphor for a contagious, toxic character or spiritual ignorance that can influence those who associate with it.</note>."

May the affliction of foolishness never strike even an unbeliever; the fool's misfortune is so great that it keeps the clouds from raining.

❦ **1945.** Because of his bad luck, the clouds shed no moisture; by his "owlish" nature <note>In Persian poetry, the owl is often a symbol of bad luck or a dweller in ruins.</note>, a flourishing city is turned into a desert.
It was because of the agitation of those foolish people that the Flood of Noah <term>Flood of Noah: the Great Deluge described in scripture as a divine cleansing of the world's wickedness.</term> devastated an entire world in disgrace.
The Prophet <note>The Prophet Muhammad.</note> said, “Whoever is foolish is our enemy and a demon <note>original: "ghoul," a desert-dwelling spirit said to lead travelers off the path</note> who waylays the traveler.
But whoever is intelligent is as dear to us as our own soul; their presence is like a fragrant breeze of sweet basil.”
If an intelligent person speaks harshly to me, I am well-pleased, because their words come from a source that is part of my own spiritual essence.

❦ **1950.** The criticism of the wise is never without benefit; their hospitality always offers a full table.
But if a fool puts a sweet treat upon my lips, I feel as though I am suffering from a fever just by tasting it.
If you are good and enlightened, know for certain that there is no sweetness to be found in the company of the ignorant.
The fool only makes your reputation foul; he is like a blackened kettle that stains your clothes without ever providing a meal.
True intelligence is the "table" itself, not just bread and roasted meat—the light of the intellect, my friend, is the true nourishment for the soul.

❦ **1955.** Humanity has no real food but light; the soul cannot find nourishment in anything else.
Little by little, detach yourself from these material foods—for these are the fodder of animals, not the food of a noble person—
So that you may become capable of absorbing your original nourishment and can begin to feast on the delicacies of divine light.
It is only by the reflection of that light that physical bread has become bread at all; it is from the overflowing of the rational soul that the animal soul gained its life.
Once you have tasted the light, you will want to throw dust over the ovens and bread of this material world.

❦ **1960.** Understand that intelligence consists of two different types. The first is the acquired intelligence which you learn at school, like a boy in a classroom,
Gleaned from books, teachers, reflection, and memory, and from studying new and specialized sciences.
Through this, your intellect becomes greater than others, but you are heavily burdened by the weight of retaining all that information.
In your constant search for knowledge, you are merely a recording tablet; the "preserved tablet" <note>original: "lawh-i mahfūz," referring to the celestial tablet in Islamic theology where all things are written.</note> is the one who has moved beyond this mechanical learning.
The second intelligence is the gift of God; its fountain rises from the very center of the soul.

❦ **1965.** When the water of God-given knowledge gushes from the breast, it never becomes stagnant, old, or discolored.
And if its outward path is blocked, what harm is there? For it continues to flow fresh from the "house" of the heart.
Acquired intelligence is like the pipes and gutters that bring water into a house from the outside streets.
If those channels are blocked, the house is left dry. Seek the fountain from within yourself!

## ***Story of a man who was consulting another, who said, "Consult someone else, for I am your enemy."***

<summary>Rumi warns against the spiritual toxicity of foolishness and distinguishes between acquired intellectual knowledge—which is burdensome—and the innate, divine wisdom that flows directly from the heart.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page transitions from a general discussion on the nature of intelligence into a specific narrative dialogue. It explores the idea that a truly rational and spiritual person can be trusted for counsel even if they are a personal enemy, because their higher intellect—the "Faith-regarding reason"—governs their lower impulses.</meta>

A certain person was consulting someone, seeking to be delivered from his confusion and from a difficult quandary.

❧**1970.** “O honorable man,” the other replied, “look for someone else, not me, and explain the matter to them for consultation.
I am an enemy to you: do not attach yourself to me; one never finds success through the counsel of an enemy.
Go, seek one who is a friend to you: undoubtedly a friend seeks what is best for his friend.
I am an enemy: it is inevitable that out of egoism I should act falsely and show enmity toward you.
It is not right to ask a wolf to perform the duty of a shepherd; to demand something from the wrong source is a failure of the request itself.

❧**1975.** Without any doubt, I am your enemy: how should I show you the way? I am a highwayman.
Whoever sits with friends is in a garden of flowers, even if they are in a furnace room <note>original: "gulkhan," the hot, soot-filled room where the water for a public bath is heated; a metaphor for a wretched place.</note>.
Whoever sits with an enemy in this world is in a furnace room, even if they are in a garden of flowers.
Do not annoy your friend through your own egoism, lest your friend become your adversary and foe.
Do good to people for the sake of your God, or for the peace of your own soul,

❧**1980.** So that you may always see them as friendly in your sight, and so that ugly thoughts arising from hatred do not enter your heart.
Since you have behaved with enmity toward me, stay away from my counsel; consult a friend who awakens your affection.”
The man replied, “I know you, O Bu ’l-Hasan <note>Referring to Abu 'l-Hasan al-Kharaqani, the Persian Sufi master.</note>, to be one who has long considered me an enemy;
But you are a reasonable and spiritual man: your reason will not allow you to act falsely or play me foul.”
The lower nature <term>lower nature: the "nafs" or carnal self, which is driven by instincts, ego, and revenge.</term> desires to take revenge on its adversary, but the reason is an iron chain upon the flesh.

❧**1985.** Reason comes and prevents the fleshly self, restraining it; reason acts like a police inspector over its good and evil actions.
The reason that is allied to Faith is like a just police inspector: it is the guardian and magistrate of the city of the heart.
It is mentally alert like a cat; the thief remains in his hole, like a mouse.
Wherever the mouse gets the upper hand, no cat is there—or at best, there is only the hollow image of a cat.
What kind of cat is this reason? The Faith-regarding reason within the body is the lion that overthrows all other lions.

❧**1990.** Its roar is the controller of the predatory animals; its shout stops the grazing animals in their tracks.
If a city is full of thieves and robbers, it makes no difference whether there is a police inspector or not if the inspector has no power.

### *How the Prophet—on whom be peace—appointed a youth of the Hudhayl tribe to be commander of an expeditionary force in which there were elders and veteran warriors.*

The Prophet <note>The Prophet Muhammad.</note> was sending a force to fight against the unbelievers and to repel their insolence.
He chose a youth from the Hudhayl <note>An ancient Arabian tribe known for their poetic eloquence and archery.</note> and appointed him commander of the army and leader of the cavalry.

### The Necessity of a Leader

The foundation of an army is unquestionably the chief in command: a people without a chief are like a body without a head.

❦**1995.** The reason you feel spiritually dead and worn out is entirely because you have abandoned your leader.
Because of laziness, greed, and your own ego, you are pulling back like a stubborn animal and trying to make yourself the master.
You are like a beast of burden that flees from its load and runs off into the mountains to have its own way.
Its master runs after it, crying, “O you light-headed creature! On every side there is a wolf searching for a stray.
If you disappear from my sight now, the powerful wolf will close in on you from every direction.

❦**2000.** He will crunch your bones like sugar, and you will never see life again.
Even if you do not face immediate death, you will eventually be left without food; a fire is eventually put out when it runs out of wood.
Beware! Do not run away from my guidance or the weight of your responsibilities, for I am your <term>rational soul<gloss>The higher, spiritual intellect—in Persian, 'nafs-i natiqa'—which distinguishes humans from animals.</gloss></term>.”
You, too, are like a beast of burden because your <term>carnal soul<gloss>The lower, impulsive self—'nafs-i ammara'—driven by base desires.</gloss></term> is in control; and whatever quality is dominant defines your nature, O worshipper of yourself.
The Almighty did not call you a donkey; He called you a horse. This is why the Arabs say to a noble horse, “Come” <note>original: “ta'ál”</note>.

❦**2005.** <term>Mustafa<gloss>A title for the Prophet Muhammad meaning 'The Chosen One.'</gloss></term> was God’s stable-master for these "beasts"—which are actually our rebellious carnal souls.
Moved by loving-kindness, God said, “Say: ‘Come ye’ <note>original: “ta'álaw”</note>, so that I may train you; for I am the true Trainer.”
The Prophet said, “Because I have taken on the task of training these carnal souls, I have suffered many 'kicks' from these animals.
Anyone who is dedicated to training others has no way to avoid being hurt by them.
Necessity dictates that the greatest suffering falls upon the prophets, for it is a great affliction to try to teach the ignorant and the unrefined.”

❦**2010.** You are currently stumbling along. At my command, move at a steady jog-trot, so that you may become gentle and fit for the King to ride.
The Lord said, “Say: ‘Come ye,’ say: ‘Come ye,’ O beasts that have shied away from the path of discipline.
If they do not come, O Prophet, do not be grieved; do not feel hatred toward those two-faced people who lack steadfastness.”
The ears of some are deaf to these cries of “Come ye” <note>original: “ta'álaw”</note>; every animal has a different stable.
Some are frightened away by this call; the stall of every horse is separate.

❦**2015.** Some are annoyed by this teaching, for every bird has its own cage.
Even the angels were not all equals; for this reason, they formed different ranks in Heaven.
Children, even when they attend the same school, differ from one another in their lessons.
Both the person in the East and the person in the West have senses, but the actual power of sight belongs only to the eye.
Though a hundred thousand ears might be lined up in a row, they all still need the guidance of a clear-seeing eye.

❦**2020.** Furthermore, the ranks of ears have a specific purpose: to hear the words of the Spirit, the <term>Traditions<gloss>The Hadith, or the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.</gloss></term>, and the Divine Revelation.
A hundred thousand eyes do not have that specific ability; no eye is capable of the act of hearing.

### *How a critic objected to the Prophet—peace be upon him—appointing a man from the Hudhayl tribe as commander.*

❦**2030.** When the Prophet appointed a leader from the Hudhayl tribe to command the army—an army aided by Divine grace—
A prideful man, consumed by envy, could not remain silent; he stood up to object and oppose the decision.
Look at how darkened the human soul can be, and how people perish for the sake of temporary, worldly goods!
Out of pride, they remain separated from God, dead in spirit while living in a world of illusions.
It is a marvel that the spirit is in a prison, yet the key to that prison is in its own hand!

❦**2035.** That youth—the spirit—is covered in filth from head to foot, even though the pure, flowing river is nearly touching his robes!
He tosses and turns restlessly from side to side, right next to the place of rest and the bed where he could find peace.
The Divine light is hidden, yet the very act of searching is proof of its existence, for the heart does not seek a refuge that does not exist.
If this world’s prison had no escape, the heart would never feel this sense of repulsion or the desire for freedom.
Your very discomfort is like a guard pulling you along, saying, "O wandering soul, seek the path of truth."

❦**2040.** The path is there, but it is tucked away in a secret place; it can only be found after much seemingly "vain" searching.
This state of separation is secretly a quest for union; look closely at the seeker and you will see the face of the Beloved they seek.
The dead trees and plants of the garden spring up from their roots as if to say, "Witness the Giver of Life!"
How could the eyes of those imprisoned in this world always look toward the horizon if there were no messenger bringing good news of rescue?
How could there be a hundred thousand thirsty people searching for water if there were no water in the river?

❦**2045.** Even if your side finds no rest on this earth, know that there is a bed and a pillow waiting for you at home.

From within me a hundred sweet-breathing silent ones put their hands on their lips, signifying, “It is enough.”
Silence is the sea, and speech is like the river. The sea is seeking thee: do not seek the river.
Do not turn thy head away from the indications given by the sea: conclude the subject—and God best knoweth the right course.
That irreverent objector made no pause in the words which he poured forth in this fashion from those cold and insipid lips of his in the presence of the **Prophet**.

❧**2065.** Words were assisting him and did not fail him, but he was ignorant that hearsay or traditional knowledge is mere babble in the presence of sight and immediate vision.
Indeed, these matters of hearsay are only a substitute for sight: they are not for him who is present, but for him who is absent.
Whoever has been caused to attain unto sight, before him these matters of hearsay are idle.
When you have sat down beside your beloved, after this banish the *<term>dallálas<gloss>Plural of dallála; female go-betweens or matchmakers who describe a bride to a groom. When any one has passed beyond childhood and has become a man, the letter and the *<term>dallála</term>* become irksome to him.

❧**2070.** He reads letters, but only for the purpose of teaching others; he utters words, but only for the purpose of making others understand.
It is wrong to speak by hearsay in the presence of those who are endowed with vision, for it is a proof of our heedlessness and deficiency.

He argues that direct spiritual vision renders intermediaries and traditional learning—likened to "matchmakers"—unnecessary once the seeker has reached the presence of the Beloved.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page follows a scene where a man is disputing the Prophet Muhammad’s appointment of a young man as a commander. The previous verses used the metaphor of a tree's fruit versus its leaves to explain that spiritual maturity is not always tied to physical age.</meta>

In the presence of the seer, silence is to your advantage. For this reason, the Divine command was sent: *Be silent.* <note>original: "Anṣitū" — a reference to Quran 7:204, which commands silence when the Word of God is heard, here applied to the presence of a spiritual master.</note>
If the seer bids you speak, do so gladly, but say little and do not drag your words out.
And if he bids you speak at length, do so with that same modesty, complying with his command.

**2075.** Just as I am doing now, in this beautiful, enchanting poem, by the command of the <term>Radiance of Truth<gloss>Ziyá’u ‘l-Haqq</gloss></term>, Husámu’ddín.
Even when I try to shorten my talk about the Way of righteousness, he draws me back to speak through a hundred different methods.
O Husámu’ddín, Radiance of the Almighty! Since you can see the truth directly, why do you seek words from me?
Perhaps this request comes from your love for the Desired One; as the poet said, “Give me wine to drink, and tell me that it is wine.” <note>This refers to the lover's desire to hear the name of the beloved even while they are experiencing the beloved's presence.</note>
At this moment, His cup is at your mouth, yet your ear asks, “Where is the ear's portion?”

**2080.** O ear, your portion is the heat of love: look, you are already heated and intoxicated. The ear replies, “My greed for this is greater still.”

## *How the Chosen One <note>original: Mustafá, a title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note>, peace be upon him, answered the objector.*

When that Arab carried his argument too far in the presence of the sweet-tempered <term>Chosen One<gloss>Mustafá</gloss></term>,
That king of the chapter *By the Star* <note>original: Wa ’l-Najm (Quran 53)</note> and that sultan of the chapter *He Frowned* <note>original: ‘Abas (Quran 80)</note> bit his lip in anger and told the foolish talker, “Enough!”
He placed his hand over the man's mouth to stop him, as if to say, “How long will you speak in the presence of one who knows the unseen?”
You have brought dry waste to one who has spiritual vision, saying, “Buy this instead of a bag of musk!” <note>Musk was a highly prized perfume; the poet contrasts the man's worthless arguments with the Prophet's spiritual fragrance.</note>

**2085.** O you of foul mind and spirit, you place camel dung beneath your nose and call it delicious!
O squinting, foolish man, you cry out in delight just so your poor-quality goods might sell,
And so you might deceive that pure sense of spiritual smell—the one that grazes in the gardens of heaven.
Though the saint’s patience makes him appear simple, you must gain some self-awareness.
If the lid of the cooking pot is left open tonight, the cat should still have some restraint. <note>A proverb suggesting that even if an authority figure allows someone to speak, that person should have the decency not to overstep.</note>

**2090.** If that glorious saint has pretended to be asleep, he is actually very much awake; do not try to steal his turban!
How long, O stubborn man without spiritual merit, will you speak these devilish charms in the presence of God’s chosen one?
This company of the elect possesses a hundred thousand kinds of patience, each one as immovable as a hundred mountains.
Their patience makes a fool of the cautious and causes the clever man with a hundred eyes to lose his way.
Their patience, like a fine, choice wine, rises slowly and surely to the brain.

**2095.** Look at the man drunk on that miraculous wine: he has begun to move crookedly, like the queen in a game of chess. <note>In traditional chess, the "Farzin" (the vizier or queen) moves diagonally, which the poet uses as a metaphor for the "crooked" or ecstatic movement of the spiritually intoxicated.</note>
From the effects of that potent wine, the vigorous youth falls in the middle of the road like an old man.

<meta>Continuity: This page follows a discussion on spiritual maturity and the necessity of silence and humility in the presence of a spiritual master. Consider especially the effect of this divine wine, drawn from the jar of the primordial Covenant <note>original: *Balá*, referring to the day souls answered "Yes" to God's sovereignty.</note>—not the common wine whose drunkenness lasts only a single night.
It is the wine that sustained the **Men of the Cave** <note>The "Seven Sleepers," a group of youths who hid in a cave to escape persecution and slept for centuries under divine protection.</note> during their long rest and their migrations, causing them to lose all worldly reason for three hundred and nine years.

**2100.** The magicians who faced Moses were likewise intoxicated by his divine power: they reached a state where they welcomed the gallows as if it were their beloved.
**Ja'far the Flyer** <note>original: *Ja'far-i Tayyár*, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad and a martyr who, according to tradition, was granted wings in Paradise after losing his arms in battle.</note> was so drunk with that wine that, in his ecstasy, he sacrificed his hands and feet for the sake of God.

### -> ***The story of Báyazíd—may God sanctify his spirit—and his saying, "Glory be to me! How great is my state!" It describes the objections raised by his disciples and how he answered them, not through words, but through a spiritual vision.*** <-

That venerable mystic, **Báyazíd**, came to his disciples and declared, "Behold, I am God."
That master of spiritual sciences spoke plainly in his drunken ecstasy, saying, "Listen! There is no god but I; therefore, worship me."
When the state of ecstasy had passed, his disciples told him at dawn, "You said such and such, and this is a sacrilege."

**2105.** He replied, "If I cause such a scandal again, come at once and strike me with your knives.
God is beyond the physical body, while I am bound by it; you must kill me if I speak such things again."
After that free-spirited man gave this command, each disciple prepared a knife.
Once again, Báyazíd became intoxicated by that powerful cup; the instructions he had given vanished from his mind.
The spiritual feast <term>Dessert<gloss>Nuql</gloss></term> arrived and his worldly reason became distracted; the Dawn of truth rose, and his individual light was extinguished.

**2110.** Reason is like a local official: when the Emperor arrives, the lowly official hides in a corner.
Reason is merely a shadow of God; God is the Sun. What power does a shadow have to stand against the Sun?
When a spirit <term>genie<gloss>jinn</gloss></term> takes possession of a human, the person's human qualities disappear.
Whatever that person says is actually spoken by the spirit; the person on this side is merely a mouthpiece for the one on the other side.
If a spirit can have such influence and control, how much more powerful must be the Creator of that spirit!

**2115.** The man’s own "I" is gone; he has truly become the spirit. A man of the Steppes <note>original: *Turk*</note>, without any prior study, suddenly begins to speak perfect Arabic.
When he returns to himself, he does not know a single word of that language. Since a spirit has this nature and quality,
How could the Lord of both spirits and men be less powerful than a spirit?
If a man, emboldened by drink, slays a fierce lion, you would say the wine did it, not the man.
And if he speaks words of pure gold, you would say the wine has spoken through him.

**2120.** If a common wine has the power to cause such a commotion, does the **Light of God** not have the strength
To empty you entirely of yourself, so that you are humbled and He makes His Word rise high within you?

❧ **2140.** His physical form has vanished and he has become a mirror; there is nothing there but the reflection of whoever looks into it.

When the discussion reached this point, its lips were sealed; when the pen reached this mystery, it broke to pieces.

❧ **2145.** Close your lips now: even if you are a master of eloquence, do not breathe another word—and God knows the right path best.
O you who are intoxicated by the wine of divine love, you are standing on the very edge of the roof; sit down or come down, and peace be with you!
Every moment that you enjoy union with the Beloved, consider that delightful moment to be the "edge of the roof."
Be mindful and fear losing that moment; hide it like a secret treasure and do not boast of it.
Lest a sudden calamity strike your devoted love, take heed, and walk with great care in that place of spiritual ambush.

❦ **2150.** The spirit's fear of loss at the very moment of enjoyment is a sign of its departure—its descent from the hidden roof-edge. <note>The "roof-edge" is a metaphor for a precarious peak of pleasure or ego; the fear of losing that state indicates that the soul is already slipping away from its spiritual height.</note>
If you do not see the mysterious roof-edge itself, your spirit still senses it, for it is shuddering with fear.
Every sudden punishment that has ever come to pass has taken place on the edge of the turret of enjoyment.
Indeed, there is no fall except from the edge of a roof: take warning from the fate of the people of **Noah** and the people of **Lot**. <note>original: *Qawm-i Nūḥ* and *Qawm-i Lūṭ*. In sacred history, these communities were destroyed at the height of their earthly prosperity and defiance.</note>

### *Explaining the cause of the eloquence and loquacity of that impertinent man in the presence of the Prophet, on whom be peace.*

When the reflection of the **Prophet’s** <note>original: *Payghambar*, referring to Muhammad.</note> boundless spiritual intoxication struck that man, even that stupid fellow became drunken and merry.

❦ **2155.** Naturally, because of this drunken glee, he became talkative: the intoxicated man forgot to show proper respect and began to rave.
It is not that selflessness and intoxication always work mischief, but rather that wine makes an unmannerly person even more so.
If the one who drinks is intelligent, he becomes more decorous and displays good qualities when he is beside himself; but if he is evil-natured, he becomes worse.
But since the majority of people are evil and wayward, wine has been forbidden to everyone.

### *How the Prophet, on whom be peace, explained the cause of his preferring and choosing the young man of Hudhayl as commander and chief of the army over the heads of the elders and veterans.*

Cases are decided by the general rule, not by the exceptions: since the majority are evil, the sword was taken away from the hand of the highwayman.

❦ **2160.** The Prophet said, “O you who look only at externals, do not look upon him as merely a youth or someone unskilled.
Oh, there is many a black beard that belongs to a man old in wisdom; and oh, there is many a white beard with a heart as black as pitch.
I have tested his understanding many times: that youth has shown the ripe experience of age in handling affairs.
O son, the person who is truly 'old' is the one who is old in understanding; it is not merely the whiteness of the hair in the beard or on the head.
How could any old man be older than **Iblis**? <note>original: *Iblīs*, the primary devil or Satan in Islamic tradition, famed for his ancient age but also for his lack of spiritual insight.</note> Yet when he lacks understanding, he is worth nothing.

❦ **2165.** Suppose he is a child: what does it matter if he possesses the life-giving breath of **Jesus** <note>original: *dam-i ‘Īsā*. In Sufi poetry, the 'breath of Jesus' symbolizes the power to revive the spiritually dead.</note> and is purged of vainglory and vain desire?
That whiteness of hair is only a proof of maturity to the bandaged eye that lacks deep penetration.
Since the blind imitator recognizes nothing but external proof, he continually seeks the way to the truth through outward signs.
It is for his sake that we have said, 'When you wish to plan anything, choose an elder to advise you.'
But he who has escaped from the **purdah** <term>Purdah: Literally a 'curtain' or 'veil'; here referring to the barrier of superficial thinking or blind imitation (taqlíd) that prevents one from seeing the Truth directly.</term> of blind imitation sees by the light of God that which really exists.

❦ **2170.** Without need for proof or explanation, the pure Light cleaves through the skin of an object and enters directly into its core.”

❧ **2180.** Of those sweet-breathing names, the least is this: that Intelligence is not in need of anyone.

❧ **2185.** The bat-like person is a lover of every place where there is difficulty and perplexing doubt, and an enemy of every place where the lamp of spiritual success shines.
The intelligent man is he who carries the lamp; he is the guide and leader of the caravan.
That leader is one who follows his own light; that selfless traveler is a follower of his own true nature.
The fool’s heart seeks the darkness of confusion so that his meager accomplishments may seem greater than they truly are,
So that he may distract you with difficult questions and make you forget his own evil nature.

### **_The marks of the wholly intelligent and the half-intelligent and the whole man and the half-man and the deluded worthless wretch doomed to perdition._**

The intelligent man is he who carries the lamp; he is the guide and leader of the caravan.
That leader is one who follows his own light; that selfless traveler is a follower of his own true nature.

❧ **2190.** He is the one who puts faith in himself; and you too should put your faith in the light upon which his soul has fed.
The other, who is only half-intelligent, considers a truly intelligent person to be his "eye,"
And he has gripped him just as a blind man grips a guide, so that through the guide he becomes seeing, active, and illustrious.
But as for the "ass" who did not possess even a barley-corn’s weight of intelligence—who had no wisdom of his own and yet abandoned the wise guide—
He knows neither much nor little of the way, yet he disdains to walk behind the guide.

## *The Story of the Lake, the Fishermen, and the Three Fish: One Wise, One Half-Wise, and the Third Deluded, Foolish, and Worthless; and the Fate of All Three.*

This, O stubborn man, is the story of the lake in which there were three great fish.
You will have read this story in <term>Kalila|Refers to *Kalila and Dimna*, a famous collection of ancient animal fables (originally the *Panchatantra*) used to teach moral and political lessons</term>, but that version is merely the husk; this version is the spiritual kernel.
Some fishermen passed by the lake and saw that hidden prey.

**2205.** They hurried away to bring their net. The fish noticed and became aware of their intentions.
The intelligent fish resolved to leave; he chose to undertake the difficult and unwelcome journey to safety.
He said to himself, “I will not consult these others, for they will surely weaken my resolve.
Their love for their familiar home and their dwelling place holds power over their souls; their laziness and ignorance will infect me.”
To seek counsel, one requires a person who is spiritually alive to bring life to you—and where is such a living soul to be found?

**2210.** O traveler, take counsel with another traveler, for the advice of a <note>original: "woman's counsel" – Rumi often uses "woman" as a metaphor for the *nafs* (the lower, impulsive soul) which lacks foresight and hinders the spiritual journey</note> lower soul will keep your feet crippled.
Look past the literal expression, “love of one’s country.” Do not stop at its surface meaning, for your real country is Yonder, O soul; it is not on this side of existence.
If you desire your true country, cross to the other bank of the stream: do not misinterpret this true <term>Hadith|A recorded saying or tradition of the Prophet Muhammad; Rumi is referencing the famous saying: "Love of one's homeland is part of faith"</term>.

## *The Inner Meaning of the Prayers Recited During Ritual Ablution.*

In the ritual of <term>ablution|Wudu, the ritual washing performed by Muslims to maintain physical and spiritual purity before prayer</term>, tradition has handed down a specific prayer for each part of the body.
When you sniff water into your nose, ask the self-sufficient Lord for the scent of Paradise,

**2215.** So that that fragrance may lead you toward Heaven; for the scent of the rose is what leads one to the rose-tree.
When you perform the act of <note>original: *istinja* – the ritual cleaning of the body after waste</note> cleansing, the proper prayer is this: “O Lord, wash me clean of this defilement.
My hand has reached this place and washed it, but my hand is powerless to wash my spirit.”

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the introduction to the parable of the three fish. > O Thou by whom the spirit of the unworthy is made worthy, the hand of Thy bounty is reaching even to the lowly spirits.
> This which I, vile as I am, have done was my limit <note>The utmost within my power.</note>: do Thou make clean that which lies beyond my limit, O gracious One.

> ❦**2220.** O God, I have washed my skin clean of filth: do Thou wash this beloved spirit clean of worldly taints.”

***A certain person used to say at the time of <term>abstersion|The ritual washing of the private parts after using the bathroom.</term>, “O God, let me smell the sweet odor of Paradise” <note>original: "Allahumma arihni ra’ihat al-jannah"</note> instead of “O God, make me one of those who repent much, and make me one of those who purify themselves,” <note>original: "Allahumma-j’alni minat-tawwabina waj’alni minal-mutatahhirin"</note> which is the proper form of prayer during such washing; and he also used to recite the formula proper to washing the body at the time of rinsing his nose. A certain man said at the time of washing himself, “(O God), unite me with the scent of Paradise!”
Thereupon a sage said, “You have used a good prayer, but you have missed the proper hole for it.
Since this prayer was the formula meant for the nose, why have you applied the nose-formula to the backside?
A person free from worldly desires catches the scent of Paradise through his nose: how should the scent of Paradise come from the rump?”

> ❦**2225.** O you who have behaved with humility in the presence of fools, and O you who have acted with pride in the presence of spiritual kings,
> The pride shown to the base and lowly is goodly and fitting. Take heed, do not behave in the reverse manner: the reverse of this is the cause of your spiritual bondage.
> The rose grew for the sake of the nostrils: sweet scent is the rightful due of the nose, O churlish man.
> The scent of the rose is for the organs of smell, O bold man: this lower opening is not the place for such a fragrance.
> How should the scent of Paradise come to you from this place? If you require the sweet scent, seek it from its proper place.

❦**2230.** Likewise, the saying “love of country is a matter of faith” <note>A famous tradition (hadith) in Islamic thought.</note> is right, but first, O master, you must know what your true country is.
That <vocab>sagacious fish</vocab> said, “I will journey; I will withdraw my heart from the advice and counsel of these others.”
It is no time for talk. Listen, begin the journey! Like <term>’Alí|Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin, who according to mystical tradition would whisper his deepest spiritual secrets into a well because he found no humans capable of bearing them.</term>, sigh your secret into the well.
Very seldom is a fit confidant found for such a sigh: go by night and let your movement be hidden, like that of the <vocab>night-patrol</vocab>.
Set out from this lake toward the sea: seek the sea and take leave of this <vocab>whirlpool</vocab> of worldly life.

❦**2235.** That wary fish made its breast its feet <note>It swam with all its might.</note> and was going from its perilous home toward the **sea of light**,
Like a deer pursued by a dog, which keeps running so long as there is a single nerve left in its body.
A "hare’s sleep" <note>A state of heedlessness or feigned sleep while danger is near.</note> while the dog is in pursuit is a sin: how indeed can there be sleep in the eye of one who feels true fear?
That fish departed and took the way to the sea: it took the long path and the vast expanse.
It suffered many afflictions, and in the end, it moved toward safety and spiritual welfare.

❦**2240.** It cast itself into the **deep Sea** whose boundary no eye can reach.
So when the fishermen eventually brought their net to the lake, the half-intelligent fish was bitterly grieved.
And it said, “Alas, I have lost the opportunity: why did I not accompany that wise guide?”

### ***Story of the captive bird which gave the following instructions: do not feel sorrow for what is past, think about taking precautions for the present need, and do not spend time in repenting.***

2245. A certain man caught a bird using a clever trap. The bird said to him, "O noble sire,
You have eaten many oxen and sheep; you have sacrificed many camels;
In all your life you were never filled by them, nor will you be satisfied by my small limbs.
Let me go, and I will give you three pieces of counsel so that you may see if I am wise or foolish.
I will give the first piece of counsel while on your hand, the second from your plastered roof,

2250. And the third counsel I will give you from a tree. Let me go, for you will become fortunate through these three lessons.
As for the saying to be told while on your hand, it is this: 'Do not believe an absurdity, no matter who tells it to you.'"
When the bird had spoken this first weighty counsel on his palm, it became free and flew to the wall of his house.
It said, "The second is: 'Do not grieve over what is past; once it has left you, do not feel regret for it.'"
After that, the bird said to him, "Inside my body is hidden a single, large, and precious pearl, weighing ten <term>dirhems|A historical unit of weight and currency used across the Islamic world.</term>.

2255. By the truth of your soul, that jewel was your true fortune and the luck of your children.
You have missed the pearl, for it was not your destiny to gain it—a pearl the like of which does not exist."
Just as a woman in labor cries out in pain, the <term>Khwája|A Persian title for a master, lord, or wealthy merchant.</term> began to wail and shout.
The bird said to him, "Did I not just warn you, saying, 'Let there be no grief in you for what passed yesterday'?
Since it is past and gone, why are you grieving? Either you did not understand my counsel or you are deaf.

2260. And as for the second counsel I gave you—that you should not foolishly believe an absurd statement—
O lion-like man, I myself do not even weigh ten dirhems! How could a ten-dirhem pearl be inside me?"
The Khwája recovered his wits and said, "Fine, tell me the third piece of excellent counsel."
"Yes," said the bird, "you have made such 'good' use of the first two that I should certainly waste the third on you!"
To give advice to a sleepy, ignorant person is like scattering seeds in <term>nitrous soil|Salty, alkaline earth that is barren and cannot support plant growth.</term>.

2265. The tear of folly and ignorance cannot be patched; do not waste the seeds of wisdom on a fool, O counselor.

### *Explaining that imagination (<term>wahm|In Sufi psychology, a faculty that mimics logic but is actually driven by the ego, fears, or physical desires.</term>) is the counterfeit of Reason and stands in opposition to it; and that although it resembles Reason, it is not Reason; and the story of the replies given to each other by Moses, on whom be peace, who was the possessor of Reason, and Pharaoh, who was the possessor of imagination.*

Reason is the opposite of sensuality: O brave soul, do not give the name of "Reason" to that which is tethered to your physical desires.
That which acts as a beggar to your senses—call it imagination. Imagination is the counterfeit of the pure, sterling gold of the rational soul.
Without a touchstone, imagination and reason are difficult to distinguish; quickly bring them both to the test.
The *Quran* and the spiritual states of the Prophets are this touchstone: like a master testing metal, they say to the counterfeit coin, "Come,

**2305.** "So that by contact with me, you may see your true self and realize you are not worthy of my higher or lower spiritual degrees."
If a saw were to cut Reason into two halves, it would remain smiling, like gold purified in the heat of the fire.
Imagination belongs to Pharaoh, the one who sets the world on fire with his ego; Reason belongs to Moses, the one who kindles the human spirit.
Moses walked the path of self-negation; Pharaoh challenged him, saying: "Tell me, who are you?"
Moses replied, "I am Reason, the messenger of the Almighty. I am the evidence of God and a protection against falling into error."

**2310.** "No," Pharaoh replied, "be silent! Cease this ecstatic shouting! Tell me instead of your ancient family lineage and your name."

I am the slave-born servant of that unique Lord—born from the womb and loins of humble servants, both female and male.
My original ancestry comes from earth, water, and clay; it was God who gave a soul and a heart to that water and clay.

❦**2480.** This is how you have acted until now; from this moment on, do so no more. You have made the water of your soul muddy; do not stir it up any further.

The spirit of man resembles the air: when it is mixed with the dust of the world, it veils the sky,

❦**2485.** And it prevents the eye from seeing the sun. But when that dust is gone, the air becomes pure and clear again. 
Despite your complete darkness, God has been showing you spiritual visions so that you might find the path to ultimate deliverance.

### The Parable of the King's Falcon and the Ignorant Old Woman

If you give a white falcon to a decrepit old woman, she will clip its talons for the sake of its supposed welfare. The blind woman will blindly cut away the very claws that allow it to hunt and survive,

❦**2630.** Saying, “Where was your mother, little prince, that your claws were allowed to grow so long?”
She trimmed its talons, its beak, and its wings; the wretched woman did this out of a misguided sense of affection.
When she offers it noodle soup <term>tutmáj: a traditional heavy pasta or dough-based soup</term>, the bird will not eat. At this, she flies into a rage, her feelings of love suddenly turning to resentment.
She shouts, “I have cooked such fine soup for you, and yet you show nothing but pride and insolence!
You deserve to stay in this misery and affliction; how could happiness or prosperity ever suit a creature like you?”

❦**2635.** She offers it the broth from the soup, saying, “Take this, if you refuse to eat the pasta.”
The falcon’s noble nature rejects the heavy broth; the old woman frowns, her anger deepening.
In her fury, she pours the scalding hot soup over the bird’s head, and the feathers on its crown are burned away.
From the searing pain, tears stream from the falcon’s eyes; it remembers the kindness of its heart-delighting King.
Tears pour from those two charming, royal eyes—eyes that hold a hundred perfections reflected from the countenance of the King.

With a single powerful breath from Salih, the very womb of the mountain would give birth to a hundred such camels.”

❦**2650.** My heart whispers, “Be silent now and practice discretion; otherwise, Divine jealousy will tear the very fabric of your existence.”

### **The Story of the woman whose child crawled to the top of the water-spout and was in danger of falling; and how she sought help from Ali, may God ennoble his person.**

A woman came to Ali <note>original: "Murtadá"; a title for Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, known for his wisdom.</note> and said, “My child has climbed onto the water-spout high above.

If I call to him, he will not come to me; and if I leave him there, I fear he will fall to his death.

He is not old enough to understand, as we do, if I were to say, ‘Come to me and escape this danger.’

❧ **2660.** Moreover, he does not understand hand gestures; or if he did, he would not listen. This approach is useless.

Many times I have shown him my breast and the milk, but he always turns his eyes and his face away from me.

For God’s sake—since you, O noble ones, are those who provide help in this world and the next—

Quickly find a remedy, for my heart is trembling with the fear that I will be painfully separated from the fruit of my heart.”

Ali said, “Take another child up to the roof, so that the boy may see one of his own kind.

❧ **2665.** He will then come nimbly from the water-spout to his playmate: like is always in love with like.”

The woman did so, and when her child saw his peer, he turned his face toward him with delight,

And crawled from the edge of the water-spout back to the roof: know that like attracts like.

The child came crawling to the other child and was saved from falling to the ground below.

The Prophets are sent from among humankind for this very reason: so that humanity, through the affinity they feel for these messengers, may be saved from the "water-spout" of the world.

❧ **2670.** Therefore, the Prophet called himself *a man like you* <note>A reference to the Quranic verse 18:110, "I am only a man like you, to whom has been revealed that your God is one God."</note>, so that you might come to your own kind and not be lost.

For affinity is a wondrous magnet: wherever there is a seeker, his own kind is attracting him.

Jesus and Idris <note>Idris is a prophet in the Quran, often identified with the biblical Enoch.</note> ascended to heaven because they shared a nature with the angels.

Conversely, the fallen angels Harut and Marut <note>Two angels mentioned in the Quran who were sent to Babylon and became entangled in human desires.</note> shared an affinity with the physical body; hence they descended from the heights.

The unbelievers have become kindred with Satan; therefore, their spirits have become disciples of devils.

### ***Explaining that one who knows the power of God will not ask, "Where are Paradise and Hell?"***

God creates Hell wherever He wills: He can turn the very heights of the sky into a snare and a trap for a bird.
In the same way, when a sharp pain rises from your teeth, it is there to make you say, "This is Hell and the dragon."
Or He can make the saliva in your mouth taste like honey, so that you might say, "This is Paradise and the silken robes <note>Referring to the luxurious garments promised to the faithful in the afterlife.</note>."
He makes sugar grow from the very roots of your teeth, so that you may recognize the power of His divine decree.

2815. Do not, then, use your teeth to bite the innocent: think instead of the blow from God that cannot be blocked.
God turned the Nile into blood for the Egyptians; yet He kept the Israelites safe from that calamity,
So that you may know that God distinguishes between the sober traveler on the Right Path and the one who is intoxicated by pride.
The Nile learned from God how to discriminate between people, for it opened its "door" for the Israelites and slammed it shut against the Egyptians.
His grace makes even a river like the Nile intelligent; His wrath makes a man like Cain <note>The son of Adam who killed his brother, often used as a symbol of someone blinded by envy and rage.</note> act foolishly.

2820. Out of kindness, He created intelligence within lifeless things; yet because of His anger, He can strip intelligence away from the "wise" man.
By His grace, a soul appeared in inanimate matter, and through His punishment, knowledge fled from the scholar.
In one place, by His command, intelligence poured down like rain; in another, intelligence saw God’s anger and turned to flee.
The clouds, the sun, the moon, and the soaring stars—all come and go according to a divine arrangement.
None of them arrives except at its appointed hour; they never lag behind nor arrive too early.

2825. Have you not understood this from the lives of the prophets? They brought awareness into stones and wooden rods,
So that you, by comparing them, might realize that all other "lifeless" things are just like that rod and stone—filled with hidden life.
The way the stone and rod obey God is a sign; it gives us news about all other inanimate objects.
They seem to say: "We are aware of God and obedient to Him; none of us exists by mere chance or in vain."
Take the water of the Nile as an example: you know that at the moment of drowning, it chose a side and made a distinction between the two nations.

2830. Consider the Earth: you know it possessed knowledge at the moment it swallowed Qárún <term>Qárún: Known in the Bible as Korah, a wealthy man who was punished for his arrogance and greed by being swallowed up by the earth.</term>, whom God subdued and swept away.
And consider the Moon, which heard the Divine command and hurried to obey, splitting into two halves across the sky <note>This refers to the miracle of the 'Splitting of the Moon,' signifying the authority given to the Prophet Muhammad.</note>.

<summary>This passage explains that the entire physical world—including rivers, stones, and planets—is conscious and obedient to God’s will. Using the miracles of Moses and Muhammad as evidence, Rumi argues that "lifeless" matter can distinguish between the righteous and the proud.</summary>

### ***A reply to the materialist who disbelieves in God and claims the world is eternal.***

Someone was saying yesterday, "The world was created at a point in time; this heaven is passing away, and God is its ultimate heir."
A philosopher replied, "How can you know it had a beginning in time? How could the rain possibly know the age of the clouds?"

<note>Small floral ornaments precede the line numbers in the following text.</note>

**2835.** You are not even a tiny speck within the great celestial cycle; how could you know the age of the sun?
How could the small worm buried in the dirt know the beginning or the end of the earth?
You have simply memorized this from your father; out of foolishness, you have clung to this belief.
What is the logical argument for its beginning? Speak, or else stay silent and stop your excessive talk."
He replied, "One day I saw two groups searching in this deep sea,

**2840.** Engaged in a desperate battle of arguments and controversy; a crowd had gathered around those two.
I went toward the crowd and observed their dispute.
One was saying, 'The sky will eventually perish; without any doubt, this building has a builder.'
The other said, 'It is eternal and timeless; it has no builder, or perhaps it is its own builder.'
The first said, 'You have denied the Creator, the one who produces day and night and provides all sustenance.'

**2845.** The philosopher replied, 'Without clear evidence, I will not listen to what an ignorant person has accepted by rote.
Come, bring the proof and the evidence, for I will never listen to this without proof.'
'The proof,' he replied, 'is within my soul; my evidence is hidden deep within my spirit.
If your eyes are too weak to see the new moon, do not be angry with me just because I can see it.'
There was much debate, and the people became confused about the beginning and the end of this well-ordered celestial sphere.

**2850.** The pious man said, 'My friend, I have a decisive proof within me; I have a clear sign that the sky was created in time.
I possess certainty; for the one who has certain knowledge, the test of that knowledge is that he will willingly enter the fire.'
Know that this proof, like the secret feelings of love in a lover’s heart, cannot be expressed by the tongue.
The inner meaning of my words is not visible, except through the paleness and exhaustion shown on my face.
Tears and blood flow down my cheeks, serving as the proof of the Beloved’s <note>In Sufi poetry, the "Beloved" refers to God.</note> beauty and grace.'

**2855.** The philosopher replied, 'I do not consider these things to be the kind of proof that would be a clear sign to ordinary people.'
The other said, 'When a counterfeit coin and a genuine one both boast, each saying, "You are fake; I am good and valuable,"
The fire is the final test; the test is that these two rivals should be dropped into the flames.'

<summary>This passage depicts a debate between a materialist philosopher, who argues the world is eternal, and a believer who asserts it was created by God. **2880.** The true usefulness of every external object is, in fact, internal. It is hidden, just like the healing properties found within a medicine.

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the spiritual victory of a believer over a skeptical philosopher. Nay, the artist paints for the sake of guests and young people, so that by diverting themselves with the art, they may be relieved of their cares.
From his picture arises the joy of children and the remembering of departed friends by those they loved.
Does any potter make a pot in haste for the sake of the pot itself, and not in the hope of the water it will hold?

**2885.** Does any bowl-maker make a finished bowl for the sake of the bowl itself, and not for the sake of the food it will carry?
Does any calligrapher write artistically for the sake of the writing itself, and not for the sake of it being read?
The external form exists for the sake of the unseen meaning; and that meaning took shape for the sake of yet another unseen reality.
Count these connected results to the third, fourth, or even tenth level, in proportion to your own spiritual insight.
Consider, for example, the moves in chess, my friend <note>original: "O son"</note>: observe the result of each move in the one that follows it.

**2890.** They made this move for the sake of that hidden move, and that for the next, and that again for another specific goal.
In this same way, proceed by perceiving reasons within reasons, one after the other, so that you may finally arrive at victory and "checkmate."
The first step is for the sake of the second, like climbing the rungs of a ladder;
And consider the second to be for the sake of the third, and so on to the end, so that you may arrive, step by step, at the roof.
The desire to eat is for the sake of the life-seed <note>original: "semen"</note>: that seed is for the sake of procreation and the light of life that glows in the eyes of parents.

**2895.** The person of dull sight sees nothing but this immediate step: their intelligence is motionless, like the plants of the earth.
Whether the plant is called to move or not, its foot remains stuck fast in the mud.
If its head moves with the motion of the wind, go, do not be deceived by the swaying of its head.
Its head says, "We obey, O gentle breeze <note>original: "zephyr"</note>!" but its foot says, "We refuse to obey: leave us alone!"
Since the person of dull sight does not know how to move on the <term>Way to God: the spiritual path of internal transformation and journey toward the Divine</term>, they advance like the common crowd, stepping forward on blind trust, like one who cannot see.

**2900.** Consider what comes of acting on blind trust in warfare: it is as useless as the trust of those playing with dice.
But those insights that are not "frozen"—meaning those that are not dense or dull—are nothing if not piercing and capable of rending the veil of appearance.
Such a person sees with their own eye in the present moment that which will come to pass ten years from now.
Similarly, everyone sees the unseen and the future, both good and evil, according to the measure of their spiritual insight.
When the barrier in front and the barrier behind are removed, the eye penetrates and reads the <term>Tablet of the Unseen: also known as the "Preserved Tablet" (al-lawh al-mahfuz), the celestial record of all existence and destiny</term>.

**2905.** When such a person looks back to the origin of existence, the past circumstances and the very beginning of life display themselves to them—
Namely, the debate of the earthly angels with the Divine Majesty regarding the creation of our Father, Adam, as the <term>Vicegerent: God's deputy or steward on earth (Khalifa)</term>.
When they cast their eye forward, they see plainly all that shall come to pass until the <term>Last Congregation: the gathering of all souls on the Day of Resurrection</term>.
Therefore, they see back to the root of the root—the primal origin—and they see forward with clairvoyance to the Day of Decision <note>the final judgment where truth is separated from falsehood</note>.

Every person, according to the level of their spiritual insight, perceives the unseen world in proportion to how well they have polished the mirror of their heart.

❦**2910.** The more one polishes that mirror, the more clearly they see, and the more the hidden forms of the spiritual realm become visible to them.
If you argue that such spiritual purity is a gift of God's grace, remember that the very ability to succeed in polishing the heart is also a result of that divine bounty.
A person’s devotion and prayer are proportional to their spiritual ambition: *A human being has nothing except that which they have striven for.* <note>original: "Laysa lil-insani illa ma sa'a" (Quran 53:39)</note>
God alone is the source of such ambition; no lowly or small-minded person aspires to be a king.

❦**2915.** But when God brings hardship upon an unfortunate soul, that person ungratefully flees away;

❦**2920.** Trials and the fear for one’s life act as a <term>touchstone</term> <note>A stone used to test the purity of gold; here, a metaphor for how character is tested by adversity.</note>: through them, the brave are distinguished from the cowards.

### ***How God revealed a message to Moses (peace be upon him) saying, "O Moses, I, the Exalted Creator, love you."***

God spoke to the heart of Moses through inspiration, saying, “O chosen one, I love you.”
Moses replied, “O Bountiful One, tell me what quality in me causes this, so that I may increase it.”
God said, “You are like a child in the presence of its mother: even when she punishes the child, it still reaches out for her.
The child does not even realize there is anyone else in the world except her; she is the source of both the child's sorrow and its intoxicating joy.

❦**2925.** If the mother gives the child a slap, it still runs back to her and clings to her.
It seeks help from no one but her; she is its entire world, both the perceived 'bad' and the 'good.'
Likewise, your heart, whether in good times or bad, never turns away from Me toward anyone else.
In your eyes, everything other than Me is as insignificant as stones or dirt, whether they be children, youths, or the elderly.”
Just as we say *You alone we worship* <note>original: "Iyyaka na'budu" (Quran 1:5)</note> in our longing prayers, so too in times of trouble *we seek help from none but You.* <note>original: "Iyyaka nasta'in" (Quran 1:5)</note>

❦**2930.** The phrase *You alone we worship* is used to show "appropriation" <note>In grammar, this refers to making something exclusive; here, it means directing all devotion exclusively to God.</note>—and the purpose of this exclusivity is to eliminate hypocrisy.
*From You alone we ask for help* is also for this purpose of appropriation; the person reciting these words restricts their plea for assistance to God alone.
It means: “We perform our acts of worship for You alone; we place our hope for help in You alone.”
