### ***The story of the offender; and how, when the king accepted his intercession, the boon-companion resented the action of the intercessor and asked, "Why did you intercede?"***

A king grew furious with a <term>boon-companion</term> <note>A close friend and confidant of a monarch who shared in his private leisure and conversation.</note> and was ready to reduce him to smoke and dust. The king drew his sword from its scabbard to inflict the punishment for that act of disobedience.

2935. No one had the courage to utter a word, nor did any intercessor venture to step forward,
Except for one courtier named ‘Imádu ’l-Mulk, who possessed the special privilege of <term>intercession</term> <note>The act of pleading on behalf of another; in this context, it reflects the spiritual station of the saints who plead for sinners.</note>, much like <term>Mustafá</term> <note>A title for the Prophet Muhammad, meaning "The Chosen One," known for his role as an intercessor for his community.</note>.
He rushed forward and immediately prostrated himself; the king at once set aside the sword of vengeance,
And said, “Even if he were the Devil himself, I forgive him; and if he has committed a satanic deed, I shall cover it up.
Because you have intervened, I am satisfied, even if the culprit has caused a hundred acts of harm.

2940. I can set aside a hundred thousand instances of anger, seeing that you possess such excellence and worth;
In no way can I refuse your supplication, for your prayer is, in truth, my own prayer.
Even if he had thrown the heavens and the earth into chaos, this man would not have escaped my vengeance;
And if every atom in the world had pleaded for his release, he would not have saved his head from the sword at this moment.
I am not placing you under any obligation by doing this, O noble one; rather, I do it to demonstrate the high honour in which I hold you, O companion.

2945. It was not truly you who made this intercession; rather, I made it through you, O one whose qualities are dissolved into my own.
In this matter, you are the instrument used to do the work, not the primary actor, for you are carried by me and are not the one carrying yourself.
You have become the instrument of my action, according to the verse: *You did not throw when you threw* <note>original: "wa ma ramayta idh ramayta" (Quran 8:17). This verse suggests that God is the true actor behind the Prophet's actions.</note>; like foam, you have surrendered yourself to the wave.
You have become 'not'; now take up your dwelling place beside 'except' <note>A reference to the first half of the Islamic testimony of faith: "There is no god (negation/not) except God (affirmation/except)." To be "not" is to lose one's ego in the Divine.</note>. This is the wonder: that you are both a prisoner and a prince.
You did not give what you gave; the King gave it. He alone exists. God knows the right course best.”

2950. Yet the companion who had been saved from the stroke of calamity grew offended with this intercessor and withdrew his loyalty.
He severed all ties of friendship with that sincere man and turned his face to the wall so that he would not have to offer the <term>salaam</term> <note>The traditional greeting of peace.</note>.
He became completely estranged from his savior; the people, in their astonishment, began to gossip,
Saying, “Unless he is mad, how could he break off relations with the very person who redeemed his life?
That man saved him from being beheaded; he should have become the very dust beneath the intercessor's shoe.

2955. He has done the opposite and chosen to renounce his friend; he has taken to harboring enmity against such a beloved protector.”
Then a certain <term>mentor</term> <note>A spiritual guide or wise advisor.</note> reproached him, saying, “Why are you acting so unjustly toward a loyal friend?
That chosen beloved redeemed your life and saved you from execution in that moment.”

For they took on the veil of letters and breath only so that their essential reality might gradually be revealed to the physical world.
Although from one perspective speech is a revealer of truth, from ten other perspectives, it acts as a curtain and a concealer.

### ***How Abraham answered Gabriel—peace be upon them both—when asked, "Do you have any need?"—"As for help from you, no!"***

“I am the <term>Khalíl</term> <note>The "Friend of God," a title for the Prophet Abraham.</note> of the present time, and he is the Gabriel: I do not want him as a guide to rescue me from this calamity.”

❧ **2975.** He did not learn this sense of respect from the noble Gabriel, who asked the "Friend of God" (Abraham) what his wish was,
Saying, ‘Do you have a wish? Tell me, so that I may help you obtain it; otherwise, I will depart quickly.’
Abraham said, ‘No; get out of the way! After one has achieved direct vision of the Beloved, the intermediary is only an inconvenience.’
For the sake of this worldly life, a messenger is a necessary link for the believers, acting as the bridge between them and God.
If every heart were capable of hearing the hidden divine revelation directly, why would there be any need for words and sounds to make it known?

❧ **2980.** Though the intercessor is "headless"—meaning he has lost his own ego in God—my own situation is even more delicate than that.
His act is the act of the King, yet to my weak perception, the "good" he did by intervening feels like an "evil" because it broke my direct contact.”

<summary>Rumi explores the paradox of spiritual intimacy, where the seeker prefers the "wrath" of God over the "mercy" of an intermediary. Using the example of Abraham refusing Gabriel's help in the fire, he argues that true union requires the removal of all third parties, including language and prophets.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discourse on the nature of spiritual intimacy. What appears as the purest grace to the common people is felt as divine wrath by the noble favorites of God.
The common folk must endure much tribulation and pain before they can perceive this subtle difference;

And even that superiority is sought for the sake of some other desire: for outward forms provide no true relish without their <term>essential meanings</term> <note>original: *ma'na*. In Sufi thought, the inner reality or spirit that gives life to the external 'form' (*surat*).</note>.
You ask, "Why are you doing this?" because the forms are merely the oil, while the essential meaning is the light.

**2995.** Otherwise, why would we even ask "why"—if the form existed only for the sake of the form itself?
The word "why" is a question regarding the purpose or utility of a thing; it is only meaningful to ask "why" when looking for a cause.
Why, O trustworthy friend, would you desire to know the reason, if the utility of a form was only the form itself?
Therefore, it is not consistent with wisdom to suggest that the forms of the heavens and the people of the earth were created for no further purpose.
If there is no Wise Creator, what is the source of this orderly arrangement of the <term>cosmos</term>? And if there is a Wise Creator, how could His actions be devoid of meaning?

**3000.** No one creates paintings or applies colors in a bath-house except for some purpose, whether that purpose be right or wrong.

### **How Moses (Peace be upon him) petitioned the Lord, saying, “You created creatures only to destroy them,” and how the answer came.**

->Moses said, "O <term>Lord of the Reckoning</term> <note>original: *Rabb al-Hisab*. God as the final judge who settles all accounts.</note>, You created this form; why then do You destroy it again?<-
->You have made these forms, both male and female, which bring such joy to the spirit; and then You ruin them—why?"<-
->God replied, "I know that your question does not come from disbelief, heedlessness, or idle fancy;<-
->Otherwise, I would have corrected and chastised you; I would have afflicted you for such a question."<-

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the dialogue between God and Moses (Kalim) regarding the mysteries of divine action. # The Mystery of the Harvest: Why God Creates and Destroys

**3005.** But I know that you wish to discover the wisdom and hidden meaning within My actions and the span of time,
So that you may explain it to the common people and, by doing so, help every "raw" and ignorant person to become "cooked" and mature.
You have asked this question on purpose to reveal this matter to the masses, even though you already understand it yourself;
For asking the right question is half of knowledge, and this ability to ask is not a gift given to every outsider.
Both the question and the answer grow from the soil of knowledge, just as the rose and the thorn grow from earth and water.

**3010.** Both destruction and salvation arise from knowledge, just as bitter and sweet fruits come from moisture.
Hatred and love grow from deep acquaintance, and from wholesome food come both sickness and bodily strength.
The <term>Kalim</term> <note>original: *Kalím*. A title for Moses meaning "The one who spoke with God."</note> acted like an ignorant seeker so that he might guide the truly ignorant toward this mystery.
Let us also pretend to be ignorant and seek the answer as if we were strangers looking for information.
In the same way, <term>donkey-sellers</term> <note>Referring to a marketplace tactic where sellers pretend to be rivals to draw in a buyer and finalize a contract of sale.</note> act like rivals to one another just to open the way for a deal.

**3015.** Then God spoke to him, saying, "O you who possess the finest understanding, since you have asked, come and hear the answer.
O Moses, sow some seeds in the earth, so that you may discover the justice in this matter for yourself."
When Moses had sown the seeds and the wheat had grown tall, with its ears of grain showing beauty and perfect balance,
He took up his sickle and began to harvest the crop. Then, a voice from the <term>Unseen</term> <note>original: *Ghayb*. The hidden or spiritual realm that exists beyond human sensory perception.</note> reached his ear,
Crying out, "Why do you sow and tend to this grain, only to cut it down just as it has reached perfection?"

**3020.** He replied, "O Lord, I strike it down and level it because here we have both the grain and the straw.
The grain is not fit to be kept in the straw-barn, and the straw is out of place in the corn-barn.
It is not wise to mix these two; wisdom demands that they be separated during the <term>winnowing</term> <note>The process of blowing air through grain to separate the light chaff/straw from the heavy, valuable seed.</note> process."
God said, "From whom did you learn this knowledge, so that you could build a <term>threshing-floor</term> based on it?"
He replied, "You, O God, gave me this discernment." God said, "Then how could I, the Creator, lack that same discernment?"

**3025.** Among created beings, there are pure spirits, and there are also spirits that are dark and clouded.
These shells are not all of the same quality; one contains a pearl, while another holds only a worthless bead.
It is necessary to make the difference between good and evil visible, just as it is necessary to distinguish the wheat from the straw.
The creation of the world's creatures serves the purpose of manifestation, so that the treasure of Divine providence does not remain hidden.
God said, "I was a <term>Hidden Treasure</term> <note>original: *Kanzan Makhfiyyan*. A reference to a famous *Hadith Qudsi* (divine saying) where God explains: "I was a hidden treasure and I loved to be known, so I created the world that I might be known."</note>." Listen! Do not let your spiritual essence be lost; let it be revealed!

<summary>Through the metaphor of Moses harvesting wheat, this passage explains that God creates and ends life to separate pure souls from "muddy" ones, revealing the "hidden treasure" of divine reality. It emphasizes that creation exists to manifest the inherent differences between the pearl-like spirit and the worthless shell.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the metaphorical explanation of why the Divine creates and destroys physical forms. ## ## Explaining how the animal spirit, discursive reason, imagination, and fancy are like buttermilk, while the everlasting spirit is hidden within them like butter.

❦ **3030.** Your true essence is hidden within what is temporary and false, just as the taste of butter is hidden within the taste of buttermilk.
Your "falsehood" is this perishable body; your "truth" is that noble, divine spirit.
For many years, this buttermilk—the body—is visible and obvious, while the butter—the spirit—seems lost and nonexistent within it,
Until God sends a messenger, a chosen servant, to act as the one who shakes the buttermilk in the churn.
He shakes it with specialized method and skill, so that I may finally realize that my true "I" was hidden there all along.

❦ **3035.** Or perhaps the words of a chosen servant, who shares in the spirit of the Prophet, enter the ear of someone seeking divine inspiration.
The ear of a true believer holds onto our inspiration; such an ear is deeply connected to the "caller" <note>Referring to the perfect saint or spiritual guide who calls the soul back to God.</note>.
Consider how an infant’s ear is filled with its mother’s words, and only then does the child begin to speak clearly;
But if the infant does not have a functioning ear, it cannot hear its mother’s voice and thus remains mute.
Anyone born deaf has always been unable to speak; only the one who first heard speech from a mother becomes a speaker themselves.

❦ **3040.** Understand that a deaf ear and a mute tongue are the results of a specific limitation, for the ear is not yet capable of receiving words or being taught.
The only one who possesses speech without ever being taught is God, whose attributes are entirely free from any such weaknesses.
Another exception is <term>Adam</term> <note>In Islamic tradition, Adam was taught the "names of all things" directly by God without human mediation.</note>, whom God instructed directly without the need for a mother, a nurse, or any material necessities.
Or the <term>Messiah</term> <note>Jesus (Isa), who in the Quranic tradition spoke while still in the cradle to defend his mother's honor.</note> who, having been taught by the Loving God, came into the world speaking at the very moment of his birth,
This was done to clear away any suspicion regarding his birth and to prove that he was not born of sin or wickedness.

❦ **3045.** A great "shaking" or spiritual effort was required so that the buttermilk might give up the butter from its innermost heart.
The butter inside the buttermilk seems as if it does not exist, while the buttermilk itself holds its banner high and appears manifest.
That which seems to you to be the "real" reality is actually just the skin or husk, while that which seems to have vanished is, in truth, the root.
The buttermilk has not yet turned into butter and is aging; keep it safely and do not waste it until you have extracted the butter from within.
Listen: turn it knowingly from side to side—practice your spiritual disciplines—so that it may reveal what it has kept hidden.

❦ **3050.** For this perishable body is actually proof of the everlasting spirit: just as the rambling talk of a drunkard is proof of the existence of the <term>Cupbearer</term> <note>In Sufi poetry, the Cupbearer (Saqi) represents God or the spiritual guide who provides the "wine" of divine love.</note>.

### ### Another parable on the same subject.

The way a lion embroidered on a banner leaps and dances is a sign of the hidden winds blowing against it.
If the movement of those winds did not exist, how could a "dead" lion made of fabric leap into the air?

<summary>Rumi uses the metaphor of churning buttermilk to explain that the eternal spirit is hidden within the physical body and requires the intervention of a Prophet or spiritual guide to be revealed. He emphasizes that spiritual "hearing" is the prerequisite for spiritual "speaking" and growth.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the metaphor of butter hidden in buttermilk, Rumi now explains how our thoughts and dreams reveal the hidden movements of the spirit. He contrasts worldly thoughts with spiritual inspirations, using the metaphor of an elephant dreaming of its distant homeland to describe the soul's yearning for the Divine.</meta>

By those movements, you can tell whether the wind is blowing from the east or the west; the movement of the "lion" <note>Referring to the lion on a banner mentioned in the previous verse, which moves only because the wind (the spirit) blows through it.</note> is the visible explanation of that hidden force.
This physical body is like that lion on a banner: it is our inner thought that keeps it in constant motion.

❀ **3055.** The thought that arrives from the "east" <note>The "East" symbolizes the direction of the rising sun and spiritual enlightenment.</note> is like a refreshing breeze, while the thought from the "west" is like a wind carrying sickness.
The source of this spiritual wind is different from the physical world; its "east" and "west" belong to the Beyond.
The physical moon is lifeless, and the place where it rises is inanimate; but the "east" of the heart is the very soul of the soul of the Soul.
The Sun that lights up our inner being is the true reality; the sun of our sky is merely its outer shell and a dim reflection.
When the body dies and its vital flame is gone, it can no longer perceive the day or the night;

❀ **3060.** But even when that physical flame is gone, the spiritual Sun remains perfect; it sustains itself eternally, independent of day and night.
It is like the eye which, even without the light of the moon or sun, can see both moon and sun in a dream.
Since our sleep is the "brother of death" <note>A traditional saying suggesting that sleep is a temporary departure of the soul, much like death is a permanent one.</note>, understand the difference between these two brothers.
If someone tells you that the spiritual world is merely a derivative of this physical one, do not believe them, O seeker, unless you have certain, direct knowledge.
In your sleep, your spirit witnesses realities that you could not see in twenty years of being awake.

❀ **3065.** And after waking, you spend lifetimes running to wise spiritual guides to ask for the meaning of those visions,
Saying, "Tell me, what is the interpretation of that dream?" To call such a profound mystery a mere "branch" of waking life is a great error.
While this may be the sleep of ordinary people, the sleep of the God-conscious is the very root of their spiritual rank and chosen state.
A spirit must be like a great elephant so that, when it falls into a deep sleep, it may dream of its true home in India <note>original: "Hindustán". In Persian poetry, India is often a metaphor for the soul’s original, lush, and beautiful homeland.</note>.
A common donkey never dreams of India; a donkey has never traveled from that distant homeland to a foreign country.

❀ **3070.** One needs a spirit as robust and majestic as an elephant to be able to travel back to that spiritual India in their sleep.
Because of its deep longing, the elephant remembers its home; then, during the night, that memory takes shape in its dreams.
The command to *"Remember God"* <note>original: "Allah". Refers to the practice of Dhikr, or rhythmic remembrance of the Divine.</note> is not a task that a person of low character can truly grasp; the command to *"Return"* <note>Refers to the Quranic verse 89:28, "Return to your Lord," an invitation for the soul to come back to its source.</note> is not a chain that can hold the feet of those who have lost their way.
Even so, do not despair—strive to be like the elephant; and if you are not yet an elephant, seek the path of transformation.
Look to the alchemists of Heaven; listen at every moment for the sounds coming from those who can turn leaden souls into spiritual gold.

❀ **3075.** They are the architects working in the celestial atmosphere; they are working for your sake and mine.
If you cannot see these people of pure, fragrant character, at least notice the "touch" they lay upon you, O you who are spiritually blind.
At every moment, a divine touch is laid upon your understanding; look at the new thoughts, like plants, constantly springing up from the soil of your mind!
Of this kind was Abraham, son of Adham <note>Ibráhím ibn Adham, a famous king of Balkh who renounced his throne to become a wandering mystic after a spiritual awakening.</note>, who in his sleep beheld the unfolding of the spiritual India without any veil.

<summary>Rumi explains that thoughts are like winds from a spiritual "East" or "West" that move the body. He uses the famous metaphor of an elephant dreaming of its home in India to illustrate how noble souls long for their divine origin during sleep.</summary>

(Therefore), of necessity, he burst his worldly chains asunder, dashed his kingdom to pieces, and disappeared.

❧ **3080.** The sign of beholding India <note>original: "Hindustán". In Persian poetry, India represents the spiritual homeland or the world of the soul from which we are exiled.</note> is that he who beholds it starts up from sleep and becomes "mad" with longing.

### *Story of the prince to whom the true kingdom revealed itself, so that the reality of the verse **"on the Day when a man shall flee from his brother and his mother and his father"** <note>A reference to Quran 80:34-35, describing the Day of Judgment when worldly ties vanish.</note> became his direct experience; and he saw that the kingdom of this world—this "earth-heap" of the childish—is like the game called **"castle-taking,"** in which the child who wins climbs the mound and says boastfully, **"The castle belongs to me,"** while the other children envy him; for playing with earth is the pastime of boys. When the prince was delivered from the bondage of "colors" <note>Diversity, superficiality, and worldly distinctions.</note>, he said, **"I see that these colored pieces of earth (earthly luxuries) are just the same vile earth; I do not call them gold and satin and brocade: I have been delivered from this multicolored brocade (aksún) and have gone toward that which is simple and unified (yaksún)."** <note>Rumi uses a wordplay here: "aksún" refers to expensive black or colored fabric, while "yaksún" refers to being of one color or essence, representing spiritual unity.</note> As God has said, **"And We bestowed wisdom upon him whilst he was yet a boy"**; it does not require many years to receive God’s guidance: no one speaks of "capacity" when it comes to the Divine Power of **"Be, and it is."** <note>The creative command "Kun fa-yakun," which brings all things into existence instantly.</note>*

❧ **3085.** A certain king had a young son, adorned with excellence both inside and out.
He dreamed that suddenly that son died; the pure pleasure of the world turned to bitter dregs for the king.
His "water-skin" <note>The eye, compared here to a leather bag for carrying water.</note> was dried up by the heat of his grief; because of the intensity of his inner fire, no tears remained.
The king became so full of "smoke" and grief that his sighs could find no way to escape.
He was on the verge of death; his body became lifeless. But because his life was not yet finished, the king awoke.

❧ **3090.** Upon waking, a joy came to him such as he had never experienced in all his life;
Indeed, he was now about to perish from joy! This spirit and body are heavily burdened by the collar of mortality.
This lamp dies—is extinguished—by the breath of sorrow, and it also dies from the breath of joy. Look, here is a strange irony!
Man lives between these two "deaths": this being who resembles one bound in a collar is truly a cause for laughter.
The king said to himself, "By the Lord's mysterious decree, such a sorrow was actually the cause of this joy."

❧ **3095.** Oh, how wonderful that the same thing from one perspective is death, and from another is a quickening of life and a gift!
The same thing is destructive in one circumstance, yet it is preservative in another.
Physical joy is "perfection" relative to this present world, but it is a "defect" and a failure relative to the Day of the End.
The dream-interpreter <term>oneiromancer: a specialist who interprets the spiritual meaning of dreams</term> also declares that laughter in a dream is a sign of future weeping, regrets, and griefs.

<summary>Rumi explores the paradox of worldly experience through the story of a king who dreams of his son's death, discovering that earthly sorrow can lead to spiritual awakening. In order that on the day this physical lamp suddenly dies, he may have the candle of the spirit before his eyes.
The king did not understand this spiritual truth; therefore, in his lack of awareness, he tried to light one perishable candle from another.

### ***How the king brought his son a bride for fear of his race coming to an end.***

(The king said to himself), "It is necessary, then, to find a bride for him, so that children may come from this marriage,
(So that) if this falcon <note>A common Sufi metaphor for the noble soul or a high-born person.</note> returns to the state of mortality, his young may become a falcon in his place,

**3115.** (And that) if the physical form of this falcon leaves this world, his inner essence may live on in his son."
Because of this, that renowned spiritual king, the Chosen One <note>original: "Mustafá," a title for the Prophet Mohammed.</note>, said: "The son is the very marrow of his father."
For this reason, all people—moved by a deep, heartfelt love—teach their children their own trades,
So that these inner meanings and skills may remain in the world even when their own bodies are hidden in the grave.
God, in His wisdom, has given parents an intense desire to guide every child who is capable of learning.

**3120.** "I too, to ensure the survival of my lineage, will seek a wife of good character for my son.
I will seek a girl who is the daughter of a righteous man, not the daughter of some harsh and powerful king."

This righteous man is himself a king; he is truly free, for he is not the prisoner of lust and gluttony.

### ***How the king chose the daughter of a poor ascetic for his son and how the ladies of the harem raised objections and disdained the proposed alliance with the dervish.***

The prince's mother, lacking deep spiritual understanding, said, “According to both reason and tradition, equality of social rank is required for marriage.

**3130.** Out of stinginess, miserliness, and some misguided shrewdness, you wish to ally our son with a beggar!” 
The king replied, “It is a mistake to call a righteous man a beggar, for through the grace of God, he is spiritually wealthy. 
He takes refuge in contentment because of his piety—not because of meanness or laziness like a common beggar. 
The lack of money that arises from contentment and piety is entirely distinct from the poverty and destitution of the base. 
If a common beggar finds a single small coin, he bows his head in homage; but this righteous man, in his lofty spiritual aspiration, would recoil even from a treasure of gold.

**3135.** The king who, out of greed, reaches for everything unlawful—it is *him* the noble-minded man calls a beggar.” 
The prince's mother said, “Where are this man's cities and castles to provide a wedding outfit? Where are his means to scatter gems and gold at the ceremony?” 
The king replied, “Be gone! Whosoever chooses to care for religion, God relieves them of all other worldly cares.” 
The king prevailed and married his son to a maiden of beautiful nature, belonging to the family of a righteous <term>dervish</term>. <note>A dervish is a member of a Muslim religious order, often associated with poverty and austerity.</note>
Truly, she had no rival in loveliness; her face was brighter than the sun at dawn.

**3140.** Such was the maiden's beauty; and her character was so excellent that her virtues cannot be contained in any description. 
Make religion your primary goal, and as a result, beauty, riches, power, and good fortune will follow. 
Know that the next world, in terms of true ownership, is like a great caravan of camels: the present world is merely a byproduct, like the camels' hair and dung. 
If you only seek the hair, you will never own the camel; but if the camel is yours, what value is the hair? <note>This metaphor suggests that focusing on spiritual reality brings the material world as an effortless byproduct, whereas focusing on the material world results in losing both.</note>
When the marriage alliance with the family of those peaceful, righteous folk was successfully arranged by the king,

**3145.** By divine destiny, a decrepit old witch—who had fallen in love with the handsome and generous prince—

**3155.** For whatever cure the father tried to apply, the son’s infatuation with the old woman only seemed to grow.

### ***How the king's prayer for the deliverance of his son from the witch of Kabul was granted.***

**3160.** This master-magician had heard the news from afar: that the boy was being held captive by an old woman,
A crone whose skill in witchcraft was unrivaled—she stood alone in her dark art.
But remember, young man: there is always a hand above another hand in skill and strength, all the way up to the Essence of God.
The final end of all power is the Hand of God, just as the final destination of every stream is undoubtedly the sea.
From the sea the clouds are born, and in the sea, the rushing torrent finally finds its peace.

**3165.** The king said to him, “This boy has lost his mind.” The magician replied, “See, I have come as a powerful remedy.
None of these local sorcerers can match that old woman except for me, the wise one, who has arrived from the distant shore.
Look! By the command of the Creator, I shall destroy her magic just as the staff in the <term>Hand of Moses</term> swallowed the illusions of the Egyptians. <note>A reference to the Quranic and Biblical story of Moses defeating Pharaoh’s magicians.</note>
My knowledge comes from the divine region, not from the cheap tricks of common sorcery.
I have come to break her spell so the prince’s face may regain its color.

**3170.** Go to the graveyard during the <term>Sahar</term>; beside the wall, you will find a white-washed tomb. <note>original: "Sahar"; the time of the pre-dawn meal, considered a sacred hour for spiritual work.</note>
Dig into that spot in the direction of the <term>Qibla</term>, so that you may witness the power and the handiwork of God.” <note>original: "Qibla"; the direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims pray.</note>

This story is very long, and you, dear reader, may be weary; I will give you only the best of it, setting aside what is unnecessary.
The physician untied those heavy knots of sorcery, providing the king's son a path of escape from his long suffering.
The boy finally returned to his senses and, through a hundred trials, went running back toward his father’s throne.

☞ **3175.** He fell in prostration, touching his chin to the earth; the boy held a sword and a shroud in his arms. <note>Offering a sword and a shroud was a traditional gesture of total submission, signaling that the subject was ready to be executed or forgiven at the king's mercy.</note>
The king ordered the city to be decorated, and the citizens—along with the bride who had been left in despair—rejoiced.

He was so overwhelmed by her beauty that he fell unconscious; for three days, his spirit seemed to leave his body.
For three days and nights he remained in this swoon, leaving the people deeply worried by his state.
Only through the use of rose-water and other medicines did he return to himself; slowly, he regained his ability to distinguish between good and evil.

☞ **3185.** After a year had passed, the king said to him jokingly in conversation: "My son, do you ever think of that old friend of yours?
Do you remember that bedfellow and that bed? Do not be so unfaithful and cold to your old love!"
"Enough!" the prince replied. "I have found the true home of joy; I have been delivered from the dark pit of delusion."
And so it is: when a true believer finds the way toward the Light of God, they forever turn their face away from the darkness of this world.

### ***An explanation that the Prince represents the Human Soul, the deputy of God; his Father represents Adam, the Chosen One, to whom the angels bowed; the Hag of Kabul represents the Material World which uses its charms to separate Man from his Father; and the Physician represents the Prophets and Saints who bring the healing word of God.***

Know, my brother, that you are that prince, born into this aging world.

☞ **3190.** The witch of Kabul is this Material World, which holds men captive through the allure of colors and perfumes.
Since she has cast you into this muddy stream, you must constantly recite the prayer: *I seek refuge in the Lord.* <note>original: "Qul a'udhu"; a reference to the opening of the 113th and 114th chapters of the Quran, used as protection against evil and sorcery.</note>
To be delivered from this witchcraft and distress, beg the <term>Lord of the Daybreak</term> <note>original: "Rabb al-Falaq"; the title of the 113th Sura, which specifically asks for protection from "the evil of those who blow on knots" (sorcerers).</note> for safety.
The Prophet called this world of yours an enchantress, because her spells have trapped all of humanity in a pit.
Be on your guard! This foul hag has potent spells; her "hot breath" has made even kings her prisoners.

<meta>Continuity: After the prince’s recovery and the death of the sorceress, the narrative shifts from the literal story to a spiritual lesson. Rumi now interprets the "sorceress" as a metaphor for the material world, which entangles the soul in "knots" of desire and distraction, just as the witch of Kabul entangled the prince.</meta>

**3195.** She is **the witches who blow on knots** <note>original: *al-naffathati fi’l-‘uqad*. A reference to Surah Al-Falaq (113:4) in the Quran, which seeks refuge from those who practice secret or manipulative arts.</note> within your breast: she is the means of maintaining the knots of sorcery.
The sorceress, who is the World, is a mightily cunning woman: it is not in the power of the ordinary people to undo her sorcery;
And if human understandings could loose her knot, why would God have sent the prophets?
Hark, seek one whose breath is pure, a looser of knots, one who knows the mystery of **God does whatever He wills**. <note>original: *Yaf‘alu Allahu ma yasha’*. A Quranic phrase highlighting that Divine power transcends all natural causes and human logic.</note>
She (the World) has imprisoned you, like a fish, in her net: the prince remained there for one year, but you have remained for sixty.

**3200.** From being enmeshed in her net, you have been in tribulation for sixty years: you are neither happy, nor do you walk in the way of the **Sunna**. <term>Sunna</term> <note>The "way" or traditional practice of the Prophet, representing a path of spiritual balance and alignment with Divine law.</note>
You are a miserable, unrighteous man: neither is your worldly life happy, nor are you delivered from guilt and sins.
The "breathing" of the World has made these knots tight; seek, then, the breathing of the unique Creator,
In order that the promise, **“I breathed of My spirit into him,”** <note>original: *Wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi*. Referring to the creation of Adam (Quran 15:29), suggesting that only the Divine spirit within can overcome worldly entanglement.</note> may deliver you from this sorcery and say to you, “Come higher!”
The breath of sorcery is not destroyed except by the breath of God: the former is the breath of Divine wrath, while the latter is the breath of Divine love.

**3205.** His mercy is prior to His wrath: if you desire priority in spiritual rank, go, seek that attribute which is prior, <note>A reference to the Hadith Qudsi: "My mercy preceded My wrath."</note>
That you may attain unto the souls that are **wedded**; <note>A reference to Quran 81:7, interpreted here as the union of the soul with its spiritual essence or the company of the righteous.</note> for look, O ensorcelled prince, this is your way of escape.
As long as the "old woman" (the world) exists in your heart, there can be no undoing of the knots, while you are in the net and in the arms of that paramour full of false charms.
Has not the Prophet, the Lamp of the peoples, called this world and the next "the two fellow-wives"? <note>A traditional metaphor depicting the physical world and the spiritual hereafter as rival spouses who are never both satisfied at once.</note>
Therefore, union with this world is separation from that world: the health of this body is often the sickness of the spirit.

**3210.** Hard is the separation from this temporary home: know, then, that the separation from that permanent home is harder.
Since it is hard for you to be separated from the "form" (the physical world), how hard must it be to be parted from its Maker!
O you who do not have the patience to do without the vile world, how, my friend, do you have the patience to do without God?
Since you do not have the patience to do without this murky "black water," how do you have the patience to do without God's pure fountain?
Since you are restless without this worldly drink, how can you remain patiently apart from **the righteous and from what they shall drink**? <note>original: *Inna al-abrar yashrabun*. Reference to Quran 76:5, describing the pure, spiritual wine given to the virtuous in Paradise.</note>

**3215.** If for one moment you could behold the beauty of the Loving One and cast your soul and existence into the fire of His love,
After that, you would regard this worldly drink as a **carcass**, <note>original: *murdar*. A common Sufi term for the material world, emphasizing its lack of true life or value compared to the Divine.</note> once you behold the glory and splendor of being near to Him.
Like the prince, you will finally reach your Beloved; then you will draw out from your foot the thorn of the "self."
Strive for selflessness, find your true self as soon as possible—and God knows best the right course.
Take heed, never be wedded to your ego: do not, like a donkey, be always falling into the water and mud.

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the world as a sorceress who entangles the soul, Rumi now transitions to the theme of spiritual perception. ❧**3220.** That stumbling arises from shortsightedness; for like a blind man, he (such a one) does not see the ups and downs.
Make the scent of Joseph's shirt thy stay, because his scent makes the eye clear. <note>In the Quranic and Biblical story, the scent of Joseph’s shirt miraculously restored the sight of his father, Jacob. Here, it symbolizes the spiritual influence of a saint or prophet.</note>
The hidden Form and the Light of that Brow have made the eyes of the prophets far-seeing.
The Light of that Countenance will deliver (thee) from the fire: hark, be not content with borrowed light. <note>Borrowed light refers to intellectual or worldly knowledge that is merely a reflection, rather than the direct "sunlight" of divine revelation.</note>
This (borrowed) light makes the eye to see that which is transient: it makes body and mind and spirit to be scabby (diseased).

❧**3225.** It has the appearance of light, but in reality it is fire: keep thy hands off it, if thou desire the (true) radiance.
The eye and spirit that sees (only) the transient falls on its face continually wherever it goes.
A far-seeing man who lacks knowledge may see far, just as (one has) far sight in dreams.
You are asleep with parched lips on the bank of the river, and (in your dream) are running in search of water towards the mirage.
You see the mirage far away and run (towards it): you become in love with your own sight.

❧**3230.** In the dream you boast to your friends, saying, "I am the one whose heart possesses vision, and (I am) the one that rends the veil.
Lo, I see water yonder: hark, make haste that we may go there"—and 'tis (only) the mirage.
At every step you hurry farther away from the water, whilst you keep running on towards the perilous mirage.
Your very setting-out has become the barrier (which prevents you) from (seeing) this that has come close to you.
Oh, many a one sets out to some place from the spot where the object of his quest is (to be found).

❧**3235.** The (far) sight and boasting of the sleeper is of no avail; it is naught but a phantasy: hold aloof from it.
Thou art sleepy, but anyhow sleep on the Way: for God's sake, for God's sake, sleep on the Way of God, <note>Rumi suggests that even if one is spiritually "asleep" or unaware, it is better to remain within a spiritual discipline or community where help might find you.</note>
That perchance a Traveller (on the Way) may attach himself to thee and tear thee from the phantasies of slumber.
(Even) if the sleeper's thought become (subtle) as a hair, he will not find the way to the Abode by that subtlety.
Whether the sleeper's thought is twofold or threefold, still it is error on error on error.

❧**3240.** The waves are beating upon him without restraint, (whilst) he asleep is running in the long wilderness.
The sleeper dreams of the sore pangs of thirst, (whilst) the water ***is nearer unto him than the neck-vein.*** <note>original: *habl al-warid*. A reference to Quran 50:16: "And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." It emphasizes God’s total immanence.</note>

### ***Story of the ascetic who, notwithstanding his destitution and numerous family, was rejoicing and laughing in a year of drought whilst the people were dying of hunger. They said to him, "What is the occasion for joy? It is an occasion for a hundred mournings." "For me at any rate 'tis not (so)," he replied.***

Even as (for example) that ascetic was laughing in a year of drought, while all (his) folk were weeping.
So they said to him, "What is the occasion for laughter, (when) the drought has uprooted (destroyed) the true believers?
The (Divine) mercy hath closed its eyes to us: the plain is burnt by the fierce sun.

<summary>Rumi compares worldly pursuit to a thirsty man dreaming of a mirage while sleeping next to a river. The text transitions into a story about an ascetic whose internal spiritual connection allows him to remain joyful during a famine that devastates others.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the world as a sorceress and the "borrowed light" that leads to spiritual blindness, Rumi now presents a dialogue between a suffering person and an ascetic. While the common person sees only drought and death, the spiritually awakened ascetic perceives the same world as a lush paradise, illustrating that external reality is a reflection of one’s internal state and relationship with the Divine.</meta>

❧**3245.** The crops, the vineyards, and the vines stand blackened and withered; there is no moisture to be found in the earth, neither on the surface nor deep below.
The people are perishing from this drought and agony, dying by the tens and hundreds like fish gasping far from the water.
You show no pity for the Muslims; <note>The original term is *Moslems*. The text refers to the Islamic concept of the *Ummah*, or the global community of believers.</note> yet the true believers are like kinsmen, forming a single body of flesh and fat.
“The pain of one part of the body is the pain of all its parts, whether in times of peace or during war.” <note>This is a reference to a well-known saying (Hadith) of the Prophet Muhammad: "The believers in their mutual kindness, compassion and sympathy are just like one body..."</note>
The ascetic replied, “In your eyes, this appears as a drought; but to my eyes, this very earth is like Paradise.”

❧**3250.** In every desert and in every direction, I behold ears of grain in such abundance that they reach up to the waist.
I see the wilderness overflowing with stalks of corn, tossed in waves by the east wind, appearing greener than a leek.
I reach out and put my hand upon them to test their reality: how could I ever turn my eyes or my hand away from such a sight?
O base people, you are friends of Pharaoh—symbolizing the carnal body—and because of this, the Nile appears to you as nothing but blood. <note>In the Quranic and Biblical story, the Nile was turned to blood as a plague upon Pharaoh. Rumi uses this to show that the "ego" perceives God's blessings as a curse.</note>
Hasten to become friends with Moses—who represents the intellect—so that the blood may vanish and you may behold the clear river water.

❧**3255.** If you act with injustice toward your father, that father will appear to your eyes as a biting dog.
The father is not truly a dog; it is simply the effect of your own injustice that makes such a source of mercy look like a beast to your sight.
Because the brothers of Joseph harbored envy and anger, they looked upon Joseph and saw only a wolf. <note>Referring to the story of Joseph, whose brothers told their father a wolf had eaten him, reflecting their own predatory intent.</note>
When you make peace with your father, your anger vanishes; that perceived ferocity departs, and your father immediately becomes your friend again.

### ***Explaining that the whole world is the form of Universal Reason, and that when by trespassing you act unjustly towards Universal Reason, in most cases the aspect of the world increases your vexation, just as when you show ill-feeling to your father the aspect of your father increases your vexation and you cannot bear to look on his face, though before that he will have been the light of your eye and the comfort of your soul.*** <note>Universal Reason (or *'Aql-i Kull*) is a philosophical and mystical concept representing the first manifestation of God's wisdom that sustains the universe.</note>

The entire world is the outward form of Universal Reason, which is the "father" of anyone who follows the Divine Word.

❧**3260.** When anyone shows excessive ingratitude toward Universal Reason, the form of the universe appears to him as a threatening dog.
Make peace with this Father and abandon your disobedience, so that the world—made of mere water and clay—may appear to you as a carpet of gold.
Then the Resurrection will become your present reality and immediate experience; heaven and earth will be transformed and transfigured before your eyes. <note>In this context, Resurrection refers not just to the end of the world, but to a spiritual awakening where the soul "wakes up" to divine truth while still in this life.</note>
Since I am forever at peace with this Father, this world appears as Paradise in my sight.
At every moment, a new form and a new beauty appear, so that the weariness of the soul dies away through the sight of these new visions.

❧**3265.** I see the world as full of bounty, with waters constantly gushing from hidden springs.
The sound of those waters reaches my ears; my inner consciousness and intelligence are becoming intoxicated by the melody.
I see the boughs of the trees dancing like people in a state of spiritual ecstasy, and the leaves clapping their hands like musicians.

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the world as a sorceress and the "borrowed light" that leads to spiritual blindness, Rumi continues the theme of perception. He previously described how an ascetic sees a lush paradise where others see a drought; now, he uses the story of the Prophet Ezra to illustrate the difference between "opinion"—which hears a promise of the future—and "reason," which experiences the divine presence in the here and now.</meta>

The light of the mirror flashes through its felt cover; imagine how it would be if the mirror itself were revealed! 
I am not telling even one mystery out of thousands, because every ear is currently filled with doubt.

⚓︎**3270.** To <term>Opinion (Zann)<note>In Sufi psychology, *Zann* refers to speculative knowledge or assumption—something heard but not yet personally experienced.</note></term>, this saying of mine is only a joyful promise of what is to come. But <term>Reason (Aql)<note>Here, *Aql* refers to the "Universal Intellect" or spiritual reason that perceives Truth directly.</note></term> says, "Why call it a promise? This is my actual, present experience; it is cash in hand."

### ***The story of the sons of Ezra (Uzayr), peace be upon him, who were asking for news of their father from a man who was actually their father. He replied, "Yes, I have seen him; he is coming." Some recognized him and lost consciousness in ecstasy, while others did not recognize him and said, "He has only given us news; why this loss of consciousness?"***

This is like the story of the sons of Ezra who went out into the street, asking for news of their father. 
The sons had grown old, while their father had been miraculously restored to youth. Suddenly, their father met them on the road. 
They questioned him, saying, "O traveler, do you happen to have news of our father, Ezra? 
For someone told us that today that man of great authority would arrive from abroad, just as we had given up hope of ever seeing him."

⚓︎**3275.** "Yes," Ezra replied, "he will arrive right after me." One son rejoiced at hearing these good tidings, 
Crying out, "Joy to you, O bringer of good news!" But the other son recognized his father and fell to the ground, unconscious with joy, 
Thinking, "What is the point of 'good news,' you scatterbrain, when we have already fallen into the very heart of the sugar mine?" 
To Opinion, it is merely a happy report; but in the eyes of Reason, it is a present reality, because the eye of Opinion is veiled by the fact that it is still searching for what is 'missing.' 
This truth is painful to the deniers and glad news to the faithful, but in the eye of the Seer, it is an immediate, lived experience.

⚓︎**3280.** Because the lover is intoxicated by this immediate presence, he has risen above the categories of "infidelity" and "faith." 
Indeed, both infidelity and faith serve as his doorkeepers; he is the inner essence, while religion and irreligion are merely his two outer skins. 
Infidelity is like a dry peel that has turned away from the fruit; faith is the inner skin that has stayed attached and gained a delicious flavor. 
The place for dry peels is the fire, but the skin attached to the spiritual essence is sweet. 
The essence itself is beyond the grade of "sweetness"—it is higher than sweetness because it is the very source of all delight.

⚓︎**3285.** This discussion has no end. Let us turn back, so that my Moses may part the sea. 
The previous part of this discourse was spoken to suit the understanding of the common people; the rest of it remains hidden. 
The gold of your intelligence is in fragments: how can I strike a royal stamp upon mere clippings? 
Your intellect is scattered over a hundred "important" affairs, over thousands of desires, and matters both great and small. 
You must unite these scattered parts through the power of Love, so that you may become as sweet and prosperous as the cities of Samarcand and Damascus.

<summary>Rumi uses the Quranic figure of Ezra (Uzayr) to distinguish between those who believe in God as a distant promise (Opinion) and those who experience the Divine as a present reality (Reason). He argues that the true mystic transcends the outward forms of religion, reaching the "kernel" or essence of spiritual truth.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the story of Ezra's sons—where some recognized their father through spiritual intuition while others only heard his words as news—Rumi moves to the necessity of internal transformation. 3290. When you become united, grain by grain—after your dispersion in confusion—then it becomes possible to stamp you with the King’s seal.
And if you, foolish man, grow to be worth more than a <term>mithqál<note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 4.25 grams, used for measuring gold coins like the dinar.</note></term>, the King will craft you into a golden chalice.
Then, both the King’s name and titles, as well as his likeness, will be engraved upon you, O seeker of arrival!
So that the Beloved becomes your bread, water, lamp, companion, dessert, and wine.
Unite yourself—for unity is a Divine mercy—so that I may be able to speak the truth of what is to you.

3295. For speech is intended to create belief, but the spirit of <term>polytheism<note>original: "shirk"—in this context, it refers to spiritual duality or the failure to see the underlying unity of God.</note></term> is devoid of faith in God.
That spirit which is scattered across the contents of the world is divided among sixty different passions.
Therefore, silence is best; it brings peace to that spirit. Thus, the proverb says, "Silence is the answer to fools."
I know this, yet the intoxication of the body opens my mouth without my own will.
Just as in sneezing or yawning, the mouth opens without your intent.

### ***Commentary on the Prophetic tradition: "Truly, I ask God for forgiveness seventy times every day."***

3300. Like the Prophet, I repent seventy times a day for speaking and revealing these mysteries.
But that divine intoxication breaks my vows of penitence; this physical drunkenness brings forgetfulness and tears the robe of my resolve.
The Divine purpose of revealing eternal things has intoxicated the one who knows the mystery.
With such fanfare—drums and banners—the hidden secret has become water gushing from the fountain of <term>the Pen is dry<note>A reference to the Prophetic tradition: "The Pen has dried regarding what shall be," meaning the Divine decree and the ultimate truths of existence are fixed and eternal.</note></term>.
The infinite Mercy flows continuously; but you are asleep to the perception of it, O people!

3305. The sleeper’s clothes are soaked by the river’s water, yet in his dream, he searches for a mirage.
He keeps running to and fro, saying, "There is hope for water over there!" By this false thought, he has blocked his own path.
Because he said "over there," he wandered far from "here" where the water actually is; through a vain imagination, he was exiled from reality.
Worldly people are far-sighted for their own gain but deeply asleep in spirit; have mercy on them, O travelers of the Path!
I have never seen true thirst cause sleep; only the "thirst" of the ignorant leads to slumber.

3310. True intelligence is that which is nourished by God, not the cleverness bestowed by the planet <term>Mercury<note>In medieval Islamic astrology, Mercury was associated with the rational, calculating, and discursive intellect used for worldly affairs.</note></term>.

### ***Explaining that the limited, discursive intellect cannot see beyond the grave, and in all other matters, it must submit to the authority of the saints and prophets.***

The foresight of this human intellect reaches only to the grave, while the foresight of the spiritual man lasts until the <term>blast of the trumpet<note>The trumpet call of the Archangel Israfil, signaling the Resurrection and the end of time.</note></term>.
This intellect cannot step beyond the tomb or the sepulcher; its foot cannot enter the arena of divine wonders.
Go, rid yourself of this foot and this limited intellect; seek the inner eye of the unseen and find joy in contemplation.

<summary>Rumi discusses how divine intoxication compels the mystic to speak mysteries despite a desire for silence. He contrasts the limited "discursive intellect," which only understands worldly life and death, with the spiritual vision that perceives eternal reality.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous passage where Rumi described how divine intoxication forces the mystic to speak despite the virtues of silence, he now pivots to the limitations of the bookish, rational mind. He contrasts the "particular intellect" with the spiritual light of the prophets and saints.</meta>

How can someone who is subservient to a teacher and dependent on a book find light from within their own heart, as Moses did?

**3315.** From this academic study and this limited intellect, nothing comes but confusion; therefore, leave this study behind and embrace <term>waiting<note>original: "intizār"—the state of spiritual expectation or waiting for Divine inspiration rather than forcing knowledge through logic.</note></term>.
Do not seek spiritual greatness through arguments: for the one who waits for Divine inspiration, listening is better than speaking.
The desire to teach is often a form of worldly craving; every such fancy is an <term>idol<note>In Sufi thought, anything that distracts the soul from God—even intellectual pride or the ego-driven desire to be a "teacher"—is considered a form of polytheism or an "idol."</note></term> on the path.
If every busybody could have found the track to His grace, why would God have sent so many prophets?
The <term>particular intellect<note>original: "aql-i juz’i"—the limited, rational, and calculating mind as opposed to the Universal Intellect or spiritual intuition.</note></term> is like a flash of lightning: how is it possible to reach the distant land of <term>Wakhsh<note>A city in present-day Tajikistan, used here to symbolize a very distant destination that cannot be reached by a momentary flash of light.</note></term> by a mere spark?

**3320.** The flash of lightning is not meant to guide you on the road; rather, it is a command for the cloud to weep.
The "lightning" of our rational intellect exists so that we might weep—so that our "nonexistence" may cry out in longing for true existence.
A child’s intellect says, "Go to school," but the child cannot learn the lessons by itself.
A sick man’s intellect leads him to the physician, but his intellect is not the thing that actually cures him.
Consider how the devils used to fly toward heaven to eavesdrop on divine secrets,

**3325.** Carrying away scraps of those mysteries, until the shooting stars drove them quickly from the sky,
Saying, "Go away! A Prophet has come to earth: from him, you will obtain whatever you truly crave.
If you are seeking priceless pearls, *enter the houses by their doors.*" <note>A reference to Quran 2:189, often interpreted by mystics to mean one must approach God through the "door" of the Prophet or a spiritual guide.</note>
Keep knocking that door-ring and stand at the entrance; there is no path for you through the vaults of heaven.
You do not need to take this long, celestial road: We have bestowed the secrets of the Mystery upon an earthly being.

**3330.** Come to him, if you are not disloyal; let him turn you into sweet sugar-cane, even if you are currently just empty reeds."
That Guide will cause greenery to grow from your earth; he is no less powerful than the hoof of Gabriel’s horse.
You will be made green and fresh again if you become the dust beneath the horse of a Gabriel—
The life-giving dust which <term>Sámirí<note>In Islamic tradition, Sámirí was the figure who fashioned the Golden Calf. Legend says he used dust from the hoofprints of the archangel Gabriel’s horse to give the statue a temporary, illusory life.</note></term> put into the golden calf, so that it seemed to possess a living soul.
From that dust, it took life and bellowed—a sound that confounded the enemies of Moses.

**3335.** If you come loyally to those who possess the Mystery, you will be freed from the hood, like a hunting falcon—
The hood that binds the eyes and ears, making the falcon wretched and lowly.
The hood is placed over the falcon's eyes because its only desire is to return to its own kind.
When it is separated from its own kind, it learns to associate with the King; then the falconer unveils its eyes.
God drove the devils from His watchtower, and He stripped the "particular intellect" of its independence,

**3340.** Saying, "Do not try to dominate: you are not autonomous; rather, you are the pupil of the heart, designed to learn from it."

<summary>Rumi argues that the rational, "particular" intellect is insufficient for spiritual journeying, comparing it to a brief flash of lightning that cannot guide a long journey. He emphasizes that true spiritual knowledge must be sought through the "door" of a Prophet or spiritual guide, who can animate the soul just as the dust of Gabriel's horse once gave a semblance of life to the golden calf.</summary>

Go to the heart, go, for you are a part of the heart. Take heed, for you are a servant of the Just King.

### ***Explaining the Verse: "O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward in the presence of God and His Apostle." Since you are not the Prophet, be a follower; since you are not the sovereign, be a subject.***

Go, therefore, and be silent in submission beneath the shade of the command of the <term>Shaykh<note>A spiritual master or elder who guides seekers on the Sufi path.</note></term> and Master;
Otherwise, even if you are talented and capable, you will become spiritually deformed by boasting of your own "perfection."

❧ **3350.** You will be stripped even of your natural talents if you rebel against the Master of the Mystery, who is filled with divine knowledge.
Be patient while "stitching old rags"; for if you are impatient, you will never be more than a common mender.
If the menders of old clothes had patience and endurance, they too would eventually become makers of new garments through the acquisition of true knowledge.
You strive so hard, yet in the end, you yourself admit in weariness that the rational intellect is a shackle—
Just like the philosopher who, on the day of his death, realized his intellect was actually poor and weak.

❧ **3355.** In that final hour, he honestly confessed the truth, saying: "Driven by a sharp mind, we galloped in vain.
In our delusion, we turned away from the holy men; we swam only in the sea of our own imagination."
In the spiritual Sea, "swimming" <note>Rumi uses swimming as a metaphor for relying on one's own intellectual efforts rather than divine grace.</note> is useless; there is no safety here except for the Ark of Noah.
Thus said that King of the Prophets: "I am the Ship in this universal Sea—
I, and those who have become my true representatives through spiritual vision."

❧ **3360.** We saints are the Ark of Noah in this Sea, so that you might not turn your face away from the ship, O youth.
Do not go, like <term>Canaan<note>In Islamic tradition, Canaan was a son of Noah who refused to enter the Ark, believing he could survive the Great Flood by climbing a high mountain. He represents the failure of human reason against divine decree.</note></term>, to every mountain of thought; listen to the warning of the <term>Qur’án<note>The holy book of Islam.</note></term>: "There is no protector today from the decree of God."
Because of the bandages over your eyes, this ship seems "low" to you, while the mountain of intellectual thought seems very high.
Beware, beware! Do not look at this "lowliness" with contempt; look instead at the grace of God that is bound to it.
Do not admire the height of your mountain of thought, for a single wave of the Divine can turn it upside down.

<summary>Rumi warns against the pride of the rational intellect, using the story of Noah's Ark to argue that true safety lies in humble submission to a spiritual master rather than self-reliant logic. ### *The Story of the mule complaining to the camel, saying: "I often fall on my face while traveling, while you seldom do—why is this?" and the camel's answer.*

One day, a mule saw a camel, as they had been placed in the same stable together.
The mule said, "I often fall on my face on the hills and the roads, in the marketplace and on the streets.
Particularly when descending from a mountain peak to the bottom, I fall on my head every moment out of sheer terror.

**3380.** But you do not fall on your face: why is this? Or perhaps, in truth, your pure spirit was simply destined for happiness.
I fall on my head every instant and strike my knees against the ground; through that slipping, my muzzle and knees are always bloody.
My saddle and harness end up crooked and messy on my head, and I am always being beaten by the mule-driver;
I am like the unintelligent man who, because of a corrupt understanding, constantly breaks his vows of repentance whenever he commits a sin.
Through a weak will, that person who breaks their vows becomes the laughing-stock of <term>Iblís<note>The personal name of the Devil or Satan in Islamic theology, representing pride and the refusal to submit to God's command.</note></term> in this world.

**3385.** He is constantly falling on his head like a lame horse, for his burden is heavy and the road is full of stones.
He is always receiving blows to his head from the Unseen realm—that man of unlucky nature—because he breaks his promises of reform.
Then again, he repents with a weak resolution; the Devil spits in scorn and shatters his repentance once more.
Weakness upon weakness! Yet his arrogance is such that he looks with contempt upon those who have actually reached God.
O camel, you who are a model of the true believer: you do not fall on your face, nor do you turn up your nose in disdain."

<summary>Rumi contrasts the spiritual blindness of "Canaan" with the foresight of the believer, using an allegory of a mule and camel to show how spiritual height and vision prevent one from "stumbling" into sin and broken vows.</summary>

### *How the mule admitted the camel's words were true, acknowledged the camel's superiority, and sincerely sought his help and refuge; and how the camel treated him with kindness, showing him the way and helping him in a fatherly and regal manner.*

The mule said, "You have spoken the truth, O camel." As he said this, his eyes filled with tears.
He wept for a while and fell at the camel's feet, saying, "O chosen one of the Lord of men,
What harm will it do if you, by the grace of your blessedness, receive me into your service?"

**3410.** The camel said, "Since you have made this confession in my presence, go in peace, for you are saved from the pollutions of Time.
You have offered justice and made amends; thus, you are saved from tribulation. You were once an enemy, but now you have become one of the loyal.
That evil disposition was not innate to your being; for from original, essential evil comes nothing but denial.
A borrowed or temporary evil is such that the person in whom it appears confesses it and desires to repent;
Like Adam, whose lapse was only temporary: of necessity, he showed his penitence at once <note>In Islamic tradition, Adam’s sin was a temporary lapse or mistake, leading to immediate repentance and forgiveness, unlike the eternal defiance of Iblis.</note>.

**3415.** But since the sin of Iblís <term>Iblís<note>The name of the primary devil in Islam, who refused to bow to Adam out of pride.</note></term> was essential and original to his nature, there was no path for him toward precious repentance.
Go, for you are delivered from your self, from your evil nature, from the flaming tongue of the Fire, and from the teeth of the wild beasts of Hell.
Go, for now that you have grasped true happiness, you have thrown yourself into everlasting good fortune."

## ***How the Egyptian besought blessing and guidance from the Israelite, and how the Israelite prayed for the Egyptian and received a favourable answer to his prayer from the Most Gracious and Merciful God.***

The Egyptian said, “Offer a prayer for me, since from the blackness of my heart I do not have a mouth fit for offering an acceptable prayer,

**3495.** For it may be that the lock of this heart will be opened, and that a place will be granted to this ugly one at the banquet of the beautiful.
Through you, the deformed may become endowed with beauty, or even a Satan <note>original: "Iblís"—the primary devil or fallen angel in Islamic tradition</note> may once again become one of the Cherubim;
Or, by the noble influence of Mary's hand, the withered branch may acquire the fragrance of musk, freshness, and fruit.” <note>This refers to the Quranic account of Mary, mother of Jesus, who was told to shake the trunk of a withered palm tree, which then dropped fresh dates for her.</note>
Thereupon the Israelite fell to worship and said, “O God who knows the manifest and the hidden,
To whom but You should Your servant lift his hand? Both the prayer and the answer to prayer are from You.

**3500.** You at first give the desire for prayer, and You at last give the reward for prayers.
You are the First and the Last: we in between are nothing—a nothingness that cannot even find expression.”
He was speaking in this way until he fell into a spiritual ecstasy and his heart became senseless.
While engaged in prayer, he came back to his senses and witnessed the effect of his prayer: *Humanity shall have nothing but what they have worked for.* <note>A reference to the Quranic verse: "That man can have nothing but what he strives for" (53:39).</note>
He was still praying when suddenly a loud cry and roar burst from the heart of the Egyptian,

**3505.** Who exclaimed, “Come, make haste and offer me the profession of the Faith <note>The Shahada, or declaration of belief</note>, so that I may quickly cut the old girdle of unbelief!” <note>original: "zunnār"—a belt or cord historically worn by non-Muslims in Islamic lands to distinguish them. Here, cutting it symbolizes a total conversion and breaking from his past life.</note>
“They have cast a fire into my heart; they have shown affection with all their soul for a Satan like me.
Praise be to God! Your friendship and my inability to do without you have rescued me at last.
My associations with you were like an elixir <note>original: "elixir" (al-iksir)—the legendary substance used in alchemy to turn lead into gold, symbolizing spiritual transformation</note>: may your foot never disappear from the house of my heart!
You were a branch of the palm tree of Paradise: when I grasped it, it bore me to Paradise.

**3510.** That which carried away my body was a torrent: the torrent bore me to the brink of the Sea of Bounty.
I went towards the torrent in hope of obtaining water: I beheld the Sea and took pearls, bushel upon bushel.”
The Israelite brought the cup to him, saying, “Now take the water!” “Go,” he replied; “all waters have become lowly in my sight.
I have drunk such a draught from the verse *God has purchased* <note>original: "Innallāha-sh-tarā"—Referring to Quran 9:111: "Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties [in exchange] for that they will have Paradise."</note> that no thirst will come to me until the Gathering on the Day of Judgment.
He who gave water to the rivers and fountains has opened a fountain within me.

**3515.** This heart, which was once hot and thirsty for water—to its high aspiration, physical water has now become worthless.”

<summary>In this passage, an Egyptian man, recognizing his spiritual darkness, asks an Israelite for prayer. The prayer leads to a miraculous transformation where the Egyptian experiences a spiritual awakening, rejecting his former life and finding eternal satisfaction in divine love.</summary>

He (God), for the sake of His servants, became the letter **K** of the **All-sufficing** <note>original: "Káf of Káfí"—Káf is the Arabic letter K, and Káfí is a name for God meaning the One who is enough or all-sufficient</note>, as a sign of the truth of the promise of the mystical letters **K, H, Y, A, S** <note>original: "Káf, Há, Yá, 'Ayn, Sád"—these are mysterious "disjointed letters" that open Chapter 19 (Mary) of the Quran; they are often interpreted as symbols of divine secrets</note>.

I thought I would declare my faith so that I might drink some water from this flood of blood.

❧ **3530.** How could I have known that He would change my very nature and make me into a spiritual Nile?

Just as, to the Prophet, this world is fully immersed in the praise of God, while to us it seems silent and unfeeling.
To his eyes, this world is filled with love and generosity; to the eyes of others, it is dead and motionless.
To his eyes, the valleys and hills are moving swiftly; he hears deep wisdom from a lump of clay or a brick.

❧ **3535.** To ordinary people, this whole world is a stuck and dead thing; I have never seen a veil of blindness more amazing than this.
To our eyes, all graves look the same; but to the eyes of the saints, one is a garden of Paradise, and another is a pit of Hell.
The ordinary person might say, "Why has the Prophet become so serious and why has he stopped enjoying worldly pleasures?"
The chosen ones would answer: "To your eyes, O people, he seems sour; but come for once into our eyes, so that you may see the joyful laughter described in the chapter **'Has there not come?'**" <note>original: "Hal atá"—this refers to Chapter 76 of the Quran, which describes the blissful state of the righteous in the afterlife</note>.

❧ **3540.** That appears to you as an illusion because you are sitting at the top of the **pear-tree** <note>The "pear-tree" refers to a famous story in Rumi's work where a person climbing a tree sees distorted images (like their spouse being unfaithful) due to the height and the leaves; it symbolizes how the ego distorts our perception of reality</note>: come down, O youth!
The pear-tree is the tree of physical existence: while you are up there, the new appears old.
While you are there, you will see only a patch of thorns full of the scorpions of anger and full of snakes.

<summary>God describes His ability to provide for the soul's needs without material means, using the miracles of Moses as proof. The text explains that spiritual vision allows the Prophet and the saints to see a living, joyful world where the "vulgar" see only death and illusion.</summary>

When thou comest down, thou wilt behold, free of cost, a world filled with rose-cheeked beauties and their nurses.

### Story of the lewd woman who said to her husband, "Those illusions appear to thee from the top of the pear-tree, for the top of that pear-tree causes the human eye to see such things: come down from the top of the pear-tree, that those illusions may vanish." And if any one should say that what that man saw was not an illusion, the answer is that this story is a parable, not a precise similitude. In the story regarded as a parable this amount of resemblance is sufficient, for if he had not gone to the top of the pear-tree, he would never have seen those things, whether illusory or real.

That woman desired to embrace her paramour <note>a secret lover</note> in the presence of her foolish husband.

❧ **3545.** Therefore the woman said to her husband, “O fortunate one, I will climb the tree to gather fruit.”
As soon as she had climbed the tree, the woman burst into tears when from the top she looked in the direction of her husband.
She said to her husband, “O wicked pervert <note>original Latin: "cinaede improbe"—an archaic and vulgar insult regarding sexual deviancy</note>, who is that sodomizer <note>original Latin: "paedicator"</note> who is lying on top of you? You are as still as a woman beneath him: O man, you have truly turned into a catamite <note>original Latin: "catamitus"—the passive partner in a sexual act</note>!”
“Nay,” said the husband: “one would think thy head is turned; at any rate, there is nobody here on the plain except me.”

❧ **3550.** The wife repeated her claim. “Aha!” she said, “who is that man wearing a cap who is lying on your back?”
“Hark, wife,” he replied, “come down from the tree, for thy head is turned and thou hast become very foolish <note>original: "dotish"—senseless or senile</note>.”
When she came down, her husband went up: then the woman drew her paramour into her arms.
The husband cried out, “O harlot <note>original Latin: "scortum"</note>, who is that coming over you like a monkey?”
“Nay,” said the wife, “there is no one here but me. Hark, thy head is turned: don't talk nonsense.”

❧ **3555.** He repeated the charge against his wife. “This,” said the wife, “is because of the pear-tree. From the top of the pear-tree I was seeing just as falsely as you, O cuckold <note>a man whose wife is unfaithful</note>.
Hark, come down, that you may see there is nothing: all this illusion is caused by a pear-tree.”
Jesting is teaching: listen to it in earnest, do not thou be taken up with its appearance of a jest.
To jesters every earnest matter is a jest; to the wise, all jests are earnest.

❧ **3560.** Lazy folk seek the pear-tree, but it is a long way to *that* pear-tree.
Descend from the pear-tree on which at present thou hast become giddy-eyed and giddy-faced.
This pear-tree is the **primal egoism** and **self-existence** wherein the eye is awry and squinting.
When thou comest down from this pear-tree, thy thoughts and eyes and words will no more be awry.
Thou wilt see that this tree has become a tree of fortune, its boughs reaching to the **Seventh Heaven** <note>the highest level of paradise in Islamic cosmology</note>.

❧ **3565.** When thou comest down and partest from it, God in His mercy will cause it to be transformed.
On account of this humility shown by thee in coming down, God will bestow on thine eye true vision.
If true vision were easy and simple, how should **Mustafá** <note>a title for the Prophet Mohammed, meaning "The Chosen One"</note> have desired it from the Lord?
