### The diverse stages of Human Nature from the beginning

First, man came into the realm of inorganic things <note>the world of minerals and inanimate matter</note>, and from that state, he passed into the life of a plant.
For many years he lived as a plant, and he held no memory of his time as a mineral because the two states are so different.
And when he passed from the plant state into the animal state, he remembered nothing of his life as a plant,

✻**3640.** Except for a lingering attraction he feels toward that state, especially during the spring and among sweet herbs—
Just like the attraction a babe feels toward its mother: the infant does not understand the secret reason why it longs for the breast.
Or like the intense attraction a seeker feels toward a great spiritual Teacher <note>the "Elder" or *Pir*</note>, whose spiritual fortune is young and vibrant.
The individual intelligence of the disciple is a branch of that Universal Intelligence; the movement of this shadow is guided by that Rose-bough.
Eventually, the disciple’s shadow disappears into the Teacher; only then does he understand the secret of his long search and seeking.

✻**3645.** How could the shadow of a branch move, O fortunate one, if the Tree itself did not move?
Again, the Creator, whom you know, was leading man from the animal state toward humanity.
Thus, he advanced from one world of being to another, until he became the intelligent, wise, and mighty being he is now.
He has no memory of his previous forms of soul; and from this current human intelligence, there is yet another migration he must make,
So that he may escape this intelligence full of greed and self-seeking, and instead behold a hundred thousand marvelous Intelligences.

✻**3650.** Though man fell into the "sleep" of this world and became forgetful of his past, how could God leave him in such self-forgetfulness?
From that sleep, they will eventually bring him back to wakefulness, so that he may look back and laugh at his current state.

<summary>Rumi explains that once the ego is purified, the world reveals God's presence, much like the Burning Bush. He then outlines the soul's journey through the mineral, vegetable, and animal kingdoms toward human and eventually divine intelligence.</summary>

### **_Explaining that the people of Hell are hungry and make lamentable entreaty to God, saying, "Make our portions fat and let the food reach us quickly, for we can endure no more."_**

This story has no end. God said, “Listen, O Moses! Let those asses <note>In Rumi's poetry, "asses" often represent the lower, animalistic self (the *nafs*) that cares only for physical appetite.</note> go to the grass,

**3670.** We know the hungry cries of Our wolves; We use these asses to sustain them.
The holy alchemy <note>term: *Al-Kimiya*—the spiritual process of transforming the "lead" of the ego into the "gold" of the soul.</note> breathed from your lips wanted to turn these 'asses' into humans.

**3680.** What wonder is it if the Creator of that intellect is also with you? Why do you not acknowledge this truth?

Your intellect is indescribably close to you: it is neither to the left nor the right, nor behind nor in front.
How then should the King not be indescribably near? For mere intellectual searching cannot find the way to Him.
The movement you have in your finger is not in front of the finger, or behind it, or to the left, or to the right.
At the time of sleep or death, that movement leaves the finger; at the moment of waking, it rejoins it.

**3690.** By what path does it enter your finger—that movement without which your finger is useless?
The light of the eye and the pupil—by what path other than the *six directions* <note>The "six directions" refer to the physical dimensions of the material world: up, down, left, right, front, and back.</note> does it enter your eye?
The world of physical creation is defined by quarters and directions, but know that the **world of the Divine Command** <term>world of the Divine Command: *'Alam al-Amr*—the spiritual realm of direct creation, existing beyond the laws of time, space, and matter.</term> and the Divine Attributes is without direction.
Know, O beloved, that the world of the Command is beyond direction; therefore, the Commander must certainly be even more beyond direction.
The intellect has always been beyond direction, and the One who knows its inner meaning is more intelligent than the intellect and more spiritual than the spirit itself.

**3695.** No created being is disconnected from Him: that connection, O friend, is beyond description,
Because in the realm of the spirit, there is no such thing as "separating" or "uniting," while our human thought cannot conceive of anything except in terms of separating and uniting.
Seek that which exists without separation and union by the aid of a spiritual guide; but know that the search itself will not fully quench your thirst.
Yet pursue it incessantly, even if you feel far from the Source, so that the strength of your true humanity may bring you to your heart's desire.
How could the intellect find the way to this Divine connection? This intellect is a prisoner to the concepts of separation and union.

3700. Therefore, the Chosen One <note>original: *Mustafá*—an honorary title for the Prophet Muhammad, meaning "The Chosen."</note> commanded us, saying, “Do not seek to investigate the very Essence of God.”

### ***How Dhu 'l-Qarnayn went to Mount Qáf and made petition, saying, "O Mount Qáf, tell me of the majesty of the Attributes of God"; and how Mount Qáf said that the description of His majesty is ineffable, since all perceptions vanish before it; and how Dhu 'l-Qarnayn made humble supplication, saying, "Tell of His works that thou hast in mind and of which it is more easy for thee to speak."***

Dhu 'l-Qarnayn <note>literally "The Two-Horned One"—a legendary figure often associated with Alexander the Great, portrayed here as a spiritual seeker.</note> traveled toward Mount Qáf: he saw that it was made of pure emerald,
And that it formed a great ring surrounding the entire world. He was struck with wonder at that immense creation.
He said, “You are a mountain indeed! What are these others? Compared to your magnitude, they are but playthings.”
The mountain replied, “Those other mountains are merely my veins; they do not compare to me in beauty or glory.

3715. I have a hidden vein reaching into every land; all the regions of the world are fastened to my roots.
When God wills an earthquake in any land, He commands me, and I cause that specific vein to throb.
I then move the vein connected to that particular land with great might.
When He says, ‘Enough!’ my vein comes to rest. I appear to be still, but I am actually in constant, rapid motion.”
I am like a medicinal ointment—outwardly at rest but actively working; I am like the intellect, which stays still while the speech it inspires is in motion.

3720. In the view of those whose intelligence cannot perceive this spiritual cause, they claim earthquakes are caused only by vapors trapped within the earth.

### ***An ant, walking on a piece of paper, saw the pen writing and began to praise the pen. Another ant, which was more keen-sighted, said, "Praise the fingers, for I deem this accomplishment to proceed from them." Another ant, more clear-sighted than either, said, "I praise the arm, for the fingers are a branch of the arm," and so forth.***

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discourse on the limitations of human perception. Rumi uses the analogy of ants debating the source of writing to illustrate how humanity often mistakes secondary causes (like the pen or the intellect) for the Primary Cause (God). He then introduces the legendary traveler Dhu 'l-Qarnayn and his conversation with the cosmic mountain, Qáf, to explain the balance between Divine Wrath and Mercy.</meta>

A little ant saw a pen writing on a paper, and told this mystery to another ant,
Saying, “That pen made wonderful pictures like sweet basil and beds of lilies and roses.”
The other ant said, “That artist is the finger, and this pen is actually no more than the instrument <term>instrument: *athar*—literally a "trace" or "sign," referring here to a tool that lacks its own agency.</term> and the sign.”
A third ant said, “It is the work of the arm, by whose strength the slender finger depicted it.”

❧ **3725.** In this fashion, the argument was carried upward until a chief of the ants, who was a little bit more sagacious,
Said, “Do not regard this accomplishment as proceeding from the material form, which becomes unconscious in sleep and death.
Form is like a garment or a staff; bodily figures do not move except by means of intellect and spirit.”
He, the wise ant, was unaware that without the controlling influence of God, that intellect and heart <note>original: *dil*—referring to the spiritual mind or seat of consciousness.</note> would be inert.
If He withdraws His favor from it for a single moment, the acute intellect will commit many follies.

❧ **3730.** When Dhu ’l-Qarnayn <note>original: *Dhu ’l-Qarnayn*—literally "The Two-Horned One," a figure usually identified with Alexander the Great, portrayed in Islamic tradition as a world-traveling seeker of wisdom.</note> found Mount Qáf <note>In Islamic cosmology, Qáf is the legendary mountain range that encircles the entire world.</note> speaking—after Mount Qáf had "bored the pearls" <note>A Persian idiom for speaking eloquently or revealing precious truths.</note> of speech—he said:
“O eloquent one, who art wise and knowest the mystery, expound to me the Attributes of God.”
It answered, “Go, for those qualities are too terrible for oral exposition to put its hand on them,
Or for the pen to dare inscribe information concerning them with its point on the pages of books.”
He said, “Relate a lesser tale concerning the wonders of God, O goodly divine.”

❧ **3735.** It said, “Look, the King <note>meaning God.</note> has made a plain full of snow-mountains, for the distance of a three-hundred-year journey—
Mountain upon mountain, beyond count and number; the snow comes continually to replenish them.
One snow-mountain is being piled on another; the snow brings coldness to the earth.
At every moment, a snow-mountain is being piled on a snow-mountain from the illimitable and vast storehouse.
O king, if there were not a valley of snow like this, the glowing heat of Hell would annihilate me.”

❧ **3740.** Know that in this world, the heedless <term>heedless: *ghāfilān*—those who are spiritually unaware or distracted by the physical world.</term> are like those snow-mountains, so that the veils of the intelligent may not be consumed.
Were it not for the reflection <note>meaning the cooling effect.</note> of "snow-weaving" ignorance, that Mount Qáf would be consumed by the fire of longing.
The Fire of Hell is in truth only an atom of God's wrath; it is only a whip to threaten the base.
Notwithstanding such a wrath, which is mighty and surpassing all, observe that the coolness of His clemency <note>original: *rahmat*—Divine mercy or compassion.</note> is prior to it.
It is a spiritual priority, unqualified and unconditioned. Have you seen the "prior" and the "posterior" without duality? <note>Rumi alludes to the famous Hadith Qudsi: "My Mercy precedes My Wrath." He challenges the reader to see these two attributes as united in the Divine Essence.</note>

❧ **3745.** If you have not seen them as one, that is because of feeble understanding; for the minds of God's creatures are but a single grain of that mine.
Lay the blame on yourself, not on the evidences of the true Religion; how should the bird of clay reach the sky of the true Faith?
The bird's lofty soaring-place is only the air, since its origin is from lust and sensuality.

<summary>Rumi uses a fable about ants to show that humans often mistake secondary causes for the Divine Cause. He then describes Dhu 'l-Qarnayn’s encounter with Mount Qáf, explaining that "snowy" ignorance serves as a necessary veil to protect the world from the intense heat of Divine wrath and longing.</summary>
<keywords>parable of the ants, secondary causes, Dhu ’l-Qarnayn, Mount Qáf, Divine Attributes, Mercy and Wrath, spiritual ignorance, human intellect</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the conversation between Dhu ’l-Qarnayn and Mount Qáf, where the mountain explained that God’s Mercy outweighs His Wrath. This section transitions from the ant’s limited perspective of secondary causes to the necessity of spiritual bewilderment (hayrat) when faced with the Divine. Therefore, remain in a state of bewilderment <term>bewilderment: *hayrat*—a high spiritual state where the seeker is so awestruck by God's majesty that they are left speechless, transcending logical "yes" or "no" arguments.</term> without saying "no" or "yes," so that a litter <note>original: *mahdi*—a cradle or a litter used for carrying passengers.</note> may come from Divine Mercy to carry you. 
Because you are too dull to understand these wonders of God, if you say "yes" you will be lying;

❦ **3750.** And if you say "no," that "no" will undo you: because of that "no," the Divine Wrath will shut your spiritual window. 
Instead, simply be bewildered and distraught, and nothing else, so that God's help may come to you from both before and behind. 
When you have become bewildered, crazed, and reduced to nothing, you have truly said, "Lead us" with a silent but powerful eloquence. 
The Wrath of God is mighty, truly mighty; but when you begin to tremble in awe, that mighty power becomes calm and balanced. 
For the terrifying shape of God's power is meant for the unbeliever; once you have become helpless and humble, it reveals itself as mercy and kindness.

## ***How Gabriel, on whom be peace, showed himself to Mustafá <note>original: *Muṣṭafā*—The Chosen One, a common title for the Prophet Muhammad.</note>, God bless and save him, in his own shape; and how, when one of his seven hundred wings became visible, it covered the horizon on all sides, and the sun with all its radiance was veiled over.***

❦ **3755.** Mustafá said in the presence of Gabriel, "O friend, show me your true form as it really is. 
Show it to me clearly and visibly, so that I may look upon you as spectators fix their eyes on something of great interest." 
Gabriel replied, "You cannot bear this, for you do not have the strength to endure it; the human senses are weak and fragile. It would be too painful for you to see me." 
"Show yourself," Muhammad replied, "so that this body may realize exactly how frail and resourceless its senses truly are." 
A man’s physical senses are indeed weak, but he possesses a powerful nature within.

❦ **3760.** This body is like flint and steel, but in its true quality it is the striker of fire <note>Rumi uses the analogy of flint and steel to show that while the human body appears cold and hard, it contains the "fire" of the divine spirit.</note>. 
Flint and steel are the birthplace from which fire is created; the fire is born from them, yet it dominates both its parents. 
Fire, in turn, holds power over physical nature; it is dominant and flaming over the body; 
Yet again, there is a flame like that of Abraham <note>A reference to the Quranic story where the fire of Nimrod became a "cool garden" for the Prophet Abraham.</note> within the body, by which even the strongest tower of fire is subdued. 
As a result of this, the all-accomplished Prophet said symbolically, "We are the last and the first." <note>original: *al-ākhirūn al-sābiqūn*—a reference to a Hadith meaning that although Muhammad's community came last chronologically, they are first in spiritual rank.</note>

❦ **3765.** The physical form of flint and steel is broken by a hammer and anvil, but in their essence, they are superior to any iron mine. 
Therefore, Man appears to be a mere derivative of the world, but in his inner essence, he is the origin of the world. Observe this! 
A tiny gnat can make a man's physical body spin in pain and agitation, yet his inner nature encompasses the Seven Heavens. 
When the Prophet persisted in his request, Gabriel displayed a small amount of his awesome majesty—a majesty that would reduce a mountain to dust. 
A single royal wing of his covered the east and the west; Mustafá became unconscious from the sheer awe of it.

❦ **3770.** When Gabriel saw him unconscious from fear and dread, he came to him and took him into his arms. 
That terrifying awe is what strangers feel, while this tender affection is freely given to friends.

<summary>Rumi explains that spiritual growth requires surrendering the intellect to "bewilderment" (hayrat) and illustrates the hidden greatness of the human spirit through the Prophet Muhammad’s encounter with Gabriel’s true celestial form.</summary>
<keywords>Mustafá, Gabriel, Muhammad, Seven Heavens, flint and steel, Divine Mercy, Divine Wrath, bewilderment, hayrat, macrocosm, microcosm</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the explanation of why the Prophet Muhammad was overwhelmed by the sight of the Angel Gabriel. Kings, when seated on the throne, have formidable guardsmen around them with swords in their hands,
Staves and lances and scimitars, so that even lions would tremble in awe;
The shouts of sergeants with their maces create a terror by which men’s souls are enfeebled.

❧ **3775.** This display is for the high and low in the street, to announce to them the presence of an emperor.
This pomp is for the sake of the common people, so that those people may not put on the tiara of arrogance;
It is meant to break their egoism so that the <term>carnal soul: *nafs*—the lower self or ego that drives selfish desires and pride.</term> may not work mischief and evil.
The country is preserved from chaos because the king has the force and authority to inflict punishment.
Therefore, those vain desires are extinguished in men's souls: awe of the king prevents that disaster.

❧ **3780.** Again, when the king comes to the private banquet, how could awe or retaliation have a place there?
There, clemency upon clemency is shown and mercies are overflowing; you will hear no noise but that of the harp and flute.
In time of war there is the terrible drum and kettle-drum; but in the hour of feasting with favorites, there is only the sound of the harp.
The <note>original: *dīvān-e muhāsiba*</note> Office of Accounts is for the commoners, while the fair ones resembling <term>peris: supernatural, butterfly-like spirits in Persian mythology known for their beauty and grace.</term> are for the king's companions.
The coat of mail and the helmet are for the battle, while this silken raiment and music are for the private bower.

❧ **3785.** This topic has no end, O generous one: conclude it, and God best knows the right course.
The physical senses of Ahmad <note>Ahmad is another name for the Prophet Muhammad.</note>, which are mortal, are now laid asleep under the soil of Yathrib <note>The ancient name for the city of Medina.</note>,
But that mighty-natured part of him, which is unconquerable, dwells—without having suffered any decay—within the *abode of truth* in Paradise.
The bodily attributes are exposed to corruption; the everlasting spirit is a shining sun,
Incorruptible, for it is not of the east; unchangeable, for it is not of the west.

❧ **3790.** How was the sun ever confused by a tiny speck of dust? How was the candle ever made senseless by a moth?
The body of Ahmad was liable to that decay: know that this corruption belongs only to the body,
Such as sickness and sleep and pain; the spirit is untouched by these conditions and is wholly detached from them.
Indeed, I cannot describe the spirit, and if I did describe it, a trembling would fall upon this world of physical existence and space.
If its fox <note>A metaphor for the physical body or the humble human form.</note> was perturbed for a moment, perhaps the lion-spirit was then asleep.

❧ **3795.** That lion which is immune from sleep was only apparently asleep: look, a gentle yet terrible lion!
The lion feigns sleep so well that those curs think he is quite dead;
Otherwise, who in the world would dare to rob a poor man of even a grain of <term>turpeth mineral: *turbid*—a medicinal root used as a purgative; here used to represent something of very small value.</term>?
The "foam" <note>A metaphor for the physical body or the outer form of the Prophet.</note> of Ahmad was powerfully affected by that sight of Gabriel, but his "sea" <note>A metaphor for the Prophet's vast, infinite spirit.</note> surged up for love of the foam.
The moon <note>Referring to the spirit of the Prophet.</note> is entirely a bounteous, light-diffusing hand: if the moon has no physical hand with which to give, let it be so!

<summary>This passage explains the distinction between the Prophet's mortal body and his immortal spirit, using the metaphor of a King's public majesty versus his private mercy. It clarifies that while Muhammad's physical form was overwhelmed by Gabriel's celestial sight, his spiritual essence remains incorruptible and divine.</summary>

**3800.** If <note>original: *Ahmad*—one of the names of the Prophet Muhammad, meaning 'the most praised.'</note> Ahmad should display that glorious pinion of his spiritual nature, Gabriel would remain dumbfounded for all eternity.
When Ahmad passed beyond the <term>Lote-tree: *Sidrat al-Muntaha*—in Islamic tradition, the boundary tree at the farthest edge of Paradise which no angel or human may pass, except for the Prophet during his Night Journey.</term> and beyond Gabriel’s place of watch, station, and farthest limit,
He said to Gabriel, "Hark, fly after me." Gabriel replied, "Go, go; I am not your companion any farther."
The Prophet answered him, saying, "Come, O destroyer of veils: I have not yet reached my highest point."
Gabriel replied, "O my illustrious friend, if I take even one flight beyond this limit, my wings will be consumed by the divine light."

**3805.** This tale of the elite losing their senses in contemplation of the most elite is nothing but wonder upon wonder.
In this state, all other forms of unconsciousness are mere child’s play. How long will you try to keep possession of your soul? For this is a matter of abandoning the self entirely.
O "Gabriel"—though you are noble and revered—you are neither the moth nor the candle.
When the candle of Divine Light calls at the moment of illumination, the soul of the moth does not shrink from the burning.
Bury this confusing discourse: let the lion, in a strange reversal, become the prey of the <term>onager: a wild donkey, usually the prey of a lion; here symbolizing a reversal of the natural or worldly order.</term>.

**3810.** Stop up your "word-sweating" water-skin; do not open the bag of your reckless talk.
To one whose intellectual and spiritual parts have not yet moved beyond the earth, this talk seems absurd and reckless.
Do not resist such people, O my beloved; deal gently with them, for you are a stranger lodging in their home.
Give them what they wish and desire, and satisfy them, O emigrant dwelling in their land.
Until the hour of coming before the King and finding sweet delight, O man of <note>Rayy: An ancient city near modern Tehran.</note> Rayy, be on good terms with the man of <note>Merv: An ancient city in modern Turkmenistan; the two cities together represent people of vastly different backgrounds or temperaments.</note> Merv.

**3815.** O "Moses," in the presence of the Pharaoh of your time, you must <note>original: *qawlan layyinan*—a reference to Quran 20:44, where God commands Moses to speak "mild words" to Pharaoh.</note> speak softly with mild words.
If you put water into boiling oil, you will destroy both the trivet and the kettle.
Speak softly, but speak nothing except the truth: do not allow your mildness to become a temptation or a compromise.
The time of afternoon has come: cut short this discourse, O you whose expression of hidden truth makes the people of this age acquainted with reality.
Tell the <term>clay-eater: a metaphor for someone addicted to worldly, "earthly" pleasures or base desires.</term> that sugar is better, but do not show such softness that you end up giving him more clay.

**3820.** Speech would be a spiritual garden to the soul, if only it were independent of letters and sounds.
Oh, there is many a person in whom this "donkey's head" in the middle of a sugar plantation has fixed a thorn!
Seeing it from afar, he supposed the plantation was nothing more than that donkey's head; so he retreated, like a ram defeated in a fight.
Know for certain that the literal form of speech is like that <note>original: *sar-e khar*—a donkey's head, often used as a scarecrow in gardens; here it represents the outer, sometimes "ugly" or "crude" form of words that hide a beautiful inner meaning.</note> donkey's head in the vineyard and the highest Paradise of spiritual reality.
O <note>Husámu’ddín: Rumi's favorite disciple and the inspiration for the Masnavi.</note> Ziyá’u ’l-Haqq Husámu’ddín, bring this "donkey’s head" into that melon-field,

**3825.** So that, when the donkey's head has "died" to the skinning-place, the Divine Kitchen may bestow upon it a new, spiritual growth.
Hark! The shaping of this poem is from me, and the spirit of it is from you; or rather—I spoke in error—truly both the form and the spirit are from you.
You are glorified in Heaven, O conspicuous Sun: be you also glorified on earth forever.

He advises the spiritual seeker to speak gently to the worldly while keeping their focus on the "sugar" of spiritual truth rather than the "clay" of material existence.</summary>

That the inhabitant of the earth may become one in heart and one in aim and one in nature with the sublime celestial. 
(Then) separation and <term>polytheism: the belief in or worship of more than one god; here referring to spiritual fragmentation.</term> and duality will disappear: in real existence there is only unity.

❦ **3830.** When my spirit fully recognises your spirit, they both remember being one in the past,

Many a person who recognised part of the truth eventually turned away: that <term>Moon: a common Sufi metaphor for the Prophet or the Divine Light reflecting in the world.</term> was angered by such ingratitude.

❦ **3835.** You have read all this: now read the <term>Chapter: *Súra Lam yakun*—referring to Súra 98 (The Clear Proof), which discusses how those who received previous scriptures expected a Prophet but rejected him when he arrived.</term> that begins with the words "Those who disbelieve," so that you may know the obstinacy of that old infidel.
Before the bodily form of <note>original: *Ahmad*—the celestial name of the Prophet Muhammad.</note> Ahmad displayed its glory, the description of him in the <term>Pentateuch and the Gospel: the Torah and the New Testament.</term> was used as a protective <term>phylactery: a religious amulet or charm containing scriptural texts worn for protection.</term> by every unbeliever.
“There is someone like this coming,” they said, “let us wait until he shall appear”; and their hearts were throbbing at the thought of seeing his face.
They were prostrating themselves in prayer, crying, “O Lord of mankind, will You bring him before our eyes as quickly as possible?”
They did this so that, by asking God for victory in the name of Ahmad, their enemies might be overthrown.

❦ **3840.** Whenever a formidable war arose, calling upon Ahmad’s persistence in battle was always their help;
Wherever there was a chronic sickness, the invocation of Ahmad’s name was always their healing medicine.
In every way, his form was entering their hearts, their ears, and their mouths.
But how should every jackal perceive his real form? No, they perceived only a derivative of his form—the mental idea of him.
If his real form should fall upon the face of a wall, heart's blood would trickle from the very stones;

❦ **3845.** And his form would be so auspicious—bestowing such a blessing—that the wall would at once be saved from having a "double face."
Compared to the <term>single-facedness: sincerity or purity of heart, having no hidden motives.</term> of those pure in spirit, having two faces is considered a fault even in a wall.
All the veneration, honor, and affection they had shown toward the Prophet was swept away by the wind as soon as they saw him in a human body.
The false coin saw the fire of the test and immediately turned black: when has there ever been a way for the false coin of hypocrisy to enter a pure heart?
The false coin used to boast of how much it desired the touchstone, simply to lead the sincere disciples into doubt.

❦ **3850.** A worthless person falls into the snare of such deceit; for every base fellow thinks to himself:
"If this were not a genuine coin, why would it be so eager to be tested?"
The hypocrite desires the <term>touchstone: a hard stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak produced when rubbed on it.</term>, but only one that is flawed—one that will not clearly expose his falseness.
A touchstone that keeps the true quality of a metal hidden is not a true touchstone, nor is it the discriminating light of divine knowledge.

<summary>This passage explores the irony of those who revered the Prophet Muhammad's name and sought his help before his birth, yet rejected him when he appeared in human form. Rumi uses the metaphor of the touchstone and false coin to describe how true spiritual character is revealed through the "fire" of divine manifestation.</summary>

## VOLUME IV
->CONTAINING THE TRANSLATION<-
->OF THE THIRD & FOURTH BOOKS<-

->1925—1940<-

### INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have hitherto been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2,000 were translated by Whinfield in his abridged version (*Trübner's Oriental Series*, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and so far as I am aware, this is the only contribution that has yet been made by a Western scholar towards the study of Books III–VI. Good as his renderings are from a general point of view, I cannot say that I owe much to them, since they are seldom precise enough to afford help in dealing with obscure and doubtful passages. Regarding the character and purpose of my translation I have nothing to add to what was said in the Introduction to the previous volume. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. Growing familiarity with the author's thought and style has removed some difficulties and lightened others; but there are still many to be cleared up.

For reasons which are set forth in the Introduction to Volume III, I consider the <note>Qóniya is the modern city of Konya, Turkey, where Rumi lived, taught, and is buried.</note> Qóniya Manuscript (*G*), dated 677 <note>original: "A.H." (Anno Hegirae). This date in the Islamic calendar corresponds to approximately 1278 CE, just a few years after Rumi's death.</note>, to be the most authoritative text of the *Mathnawí*. The text of the present edition from Book III, verse 2836, to the end of Book IV is founded on that ancient and admirable manuscript, and in the Appendices to Volume III I have recorded those readings of *G* which differ from the text of my edition in the First and Second Books and in the first half of the Third Book. The present volume, therefore, contains an Appendix showing what changes the adoption of these readings would involve in the English version of the corresponding portions of the poem. As it will be some time before the Commentary on the First and Second Books can appear, a few suggestions for improving the translation of these Books are now brought together in a separate list.

**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**

CAMBRIDGE,
*April 1930*

### INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have hitherto been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2000 were translated by <note>E.H. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. ->INTRODUCTION<-

## INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already available to European readers before this translation was published, the remaining four Books—which make up more than two-thirds of the entire poem—have been very poorly understood until now. These sections contain roughly 17,500 verses. Of these, only about 2,000 were previously translated by <note>E.H. Whinfield (1836–1922) was an early English translator who produced a shortened version of Rumi's work.</note> Whinfield in his shortened version (*Trübner's Oriental Series*, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898). As far as I know, this is the only contribution a Western scholar has made toward studying Books III through VI. Although Whinfield's translations are good in a general sense, I cannot say I relied on them much, as they are rarely precise enough to help with confusing or uncertain passages. Regarding the style and goal of my own translation, I have nothing to add to what I wrote in the introduction to the previous volume. While this translation can help readers understand the meaning of the text on its own, its primary purpose is to provide a solid base for the commentary, which is necessary to fully grasp the poem. As I have become more familiar with the author’s way of thinking and writing, some difficulties have disappeared and others have become easier to manage, though many challenges still remain to be solved.

For reasons explained in the introduction to Volume III, I consider the <term>Qóniya manuscript: A famous early copy of the Mathnawí preserved in Konya (modern-day Turkey), where Rumi lived and died.</term> (referred to as "G"), dated <term>677 A.H.: An Islamic calendar date corresponding to approximately 1278 AD, only five years after Rumi's death.</term>, to be the most reliable version of the *Mathnawí*. The text of this edition, from Book III, verse 2836, until the end of Book IV, is based on that ancient and excellent manuscript. In the supplements to Volume III, I recorded the instances where the readings in the Konya manuscript differ from the text I used for my editions of the First and Second Books and the first half of the Third Book. Therefore, this volume includes an appendix showing the changes that would need to be made to the English version if we adopted those specific readings. Since it will be some time before the Commentary for the First and Second Books is ready, I have collected a few suggestions for improving the translation of those Books here in a separate list.

**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**

CAMBRIDGE,
*April 1930*

### INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have until now been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2,000 were translated by <note>E.H. Whinfield (1836–1922) was an early English translator of Persian poetry whose work introduced Rumi to a wider Victorian audience.</note> Whinfield in his shortened version (*Trübner's Oriental Series*, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and so far as I am aware, this is the only contribution that has yet been made by a Western scholar towards the study of Books III—VI. Good as his translations are from a general point of view, I cannot say that I owe much to them, since they are seldom precise enough to afford help in dealing with obscure and doubtful passages. Regarding the character and purpose of my translation I have nothing to add to what was said in the Introduction to the previous volume. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. Growing familiarity with the author's thought and style has removed some difficulties and lightened others; but there are still many to be cleared up.

For reasons which are set forth in the Introduction to volume III, I consider the <term>Qóniya MS. (G): The Konya manuscript, an exceptionally early and accurate copy of the Mathnawi kept in Konya, Turkey, the city where Rumi lived and died.</term>, dated 677 <term>A.H.: "Anno Hegirae," the Islamic calendar. 677 A.H. corresponds to approximately 1278 CE, just five years after Rumi's death.</term>, to be the most authoritative text of the *Mathnawí*. The text of the present edition from Book III, verse 2836, to the end of Book IV is founded on that ancient and admirable manuscript, and in the Appendices to volume III I have recorded those readings of G which differ from the text of my edition in the First and Second Books and in the first half of the Third Book. The present volume, therefore, contains an Appendix showing what changes the adoption of these readings would involve in the English version of the corresponding portions of the poem. As it will be some time before the Commentary on the First and Second Books can appear, a few suggestions for improving the translation of these Books are now brought together in a separate list.

**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**

CAMBRIDGE,
*April 1930*

### INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already available to European readers before this translation appeared, the four remaining Books—which make up more than two-thirds of the poem—have until now been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2,000 were translated by <note>Edward Henry Whinfield, an earlier English translator of Persian poetry.</note> Whinfield in his shortened version (*Trübner's Oriental Series*, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and as far as I am aware, this is the only contribution yet made by a Western scholar toward the study of Books III through VI. Though his translations are good from a general perspective, I cannot say I owe much to them, as they are rarely precise enough to provide help when dealing with difficult or uncertain passages. Regarding the nature and purpose of my translation, I have nothing to add to what I said in the introduction to the previous volume. Although it can serve on its own as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main purpose is to provide a solid foundation for the commentary, without which the poem cannot be fully understood. A growing familiarity with the author’s thought and style has solved some difficulties and eased others, but many still remain to be explained.

For reasons explained in the Introduction to Volume III, I consider the <term>Qóniya MS. (G): A manuscript from Konya, Turkey, the city where Rumi lived and died. This copy is dated 1278 CE (677 A.H.), just five years after Rumi's death.</term>, dated 677 A.H. <note>Anno Hegirae: The Islamic calendar year, corresponding to roughly 1278–1279 CE.</note>, to be the most authoritative text of the *Mathnawí*. The text of this edition from Book III, verse 2836, to the end of Book IV is based on that ancient and excellent manuscript. In the appendices to Volume III, I recorded the readings from this manuscript that differed from my edition of the first two books and the first half of the third. Therefore, this volume contains an appendix showing what changes those readings would require in the English translation of those parts of the poem. Since it will be some time before the commentary on the First and Second Books can be published, I have gathered a few suggestions for improving their translation into a separate list here.

**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**

CAMBRIDGE,
April 1930

## INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have hitherto been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2,000 were translated by <note>Edward Henry Whinfield (1836–1922) was an early British translator whose condensed version of the Mathnawí was the primary English reference before Nicholson's work.</note> Whinfield in his abridged version (*Trübner's Oriental Series*, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and so far as I am aware, this is the only contribution that has yet been made by a Western scholar towards the study of Books III—VI. Good as his renderings are from a general point of view, I cannot say that I owe much to them, since they are seldom precise enough to afford help in dealing with obscure and doubtful passages. Regarding the character and purpose of my translation I have nothing to add to what was said in the Introduction to the previous volume. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. Growing familiarity with the author's thought and style has removed some difficulties and lightened others; but there are still many to be cleared up.

For reasons which are set forth in the Introduction to vol. III, I consider the <note>Modern-day Konya, Turkey, where Rumi lived and is buried.</note> Qóniya MS. (G), dated <note>original: "677 A.H." This is the Islamic Hijri year, corresponding to approximately 1278 AD, just five years after Rumi's death.</note> 677 A.H., to be the most authoritative text of the *Mathnawí*. The text of the present edition from Book III, v. 2836, to the end of Book IV is founded on that ancient and admirable manuscript, and in the Appendices to vol. III I have recorded those readings of G which differ from the text of my edition in the First and Second Books and in the first half of the Third Book. The present volume, therefore, contains an Appendix showing what changes the adoption of these readings would involve in the English version of the corresponding portions of the poem. As it will be some time before the Commentary on the First and Second Books can appear, a few suggestions for improving the translation of these Books are now brought together in a separate list.

## INTRODUCTION

While the First and Second Books of the *Mathnawí* were already accessible to European readers before the appearance of the present translation, the four remaining Books, comprising more than two-thirds of the poem, have until now been known very imperfectly. These contain about 17,500 verses, of which some 2,000 were translated by <note>Edward Henry Whinfield (1836–1922) was an early British translator of Persian poetry.</note> Whinfield in his abridged version (Trübner's Oriental Series, 1880; 2nd edition, 1898); and so far as I am aware, this is the only contribution that has yet been made by a Western scholar towards the study of Books III—VI. Good as his renderings are from a general point of view, I cannot say that I owe much to them, since they are seldom precise enough to afford help in dealing with obscure and doubtful passages. Regarding the character and purpose of my translation I have nothing to add to what was said in the Introduction to the previous volume. Although, by itself, it may serve as a guide to the meaning of the text, its main function is to provide a sound basis for the commentary without which it cannot be fully understood. Growing familiarity with the author's thought and style has removed some difficulties and lightened others; but there are still many to be cleared up.

For reasons which are set forth in the Introduction to volume III, I consider the <term>Qóniya MS. (G): The manuscript found in Konya (Turkey), where Rumi lived and is buried. This manuscript is considered the most reliable version of the text.</term>, dated 677 <term>A.H.: "Anno Hegirae," the Islamic lunar calendar. 677 A.H. corresponds to approximately 1278 AD, just five years after Rumi's death.</term>, to be the most authoritative text of the *Mathnawí*. The text of the present edition from Book III, verse 2836, to the end of Book IV is founded on that ancient and admirable manuscript, and in the Appendices to volume III I have recorded those readings of G which differ from the text of my edition in the First and Second Books and in the first half of the Third Book. The present volume, therefore, contains an Appendix showing what changes the adoption of these readings would involve in the English version of the corresponding portions of the poem. As it will be some time before the Commentary on the First and Second Books can appear, a few suggestions for improving the translation of these Books are now brought together in a separate list.

->**REYNOLD A. NICHOLSON**<-

CAMBRIDGE,
*April 1930*
